This is a World War 2 themed shooter which is similar to Planetside 2 with elements from Battlefield 4. There are modes which are more closer quarters and there are massive, all-out wars with vehicles (planes, cars, half-tracks, tanks) and unlockable equipment which you get by completing ribbon challenges akin to Battlefield 4. While it takes work to unlock guns and more equipment it is not as bad as many say because the process itself is fun. The core mechanics of the game work well with responsive gunplay where good aim, keyboard dexterity, action game skills and situational awareness is rewarded.
You choose to either play as US, USSR or German soldier who can be either airborne, pilot, tank driver, recon, general or simple infantry; there are differences in equipment where an M1 Garand behaves different from a Tokarev SVT-43 rifle. Weapons can be upgraded with unlockable modules which give minor benefits; but remain balanced nonetheless. The player can also equip badges which behave like perks from the later CoD games; typical faster reload, more health and stamina nature. They are also balanced and therefore not break the game. There is no "perfect" set-up therefore, its all up to your ability to play FPS games.
There are no OP weapons in the game; if you are good with your weapon than you should be fine.
There is also scope for teamwork where its possible to form a squad and work together with your friends or random people; who most of the time are fine and make the experience better.
There are no differences between players; its all down to skill and the ability to hit your target like any FPS out there so claims of "Pay to Win" are false; from my experience.
I would take this kind of MMO game over any WoW tab-targetting clone any day because the gameplay loop is fun and challenging.

I've been playing this game since almost the start of alpha, and while it started out rough, the last few major version revisions have really made it shine.
Pros:
Beautiful Graphics- The color palette is beautiful, with a lot of variety between the different biomes. The lighting FX are also very well done- light shafts, god rays, shadows, etc, but not too over-bearing.
Easy Controls- The controls are easy to learn, especially if you've ever played something like MC or any other sandbox RPG. Built in support for controllers as well is a nice plus. At first I didn't like the combat camera (lock-on function) but once you play with it for a bit, it becomes invaluable to my next pro..
Fun, Engaging Combat- No matter what class you choose (Warrior, Mage, Ranger) you will have a lot of fun dynamically dodging attacks, using your weapon of choice, and slinging powerful spells. All classes can learn ANY spells, as long as you have the points to cast them! My Spellblade (warrior mage) is a ton of fun to play in a group!
RPG Stats- For customizing your character! Put points in intellect, strength, etc and pick up new skills, both active and passive.
Cons:
The crafting system- Can be a little bit confusing and convoluded at times, using multiple crafting tables to make components for a single item. Does't deter me from making stuff, but not as streamlined as it could be.
Better with friends- While the game has a lot to offer for a single player, and I enjoy it solo, it's without a doubt better in a group, even a small one. After a while, you will want to build something large, take on large groups of monsters, or tackle powerful dungeons, and may find it hard in single player if you are at or slightly below the level curve.
Taking all the pros and cons into account, I would still very much recommend this game for anyone who enjoys building, sandbox, RPG type games. It has a lot to offer with dynamic combat, fun monsters, bosses, levels to explore, lots of thing to build, loot and craft, and of course offering co-op gameplay with hot join capability. At the price of $12 (at current time of this review) it's well worth it IMO if you enjoy these kinds of games.

One of the best damn games I've ever played. A sort of cross between RPG, Strategy, Sandbox and Adventure.
The most notable thing about this game for me is the combat system. The hand to hand controls are the best I've ever used in a game - you control the direction you swing or stab, as well as where to block. It's challenging, but not over-complicated.
The sandbox aspect is awesome, it is purely down to you, your preparation and your own tactics as to whether you win or lose a battle, and you generally have to fight as a part of your army to win, rather than go off being some kind of swashbuckler.
The tournaments are awesome too, great way to make money and feel like a sort of medieval Russell Crowe at the same time, after you kick everyone's♥♥♥♥♥(if you can) and look up at the crowds.
The Viking Conquest story mode is actually very gripping. I thought it was funny when I realised I was having more influence on the outcome of the story than I did in any huge RPG title. The graphics of Viking Conquest especially are solid.
If you like the medieval/dark ages themes, training up lots of gruff men and women to follow you around and capture other people's castles and towns, this is for you. Even if you don't, try this. It's endlessly fun, and the sandbox element means you can keep coming back to it.

The fidelity to the animated series visuals and story line is something that I thoroughly appreciate and enjoy, so much so that it allowed me to easly overlook the rough edges of the current state of the game, and have a good few hours of fun. Not to say that the game doesn't have great potential, and a lot of value in its own right.
Even at the current state of development; with only a few more chapters to the story, a boss fight, and a decent lobby system, it could deliver enough of an experience to attract a lot of support from more than just fans of the series.
Some issues that I think it would need to be addressed before the game goes out of early access:
1.- The lobby system
There is nothing more frustrating in a game that losing your progress, players should be able to preserve their current game state after disconnecting (purposely or otherwise), and be able to look for other games at the same state to join.
2.- Difficulty level
After you have mastered the combat system, most fights become monotonous, which can easily be addressed by adding higher difficulty settings.
3.- Collisions
Collisions would have to be polished a fair bit, in order to deliver a more satisfying experience when hitting enemies and objects.
At its current state, I would recommend the game only for fans of the series that are willing to look past a few quirks, in exchange to be able to play your favorite RWBY character for a little while.

Overview
Great but very sad story, definitely didn't see the twist coming! The game really pulls you into the story, you can feel the mood and emotions of the characters despite not understanding their language; but rather through the background, sound effects/music as well as how the characters convey their speech. This game really delivers a masterful story of the younger brother's loss of innocence and coming of age, and the universality of what he experiences in the game.
Technical takeaway
At first it was difficult trying to play both brothers at the same but eventually you will get used to it. A tip: keep the brothers next to each based on what hand plays them (ie. Older brother should be to the left of the younger brother since left hand controls the older brother).
Playing on keyboard had some difficulties, especially when you had to hold the interaction keys down while maneuvering, or when cranking stuff (apparently on controllers you roll the sticks to make the brothers crank faster, but on keyboard that isn't possible; so try to play the game with a controller if you're just starting out).

Within a span of three hours, Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons manages to build a world more engulfing and tell a story more compelling than some of the most expensive 40-hour-gameplay titles created by big studios, and does so without the use of any real spoken language the players can understand. You won't know where you are going until you get there, but the journey to the brothers' destination is beautiful and fascinating to see unfold.
Although there is a notice saying that the game requires a controller to play, I did so with a regular keyboard. Just use WASD and spacebar for the elder brother Naia, and arrow and Ctrl keys for younger brother Naiee. Whatever you do use, controlling the two brothers simultaneously can be a bit disorienting, and I recommend keeping each brother on the side of the screen that corresponds with the side of the keyboard/controller where their buttons/joysticks are located. It is pretty fun to figure out the little puzzles along the way, as much of the game requires the boys' cooperation to move the story along.
Even though it is short, Brothers is worth every penny. If you can catch it on sale, as it is at the moment of this review being written, you really have no reason not to buy it. If you find yourself frustrated occasionally, give yourself a break and pick up the game again soon. You will want to play it through to the very end. (And grab a hanky when you get there.)

Video Version of this review:
You play as a character named Kinubo. His biggest desire throughout the game is to go to the moon, and you have to find someone who’s willing to help you get there. But no one will talk to you, because apparently, the other Lumpos don’t like strangers. None of these guys are happy to see you… except for one, of course, because otherwise, there’d be no game.
Then starts a chain of events, all of which involve taking a character’s hat in order to talk to other characters. But all of them want you to do favors for them… because video game logic. The tasks themselves are relatively simple. There’s one in particular that I like. Lanuno wants you to get her wand back from her brother Wizupo. But to get it, you have to do a bunch of gravity-inverting puzzles. They’re not really hard, but I did end up getting bounced around a bunch of times.
This game is very calm and peaceful. There’s no violence, no enemies, no weapons, and no traps. The only way you can die is by falling out of the bottom of the screen. This game is also very pretty. I like the glow of the moon against the dark blue sky. It’s quite pleasant to look at. And the soundtrack is so relaxing.
I find the controls a little bit strange. Usually, if “X” is to interact with stuff, then “Z” would be the button to jump rather than the spacebar. But whatever.
There’s this one door in a cave that doesn’t take you anywhere. I know the sign next to it leaves a hint, but I can’t figure out how to make the door work, if it’s supposed to work at all.
There’s also this one guy who has a flaming hat that he claims makes people hate you. But that guy wasn’t kidding. Seriously, if you wear his hat, not a single one other character likes you one bit. Not even the king will talk to me.
The king is the last character you have to talk to, and he agrees to help you get to the moon. But you have to set sail for another island for someone else to help you. But this is where things get quite different than what you’d normally expect from a video game. But I don’t wanna spoil it. So I think now’s an appropriate time for me to end my review.
So far, I have no complaints about this game. You should totally check it out. It may only be an hour and a half long, but it’s got an interesting ending, and it’s also a good game to play if you simply just want to relax.

Never knew about the "Sniper Elite" games until recently, so I picked up all four in a sale and started playing 3 (chronologically the first).
I was happy in many ways with it. It's the closest there is to a "Metal Gear in World War II" style, and the sniping can be very satisfying. The missions aren't open-ended per se, but the player has a choice whether to use stealth or shoot their way through. I thought it was a bit difficult though; most my attempts at stealth failed miserably and I kept having to resort to shooting every single bad guy I found.
It is short, and there isn't a ton of story (anyone who was weary of the cinematic scenes in MGS will be happy), but I beat the game today and thought it was top-notch. I would have liked to see the final "enemy" actually moving around and fighting though. Destroying a super-tank in a hangar isn't the same as avoiding it in the open desert, climbing onto it while it's moving, and so forth.
I have also been a little spoiled by other games- the lack of a "dive" button threw me off, and I missed the opportunity to interrogate prisoners instead of killing them all. Also, the lack of development in the hand-to-hand features was unfortunate. If they know you're there, you'll lose every time. If it's a sneak attack, the player wins every time.
Would recommend, and will be playing the others shortly.

A solid action RPG in all respects, Kingdos of Amalur is a fun little gem that gives you a nice big world to explore, a big pile of questlines and sidequests to get on with, a few interesting pieces of DLC and nice, smooth combat. It brings absolutely nothing new to the genre, but if you're an avid fan of smacking loot confetti monsters in the face and scratching a completionist itch, you could be doing much worse than this.
The story doesn't ♥♥♥♥ around. It right up shows you the main antagonist laughing on his evil throne of Anal♥♥♥♥♥♥of the Innocent, you've got your snobby immortal elves, clever tinkering midgets, and bigoted, dumb humans, all the good stuff. Little story arcs and points of interest meet you on your travels and characters are likeable enough. Again, it's cliche, safe, but executes what you'd expect just fine.
The crafting system is simple enough, letting you customise gear you want based on what items you have. Loot comes in the WoW-esque colour branded system where you'll stick to your PRECIOUS PURPLEZ even though they're for characters ten levels lower than you. Levelling up is braindead basic, with three talent trees (Roughly fitting into the categories of punching ♥♥♥♥♥s in the faces, zapping ♥♥♥♥♥s in the ether, and stabbing ♥♥♥♥♥s in the back) and upgrading some skills you require along the way, like lockpicking, aforementioned crafting, persuasion, yadda yadda.
"Open world" is perhaps a little bit of an oversell. You can run around all the lovely locales at your own pace, but if you do venture a little too far, you will end up getting one-shotted by the most common of enemies if you're not quite up to standard in level and gear. The areas are at least pretty for the most part, but you might get sick of seeing the same generic caves or mines over and over.
It's got better combat than The Elder Scrolls games, and goodness knows people need to be yanked away from sucking that schpinter perhaps just a tad. I did find myself getting just a little bit bored of performing the same patterns of attacks and dodges, which whilst felt lovely to execute, you wish maybe the enemy AI would spruce things up just a little bit.
Perfect and new it isn't, but I picked this lesser-known title with all of it's DLCs for a tenner and it's eaten up plenty precious hours of my life, and I haven't even completed it yet.
(Of course, in typical EA curse fashion, despite this game getting plenty of good reviews, the company behind it went bankrupt and the brand is six feet under, so if you don't feel like feeding your hard-earned cash into their stockholder and executive board, maybe you want to pass up on buying this straight from Steam. You stay classy, EA!)

Heroes and Generals is a great fun game to play.  I have only played a little bit on the steam version but I have over 720 hours of actual battle time ingame.
Heroes and Generals is not a Pay 2 Win game. You can unlock anything and everything without paying a cent. You can even get the premium membership called Veteran Membership with credits. It is more of a pay to advance quicker game.
Pros:
Gunplay- the guns feel good and there aren't any that take a ridiculous  amount of bullets to kill.
Weapon Modding- You can make the gun you want work the way you want to.
Camos- Adding a touch of personality and concealment without having bright pink guns and soldiers walking around.
Tier System- Keeps the new players from getting destroyed by people who have been playing for years.
Spawn Protection- It is EXTREMELY hard to spawn kill, and if you do you wont be doing it for long
The Devs- While they dont post often on the forums they do Q and As in streamers chats, give out gold (premium currency) to streamers for giveaways and are active in the community. There are only about 15 content devs and the speed and quality which they put out updates is good.
Some Cons:
The Recon class is gimped right now because there is a lot of sway on BA rifles and with 8x scopes it is hard to use.
Matchmaker: Sometimes, but not often in my experience you will get bad matches, when you get a battle that doesnt fill quick and you get a team of tanks and planes.

I'm a big fan of RWBY and rooster teeth but I took my love for them aside and looked at what the game stands as it is.
Currently the game only has the main team from the show, RWBY. The team consists of Ruby, Yang, Blake and Weiss.
There only a few area's and monster you fight at the time of typing this, but they all still feel equal in difficulty.
Instead of simply leveling up and getting new abbilities, you have to USE said abilities to be able to learn specfific upgrades.
Challenges add to the replayability to this early in develpment title. I have been happily grinding my way to beating goals to learn skills for each character. Some require simply killing Grim with a certain skill, others require reviving players and reaching the cap on said character.
As for balance, the game can be easy at first, but as you level up it gets harder. It gets even harder when there are more players.
Sure, you can play in private lobbies or with friends, but I prefer having others there to talk to.
AH! On the topic of lobbies. This game is online only. AKA: No offline play.
When you hit play you will see a conecting to server popup.
In order to play Solo, you have to play in a private lobby meaning no one else can join you.
This will be fustrating for some who like to take a laptop and some games with them on Family Trips or on a air plane.
Now I'm not sure how many people are having this issue, but I couldnt use my skills/abbilities using my Xbox one controller and had to move back to my keyboard and mouse.
With Controls in mind, there are no rebounding of keys or controls. Graphics customization is heavily limted, so is audio.
I noticed when there were many sounds at once, they tend to clip the feed.
Lastly for this very Early Access version of RWBY: GE, when large amounts of enemys are on the screen the game tends to drop frames drasticly untill you clear them.
Do I reccomend it? well, as you can see I do. but with care.
This is Rooster Teeth's First jump into Making a video game. They have some talented people working on it, but there is always room for error.
I reccomend it becuase, as it stands, there is great potential in this game.
Much like any Early Access title you must take care. Even if its a big time developer or company making the biggest most popular game. There is always room for error.
So, Like I said. I reccomend this game in its current state becuase it does indeed show potential.

9.75/10: Would highly recommend!
Pros:  The combat system is very intuitive and quick to pick up.  It took me a couple of times opening up the tutorial page, but once I switched over from FFXIV controls mentally, it became very easy to pick up and play.  It's a decent difficulty, and the game apparently automatically adjusts based on how full your team is, which is nice -- you're not left to fight a boss on your own with the levels ratcheted up super high.  The music is also top-notch, as I expected from the RWBY sound team, and so far, the voices sound just as good in-game as they do in the show, although every now and again, there's the odd line that just sounds a bit not-like their character (not that this detracts from the game, since voices can be turned off easily).  Targeting is mostly on point, too, although to be fair, I've only played as Yang so far.
Cons:  The game definitely feels like it's still in beta, despite how good it is already.  It relies on gamers being familiar with the RWBY universe already, and kind of just tosses you in without any real explanation as to what's going on.  There's also no option for a solo and/or story mode, which would be nice, but for 15 bucks, it's not a game-breaker for me.  There is also a slight clipping glitch with hills and stairs -- It looks like it's supposed to be a sliding-down-an-incline animation that just didn't quite grok with the rest of the game, and I've confirmed I'm not the only one getting it.  Again, not a game-breaker, but it is a little jarring to see.  There's also no sense of "I have saved my game and can quit" during missions, either.  I'm like 99% sure the RT team pays attention to what their fans are saying, though, and I'm confident that these issues will at the very least be addressed.
Overall, it's a very fun game to pick up for a quick bit of stress relief/time wasting/whatever you use it for.  The way it drops you into a game makes it feel like a good balance between casual and more intense gaming, and personally, I think the RWBY art style looks much more polished in this medium, in a way that's hard to accomplish with the animated series.  It was money well spent on a game, and I look forward to seeing what new updates include.

Been watching South Park since it's inception back in 1996 and when it first started on television. That said, I may be biased to a fault, but both of these recent South Park games, The Stick of Truth and The Fractured But Whole continue to carry the same brand of absurdism and continue to remain sardonic while holding onto the criss cross of both subtle parody and scathing satire. Considering the fact the original creators continue to write just about everything in the games, well, if you love South Park, you should get in on this.
As for the gameplay, it's nothing particularly special, but does take a slightly more interesting and complex route when it comes to combat. Whereas The Stick of Truth was fairly bare bones and ridiculously simple to upgrade and master, Fractured But Whole uses a grid based fighting mechanic where attacks will effect certain squares on the grid and require you to move about the field to attack, avoid or block enemies. Though, with thought, you can effectively cheese most enemies with status effects, it does take a bit more thought than before. But it's nothing difficult to figure out. However, if you don't take advantage of the much higher range of abilities available from your companions, battles later in the game can easily drag out into fifteen minutes or longer.
As for equipment, rather than your costume effecting your stats, you instead get artifact slots that open up as you gain levels, to a max of ten. The artifacts come with little bonuses that can stack up quite nicely mid to late game, also granting you more health and damage. The artifacts themselves range from references to events in the show, to the downright absurd nature of South Park. With that there is a rather mediocre crafting system for making costumes and these artifacts. If you loot every container in sight and complete various side quests, you'll almost never have a lack of crafting components. As for the actual crafting, it's very simple and straightforward and nothing special, other than occasionally providing a slight edge over your enemies with some special items than can be found in the world and crafted into very rare artifacts.
As for the story, I wouldn't say it's quite as over the top as The Stick of Truth, but it sure has it's moments that move from the sickeningly hilarious to the morbidly awesome. This game is dripping with what South Park embodies and once again, it's almost like an extra long episode of the show and rightly flows like one to. I have seen people complain about the story and even some fret about the ending, but my only words for that are, "You clearly haven't seen enough South Park." The story fits the bill to the T.
Now is it worth $60(USD)? That's a tough question. Even with the bit of extra stuff aside from the main story, it's just shy of being a twenty hour game. However, I can bet it has some good replay value, given a rest of course. Some will complain about Ubisoft, but honestly, it's overlay can be disabled and creating an Ubisoft account is easy as can be. Shouldn't take more than a few minutes of your time. Other complain about Denuvo, convinced Denuvo shortens the life of their SSD's and HD's without any real proof. The consumer may have rights, but companies have rights too. I leave it up to your own volition whether you have an issue with Denuvo, just thought I'd mention it. Along with that, I have seen people complain about the game not running properly and getting a black screen. I can't speculate whether this is an issue on the development teams side or the person is attempting to run 4K on a bad rig. I've seen people have issues running 4K in other games and they don't realize that is a still relatively new thing and should be known it's unstable.
With all that said, no, I don't think it's quite a $60 game. I'd vouch for $50 or $45, but since I would like to see more of this content in the future, I guess I opted to get it fresh off the presses.

If you like top-down isometric action role playing games - let's just call them IsoRPG's - like the Diablo series, but grow tired of playing the diablo series, then this game and the original Torchlight are for you.
It has everything you'd expect in an IsoRPG; random loot drops, random maps, mobs of monstrous enemies to slay, et cetera. It's really a good game, but it suffers from balancing issues that are difficult to overlook. These issues do not make the game unplayable by any means, but it does limit your options sometimes. These issues include diminishing returns on character development making each level you gain seem less potent than the one before and equipment scaling.
Do not let these decidedly minor problems scare you away, however. This game is not without it's boons, of which it has many ranging from it's unique sense of style, gameplay, replayability, stability, sizeable mod community, and so on.
All things considered, I give Torchlight II a 7.5 out of 10.

I only needed ten minutes with Lucidity to see what it was all about. Some games are like that, they put everything they have right out from the get-go and don't ever push past that foundation. Lucidity certainly starts with plenty of promise in its storybook world and charming presentation. It's just when you actually get down to playing it that it falters.
The game opens in a quaint little house on a hill, where a little girl lives with her doting grandma. Your wee lass nods off while reading tales of adventure, and dreams of traveling to fantastical faraway lands. This is where the action is, in the dreams of this young lady, and it's up to you to help her get through her adventure in one adorable piece. And maybe collect some fireflies, too!
I'm sure that all sounds peachy until you play it. See, Lucidity is one of those platformers where you don't actually control your character. Sofi (her name is Sofi, I had to look that up) trundles along to the right at a steady clip, only stopping if she literally runs into a wall. Otherwise she'll happily plunge off a cliff or smack face-first into a dream wasp. There's no jumping, no ducking, and while we're on the subject there's no way to speed up her slow stroll, either.
To help her not toddle into certain death like an idiot, you get to place objects in the world that protect her. These include planks and stairs to walk on, springs and fans to launch her, and bombs that can clear enemies away and take chunks out of solid surfaces. You don't get to place these freely, though, because each item is chosen for you, one at a time, Tetris-style. You can bank one item for later use but in general you're going to be working with whatever the game decides to give you at the moment.
I suppose this could work with some clever level design but that's the last thing you're going to get here. Levels are vast expanses of blocky platforms and pits of death and enemies that require some quick thinking when placing objects. Honestly placing objects is always going to require quick thinking, because as slow as Sofi is she doesn't tend to give you much room to work with on her teeny-tiny platforms hanging in a deadly void. There's a huge amount of vertical space to explore as well, with elevated areas that you're only going to get to with a lucky combination of springs and fans anyway.
The end result just isn't any fun, and it's dragged even further down by a conspicuous lack of polish. The art style is a flat papier mache style but coupled with the sharp, straight lines that comprise platforms, levels end up looking like cheap vector art. Some of the backgrounds are nice to look at but others feature some terrible and distracting color combinations. The worst offender is your own interface, with flat yellow silhouettes for your objects, and flat blue silhouettes for the ones you place. It seriously looks like placeholder art, lacking any sort of effects or continuity with the world.
Platformers with indirect control are always a dicey proposition because the threshold for frustration is so much lower. You feel like most of the game is out of your hands, leaving you to simply react to what someone else is doing. Something like Kirby's Canvas Curse worked wonderfully because you had a huge amount of control over your character and the world around him, just in an indirect manner. That's not at all the case here, where you can't even choose how to save Sofi from her own stupidity, you just throw whatever you have at her and hope for the best. Coupled with the unpleasant level design and inconsistent art, Lucidity is more of a nightmare than the dream walk it's supposed to be.

The premise is to help a little girl skip her merry way through myriad  imaginary landscapes, using conjured-up items (such as staircases, giant slingshots, bombs, etc) to provide her safe passage and remove obstacles and enemies from her path.  Easy enough at first, but as it progresses, your chances of making it through seem more and more dependent on the sheer blind luck of what useable imaginary object spawns for you next.
I don't think I've ever groaned so many times in my life, and I don't even mean big, expressive, exasperated groans...just very small, noncommittal, "Oh God, do I have do this bit AGAIN?" kinds of groans.
Honestly, my main criticism is that I can't quite imagine exactly WHO the "target audience" for this product even is, as it's clearly aimed at kids, but surely way too challenging and puzzle-oriented for the average six year-old to successfully negotiate.  A game for overgrown, forty year-old, game-addicted losers, perhaps?  No, wait, that would mean that I of all people should have enjoyed it; which frankly, I didn't.
This just wasn't much "fun", I'm afraid, and I finally allowed myself to throw in the towel after dying in the exact same spot more than ten times in a row (something I will more than happily tolerate from a really good game, like Limbo or Tales From Space: Mutant Blobs Attack, but not from the more middling likes of this).

I'm almost tempted to give this a thumbs-up irrespective, in acknowledgement of the fact that it's not so much an "incompetent" game, but merely one not suited to the likes of Yours Truly.  Yet I honestly find it hard to believe that ANYONE is gonna get much pleasure from this, no matter what their age...which arguably doesn't make it a very successful "game", period.
If I ever have kids, I might force them to play this one for an hour whenever they're naughty.  "BEHAVE, OR I'LL MAKE YOU PLAY LUCIDITY FOR AN HOUR!"  "NO, DAD, PLEASE...NOT LUCIDITY!  PLEASE DAD...I'LL MOW THE LAWN...DO THE DISHES...BATHE THE DOG...BUT NOT LUCIDITY, PLEASE!!"

That oughtta learn 'em.

is a difficult game to describe. It's a puzzle game, but the puzzles are all very simple. It places a lot of focus on plot and atmosphere, but the dialogue is all in a fake language without subtitles. It's cooperative, but not really since one player is controlling both characters.
I think if I had to give this game a genre, then I would call it a fairy tale simulator. The plot is laden with vagaries and lacks context, but that makes it more surreal and engaging. The puzzles are simple, but they require you to interact with many bizarre and magical elements. The gameplay is mostly a matter of going from A to B, but doing so really gets you to empathize with the brothers and their quirks, even if they don't have very explicit personalities.
With that in mind, I think this game fulfills its goal well. It takes the surrealism and limited context that make fairy tales so iconic and evocative, and lets the player interact with them through gameplay. It takes the logic of a fairy tale and manages to make it work in a more conventional way, so that the player is never lost by the story nor put off by crazy soup can puzzles.
I recommend this game, but with caveats. The experience is powerful, but short; you'd be better off buying it during a sale. If you don't like fairy tales, with their unorthodox logic and visuals, then this game might not be for you.
If you like fairy tales, though, and you don't mind some gameplay that breaks genre conventions, then this is a experience that is absolutely worthy of your time.

Firstly, I would like to assure those who are concerned about playing this game without a controller that it can be enjoyed to the full with just a keyboard. It can make some of the gameplay mechanics awkward at times, in particular when pushing or pulling triggers through a combined effort, however it is a minor issue in the face of such a superb production.
Brothers successfully engages with its audience and builds empathy and understanding with its protagonists and those they encounter through a simple but poignant story. Without the use of comprehensible dialogue, the game instead relies upon seamlessly integrated cut-scenes and the continually pleasing cooperative mechanics to involve the player. The game is not designed to punish the player, with generous automatic save points and a very linear path which might frustrate those in search of a challenge, however this is simply an issue of adjusting expectations. One should not expect a game that tests their skill or pushes the boundaries of gameplay. Brothers is instead a marvellously well executed attempt to tell a story of adventure that can captivate without a reliance upon violence or the extraordinary ability of its characters.
The experience is enhanced by a pleasing and at times stunning aesthetic design and a soundtrack that beautifully complements the atmosphere of the game. It entrances without distracting or dominating. Depending on whether one rushes through or stops to enjoy the view and explore every available inch, it will only take on the order of 3 or 4 hours to complete, but it is well worth the afternoon or evening dedicated to it to enjoy a touching tale brought to life so beautifully.
One criticism would be the occasional need to reload the chapter or checkpoint in order to successfully complete a puzzle, however such bugs were few and far between during my playthrough. Overall though, it will certainly not distract from your enjoyment of a wonderful game. Highly recommended.

In Moonlight you play a creature fascinated with the moon and with the idea of travelling to it. A stranger to town, he needs to do the other furry NPCs favors to find someone to help him achieve his objective. The first NPC gives you a quest that rewards you with the NPC's own hat upon completion. This hat grants you instant rapport with the next NPC, as clearly if you deserved a hat, you deserve to be trusted. Thus ensues a short (less than an hour) 2D platfomer. There aren't any enemies, just a string of NPC to appease in a linear fashion. It is relaxed, has beautiful art/environment and *really* good music, there are several tracks which is surprising considering the length of the game, and they are all good.
While I do recommend this as an easy inoffensive palate cleanser between games, it did leave me slightly unsatisfied. I couldn't shake the feeling that this is more of a prototype than a complete product. It felt like the developer created this setting, mood, good 2D platforming mechanics, and then cut the project short. It doesn't help that almost all the doors you run into in the game are locked, adding  to the feeling that there was something more there that was left incomplete. I would have liked if this had more content: more NPCs, a bigger town, more tasks, etc. Just to give the entire quest some weight.
P.S.: Found it cute that the developer dedicated this game to his two daughters, I hope that one day I am able to dedicate something beautiful like this to my children :)

I originally wrote a long early access review with a thumbs up. Now after final release I am afraid I have to revert it into a thumb down to give it a fair and balanced tone on the review page.

To keep it short. This game is not fleshed out and is really lacking content and fun features. In early access state this is to be expected, but now the game has been officially released in practically the same state it was in the end stage of EA. They have added an extra Island, some vanity stuff and a few new boring quests from new 'NPC's' and thats about it.

Main reason for the thumb down is that even though the game is still lacking content they did raise the price now to €20,- +added day1 DLC's. With €15,- they were already pushing their luck, but raising it even more now with really no more new content to show for is a no no for me.
And don't get me wrong, the devs have done a lot of things right and layed down a good fundament for potentially a great game, but they dropped the ball on the end result. It's almost if they were tired of developing it half way and and then just rushed to the release date without actually putting sincere effort into fleshing out the game. It's a very nice looking game with decent building mechanics, all other aspcects are lacking and feels unfinished. The game remains a boring empty grind with rehashed content during the game. The RPG element is almost non existent besides for having 'classes' and 'bosses. There are 'NPC's' in the game , or at least the devs call them NPC's, but they are just static objects that triggers a text window with 2 looped meaningless sentences or it gives you a boring 'fetch/kill' quest. The NPC's feels like placeholder content for real NPC's, but it is actually in the 1.0 release.

My other gripe is that building which is a potential large aspcect of the game is completely trivial and still serves no purpose in the game (while building itself is fun and they put a lot of time in the building mechanics). If those 'NPC's were able to move into your house/building and your pets could roam around there then it would be something, but they can't. There is no reason to build other than to extend your game time and if want to have a break from the lackluster grindy gameplay.
If this game would still be €15, I might have left my positive original review alone, but I feel that I have to share my honest opinion about the price/quality/content now that the game is offically out.

For young kids this game is still okay, they don't require deep RPG gameplay and stuff, they just want to walk around in a pwetty world, but for adults this game in it's current state is just to boring and to much of a meaningless grind.

Depending on future updates it might still turn into a solid content rich game, but I am not all that opimistic about it anymore. Time will tell!

If you're looking for a game review, you've come to the wrong place. But if you're looking for a fantastic Banana-Bread recipe, you've come to the right place.
Tips
No need for a mixer for this recipe! Clean-up is easy too, if you want,
you can mix everything in one bowl.
The best bananas to use for banana bread are those that are over-ripe. The yellow peels should be at least half browned, and the bananas inside squishy and browning.
Ingredients
- 2 to 3 very ripe bananas, peeled
- 1/3 cup melted butter
- 1 teaspoon baking soda
- Pinch of salt
- 3/4 cup sugar (1/2 cup if you would like it less sweet, 1 cup if more sweet)
- 1 large egg, beaten
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 1 1/2 cups of all-purpose flour
Method
1. Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C), and butter a 4x8-inch loaf pan.
2. In a mixing bowl, mash the ripe bananas with a fork until completely smooth. Stir the melted butter into the mashed bananas.
3. Mix in the baking soda and salt. Stir in the sugar, beaten egg, and vanilla extract. Mix in the flour.
4. Pour the batter into your prepared loaf pan. Bake for 50 minutes to 1 hour at 350°F (175°C), or until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean.
5. Remove from oven and cool completely on a rack. Remove the banana bread from the pan. Slice and serve. (A bread knife helps to make slices that aren't crumbly.)

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided takes a dystopian world filled with believable characters with unclear agendas and near-future tech, adds hints of social commentary and cyberpunk themes, and wraps it around a stylish, well polished stealth/action shooter. Despite some minor technical flaws and gameplay kinks, it’s a satisfying game that successfully captures and improves upon the Deus Ex formula.
PROS:
Best Deus Ex yet
Engaging storyline
Breach mode adds longevity
CONS:
Some performance issues
Cover system can be frustrating
Enemy AI is a little erratic
Lovingly crafted, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided essentially takes Metal Gear Solid and drops it into a Blade Runner-esque transhumanist world full of complexities, oddities, and deception. The result is an engaging adventure with great feel and a few surprises up its sleeve. Definitely one to look into.

Mortal Kombat 10 has a robust and fluid battle system. Though it doesn't hit the technical excellence of fighters such as Virtua Fighter, it is still a satisfying fighter to play.
Mortal Kombat 10 has a fun and enjoyable story. Its shorter than the last game, but its still incredibly enjoyable to play.
Mortal Kombat 10 has a tonne of game modes, which will keep you entertained for weeks, especially if you have friends to play it with.
If the game is that good then, why am I giving it a thumbs down?
Because the release of this game has been atrociously bad. From terrible optimization, frame rate problems even on high end machines, crashes, day one problems that made the game unplayable, to patches COMPLETELY wiping people's saves, its been a bit of mess. I was lucky enough to avoid losing my saved date, but I can empathize with those who had to deal with this ridiculous blunder.
I consider myself a patient gamer, I don't get bent out of shape over bugs and problems, but the number of issues this game has had to contend to reach a playable state is well beyond the point of being acceptable.
Even if the game reaches a solid state at some point, I cannot give this game a thumbs up. Developers need to be accountable for the state they release games in, and that will not happen if these kind of problems are given a free pass.

Pretty good game if you know what you're looking for.
(PROS)
*The fighting itself is probably at it's best in the whole series.
*Good graphics. Also runs on low end machines pretty well.
*Character design is nice as well.
*Great port, better than the consoles for sure.
*Super balanced, pretty much every move has something that can beat it.
*Great training mode, has everything you need.
*Online plays good for the most part and connections are generally playable.
(CONS)
*Single player content is seriously lacking. The story is meh and only good towards the last couple of fights. The arcade mode is also lackluster compared to previous games.
*A lot of old characters from previous games are missing and some of the replacements for them are inferior (Gigas).
*Steep learning curve, learning the game isn't easy and takes awhile to get comfortable with.
*Lack of any tutorial in game, which is ridiculous for a game this difficult. Going to have to look up videos to learn the game.
Overall if you plan to play this online and spend a good chunk of time in practice mode, I'd recommend this game 100%.
If you plan on buying this for the offline, understand it's shallow and inferior to the past titles, and I'd recommend for the price to drop before buying it.

Sniper Elite 3 is a third person shooter set in Africa during World War 2. Originally released in 2014, it still holds up as an enjoyable game by today’s standards.
As you would imagine by the game’s title, your primary weapon is a sniper rifle, but you can also carry a pistol, and an SMG. There are three or four types of each weapon to choose from, but honestly the starting sniper rifle and silenced pistol felt so good to use that I just stuck with them. You can also equip various types of grenades and mines which are useful for destroying tanks.
There’s a strong focus on stealth, you can crawl along the ground to stay out of sight, perform instant melee kills with a knife, and use loud noises such as the engines of planes flying overhead to mask your rifle fire. Levels are designed to give you multiple paths to reach your objectives, allowing you to avoid or flank some enemies. Its the forgiving style of stealth that I personally enjoy - if you make a mistake and get detected, there’s no instant mission fail, you can go loud and fight your way out of the mess.
My only real problem with the game is that the AI is a bit too videogamey. After being detected, if you find a place to hide quietly for a minute or two, enemy soldiers will just give up their search and go back to their normal patrol routes. I think it would make more sense if they kept searching until they found you – especially if they’ve seen you kill their friends.
I finished the campaign in just under 8 hours, which felt a bit short, but on the other hand the fact that I wanted more, clearly meant that I was enjoying the game. I didn’t encounter any bugs or crashes. Controls are fully rebindable and work great with mouse and keyboard.
If, like me, you previously overlooked Sniper Elite 3, and you’re in the mood to shoot some Nazis, you might want to consider picking this up on the next sale.

I've been a fan of Tekken as long as I can remember. I was very excited when I found out that Tekken 7 is going to be released on Steam. I am skeptical when it comes to preordering games. Nevertheless, I ultimately decided to preorder it due to wanting to support the series.
After seeing the specs though, I had a feeling that I wasn't going to be able to play it with my 4GB RAM i5 @1.7GHz laptop. Turns out I was wrong. The optimization of this game is very good that it runs so freaking well on day one, a feat which few new gen games could even hope to achieve. It runs on a constant 38 FPS while using Medium settings on my laptop, going even beyond what I had initially expected.
Moving on to gameplay:
+ Polished fighting mechanics as a result of 20 years of refinement
+ The inclusion of Rage Drive and Rage Arts makes the fighting formula feels fresh
+ While it seems weird at first, the addition of slow motion in Tekken works well
+ Great online netcode
+ Extensive customization features. You can also unock customization items in the Treasure Battle Mode, ensuring that there's always something to be done.
+ Extensive gallery mode spanning from Tekken 1 to Tekken 7.
-
Gone are the Team Battle, Ghost Battle, Time Attack and Survival Mode that Tekken fans know and love.
- The story mode was highly teased before the release, yet it suffers from pacing issues and isn't as long as expected.
- Individual characters' story mode was replaced with character episodes,  a series of one match battles featuring the character themselves. Unlocking each characters' endings in an arcade-like mode was what made each Tekken entry special, so the removal of that has certainly made something felt missing
- Arcade Mode is very short (5 battles long)
- Versus Mode can't be played with a CPU
Due to the lack of single player content, you'll be mostly finding yourself playing Treasure Battle Mode if you're going to play offline. Nonetheless, Tekken 7 is still a great game to play, as fighting online still feels very satisfying. Tekken is one of the most fluid fighting game I have ever played that doesn't force you to memorize button inputs. With the accessibility of this game, it has never been a greater time to jump into this classic game series.

Seen as this is an Early Access title, I'll start by saying this game has so far baffled me with how much polish it has. Not for an Early Access game. For a game in any stage of development. I expect to have fun in Early Access titles, but I also expect bugs and incompleteness. That is not something that I have seen so far in Portal Knights. Keen Games is serious about this game, and
.
I remember when I first started playing Minecraft – past the initial panic of the approaching night (I knew there were zombies) – taking a more detailed look at the game's assets, textures and lighting and thinking to myself "it plays well...", a staple of sandbox games, especially first person, "...but it looks
". After a while, a bit dull as well.
On was my quest to look for the perfect resource pack (then called simply "texture pack") and add-on that would hopefully bring a little more gameplay outside of building massively intricate structures in Creative mode. Finding resource packs that were also compatible with the add-ons I had was a herculean task, but I eventually managed and had a blast while it lasted.
The issue is that, with every update, my texture packs and add-ons would take anything between weeks and months to get updated and I was stuck with playing an older version of the game, fervent to dive into the just-released gameplay.
Portal Knights takes all that anguish and throws it out the window. It delivers, out of the box, not only the smoothest gameplay I've ever seen on a block-sandbox (my 6-year-old system runs this game at 60fps, it's a work of art) but also an alluring, carefully designed graphic style complete with dynamic lighting and custom models for structures, objects and monsters.
All that is made possible, of course, because of the – admittedly, and quite positively – small bit of lore they've designed the game around. Your world has been shattered by an event called The Fracture and, as such, you will explore small floating islands one by one, by means of
portals! That not only helps gate the content while providing both some peace and an element of progression but also makes the whole game take a smaller toll on your computer. The brief loading screen between the island transition can get annoying, especially if you're moving your home base from one island to another, but in general, it doesn't hinder the gameplay.
Combat is satisfying, if not a little repetitive, at least until you get ahold of some more elaborate spells and skills. My personal opinion is that I am willing to let go of extremely developed combat systems in a game in which I focus on building. It might not be the same for everyone, but then again, if combat is your priority, perhaps you're better off tearing down the latest Diablo III seasonal event.
You can choose to play as either a wizard, warrior or ranger, and they all sell their fantasy reasonably well, each with their specific skill trees that give you access to meaningful choices based on how you prefer playing the game. If that wasn't enough, there are craftable abilities that you can equip with any class, so playing a battlemage, or a druid-like archer isn't completely out of the picture. It might not be
, but it will get you through the game just fine. Progressing through the game and seeing all the different enemy and creature models did make me feel like playing another race, but sadly that is not an option in the game's current state. It might come eventually, however, so I'll be patiently waiting. For now, the wide range of character customisation gives me enough tools to tailor a character that resonates with who I am.
More often than not I've been taken aback by how much thought has been given to details and there have been breathtaking moments in which I had to stop and watch a sunset paint the green fields of my home island yellow, and then orange. The sound of birds chirping slowly giving way to the crickets as night falls and the multicoloured sky is filled with stars. Everything looks and sounds solid and lovely – each notch (
) into the stone texture looks right, each hit of your pickax on ore or gem sounds satisfying. It's hard not to want to mine and gather
to a point where it feels like your limited bag space and restrictive eight actionbar slots are veritable ball-and-chains.
My only concern considering the state of things has to do with scale, as most of the crafting stations you are able to craft feel like they've been plucked from a giant's house and placed into your house. A drafting table that was supposed to be somewhere you sit on and draw looks like a large physician's whiteboard, the anvil is about the same height as the characters themselves, but the tables and chairs are scaled correctly, so the stark contrast between the stuff that's in your house leaves me wondering what went into their minds when designing these gigantic crafting stations. If they ever implement different races, I wonder what a halfling would feel when entering a standard sized house only to find out he needs a
in order to use his workbench.
Finally, some features might be lacking at the moment, such as passive animals, breeding and horseback riding, but those are certain to come, along with many others that will surely feel right when they're introduced.
In general, Portal Knights is an extremely quality title that has already given me multiple hours of fun and it redefines both the sandbox genre and the concept of an Early Access game. It is very close to Minecraft in terms of content (albeit it being
content) and has room to grow vastly. It plays a lot better too, so if you're looking for an upgrade, Portal Knights is the way to go.

Brothers - A Tale of Feels.

Brothers delivered to me one of the best gaming experiences I have ever had (it is up there with the best: Transistor, Bastion, Spec Ops: The Line, and even Telltale's The Walking Dead games). It is gorgeous, mechanically excellent and offers a magnificent story backed-up with a fantastical setting!
It may only be a short experience (approximately 3 hours to finish), but it is an extremely enjoyable one that is well worth the time! You play as two brothers (as TotalBiscuit puts it rightly: a "singleplayer co-op" game), which is why a gamepad is required. The left trigger and analogue stick controls the older brother, whilst the right trigger and analogue stick controls the younger brother. This takes a little while to get used to, and it seems hard to perfect, but the puzzles that have been crafted around this mechanic are simply wonderful. I never found them difficult, nor frustrating, but rather I marvelled at their cleverness time and time again, despite how simple some of them may have been.
The settings that you adventure through during your tale are just gorgeous (I mean, just check out the screenshots for this game! What you see is what you get), and the music that accompanies them at times just adds to the enjoyment. And if ever you die, it is usually because your mind is controlling two characters at once. A few times I ended up letting go of a cliff face with the wrong brother, who would fall to his death, while the other one dangled safely over solid ground. But because of the wonderful atmosphere the game creates, you do not get frustrated, you just facepalm and persevere.
The story is incredibly well presented as well. There is just enough tension at times, or joy or sadness, which is why this has to have been one of my favourite gaming experiences ever! At one point, I was even scared that... wait, you haven't played it yet, have you? Well, I best not spoil it for you! Please, buy this game, it is incredible.

In a land of giants and shapeshifters, two brothers set off in a heartbreaking adventure in search of a miraculous cure for their father's malady. The story is amazing and very emotional, and the fact that the characters communicate by gestures and a gibberish language in any way hinders the understanding of the plot.
The graphics are stunning, beautifully crafted to set a cartoonish tone to the fairy tale. Passing through grassy lands, underground mines, ruined towers, wooden villages, snowy mountains, frozen lakes and even gliding among ridges, the environment will never disappoint. Players will occasionally encounter some benches scattered throughout the scenario, where they can take a break, sit and enjoy the breathtaking landscapes.
The sound is good, allowing for a peaceful mood as you progress. The main song, though not bad, is executed a bit too much, so it can be a little repetitive.
I understand this game was meant to be played with a gamepad, but since I played with the keyboard I'll base my review through this experience. Gameplay could be better, sometimes it felt a little awkward to control both of the characters, specially the younger brother, whose action button was set in the Right Ctrl key. Maybe if it was placed in the 0 key of the numeric keypad instead... Ok, it's possible to change it to whatever key you want, but in order to do that you must first reset the game (for some reason you can't change key bindings in the ingame menus) and that's a pain. And make sure you do your changes after the prologue, or else you'll be stuck when the game flashes some instructions such as, for exemple, "press space to do action". In this case, if you have changed they key binding that was supposed to be space, you won't be able to leave this screen, making you press all buttons to no avail, until you finally give up and press Ctrl-Alt-Del.
Other than that, it was a marvelous experience, though very short. It is possible to complete the game in about 3 hours (or even less if you rush). The 12 achievements won't keep you busy for too long as well. Unfortunatelly, it's the kind of game you install, play, complete and then uninstall. Perhaps I'll come back to it in the future, but not soon. I recommend buying it if it's on sale.

This is definitely one of the coolest and most memorable games I've ever played. It really does feel like an adventure. There's no grinding, no lengthy dialogue to sit through, no real learning curve; it's just a fun journey that feels natural right from the start. You have no idea what to expect from one area to the next and it does a fantastic job of making you feel the same way the characters do with each new experience. The dual character controls make the simple puzzles fun to go through, which is great. You don't really spend time wondering "what am I supposed to do?", you just have fun doing it.

[MINOR SPOILERS for the very beginning of the game]
Lucidity would simply be about grief and loss if it were a book or a movie. The protagonist, Sofi, is a young girl who loses her grandmother and then determinedly journeys to find her while struggeling to come to terms with her death. Lucidity is a not passive linear media, however, but instead is a game, and its specific gameplay is very much about quick thinking and adaptation, as the player is asked to help Sofi navigate constantly changing environments using a continually randomized set of tools.
These themes from story and gameplay seem to be oddly paired, especially at first. As the game begins, and Sofi starts marching forward on her own, the player is taught how to use certain tools to keep her safe until she reaches the end of the environment. Sofi is not entirely helpless (she’ll climb up small rises with ease), and the game might look much like it belongs in the platformer genre when viewed from a distance, albeit one that plays itself. If left alone, however, Sofi will die, and on later levels, die often, falling victim to giant enemies and treacherous falls. It will be up to you to keep her away from those living dust bunnies and spiky pits by placing things like staircases, fans and slingshots in her path, enabling her to jump and climb past danger.
Lucasarts described Lucidity as a “challenging puzzler,” and, well, I agree. The puzzle to be solved is fairly straightforward: get Sofi to the end of the level safely, navigating through a sometimes dangerous environment and around always dangerous creatures. I think it is important to point out that this particular puzzler does not derive its challenge from obscure solutions or mind-twisting scenarios; indeed, the game thrives on offering the player a multitude of solutions at any given moment. If the ground is covered in deadly plants, you might slingshot Sofi past them, build stairs to let her climb over them, place a jump pad to let her climb to a higher level of platforms, or bomb the plants out of existence. All of these actions would probably work with some degree of success. The challenge lies in choosing the best solution with the current tools available, and then in implementing the solution before Sofi runs into danger. The time pressure makes the relatively straightforward problem solving thrilling.
Lucidity deals with is treatment of grief by cleverly separating the bereaved character from the player, casting the player as the one helping the main character through her pain. The player must continually adapt while the playing field and pieces change, as Sofi must learn to adapt to the concept of death. The symbolic journey does falter a bit toward the end as the narrative pulls apart from the gameplay, unfortunately.
There are a few technical quirks that impact the experience enough that they bear mentioning. Because gameplay essentially involves placing level pieces on a grid, a gamepad offers a smoother experience here compared to a mouse (having a mouse cursor constantly snapping to a grid is an alien and unnerving sensation).

Welcome back to South Park, all of your favorite characters are back and ready to make you ask yourself: "What the ♥♥♥♥." This amount of "what the ♥♥♥♥" is put into the fighting, visuals, plotlines and characters, and they're all fantastic (for the most part). You fight/befriend even more absurd characters than the first game, the graphics look even smoother/epic, and the fighting style is actually a challenge now. As in, the fighting is balanced and you actually have to try/use your consumables. Cruising through the game isn't as smooth this time around, because there are a ridiculous amount of fetch quests, but I for one think the jokes that come out of them are amazing (save for a small few).
If you're here for the jokes, you won't be disappointed, but you will have to put up with several crashes/glitches/resets, a Ubisoft account, and an ending that won't live up to Stick of Truth's. The amount of bugs is ridiculous, and has the abillity to render you without a computer as you realize you have to redo the entire ♥♥♥♥ing boss fight all over again because you crashed mid-cutscene when the boss was talking. On my first playthrough, this happened through 2 bossfights once, and I got soft-locked in cutscenes 4 times. On top of all that, you need to register a Ubisoft account and launch the game through it. I want Obsidian and my fulfilling endings back. Don't even get me started on the ending. If you wanted a Stick of Truth-level ending, prepare to be disappointed. Even the scene afterwards isn't a fun reward.
Even though this game has game-breakingly bad bugs, I can't help but still like it. I haven't watched South Park in a long time and I still have a great time seeing the characters and laughing alongside them, and that's all that keeps me going in the longrun because of these bugs. I can't stand these bugs. They're terrible, game breaking, and they really demotivate me from actually completing this game. If you're into South Park, I think you'll be willing to go through this game so you can see all your favorite characters/episodes/jokes make an appearance/be referenced. If you're looking for a great game that has no bugs, a fighting style like Stick of Truth and an ending worth fighting for, prepare to be sorely disappointed.
TL:DR just buy Stick of Truth instead it's much more rewarding.

GTA 5 is an entertaing singleplayer game and with friends the only has lots of fun moments. The core of GTA, the fun of the airport in GTA4, the mayhem of spawing attack helicopters in San Andreas and the cool enviroments and music of Vice City are all there. But GTA 5 is another unfortunate victim to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ization of gaming in general. Instead of embracing their fans, who made them one of the most successful media launches of all time, they turn away and strip away at the core of the very fun game. The singleplayer was a great time, and I enjoyed all three characters. A few of the things I dislike in singleplayer is leaving online content out, forcing you to unlock these things in the multiplayer, which I will get to.  Singleplayer DLC has also never come, which dosen't make any sense seeing as the DLC for GTA4 were just as, if not better, than the base game. But, making a storyline would actually require some effort on the Rockstar's part. Rockstar would rather sell their microtransactions in a $60 AAA game, then add more to the singleplayer. The online on PS3 was always a fun experience, because with just a little hard work you could keep buying better cars and guns, and making money wasn't as boring of a grind because the payouts were fairly decent and you could replay a mission as much as you wanted. But, Rockstar realized that making everything ludicrously expensive and then making the money hard to get would allow them to make much more money from Shark Cards. Shark Cards have ruined the online. Before DLC items were too expensive to actually purchase, I looked forward to getting the new weapons and playing with them. But now, a ♥♥♥♥ing SMG will cost you 30,000 dollars and the extended magazine attachment will set you back another 15,000. Dosen't sound like a lot, but when you have to spend about a long♥♥♥♥♥time making that money, it just makes you not want to play anymore. GTA Online is just not fun anymore. And if you were lucky enough for a modder to give you some money so that you could buy the fun stuff, the game opened up a lot more. Flying around in a sports car with a turbo jet on the back is insanely fun, but 95% of the people who play will never get to that point. GTA Online is just an overall bad experience in the end. There are glimpses of something that could be so amazing, but Rockstar balkanized the playerbase so that 10 percent of people get to have the cool stuff that lets them have fun, then this ten percent just flies around in a jet and blows anyone else up. If the Online was a complete sandbox and anything you wanted was allowed to you, then you could have fun moments of chasing someone in a tank while you are dodging cannon shots in an Apache. When you can actually have fun, it really is fun. But since that fun is so hard to attain, it is not worth it.

There are two things that every Spelunky player will come to learn rather rapidly within their first fledgling hours with the game. The moment of epiphany whereupon these lessons become clear might be wildly different for everyone; maybe it comes as you plummet face first into a set of spikes, or get shotgun blasted into oblivion by an irate shopkeeper for the fifth time. No matter the scenario pans out, however, the conclusions are always the same – you will rapidly realise that Spelunky is both incredibly ruthless, and extremely addictive.
On the surface of thing, the game is quite simple to understand. You spawn into a randomly generated dungeon and slowly work your way down to the next floor, overcoming all the enemies and traps thrown at you, while picking up all the gold and items that you can to help you along the way. Yet this initials simplicity, along with the cartoony visuals, hides what is in fact a deeply challenging and skilful game. You’ll die a lot, but through the process of dying you slowly learn the nuance of things; how to trigger traps safely, what to do when, and so on. You’ll slowly plod further and further only to inevitably die again, upon which the cycle begins again. I spent endless hours on the Xbox 360 version of the game, but even now victory never feels guaranteed, and I learn more with each dive back into the breach. You can feel your knowledge developing and your overall skill improving, and it’s a great feeling indeed, and one that makes you keep wanting to come back.
Part of what adds to Spelunky’s rogue-like charm, however, is the fact that even with all the skill in the world, things can still get irretrievably out of hand pretty damn fast. Pretty much every action that you can do can have unforeseen consequences that can lead to an abruptly painful death... Heck, ever the actions of enemies off screen can lead to a cataclysmic chain of events that’s nigh-on impossible to escape from. On rare occasions this can be slightly irritating, especially when a good run is mercilessly crushed in such a way. Most of the time, however, you’ll be too busy laughing at the sheer unexpectedness of events to care that much; if fact, you’ll just be ready to go again, to see what odd situations you might find yourself in next.
If you start getting REALLY into the game, then things only start to get crazier in return, with some crazy secrets to be uncovered. For instance, There’s a whole chain of events to complete one by one,  which in turn unlock a hidden city of gold and in turn the path to the true final boss... Doing so requires a fair amount of skill and a little dash of luck, but safe to say that it remains one of my favourite gaming challenges of recent years. For the die-hard player that you might become, there’s also the challenge of a high score run, or even a challenge where you do the opposite and avoid picking up points altogether. There are even daily challenges to keep you coming back to try your might against your friends and the best in the world… Put shortly, the challenge never ends.
If there’s one key criticism to be levelled against Spelunky, it’s that you really should be playing it with a controller. While there’s nothing strictly wrong with the keyboard controls, they feel a little cumbersome when it comes to doing some of the accuracy and twitch actions you need to succeed, and while the very original form of the game originated on PC, it’s hard to shake the feeling this version was designed with controllers in mind. Some people will swear by the keyboard, and that’s fair enough, but my opinion (and the opinion of most others if you look around online) would say you’ll get a much better experience if you get a controller in hand.
Overall, Spelunky is a brutal and merciless challenge, designed is such a clever way that you will always want to come back for more. Give it a shot.

Overall, I'd say the game is pretty promising. I'm not sure on the choice to make it a hack-and-slash title, even if the fighting was so central to the series, it still also prides itself on character developement and world building, whixh leads to me to think the game would lend itself better to being an action RPG, in the vein of Kingdom Hearts. But, a game like that would obviously require a MUCH bigger developement team and a considerably longer developement time, and so this choice of genre is understandable. The game does do a decent job of emulating classic arcade beat'em ups in a 3D world, though I wish they made more use of the 3D space by making it a little less linear. I won't even mention adding more game to it, because obviously there will be more, the game is not yet finished. Here is a list of things that I'd like to see improved over time:
-Add a sound effects volume control. none of these other points are in any order, but this one is at the top of the list for a reason. As a headphone user, I had to turn my steam volume down to 9% AND max out my music and voice audio in-game to get anything near a reasonable sound balance.
-rebalance some of the abilities. Having only played one character so far, (Yang) I can already see not all of the abilities are where they should be. For example, Yang's uppercut is pointless. It does pretty much the same amount of damage as a combo, with no added bonus effects or the ability to charge it.
-Ranged attacks in general are pretty much pointless. Much faster and more efficient to just get in and beat them up.
-Possibly create some sort of combo system that would let you mix up your attacks, instead of using the same ones are and over again.
-Other ways to gain "Special" back other than just combo attacks.
-Please make it so when characters walk down a gentle decline, they don't fall everything inch of the way, so that they don't constantly trigger the "landing" sound wave.
-jumping is kind of pointless, isn't it? I never really encountered any reason to use it, other than to maybe get away from a mob. ANYTHING to make jumping actually valuable, such a special jumping attacks (that actually matter) or environmental stuff, anything at all.
-rebalance some of the Grimm. For example those boar-Grimm things are a pain. They're invulnerable 50% of the time, too far away to attack the other 50%, take a lot of punishment and hurt a lot. And it's not as if they're meant to be like big boss Grimm or anything, just above-average toughies.
Potato is a graphics option. Enough said.

So far, the game has only crashed on me twice, and it was entirely my budget graphics card's fault. For an early access game, it looks remarkably well done, the character models are looking very nice though the environments and animations could use some work. The actual combat is very simple, using only three or four buttons to attack (2 for standard attacks, 1 for dodge and one that opens up the special move window) but is actually really fun. The music sounds great, I just wished they had included some of the show's soundtrack. The characters are perfectly voiced and they match the show's versions in personality.
The actual attacking animations are perfect and I'm amazed everytime I see Ruby spin and leaping around the battlefield like a red and black ball of death. The walking and running animations seem to be misstimed for their starting and stopping animations by a fair number of frames, but you only notice outside of combat.
The projectiles are incredibly random, attack whatever they feel like whether your point-blank or on the other side of the field. The skill tree is incredibly basic, but I think Rooster Teeth can easily expand upon them. There is no targeting system so the camera can get into pretty awkward angles sometimes, I can kind of understand with the large amount of enemies on screeen, but I still would like to be able to lock-on to some of the bigger Grimm at the very least.
Your character's level is not saved, but whenever you progress towards completing a challenge, your progress is saved, so you dont have to kill another 100 enemies with ranged attacks for "Sniper" again, for example. Joining online games is incredibly fast, for once "Quick Match" isnt lying.
Online, your likely to run into multiples of the same character in a single lobby, I wish they would include some way to see who is playing which character before you choose your own, or at least make it so there can only be one of each character in a lobby.
All-in-all, if you want a game that you and a few friends can kill a couple of hours on this is a pretty good buy. I'll do an edit when the game leaves early access. Until then, I definatley recommend if you're a fan of the show.

I'M BAAAAAACK!
So it's finally here the second game made by Matt Stone and Trey Parker that continues the story of the new kid who became king of elfs and wizards at the end of Stick of Truth. Now it's the next day, and the Coon has arrived from the "future" to ask the gang for help save Scrambles the missing cat for a 100$ reward in a town with a skyrocketing crime rate which turns out to be the result of a sinister political plot.
Now let's get to the good stuff by first answering the question: Is the game good? The answer is of course yes if you're a fan of the series and know what kind of humor you get from a South Park game, however it's unfortunatly a step down from its predecessor. The story is a bit weaker this time around and the jokes feel a bit more tame this time around though they do poke some fun at the madness that is identity politics, police brutality, race relations just to mention some aspects you might have a grin at.
The customization has been improved somewhat with more items to create and pick up as well as giving the player the abillity to multiclass which is something the devs should be given props for.
Unfortunatly the game has some major bugs and glitches that for some players can be completely game breaking, I was lucky to not encounter any of those I did however occationally encounter a glitch after doing a time fart which caused me to be unable to proceed combat as well as one black screen after a cutscene which i luckily got past by doing the segment again and skipping that cutscene entirely.
In terms of difficulty the game still is a bit too easy even on mastermind level. I only really had some slight problems during two or three boss battles where things got kind of challenging one of them being Morgan Freeman, that being said though; The new combat system does make it a little harder than the previous game
This game oddly enough is way harder on my machine than Stick of Truth often taking up massive amounts of resources on my processor.
The game really isn't that much longer than the Stick of Truth and you should be able to finish it in 12-14 hours
Another thing that irks me is that unlike Stick of Truth this game has very limited replayabillity value since you can easily do all the achievement and try all the classes in one playthrough wheras getting all the achievements in SoT was much harder since you had to pay attention not to miss any chinpokemons and/or items which you could only get during that one section and if you wanted to try all the classes you HAD to play through it again
So is this game worth buying?
Yes, however you might want to wait for a price drop, I'm having a really hard time finding a justification for its current price tag but if you're a fan of the show it's definitely a title you should pick up at some point

Alrighty. Beat Hell & Yama 9 times, Olmec even more. Think it's time to put Spelunky on the shelf, now that I've proven myself it was not a fluke. It's given me  great pleasure for dozens upon dozens of hours. Doing casual Hell runs has slowly lost its appeal though.
