This is quite a fantastic, fun little game.  The central conceit is essentially that of a whacky mini-fallout in the vein of Fallout 2 or New Vegas, only with more crude humour and Richard Nixon.  Your main task is to break into Coolers (preservation bunkers) to steal booze that gives your character performance enhancing hangovers.  Along the way, you will fight enemies and evade traps with a wide variety of weapons and power-ups and take on side-quests from the eccentric locals.  You will also die.  A lot.  When you die, a new character takes over your previous character's home and stash and continues on in his/her stead.  Luckily, aside from your accumulated hangovers, you don't lose too much when you die (favorite weapons and equipment can be re-acquired for a fee, and you can store huge amounts of "cash" in your personal bank), and new characters provide a nice excuse to change up your play style.
The gunplay and melee combat are the real meat of gameplay, and they provide a perfect mix of responsiveness and cartoony effects, and the weapons are varied enough that you can probably find quite a few weapon combinations that you like to use.
The only real point of contention I have is that, so far, the dungeon maps are very repetitive.  But, it has not been enough for me to lose enjoyment (also, I am only in the second dungeon so far, so maybe  things change eventually) and there is enough variety in weaponry, booze effects, and enemies that I feel the game can be forgiven one element of repetition.

Here are the good, the bad and the ugly with this game.
The colorful look to the game is wonderful.  Even for a place like the junkyard world, Deponia, looks lively.  The place has several locations to explore which can be a good and bad thing.  I’ll explain the bad later.
Characters are also lively.  Most of them aren’t just random backgrounds with one-liners.  They are pretty memorable, too.  The humor and jokes they make are alright.  Fantastic voice acting as well.
Storyline is simple but engaging.  Rufus’ main goal is to leave the junkyard and save a female who fell from Elysium.  Even though it’s cliché, I still enjoy that simple storyline concept.  As long as it’s executed well, I’m all for it.  In this case, it was alright.
Since this is a point-and-click adventure game, the root idea of taking random items and using them on something that doesn’t make sense, is still there.  In the case for Deponia, there are a lot of items to take and most of the time, I have no clue where one item goes or what I can combine them with.  Early in the game, you are allowed to travel anywhere in the residence of Deponia.  In a place so big, I can’t figure out how to progress.  Even with a boat-load of items, I had to do trial-and-error with so many items trying to combine or use them on something.  After consulting a walkthrough, the answers are sometimes ridiculous that you know you will never think of it.
Man, oh man, this Rufus guy.  Sometimes, it’s hard to appreciate the journey Rufus had to go through.  With an attitude like his, I almost don’t care what happens to him in the story.  No matter what people say to this guy, he continues to be ignorant.  Sometimes I can tolerate his conceited attitude, but what’s really annoying is how much Rufus continues to insult people.  There are a couple of character’s that Rufus continues to drill his insults, and because of that, Rufus becomes so unlikeable.  He needs a good smack behind the head sometimes.  I don’t know how Rufus will turn out in the sequels.  Maybe he’ll change, maybe he won’t.  Who knows, if I go through the entire journey, I might end up liking the guy.  For now, not so much.
Despite the bad and ugly parts of the game, I still enjoyed it.  I do recommend the game for those who like point-and-click adventure games.  The humor and the vibrant, visuals should be the biggest selling points.  I’m not sure if the sequels will turn out better but after quickly looking at the feedbacks, it looks like this game is one of the best in the series.

Egotistical, Womanizing protagonist ... check! A world that is literally a trash heap .... check! Adolf Hitlers resurrection .... absent .... so it seems Deponia doesn't quite have everything a great narrative should consist of, but it makes a good effort.
Gameplay:
So to clarify I don't usually play point and click adventure games, and I assume from the little I have played the formula is very similar: Grab every item you can find, combine them and then ... make a profit? In all seriousness there isn't exactly much gameplay wise, click to where you want to go, click items to use etc, but what can you except it is a point and click adventure game after all. Well i'd be lying if that was it, there are of course challenging puzzles that one must overcome! No this is not some shooty shooty boom your heads gone kind of game, you must use actual  intelligence to play, in actuality a lot of the puzzles are somewhat obscure and at times nonsensical (that ties in well with the narrative and world so it doesn't hurt the games atmosphere or theme negatively). This could well be a problem for you if you don't like this sort of thing, but if you get too frustrated you can always look up a guide (did that on a few occasions not going to lie). It also has some very welcomed features such as double tapping arrows to fast travel to different areas or holding down space to view all objects/things in an area, I cannot stress enough how much time this can save you making the game flow much better and be less frustrating.
Visuals/Sound:
Since the art-style was the thing that drove me to playing this game I can wholeheartedly say it did it's job and it did it pretty damn good. Deponia manages to make a dirt ridden world filled with junk look vibrant and colorful, the characters also have quite memorable designs, such as the aforementioned egotist Rufus. On the auditory side of things the sound affects and music fit well with the lighthearted and comedic nature of the game, and the "chorus guys" medleys are catchy and fun. Perhaps one of it's greatest strengths are it's voice acting, Kerry Shale hit it out of the park with Rufus, and that's not to say the other voices are bad either, their all brilliantly casted and voiced.
Story/Setting:
The junk planet of Deponia is a very interesting setting, sure things have done it before but Deponia makes the small town of Kuvaq a joy to traverse, the eccentric townsfolk, mountains of junk and the art style contribute heavily to this. It also manages to establish an interesting universe? bunch of planets? or larger set-piece? by the end of the story teasing us with Elysium, Organon and a floating black market. The locations and their respective factions seem to be the main focus of the story although it starts towards the end of the game, primarily Deponia is an adventure and that is where it's story lies. It is Rufus's adventure, that has many unanswered questions that deserve some answers. Without spoiling too much the story made me want to carry on to find out Rufus's fate ... would he leave Deponia? Get the girl? be the hero?
Writing:
Deponia has some of the best writing iv'e seen in a video game for some time, this can range from the eccentric characters and customs that have formed from it's magnificent world, to the ego heavy monologues of Rufus. The fact that Rufus thinks he's intelligent, yet he isn't ... but we the player solve these difficult yet impractical problems as Rufus shows exactly how intelligent and an absolute fool he is at the same time which to me is an example of great character writing. The comedy is also fairly smart and witty at times such as when you find some straw in a stack of needles, or when Rufus is constantly prompted to berate a man he thinks is a pirate. I honestly could go on about how good the writing in this game is but I better finish up ....
Conclusion:
Deponia is like breathing fresh, clean spring air after breathing in diesel fumes for your whole life. It presents the player with a cast of fairly likable characters (unlike a lot of games which give you a skeleton, his only personality trait being he makes puns bout bones .... seriously why do people think this is good characterization). The writing is superb and made me laugh on a good few occasions, the art is great, voices are great, music is a tiny bit less than great .... but still good. And whats this .... this is part 1 of 3 .... oh boy can't I wait to play the rest of this series!
The verdict, maybe if you've never been into Point and Click adventure games, or just aren't into them give Deponia a try anyway, it's funny, has good characters, and a promising tale to tell. The price is decent, but it goes on sale frequently so you can wait till it's like 99p which is well worth the price, alternatively and probably the smartest option is being all 3 in the complete journey edition, which also goes on sale fairly frequently for about £5!

If you aren't familiar with Torchlight, it's okay. You chose a class, killed lots of bad guys, and saved the day while loot fell from the sky. Nothing atypical of your classic dungeon crawler. However, everything it did, it did right. Itemization, drop rates, skill sets, and combat were just a joy to experience. The biggest downside was that I wanted to play with my friends, but I couldn't because it was single player only. This was everyone's biggest complaint.
Fast forward to Torchlight 2 - Runic delivered. Everything that made Torchlight so polished was implemented into Torchlight 2. Only now, there's the addition of multiplayer just like the players wanted. In fact, you can play alongside 5 friends simultaneously.
The graphics have been updated significantly from Torchlight. Lighting is improved, character models are sharper and more detailed. Weapons look fantastic and the animations are well done. Characters move fluently and quickly compared to other dungeon crawlers, so it may take some getting used to. All in all, it looks great. Mind you, this graphic style is very different from Diablo 3, but given the budget difference between the old Blizzard and new Blizzard, it does the job just fine.
But who plays these games for the graphics alone? The loot is where the money is (pun intended). Torchlight 2 does that better than most on the market. There are myriad upgrades as you level, which include set items and socket pieces. This is not your dumbed down core stat itemization either. There are so many builds that work in Torchlight 2, and the items/set bonus tailor to your playstyle. If you want strong pets, farm gear with +pet/minion speed, get gems with +attack power for pets, etc. If you want to focus on ranged, they have ranged bonus sets, gems with +% ranged damage.
You truly get the sense that your character is getting stronger as you level and you can tailor the gear to your personal build. That's what makes this game so much fun.
To top it off, you don't have to spend 25-30 hours farming for an upgrade to your character at max level (or as you level). The good drops are very fair (some would argue too easy), however the upgradable items for your specific class or build may still take adequate time to achieve.
Don't like auction houses to make your characters stronger? Me either. Torchlight 2 has no economy, which means no botters, no 3rd party messages, no WTS threads. You want an item? Play with 5 people and you'll see the community is willing to share with one another. Your in game gold is still used for enchanting items, buying from the gambler (have a chance to get very rare items), and buying various potions/scrolls/spells etc.
I can go on about this game but it's a game you should definitely try if you are a fan of the genre. You will not be disappointed, and if you aren't into the online thing there is no "online only" requirement to enjoy this masterpiece of a game. Plus, at $20, it's a steal.

Beyond the town of Torchlight lies a world shrouded in adventure and mystery. Guardian-warrior Syl appears in a prophetic dream, summoning the player to the Estherian Steppes. There, you meet with the Destroyer and soon venture across the continent of Vilderan, an exotic frontier besieged by forces of evil. A discovery unfolds, that the Alchemist, following his conquest of dark ember, disappeared on his quest to defeat the unknown corrupted force responsible for destroying the mystical race of Estherians. Aided by Syl, the remaining Estherian Guardians, and clues left behind by the missing Alchemist, you will find yourself battling a powerful enemy that threatens to unravel the elements of the entire world.
Runic Games' sequel in the award-winning action-RPG franchise features additional character classes, quests, monsters, and dungeons not found in the original game. Torchlight II also now includes cooperative play through a free, peer-to-peer matchmaking service. Play with your friends, and use the free peer-to-peer matchmaking service to meet new players of a similar level and interest. Together players will discover expansive randomized outdoor areas and deep ominous caverns; random instanced and persistent dungeons, a huge variety of all new monsters and villains, endless variations of loot to find, and quests to complete. Players journey through the perilous Overworld, enjoying all new weather features, time of day events, and a rich and cunning story to drive gameplay.

I've always loved this board game! It's sort of an abstract sumo wrestler strategy thing where you're trying to lure opponents to the edge and use their momentum against them. The weight of the pieces as they clack along the track and against each other was just perfect.
This adaptation does a great job of capturing the physical feeling and the controls are just right. It's also nice that you can try out moves and undo them without the opponent seeing, rather than having to imagine the outcome and poker-face.
Matchmaking finds me an opponent within about 30 seconds and seems to do some amount of matching based on skill. Since lag and language isn't an issue it can easily pull from the worldwide pool. There's no chat features... I wish there was at least a selection of emoticons so I could congratulate good plays. After each match you can watch the full replay at fast speed. In about 10 games I've never seen anyone rage quit when I'm clearly at an advantage.
I haven't tried the single player vs AI or non-traditional layouts. But it has a nice interactive tutorial and several simple practice levels of increasing difficulty to teach the game.
My only complaints are the missing chat feature, a way to see the total online pool of players searching, and the stupid chime sound when you knock out a piece. Otherwise I'm really happy with this version.

Even in early access, this game is a ton of fun, especially for people familiar with the RWBY series. There are already plenty of enemies, some requiring different tactics to defeat, and I'm excited to see more. Hopefully they'll include some of the giant grimm. The combat is always fast-paced, but never overwhelmingly so. Selecting different perks as you level up is very straightforward, and the different special abilities fit the characters very well, though I'm hoping more will be added as the game progresses, as it feels a bit lacking in customization so far. There is plenty to make fans of the show feel connected to the show's story, from the chess piece relics, to the professors guiding you through your missions, to the Schnee Dust Company crates scattered around the maps, to the very levels themselves, sometimes areas explored in the show; but that knowledge of the show is not necessary to enjoy the game.
There are certainly still a few bugs as of this review. If there were more subtitles than could fit on the screen at once, the subtitles that didn't fit were cut off, and were never displayed, and the walking animation tends to pause when moving over more uneven terrain, but these are very minor annoyances, and I have no doubt they will be fixed by the final release.
A solid game so far, and I'm very excited to see it progress further!

I Love this game. I've been following since the first trailer was released and thank the heavens a good friend gifted it to me. This game is exactly what Trove and Cubeworld should have been. With a vast variety of enemies with each its own combat mechanics, several environments to explore that coincides perfeclty with the games lore, and a crafting system that may take time to get used to but not complicated enough to have difficulty to understand. I also love how they've just added 3 classes, and all those classes really determine is your initial stats and and passive abilities you gain through leveling up. Basically a blank slate you can customize by increasing certin stats while using any manner of weaponry and armor available in game. And don't get me started with the Boss fights, they REALLY feel like boss fights. With that being said there are some features I'd like tweek about the gameplay.. It ain't perfect, the game ain't  done yet.
Now to begin with the grind... well specifically how it takes more ore to make an ingot when you get to metals from higher levels. I understand that this is to make it more challenging, However I can honeslty say a large chunk of my time in this game was spent mining for iron, gold and coal so far (I've only gone past the 2nd boss in a medium sized world). And I've only used the gold I've obtained to upgrade my crafting tables, well all but my anvil. I think a good fix for this would maybe to increase the amount of coal needed to smelt better ores, leaving the actual amount of ore standard for each kind of metal.
Another is maybe to add sprinting and stamina to the game. The movement speed is well... it needs some improvement. This can be currently done by incresing your agility but thats just your movement in general. Sprinting might the fix for this and stamina would definately help balance it out. Agility can still increase both walking and sprinting speed at the same rate but a new stat could be added to increase the stamina of the player. I mean, You could literally barrel roll your way out of trouble in this game, and although you cannot go any other direction other than the way you're facing and that you can only do it on flat surfaces, it still shouldnt justify how many hits you've dodged with your super abdominal muscles. Now I'm thinking like monster hunter, where both sprinting and dodging/rolling will deplete stamina and maybe even jumping, but might be going a little far...
Now... in every game like this dual weilding is a pretty common request. And damn it, make it happen. But I can definately see this come in the future. Who holds a sword without a sheild? Why have one dagger when you can have two? And so on. Balancing it would definately be the problem though.The system Minecraft has for it won't work for this game. Maybe only making certain weapons be allowed to do so? you can't carry 2 swords but both a sword and a sheild? Or adding new weapon types that are already dual weilded? Add an offhand that will only carry certain things? I don't know what would work for this game. There are layers of problems over any solution for dual weilding.
And well finally, other than some bugs that must be adresses (like how sometimes I cant scroll through my hotbar and I can't click and drag in my inventory sometimes) make an mmo server please :(

Neither Nether Realms nor High Voltage apparently seem to believe in in-house testing of their code. They release a patch which is supposed to bring the Steam port of MKX into line with the console ports, but then are required to pull that self same patch because it corrupts save data. So now Steam players neither have Jason, which they paid for, nor their save data, which they played for.
I myself have been working hard in the Black dragon faction. I was level 50, and was slaving on unlocking Wicked Laser, the last faction kill. My profile level was around 60, and I was getting so close to the level 65 achievement. I had millions of coins from constant play, which I was planning to use in the krypt. I had tons of unlocked items, including backgrounds, icons, borders, costumes, etc, etc, not to mention a lot of leveling up of Liu Kang.
All of this is now rendered moot. I now am level 6 in Black Dragon with only one Faction Kill, no leveling up of Liu Kang, only 16 thousand coins (10 thousand of that as a result of their pitiful attempt at compensation for their ridiculousness), none of my unlocked icons, borders, or backgrounds (I have a whopping 4 backgrounds available to me at present), am level 5 in my profile, etc, etc, etc.
I don't know how in the world they managed to release an update that could corrupt save data that badly, nor do I know how or indeed if they even plan to make things right. Furthermore, they required that I download 15 GB worth of data to update to the version that had Jason and destroyed my save data, and then was required to download yet again another 15 GB worth of data to remove Jason, any updates meant to bring the PC version into line with the console versions, and my game progress, just to sweeten the deal.
I can only assume that this is part of a "Fresh Start" package being offered by Nether Realms, but if so, I don't know why they didn't charge me yet another micro transaction to enjoy the concept.

I really wanted to like this game. I wanted to like it so badly that I played through 17 grueling hours of it hoping to find the fun. And don't get me wrong it did start out fun as I started to get the hang of it, or so I thought. The first world seemed fair enough but the second ramped up the difficulty so much that I debated quitting the game. I trudged through though and made it to the third world which was easier than the second and gave me high hopes that I was getting the hang of the it. I was so very wrong. The fourth world was much harder than any of the previous worlds. Almost everything either kills you or stun locks you and then kills you, and there are many more enemies that the previous worlds. The only way to beat it is either by sheer luck that the game generates levels that are beatable with very limited equipment or by starting from the beginning and managing to get enough gear and items without dying to make it through.
I did beat the boss of the fourth world and I know about the fifth and final world, but I'm really not interested in going back and starting from the beginning just to die somewhere in world four countless times losing all my progress. I think this game would really benefit from having an easy mode for casual players like me. It could remove stun, give more lives and gear to the player from the start and maybe some pocket change and make the insant kill traps not quite so deadly. I know there are a whole lot of players that have dedicated dozens or even hundreds of hours to this game, but that's not what I'm looking for in a small single player game like this. I really don't want to take the time to learn every little detail about the game, but that really is the only way to beat it. That's why I think it would be nice for the option to be there to make the game easier for those that just want to play through the game, enjoy it, and put it away.
Since there's no real story to follow, there was nothing to keep me hooked other than the drive to beat the boss. I tried to keep the game interesting by exploring the levels more than I was required to, but I just ended up getting punished by taking damage or wasting items. I paid $3 for this game on sale and although I do feel that it was a good deal, I wish I wouldn't have picked it up.

I highly recommend Deponia, well drawn, funny and a consistent storyline.
no negative points

Egotistical, Womanizing protagonist ... check! A world that is literally a trash heap .... check! Adolf Hitlers resurrection .... absent .... so it seems Deponia doesn't quite have everything a great narrative should consist of, but it makes a good effort.
Gameplay:
So to clarify I don't usually play point and click adventure games, and I assume from the little I have played the formula is very similar: Grab every item you can find, combine them and then ... make a profit? In all seriousness there isn't exactly much gameplay wise, click to where you want to go, click items to use etc, but what can you except it is a point and click adventure game after all. Well i'd be lying if that was it, there are of course challenging puzzles that one must overcome! No this is not some shooty shooty boom your heads gone kind of game, you must use actual  intelligence to play, in actuality a lot of the puzzles are somewhat obscure and at times nonsensical (that ties in well with the narrative and world so it doesn't hurt the games atmosphere or theme negatively). This could well be a problem for you if you don't like this sort of thing, but if you get too frustrated you can always look up a guide (did that on a few occasions not going to lie). It also has some very welcomed features such as double tapping arrows to fast travel to different areas or holding down space to view all objects/things in an area, I cannot stress enough how much time this can save you making the game flow much better and be less frustrating.
Visuals/Sound:
Since the art-style was the thing that drove me to playing this game I can wholeheartedly say it did it's job and it did it pretty damn good. Deponia manages to make a dirt ridden world filled with junk look vibrant and colorful, the characters also have quite memorable designs, such as the aforementioned egotist Rufus. On the auditory side of things the sound affects and music fit well with the lighthearted and comedic nature of the game, and the "chorus guys" medleys are catchy and fun. Perhaps one of it's greatest strengths are it's voice acting, Kerry Shale hit it out of the park with Rufus, and that's not to say the other voices are bad either, their all brilliantly casted and voiced.
Story/Setting:
The junk planet of Deponia is a very interesting setting, sure things have done it before but Deponia makes the small town of Kuvaq a joy to traverse, the eccentric townsfolk, mountains of junk and the art style contribute heavily to this. It also manages to establish an interesting universe? bunch of planets? or larger set-piece? by the end of the story teasing us with Elysium, Organon and a floating black market. The locations and their respective factions seem to be the main focus of the story although it starts towards the end of the game, primarily Deponia is an adventure and that is where it's story lies. It is Rufus's adventure, that has many unanswered questions that deserve some answers. Without spoiling too much the story made me want to carry on to find out Rufus's fate ... would he leave Deponia? Get the girl? be the hero?
Writing:
Deponia has some of the best writing iv'e seen in a video game for some time, this can range from the eccentric characters and customs that have formed from it's magnificent world, to the ego heavy monologues of Rufus. The fact that Rufus thinks he's intelligent, yet he isn't ... but we the player solve these difficult yet impractical problems as Rufus shows exactly how intelligent and an absolute fool he is at the same time which to me is an example of great character writing. The comedy is also fairly smart and witty at times such as when you find some straw in a stack of needles, or when Rufus is constantly prompted to berate a man he thinks is a pirate. I honestly could go on about how good the writing in this game is but I better finish up ....
Conclusion:
Deponia is like breathing fresh, clean spring air after breathing in diesel fumes for your whole life. It presents the player with a cast of fairly likable characters (unlike a lot of games which give you a skeleton, his only personality trait being he makes puns bout bones .... seriously why do people think this is good characterization). The writing is superb and made me laugh on a good few occasions, the art is great, voices are great, music is a tiny bit less than great .... but still good. And whats this .... this is part 1 of 3 .... oh boy can't I wait to play the rest of this series!
The verdict, maybe if you've never been into Point and Click adventure games, or just aren't into them give Deponia a try anyway, it's funny, has good characters, and a promising tale to tell. The price is decent, but it goes on sale frequently so you can wait till it's like 99p which is well worth the price, alternatively and probably the smartest option is being all 3 in the complete journey edition, which also goes on sale fairly frequently for about £5!

I've been a fan of RWBY the show since it was first announced.  I picked up a copy of the original fangame when it first came out, and I still have it.  I was looking forward to this game's release, and was even more looking forward to it once it was greenlit after only two days on the list, and I was extremely hyped when it dropped onto early access.  So to say I'm completely impartial would be an out and out lie.
What I got was a game that is honestly very bare bones.  It has beautiful visuals and the basic gameplay is fun and fast paced, although some things do need to be reworked, but I'll go into that later.  I don't think I'll have any trouble finding people to play this game with, especially as it continues patching and growing.  As of right now there's only one game mode, and has two missions.  The difficulty level is set on a slider based on how many characters connect, and will adjust as people connect and disconnect.  You travel on a relatively set path with some limited exploration here and there.  You know you're entering a new combat area very easily, kind of like the new Devil May Cry game or even Kingdom Hearts for that matter.  You hack and slash your way through multiple types of enemies from the show, some more easy to defeat than others.  Build up your combo meter to refresh your special abilities faster and to level up your character.  So far there are only two missions, but your leveling points don't reset between them, so you can use them next round.
This game has going for it:
Beautiful visuals
Full voice acting
Fast paced and challenging gameplay
This game's problems:
Minimal content
No customization
Graphical hiccups on the characters
Balancing issues with skills and leveling
Honestly, the $15 price tag might be a bit much for anyone but a die hard fan at this point, however there is an intangible that you get in the purchase price.  Rooster Teeth has always been very community based, and they listen and answer questions on a one on one basis in many instances.  I don't have any doubt that the bug reports from this initial release will all get addressed, including mine, and it will continue to improve at a rapid pace to be worth far more than the $15 price.

The shotgun problem is easy, just avoid meatshotting the big ones. If you really have to shoot at the big ones with the shotgun, do it with some range. Other crashes are by penetration and explosions, if you penetrate more than four little monsters at the same time with the disc gun or laser gun, it will crash. Lifeline had a lot of promise with its original pacing mechanics and immersive style, but what saddens me the most is that it has completely failed to realise its potential.
The core of the game is that you have to guide the protagonist through the dangers by helping him make decisions.
And that's where the interesting premise starts to fall apart.
First of all, the protagonist himself. He lacks any real character and at best can be described as "common", "annoying", "whiny" and only occasionally "witty". I suppose it makes him relatable but it's only a matter of time until he annoys the hell out of you, especially if he keeps dying because of random choices.
Yes, the choices. This is the perfect example of bad and meaningless choices that all CYOA games should avoid. For every situation, there are only two choices, and 90% of the time the choice is whether to go "left" or "right". That's it. You'll spend hours telling the protagonist to go in one direction or the other without any meaningful interactions. The protagonist then continiously asks you whether you are absolutely sure you want him to go this way and continues to whine. If you ignore his whining, congratulations. Most of the time, he'll end up dead and you'll have to replay a large chunk of the game.
Lastly, the story. What starts as an interesting space horror/mystery rapidly devolves into some typical b-movie and ends. Without spoiling anything, I was both surprised and dissapointed by the ending, having wandered in space for many days before reaching a quick and unsatisfying conclusion.
Oh, and if you want a good CYOA game with similiar mechanics but better story, mystery and real choices, you should play "Lost Crew" instead.

Ever since I discovered Tekken 7, I've waited about a year for the PC release.
$50 is an extremely high price for me, so I hesitated, but I regret nothing.
Fighting games have been referred to as some of the most difficult games to play, so I was pleasantly surprised when it only took me about 2 hours to get Lily's bread-and-butter combos down.
That's still a long time, but still shorter than I expected. Due to the time it takes, when you get it down, the feeling of satisfaction is second to none.
A single hit in Tekken 7 feels extremely satisfying as well. Instead of relying on over-the-top flashy attacks, Tekken has simple attacks that have hit effects that are just the right amount of flashy.
I've invested 12 hours into Tekken so far, and I know that there is still a lot for me to learn, which gives me motivation to keep playing.
I don't have enough confidence in my knowledge of the game to play against others yet, but without even participating in PVP, I'm having fun with this game—I can go ahead and spend hours and hours doing treasure battles so I can play dress-up on all of the characters.
I'd recommend this game.
The game in general is pretty, the gameplay mechanics are complex, and the feeling of satisfaction when you succeed is amazing. Although the gameplay is more or less the same thing over and over again, the large & diverse character pool means there's a large amount of replayability, even in offline play.
But I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone who enjoys seeing immediate progress or enjoys easy victories—even the veteran players say this game is difficult.
And if you're adamant on playing only one character, the entertainment and satisfaction from replaying drops a bit.
Also, I've only really played action games on PC, so I use a keyboard. So far, it's been extremely easy to use with no sense of disadvantage (which I didn't expect, because everyone and their mothers have arcade sticks or controllers), but it's pretty obvious that you need a keyboard with anti-ghosting on WASD or ↑←↓→ (or whatever else you want to use).

After 465 hours in game i finally had time to write this review -- It's a great game if you care more about gameplay than graphics.
When M&B series was originally released in 2007, it was a time when video games starts to become more casual. And by 2010 when M&B Warband was released, there are basically two types of games left: either it's originally designed for casual gaming for consoles, or it tries so hard on graphics to woo players that it basically rehash the gameplay. Very few developers had tried to innovate how RPG should be created and played.
And here comes Mount & Blade Warband, designed on a already out-of-date DirectX API, with few lightings to impress the crowd. I had ignored this game for 4 years before finally getting it. And I never regretted since:
----------  This is the game that shows how sandbox games should be designed!!! ------------
Unlike the standard standbox games which were always using some rehashed mechanics: tower captures, endless spawned enmeis for no reason, no sense of progression. Mount and Blade series standed out as being the ONLY GAME since 2010 that had acceptable graphics, deep sense of RPG immersion, and deep progression on all areas. Leveling a character should be designed not only just to increase some integer numbers (strength, agility, charimsa, goodness, evilness, and gold), but it should also take into account of the player's actions. Not in the sense bioware had tried (let's just change some dialogs if goodness > evilness).
My actions in the game matters so greatly: loot a villege, steal some cattles, keep ransoms for myself. When I decided to start a kingdom, I found out no one wanted to join my army, every peasent charges obscene amount of gold for a simple sword, and my kingdom lasted less than half a week. It wasn't much latter I found out how being nice to people can be so rewarding in this game: befriendly lords of good characters, marry a nice lady and solidfy alliance, join a faction and help out in wars in return for new land grants, help villages and towns and it propspers to allow me to sell more at a higher price, maintain good relations with village elders so I have a steady supply of new eager recruits, work on leadership skills to unify units under my command. Once the king starts to get power hungry start a rebellion, recruit the good and friendly and allied lords to my cause, manage garrisons and taxations, lead a military campaign to crush the tyrant, and then have than play the diplomatic and military game to conquer the whole ancient europe. I can do them all!
Not only actions matter greatly, the gameplay on how you perform the actions are so difficult and rewarding. The battles are absolutely unforgiving at higher settings. The only tools I have to work with are my own hands and eyes. Want to shoot the approaching band of armies? Click the mouse and aim -- except there is absolutely no aiming assistance, both the enemies and my elite units are mounted. And I only get one shot before having to spend 3 seconds to reload. Melee kills while mounted also took some time to master: I have to wait until they are precise at the position where if I extend my polearm now, at the end of my thrust it reaches precisely on the enemy!
Medieval tactics are a much harder lessons to learn: when to shieldwall, when to use ranks, when to hold and when to charge, whether to attack or to defend. And when things start to go well, where to lay siege next? When to start and when to end a military campaign so I can host feasts to improve morale and relations? These are all hard questions we have to continue to contemplate in between individual battles.
And there is no other game in the world that has this great amount of depth, the amazing combat gameplay, and the rich RPG experience than this. If you only have resource to play one RPG game, and you like medieval themes, then get this!
Also I hope the M&B2 is progressing well. I can't wait to buy it!

As of December 2, here are the cons and pros of the game. I acknowledge this is still basically in alpha and still nowhere near its full potential, but I recommend it as a game that will most likely involve into something much better than what it is currently.
Cons:
-Bugs with movement, invisible walls, movement animations
-Only team RWBY currently playable
-Skill leveling doesn't save from game to game, which is a pain to reassign points every time you start again
-Enemies are invincible while attackng (not necessarily a bad thing, adds an element of timing to using skills)
-Available missions are limited, only a short story mode is available
Pros:
-Has the same feel as the show, characters don't lose that essence
-Characters are fun to play, skills are fun
-Combat is pretty balanced
-Even with the limited number of levels, there is more than one objective type (Defense and Escort)
-Animations are nice, looks pretty much like the show

-Character leveling trees are short but interesting, and provide different unlockable options

-Lots of potential for new characters or different levels exclusive to certain characters

TL;DR- I am a big fan of the RWBY video series. I find this game is worth what I paid for it as I've throughly enjoyed the hours I've played it. While it does have flaws they're easy to over look as it's fresh release early access and I've spent more money on worse games than this. From what I see there is a solid ground work laid for the Developer to build a great game off of as it comes out of EARLY ACCESS. Worth it IMO.
Long Version- I am a fan of RWBY, while I love the series I'll be as honest as I can about the games short comings. I've spent almost 9 hours so far playing this game, and I'm still enjoying it.
The game is early access, this is sometimes brutally apparent on some of the graphical/sound glitches  you will come across (there have been far fewer visual/sound glitches since the first patch). It also only has two levels you can currently play. The character customization (skill tree) is very basic but the system is there to be built upon. So far the game has not crashed and I've been running it on max settings. I've had no problems jumping into online games or having other people jumping into my online games. While it's not really a single player option you can play solo by creating your own lobby and setting it to friends only while you're in "offline" mode, but at this point in time it's the same as multiplayer. There are no character saves, so every time you start a new game you have to progress from character Level 1. The good news is kills and unlocked skills DO stay when you make new characters so you don't have to struggle like hell. I would like to think that Rooster Teeth will finish polishing this game until is shines like the show it's based on.
PRO list:
•Voice acting has real voice actors.  (go team RWBY!)
•3 days after early release they fixed the sound glitches, no more bleeding ears!
•Also fixed the bugs where soundFX would cancel out voices.
•Also fixed many of the terrain level visual glitches. And the uneven surface gravity glitch.
•Character personas are like their series counterparts
•Visually appealing environments even though it is early access.
•Minor (very minor, like I've only seen one on each zone) route changes on maps. You're not always running down the same paths. (I can only hope this might one day have some randomization to locations like Mountain Glen.)
•Super easy controls for mindless smash and bash fun. I've used Keyboard and Xbox controllers happily.
•Quick match is actually quick, I've never spent more than 10 seconds before being connected to a game.
•Skill Challenges and Unlocked Utilities are saved so if you grind it's yours.
•It is fun
CON list:
•Only 2 maps currently. Each map has two sectors but it's still kinda small feeling.
•Skill tree is kinda basic currently. (I'd like to see more of the characters Semblance powers)
•Ranged attack kinda targets what it wants when it wants unless your enemies are close. And sometimes then also. (I'm talking to you Weiss...)
•Invisible walls, as far as the eye can see. Or can't see, they're invisible after all...
Character classes based off my opinions:
Ruby- Range OP, can also do some decent AoE damage with Crescent Rose if she's in a pinch.
Weiss- Crowd Control, dat Ice Queen freeze is nice in a pinch. Myrtenaster not that great of damage.
Blake- Airial assualt, spent most of my time juggling enemies and up in the air. Gambol Shroud gun doesn't cause knock back either
Yang- Bruiser/melee, her Ember Celica seems to hit the hardest of all though it's gun range is super short it still packs a punch.
Is it worth it?

Wasted is a fun little dungeon crawl shooter with its own brand of humor and its own take on the rouge lite genre that can be a bit confusing at first if your ar eused to games like the Binding of Isaac or Rouge legacy.
I like this game and found a lot of the complaints I see in the reviews to be unhelpful, to the extent that I actually avoided this game for some time thinking the worst of it because of those reviews. So allow me to speak on some of these issues that I see a lot of people bringing up in the hopes of helping somone like myself from wrongfully ignoring this game.
- There are a lot of complaints about the timer (the s.o,b) in the dungeons,
First, the kill bot that comes after you is very slow and easy to kite around and the game gives you ample warning that he is coming and time after he enters the dungeon, the s.o.b is there to stop you from searching every room and killing every guy because the game wants to promote quick decision making.
And if you STILL hate the s.o.b and the time limit he puts on your dungeon runs, you can turn him OFF. Google how because while it sadly is not in the games options menu (a flaw in my opinion)  there is a simple way to remove him.
- There is also a complaint about a lack of permanent progress... (except there sort of is)
Sure there are no permanent buffs, and no permanent weapons but you can HOARD like there is no tomorrow.
The game allows you to store items in your house and they never go away unless you bring them with you on a dungeon run and then die with them. This game rewards players for doing runs just to acquire backup guns, health, armor, and ammo. And while this is not the permanent progress that many expect from this genre of games, I think it does enough to scratch that itch once you understand that this is how it is done in this game. It certainly is more permanent progression than what is in say FTL and people love that game.

As a Fallout 3 & New Vegas pastiche this is great. As a game it fails imo.
I've played it both with keyboard and with Steam Controller. With keyboard this game plays as a standard shooter game (well, as Fallout 3 to be honest) but it also works pretty well with Steam Controller.
Pros:
- 80's vibe
- humor revolving around absurd NPCs and getting irradiated alcohol that gives you special abilities
- it reminds me of Fallout 3 and New Vegas games, it's a good pastiche without being a mock up parody
- graphics are a bit cartoony but this fits the overall absurd tone of the game
- well written factions and NPCs
Cons:
- this game lacks substance imo. What's the reason to do all of the Cooler runs? Just get another boost after playing 30+ minutes provided that you won't die due to some stupid error, bug, glitch or this SOB terminator with minigun(super powerful NPC with lots of health, great armor and a minigun)? Pointless of me.
- it's hard in an unfair way - you get only 10 item slots and that's a really small number we're talking here. Get some gun, some melee weapon, some armor (helmet, body and trousers), some medpacks, some ammo for your gun and you end up with 3 free slots. That results in some serious inventory management time waster as you need to constantly juggle between full ammo guns while throwing away those with no ammo as there's no point in reloading when there are so many guns here and there. The same with medpacks and mutant meat. What's the point?
- cheap shots - some enemies can stun lock you and chew away most of your health or end your run straight away (read as - game over)
- you lose all of your equipment, hangovers and other stuff after dying - new character is a clean sheet, starting maybe with some pistol or some crowbar (only hope is to stack some stuff from previous runs in your home/base, but why to stack the usefull stuff instead of using it on your current run?)
What's strange for me it's a lack of clear focus in this game? Am I supposed to comb those levels for usefull stuff or speedrun them before this SOB minigunner comes in and probably ends my run?
I can think that this SOB enforcer mechanism was introduced in order to force players to make haste while plundering those Coolers/bunkers but when in rush one tends to make mistakes and miss potentially usefull items. That is one side of this game.
There is also other side that you can see when you turn off this SOB enforcer by modding this game a bit(it's described how to in the community guides section). With no enforcer we have no time limit thus we can explore whole levels of those bunkers before going to another level. But then if we have no time limit we end up with full inventory, full stacks of ammo and medpacks and stroll casually wasting enemies and keeping full stacks of items. Totally a different game now.
Then let's move to Booze, that is this irradiated alcohol that gives you Hangovers (read as buffs/debuffs). You can pick one bottle from four (usually) and the modifier is visible thus you can take it or pass it and check another one. Bottles on earlier floors of those Coolers usually give debuffs or weak buffs thus it's better to pass them unless you need to end a current run. Ending a run comes in one of three ways:
- when you lose all of your HP - you die, new character comes, GLHF
- when you beat boss - didn't have time nor nerves to get to any boss though
- when you drink Booze - you get linked buff/debuff and wake up in your home base
Thus I can't recommend this game. There probably is some plot or storyline but I don't care. It was fun for two or three hours but after that I see nothing beside doing Cooler runs over and over again. I see no point in playing 30+ minutes in one run and then dying to be left with nothing and doing the same stuff over and over again untill... I don't know what. It was fun in Dark Souls, it's not fun here. Runs are too long, give too little and the overall progress is too slow for me.

I love roguelikes, but I am getting pretty tired of new takes on the genre. It seems like every 5th game that comes out has some roguelike elements in it, and almost none of them are the better for it. They consistently use said elements in ways that save the developers money and time but add little to the game, and almost always are worse for it. WASTED is no exception. Having played almost a dozen Roguelike FPS games, I am just about ready to say that the mashup is unworkable on a fundamental level.
I won't bore you with every petty complaint, but the biggest crime in this game is the maps. They are huge and extremely uninteresting. You can see the same room, exactly, several times per floor. Not too exciting. Oh boy, another L-shaped corridor wrapping around a room with two doors, a minor treasure chest, and some enemies appropriate to the level.
One thing I noticed when reading other reviews of this game is that people don't like the soft-timer on completing levels in the form of the big baddy that comes by and kills you if you take too long on the level. What they don't seem to realize is that without this pushing you forward, you'd have time to realize how samey and tedious the game is. Honestly, it's a very clever solution and works well. I would have gotten bored much sooner had I time to sneak through the game at a more methodical pace. Running through and shooting things feels pretty good for the first hour or so!
Anyway. This would have been a fun playthrough if it was just a standard FPS, with real maps designed by a real person. The writing and humor is not my cup of tea but it's well executed, ditto for the art style. I got a genuine laugh out of the Richard Nixon character. But it's not really worth your time, overall.

If you're a fan of dungeon crawlers a la Diablo (or if you're a flash gamer, Monster Den, etc.), Torchlight II will hold your attention for hours at a time. Although a bit more cartoony than Diablo, it still boasts gore, fun animations and evilly fun mob death noises, plus easily followed quests, side quests, fun dungeons and challenging elite mobs. There's a lot more flexibility in the abilities system than Diablo, which gives you set skills and is heavily gear dependent, with the option to upgrade any ability as much as you like until you hit the cap, as well as assign yourself stat points at whim. Functionally, it means you can adjust your abilities to suit your play style even within a play style-oriented class system! How nifty. Playing online with friends is very easy and fun, as long as you both have a decent connection (though that's not surprising). I suppose my only complaint is the run speed versus zoom limit. Playing the game zoomed in all the way would definitely give you a challenge, as you can't see very far ahead and any enemies would essentially be up your shorts by the time you noticed them (try that on hardcore, see how far it gets you). However, zooming all the way out tends to give me vertigo as I run because the (admittedly awesome) run speed almost blurs the environment. If it zoomed out just a teeny bit further, it might not make me so dizzy... though I tend to just watch the minimap outside of combat so I don't miss any hidden alcoves. There's so much to explore that sometimes I don't even care that that I already murdered every living thing within a hundred yards! Definitely fun.

I'm very pleasantly surprised with this fantastic little piece of interactive fiction.  Sure, the sci-fi premise had me interested from the start, but Lifeline turned out to be a LOT more entertaining than I expected. The writing and plot is top notch with an incredibly likeable protagonist in Taylor.  I didn't think the story would have kept me so engaged considering it's set on a desolate moon in the furthest reaches of the galaxy, but the rapport you build with the stranded science student keeps you concerned for his well being as much as you're interested in discovering just what the deal is with the creepy moon he's crash-landed on.  Heck, towards the end when things go nuts I was absolutely hooked, even having dreams about it after I'd finished!
What's most interesting is the way the mobile port paces the story segments, having the reader wait several minutes (and at times hours) between interactions with Taylor.  This does an excellent job at conveying the character's isolation while adding scope to the overall narrative, not to mention injecting suspense when Taylor goes silent at tense moments.  Although some may feel the wait is an annoyance, it's easily switched to "Fast Mode" after Taylor's first death, which will likely come early in your first play-through.  For those with a bit of patience, exiting the game in "Real-Time" mode minimizes it to your taskbar where new messages will pop up as desktop notifications.
My one and only complaint is that the text moves too fast for me to keep up with most times, being the slow reader that I am.  This isn't a huge deal as I'd often just scroll up and take my time catching up while Taylor finished his thoughts, but it would've been nice to have some type of text speed option to work with.
Anyhow, I really don't want to say much more for risk of ruining the story, but if you are at all into interactive fiction, I highly recommend this little gem.  The first in a series of games, I'm hopeful the rest make their way off our phones and onto Steam, especially since this one ends in quite the cliffhanger.
although it's all just text, this is quite an entertaining game. nice story and atmosphere.

To get right to the point, I feel that this game isn't worth the money. In my opinion, I believe this could have been a good little text adventure, but it misses its mark.
To begin with, I don't like the invariably binary "decision" prompts. Binary is fine when there are only two options, such as turn left or right, go forward or back, etc etc. But as the situation becomes more complex, two options is frustratingly limiting. There is one point at which Taylor asks whether he should try to capture it or try to kill it. There is no option for leaving it the hell alone, which I feel most people would have considered a valid option. Then there are the times that you are tasked with making a decision, but afterward, it immediately becomes obvious that it wasn't the decision that the game's writer wanted you to pick and it quickly circles back toward the other option. In a similar vein, in many cases, the two prompts that are offered effectively say the same thing. For instance, "Tell me what you see," and "What going on?" These are pointless interactions.
Secondly, in my opinion, Taylor's dialog is poorly written. He often launches into an expositional dump or describes something in more detail than a person normally would in an actual conversation --which is what it is supposed to be. He makes jokes and side remarks that undermine the anxiety and fear that he claims to be feeling. And most annoying of all is that the game is apparently set in the distant future when humans are traveling between star systems and yet Taylor repeatedly makes reference to modern pop culture. It almost feels like the game is trying to drop names to make itself sound cool. It completely breaks the immersion.
And finally, I feel that the game's visual design is poorly executed. It is supposed to be a text-based communication system, so one would think that its design would be reminiscent of modern messaging programs --such as Steam's chat system, for example. But instead, it is simply a stack of chat bubbles populated with an obnoxiously large font. The game rapid fires these text blocks at you and then goes silent for an indeterminate amount of time, making for an annoying pace of play.
I have played a number of text-based adventure games in my time and thought that Lifeline would harken back to that genre, but this game shows none of the complexity of those old DOS-based programs nor even many of the better "choose your own adventure" books.
In the interest of full discloser, I admit that I have not thoroughly investigated every aspect of this game. So I am unable to fully evaluate it. However, I will say this. I played it for several hours, getting what seemed like rather far into the plot of the game before Taylor stupidly died of a heart attack moments before being rescued. I have the option of rewinding the story and trying again, but I feel no inclination to do so. I didn't find the story particularly compelling nor fun to participate in. Take that as you will.

Lifeline is essentially a story that unfolds in real-time.
It's all diaglog based, with Taylor (the main character) describing what he is seeing and doing, and you can offer advice to tell him what to do next.
So there are times where he'll need to 'travel" from point A to point B. So nothing will happen for an hour.
You are literally expected to shut off the game for that time.
I'm not sure it really works in a desktop environment, but the story and writing are definitely very enjoyable. If you do not have a mobile device capable of running the game, then definitely pick it up on Steam, as it's definitely worth experiencing.
However, the story is best experienced from a mobile device, where you're fully immersed in the experience of the mobile-to-mobile communication, and the push notifications involved when Taylor wants your attention.
There were no push notifications for this version as far as I’ve seen since I bought it. That severely hampers the playability of this.
So overall, I cannot recommend this game on the computer.
I do, however, heavily recommend it for your mobile device, which would have push notifications properly.

I recently received this game for free from BFG_Skipper. It is a point and click text adventure game featuring two protagonists, an unnamed radio communications operator from Earth (the player) and a lone survivor Taylor from a small transport spaceship Varia which crashed onto a desert moon of 31U00W around Tau Ceti. As Taylor explores the immediate surroundings to search for other survivors of the crash, scavenge for useful supplies and to stay alive long enough to send an emergency broadcast signal and hope rescue comes, Taylor will rely on the player to make decisions through various dialogue choices.
During the first playthrough (Without Fast Mode), a large portion of the game requires waiting for the game to progress where closing the game and being offline will count towards game progression. This game can also be played and run in parallel with another Steam game that does not use up significant computational resources to get multiple achievements over more than one game. Recommended for casual gamers who enjoy short text adventure games, role-playing games or visual novels when at discount or in bundle offer as it takes less than 10 hours (actual playing time) to get all achievements.

Spelunky is addicting, fun, and very punishing. The easiest way to lose in this game is to be careless. Fall damage hurts you and while that is something I usually hate in platformers, it works here. Things like fall damage, spikes that kill you in one hit, and leaps of faith because you were too cheap to use a rope or blew em all already, really make this game something special. You have to constantly have your wits about you because any wrong mistep can kill you especially from the second world and onward. Taking a golden idol or throwing a bomb the wrong way can turn the sweet prize you just got sour if the shop keeper is disturbed and then goes on a murderous rampage. You will probably play plenty of levels over and fortunately unlike plenty of other games Spelunky's randomly generated levels are extremely entertaining and never got boring to me. The key to winning is precision and awareness.
All that said the art for this game is top notch. Enemy designs are cute and fun as are the characters and each level is full of life and color. As for the soundtrack? It gets a 10/10 from me. I almost didn't feel it was worth mentioning but the story what little there is really isn't important as its not why you should want to play this game.

It's hard to decide on a YES or NO for my recommendation on this game.
Note this review is written knowing this game is only a few days into early access and so I shall revisit and update it accordingly. I will also be trying to write it with the same open mind that I had when trying ARK.
A little background on me:
I think God of War III, II, I to be some of the best games Sony has to offer. Other hack and slash titles just haven't felt fantastic to me. I love RWBY and while it's not an avatar:the last airbender in terms of great Western animes- I love this series. It ticks all the items in traditional Japanese manga/anime, but is fantastic in its own right.
My computer:
AMD PHENOM II 955@3.6 GHz
8GB Kingston Hyper X DDR3 RAM 1600MHz
Gigabyte R9 290X
Windows 10 professional
So for those who haven't watched RWBY- I suggest you watch it. It was conceptualised and partially developed by Monty Oum of Rooster Teeth and is free to watch on YouTube and crunchyroll
Without spoiling anything I will talk about what is in the game.
I was pleasantly surprised to find the voice actors reprise their role in the game.
The graphics resemble the unique art style that made RWBY stand out
The attacks your characters perform are big and flashy- just like the anime
All the creatures(Grimm) that you fight/kill except one so far are Grimm encountered in the anime.
The ONE level you go through goes for about 40 minutes. I definitely found it fun as RUBY and will have another crackling with Blake and Yang. I never like Weiss however.
That's all the good points of the game so far
Issues:
Despite my computer being below average- I managed 40-50fps Fone, but there was definitely a stall when I used an AOE attack to get out of a horde
I have to jump off the road to get onto the sidewall. Really?
I found that the ranged weapon targeting non-existent. You just shoot in the direction you are pointing. Ruby's scythe/gun also had an inconsistent range. Why am I able to hit the small and medium Grimm like the Beowulf and diggers at a distance but not the big Ursas?
Sound effects in game drown out the voice acting.
Subtitles are still somewhat useless because when a lot has to be said- the Subtitles only show the first half of what was said. I could never hear my next objective when the building collapsed.
Options menu needs a bit of an overhaul. Give us a drop down list for screen resolution and give us finer tweaking of graphics settings
More Ursas at once does not make the stage more difficult. Just more tedious
Walls... Well everywhere and invisible
Intermittent walking animation issues
A complete lack of the awesome soundtrack in the anime
What I feel should be added:
Let us play as team JNPR or create our own characters with a shop to customise and build our signature weapon
Give us a tournament mode where it's teams versus each other with the highest scoring in the team moving to the next round
Definitely work on a full story mode
Give us a targeting system. I hate shooting the wrong grimm
Some voice chat options to your team would be nice
In summary this game shows potential but keep the updates coming hard and fast... Like Yangs fists
Will I recommend it? For now, yes for RWBY fans who want to show their support.
If you haven't already watched the anime- watch it before you play this otherwise you will be looking at enemies to kill without context and probably not liking the visual style much

Portal knights, this is how it was made:
1/2 gallon of cuteness
2 pints of anime
3 quarts of RPG
12 oz of Sandbox
2 pounds of combat
and
6 tons of awesome
Combine them in a pot and stir well, and out comes Portal Knights!!
Portal knights is a cute, lego style sandbox-RPG game full of loot, mining, chests, combat, 6 bosses, 50 (or so) levels, diversity, classes, ore, crafting, farming, exploration, co-op, building, weapons, armour, questing, leveling, and all - around awesomeness for any ARPG lover. (I am aware this isn't anime but it's a lot like it :P)
You're not convinced? It's worth the money no doubt. But let's go into more detail.
FAQ:
1. I don't like building. Is it ever required?
A1: No. Although, it is very fun to do in a unique, engaging way.
2: I don't like fighting and stuff. Is it ever required?
A2: Nope! The combat system is fun and exciting, but if you want you can stay on the first floating island for your entire game experience and still have fun building!
3: Are the achievements easy and fun?
A3: Yup! Some require you to reach certain level milestones by fighting for exp and mining, some are for doing simply done things like completing the tutorial, and some are really advanced like getting to level 30, beating the final boss no - hit, and more!
4: Is this game co-op?
A4: You are correct sir, it is! You can play with steam friends and team up to defeat monsters, get loot, build bases, quest and farm! It also has very good connection to the online server. So double up with a friend for a better - and easier experience! With this recent update you can be on different islands, so your friend can be leveling up on a monster-heavy world while you gather resources on a more peaceful map or build a house!
5: Is this game any good?
A5: Yes in a heartbeat.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The 3 classes are:
Warrior: Possibly the best class, the warrior does massive damage in single hits and has very defensive armour. Even though it's supposed to be that the warrior is slow, if you don't like the attack speed you can use a speedy sword, but if you don't think a sword's damage is enough and want to take things to another level, you can grab a battleaxe and pound foes into dust! The only drawback is that they can't hit air enemies, so you'll have to make a spell at the altar (one of the many crafting stations) to unleash a powerful shout to knock flying beasts to the ground.
Ranger: Best class for early game, stinks for later. As you might expect, the ranger is very far range. They also have good speed. Drawbacks? Minimal damage, minimal health, horrible close range, pretty defenseless. Don't pick them unless you plan to only build and stay on like the first 10 islands. On the other hand, they are really cool...
Mage: Balanced, ok for early and late game. They don't have quite the range as a ranger, but still good. They can hit aireal enemies and cast spells that greatly increase their ability. The problem is that requires mana, so unless you are stocked with mana potions, you'll have trouble late - game. They have elemental weapons so you can get a buff if you use a certain weapon against a certian enemy type. (Ex: fire wands do most damage against earth enemies.)
There are 10 different original map types (non-event) and they are as follows:
1: Forest
2: Desert
3: Cove
4: Mushrooms
5: Snow
6: Jungle
7: Volcano
8: Heaven
9: Outer-space
10: Boss arena
There are 6 bosses. The first one is the Giant worm, then the Dragon queen, the Ghost king, the Electro bug,  Ice dragon and the Bright prince. In order of difficulty it probably goes: (And the list I just made was in order of when you encounter them)
Giant worm - super-easy
Dragon queen - kinda easy
Ghost king - a little hard at first
Bright prince - kinda hard
Electro bug - hard
Ice dragon - very hard
(Note: Electro bug, Ice dragon and bright prince can only be fought if you use the correct summoning item to fight them (To get to the electro bug you must fight the giant worm until you get the relic, for the Ice dragon you have to fight the dragon queen until you get the relic drop, and same deal for the ghost bosses, you have to fight the Ghost king until you get the relic for the Bright Prince. All the relics are very rare drops so you will have to grind the first 3 a lot to get the relics.)
The ores from best to worse are as follows:
Titanium - found on outer space maps
Gold - found on volcano maps
Iron - found on snow and mushroom maps
Copper - found on desert and cove maps
As for the gems, it goes:
Moon opal - found in outer space
Angels diamond - found in heaven (Used to be sun diamond)
Sea sapphire - Found in snow maps (used to be something like ice crystal, idk why they changed it)
Electro quartz - found in jungles
Flame rubies - found in deserts
Verdant emeralds - Found in coves
If you aren't convinced yet, I don't know what can convince you. If it's any help, there are almost no bugs - nada, zilch, zipzero bugs.
For 20 dollars? Get out of here! I would pay 30 for this.
Go get yourself a copy and have fun.

TL;DR  Lifeline is a well written choose your own adventure style game that is played in real time.
I am changing my review from a negative to a positive after learning more about this game and giving it another try.  Having tried it again I found that I enjoyed Lifeline for what it is and hope to see more of these games on Steam, It looks like there are 5 other games in this series.
My main problem with the game originally was that it would keep pausing in the story and just give you a message that "Taylor is busy", and some of these pauses would take hours before the story would continue.  I have since been told that this game was originally designed as a mobile game, and was meant to be played in "real time" as Taylor was messaging you.  I bought this game from the Google store and it turned out to be a game concept that works great on your phone.  I then retried it on Steam and found it to be enjoyable to play through once I knew what to expect.
There is an option to put the game into Fast Mode once you die the first time. Fast mode allows you to play the game without any pauses in the story, so Taylor will respond to you imminently making the game play much quicker. There is also an option after you die or beat the game to go back to a previous chapter in the story and choose a different path.
A couple of changes I would like to see an option to put the game into Fast Mode from the start of the game. The real time play is an interesting idea and works well on my phone, but it was a little tedious on PC.  I would also like to see a couple of more options to go back in the story, maybe a bookmark location so that you can jump right to a choice you made that ended badly for you quickly.
One other think I would like to see is a way to exit the game properly. Right now Lifeline uses Steam Notifications to tell you when you get a message from Taylor so you know when the story is progressing, so when you exit the game, it keep running in the background. This isn't really a problem until you try to exit Steam and just keep getting a message to shut down Lifeline before you can close the game.  The only way I can close the game right now is in the Task Manager and force it to shutdown.

Wasted is a very funny and satirical take on... Well, Fallout and Borderlands. Obviously.
Wasted is a dungeon crawler roguelike that tasks you with entering bomb shelters to get drunk. And everyone is stuck in the 80's. And everyone makes♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes. And the currency is toilet paper. Yeah.
Unlike most roguelikes, you get a dedicated "home" area where everything is safe. In fact, the general "lose everything when you die" is cut down quite a bit in Wasted. There are courier boxes spread out in dungeons that can hold 6 items that will be available at any other courier box, for if you die or need to send something home. Your home can hold an essentially infinite stock of whatever you put in it, and it's all still available on death.
Well then, why do I care if I die or not? Well, once you enter a shelter, you have to find booze to drink. Once you drink it, you pass out and wake up at home. The ONLY way to end up safe and sound is to find booze. Otherwise, you die. Simple.
Now, booze gives you a hangover. This isn't necessarily a bad thing. These hangovers are permanent effects on that particular character that may be beneficial or negative. The thing is, the booze found at the first few levels in the bomb shelters are relatively weak or even downright bad, which makes you want to go farther and get better booze, which in turn, makes you more likely to die. So there's a catch.
So, overall it's relatively "safe" for a roguelike, and progression feels fair overall.
The game has some light RPG elements in the way of a few stats, which are affected by either hangovers or the gear that you wear - Gear is probably the largest form of progression in the game, providing you with better guns, better armor, and more fanny packs (that let you hold more items). The stats themselves are quite simple, such as a skill for shooting better or a skill for smacking things better or a skill for tinkering around with traps and doors.
The combat is fast and frantic, if simple. You can look down the sights of your gun, and it handles much like a typical shooter, but guns feel a bit inaccurate at times. A "high level" gun does significantly more damange than a "low level" gun, making it a bit more similar to Borderlands than Fallout. Melee is a matter of hitting, charging hits, and blocking. Pretty typical. Combat may be simple but the fast "rocket tag" aspect of gunfights make it quite enjoyable.
Graphically, the game is very enjoyable. The characters are very cute and silly, even if the number of polygons leaves a bit to be desired. The environments are somewhat more bland unfortunately, and can become very repetitive. The guns look and feel rather satisfying. As for audio, the game has a charming soundtrack and many of the NPCs are voiced. I didn't find any of the voices lacking, and some are rather... interesting (I'm looking at you,♥♥♥♥♥♥and Kissinjerk).
Overall, the game is a very enjoyable dungeon crawler with some interesting aspects and a lighthearted tone. I'm not particularly far into the game at this point, but it hints at being even deeper than it is already.
I would definitely recommend this game, and if you act fast, there's a humble bundle including it right now.

Listen, If you're on the fence about playing this. Here's what I want you to do if you were to decide to purchase it. Play the Native game first, get used to the combat, quests, recruiting, leveling up, tournaments, becoming a vassal, become a lord, become a king, own towns, villages, cities, get your butt kicked in online multiplayer et cetera until you're like "okay, I get it, it's a good game." Why do I want you to play the Native first? It is because I want you to download the Floris Mod Expanded and revel in the thousands of improvements. It is stammering the HARD work these modders completed, corroborated and combined into one just utterly fantastic mod. I know, I know, I'm giving more praise to the mod than the game, but it would not at all be possible without M&B developers. Shoot, I bet the devs at Taleworlds even play Floris Mod.
This game does not hold your hand.  You choose how you start off, your characters history, where they are from, what they did as a child, what their father did etc. You don't start with an army, or even a few friends. You are alone in the world of Calradia. Yes, depending on the life you chose at the beginning does make it easier or harder for you to get ahead in life. But this game is NOT for the feignt of heart. You are not invincible. If you're on the battlefield with your men, charging at the enemy and you get clocked with a stray arrow to the face, you're done. If you get incapacitated, in the Native version: The battle ends and you will either win or lose depending on force strength and experience. In Floris Mod, you can watch the remainder of the fight. You are not respawned, nor can you play as someone else. You're done. Combat is difficult, it's not a hack and slash, it's not quicktime action counter attacks, it is not simple. Hacknslash will get you killed quickly. You need to see how your opponent is attacking, from which side, and making sure you block that attack while hoping you're quick enough to strike him/her while they line up another attack. This becomes incredibly difficult if you're facing multiple opponents. Even if it's only two. One may stab, the other slash, the other swinging overhead. It is easy to "die", and you will a lot in the early game as a beginner, shoot, even as a veteran sometimes I still get my army killed and captured early game.
There is not enough text nor time to go over how brilliantly amazing this game is. I need you to trust me. If you buy it, go into it with an open mind, even if you have no clue what lords/villagers/kings are talking about. Do what I did, stick with it and you will learn it and love it.

People who've played Dark Souls might best understand Spelunky as a 2D version of Sen's fortress where the map rearranges every time you play, you only have 4hp, no flasks, and no shield.
This game requires a similar kind of stubbornness and masochism as the Souls games. It is hard. Death comes very easily with numerous opportunities for mistakes. Many traps can kill you with a single hit. But if you keep at it you can improve dramatically. A lot of the game is about discovery. Discovering how different traps work and how to defeat them, how enemies behave and how to conquer them, and how various other game systems work. As you begin to gain mastery of those things you will delve deeper and deeper into the game, which brings a great sense of accomplishment.
Sometimes the randomly generated levels are very unfair. This is especially true when using the shortcuts (after you unlock them) to skip the earlier stages of the game. Playing the early stages gives you time to find useful items that give you more options in tackling obstacles during the later stages. If you jump straight into those later stages however, your options are going to be a bit limited.
A fun little game, which is usually fair but severely harsh.
