To clarify, I've played a tiny bit of Tekken 4 on PS2 and Tekken 6 on PS Vita, but that's the extent of my previous experience. I barely played either of these and I just button mashed, so I'll call myself a Tekken noob and say that this game is my first 'real experience' in playing a Tekken game. I pre-ordered this game without knowing how well it will be optimized on PC, if the online servers will work, if it supports controllers, etc. To my amazement, Tekken 7 on day 1 tackled all of these.
Constant 60 fps is vital in this game as framerate drops will affect button inputs. This game is extremely smooth to run on ultra settings whilst maintaining constant 60 fps (at 1920x1080 on a GTX 1060) though borderless windowed settings forces me to run at 3840x2160 for some reason, but this does not seem to affect system performance at all. Only drops you will see are the loading cutscenes where it will run at 30 fps, but who cares about that?
Amazing. Simply amazing. Day 1 release gives you a whopping 37 characters to choose from (38 if you got Eliza as a pre-order bonus) with 10 of them being new characters. The characters all speak in their native language, so I found myself very confused when they all seemed to understand what each other was saying during the story (a great example of this is the dialogue between Nina, Heihachi and Claudio). However, this is by no means a downside as we don't have to hear horrible dubbed voices of foreign characters, but instead it feels more natural and fitting.
Not only are there a wide selection of characters, but there are also 20 stages to choose from. The stages have different layouts so it doesn't feel repetitive. You'll have stages with and without walls, some which are octagonal shaped, others which are square shaped and even stages with multiple platforms that can be broken through by using certain moves. Each stage has it's own music piece composed to it and gives it a sense of uniqueness. Oh, and they all look great too.
I found the story to be very interesting and gripping at times, but I also found it to be quite short. For the most part it's spending 5 minutes watching a cutscene, fighting someone and then rinse and repeat. Though I guess for a fighting game not much else can be done. I completed the story in a couple of hours in a single sitting along with the extra character episodes unlocked after completing the main story. I found myself hysterically laughing at certain character episodes (Paul vs. Panda and Lucky Chloe vs. Eddy are the two that come to mind) and it was just really fun overall. But as I previously mentioned it is VERY short.
I gotta say, the gameplay is near-flawless. For a fighting game noob, I was able to quickly pick up characters I have never even played before and within an hour or so I would come to grips with their playstyle and how to use them. Blocking is done simply by holding back for mid and air attacks and down-back for low attacks, there is no button input required and it is as simple as that. Most characters have very easy 3 or 4 hit combos which is helpful when starting out with a new character. One thing I am not too impressed with however is the inclusion of 'rage arts'. I understand that it is included to help give players an edge when they have low hp, but it honestly just feels cheap. Not to mention that Akuma's rage art can not be blocked, but only evaded by sidestepping or jumping at the right time.
Because who would ever dare to play a fighting game with keyboard and mouse? I play this game using my PS4 controller and seems to work flawlessly. The button layout however still shows the Xbox controller button layout, but this isn't an issue at all. I really appreciate the inclusion of custom controller input bindings so I can easily bind multiple buttons to a single button (LP+RP to L1 for example).
The soundtrack is quite possibly the best soundtrack of any game I have ever played. There isn't a single track that I have disliked and I have found myself sitting in the character select screen and certain maps in practice whilst I do other tasks just so I can listen to the soundtrack in the background. Honestly even if you don't like fighting games, at least listen to the soundtrack and you will not be disappointed.
It's honestly hard to fault this game, it is quite possibly the best fighting game of all time. I love every aspect of this game from the characters to the soundtrack. The game runs very smoothly so I have no issues with input lag and I just find myself falling in love with this game more and more each day. The only issue I have found is that you will sometimes lose connection to a host before you have even joined them, but otherwise online also works flawlessly with no noticable lag.
Truely a testament to a games ability to tell a masterful story in a way only a game could do. Absolutely beatiful. (definetly play with a controller though, the gameplay is rough without one)

Online matches are great. Matchmaking is fast and I didn't experience any lag at all. In general it feels like a good PC port.
Practice mode is one of the most important features in fighting games.
In Tekken7, this mode is well thought out. It offers a lot of different settings and makes it fun to learn new moves and combos.
There is also plenty of singleplayer content for a fighting game. You can choose from different modes like Story Mode, Arcade Mode and Treasure Mode (for unlocking new items that can be used to customize the looks of your characters).
All items that can be used for customizing the outfits of your characters must be earned through playing the game. There are no microtransactions. Also, these items don't provide any  gameplay advantage.
Controller support is also fine. All of my controllers worked without any problems.
The last Tekken game I've played was Tekken3 and this game made it easy for me to come back to the series. If you've ever played a Tekken game it should be easy for you to get into this game again.
But also for people who are new to fighting games or the Tekken series, Tekken7 is a great choice. It's one of these games that are easy to play, but hard to master.
As long as you like fighting games, I would totally recommend this game to you. Whether you prefer playing competitively in online ranked games, casually with some friends or even some singleplayer matches, this game offers it all.

So of course the mechanical core of this thing ended up being the best since Tekken 3 and I made myself look a♥♥♥♥♥for doubting it.
That said, the game modes are anemic, in terms of single player there are two (not counting story mode), the arcade mode is half the length it used to be with no cinematic endings and the trasure mode is a poor replacement of ghost battles. It is the only real single player option in the game but the stages only change every 5 or so matches and you can't even switch up the rules (you know, I really would enjoy 3-round figts with no time limit. Also, can we talk about adding the option to turn off custom outfits for NPC opponents?).
So the game gives you one of the best fighting game combat systems on the market and then doesn't really let you have any fun with it. It's kind of frustrating.
The systems, aesthetic and kinesthetics carry it well enough for me to recommend it but god damn it the game needs some updates.
Also the thing runs on my 3-year old i5+GTX770 rig on ultra and rock solid 60FPS. I'm not entirely sure how they pulled that one off.
This is now one of my favourite games, even though there are some bugs and problems with the game, for £11 in early access it's definitely worth it :)

As it is early acess you should be expecting bugs. So if you want a PERFECT game turn away now. It's bound to get better in the next 8-10 months though (at least i hope so).
So lets get into it -
Pros:
- Doesn't take up much space on your computer (small file)

A love letter to old pick-up-and-play fantasy games with a deep customization system and a co-op mode that will pull you back in for multiple sessions.
Right off the bat with its charming throwback aesthetic, Secrets of Arcadia promises to be a colorful romp through dark caves, mystical icy corridors, and old forgotten castles, harkening back to the games you played as a kid. SoA maneuvers this well-trod territory with style and never seems to overstay its welcome primarily thanks to the implementation of a (surprisingly versatile) ability system that allows players to purchase upgrades across class lines.  As healing items and gems (the game’s primary currency) are plentiful, especially in the later phases of the game, the core rhythm of the game quickly settles into clearing levels to gain gems and unlocking as many upgrades as possible in order to play with the many different character customization options.
As a solo experience the game is perfectly acceptable. You’ll find yourself upgrading your character, avoiding traps, and taking fewer hits as you learn to implement the game’s fluid dodge-and-strike rhythm. However, it must be said that the real fun to be had here is in venturing into the depths of Arcadia with a friend in co-op mode. This is where the ability to create and augment character builds on the fly really feels the most relevant and exciting.

Secrets of Arcadia is short and fun. Money well spent with high replay value, both solo and coop.

This is, without a doubt, the best Mortal Kombat game ever released.
Now, you could say that's not a high bar, as in the past, Mortal Kombat has always been more style than substance. I'm gonna run through the pros and cons at the bottom of the page, because now I'm going to address some of the more "controversial" aspects of the game.
Firstly, I see a lot of people putting day 1 DLC as a reason to downvote this game. Now I agree that Day 1 DLC is irritating, but honestly, it's not something that's going to go away any time soon. You've just gotta suck it up and deal with it.
Secondly, people are complaining about how easy fatalities are, and how you can use tokens for an "easy fatality". For the first aspect, I will agree that fatalities are easy. However I think that the difficult brutalities compensate for this extremely well. As for the quick fatalities; you don't have to use them. It doesn't help the player win. It literally just skips a few button presses for them at the end.
Lastly, DLC to unlock all of the items in the Krypt. This still doesn't affect you if you don't want to do it. Some people do not have time to unlock every thing in a game themselves. It still does not give them an advantage. Stop complaining about this everytime a game has this feature, chances are, the only people paying to unlock everything simply don't have the time to unlock everything themselves, and just want to play the game.
Pros:
- Genuinely seems to be fairly balanced.
- Good cast of classic characters (Kano, Sub-Zero, Scorpion, Johnny Cage etc.) while adding some of the best new character designs pretty much in MK history, or certainly since the dreaded PS2 era.
- Each character has three variants that change the special moves and some standard moves to varying degrees. Some are better than others, but it leaves room for experimentation.
- At the time of writing, a week or so after launch, it seems to have a healthy playerbase, I'm not struggling to find matches online
- BRUTALITIES ARE AN EXTREMELY SATISFYING ADDITION. Essentially, each character has a series of brutalities that require certain prerequisites to execute, resulting in a brutal death for your opponent. These range from the simple "final hit must be a throw, hold certain button etc) to fairly advanced (use a certain special move at the end of a 5 hit combo, for instance). The harder ones take a while to pull off, but goddamn, when you finally get it done in a multiplayer match, it is extremely satisfying.
- Plenty of unlockables, such as costumes, fatalities, brutalities, and concept art (ugh).
- I actually enjoyed and completed the Story mode, which is not something I could say I'd actually done before with a fighting game (well, okay, MK9 and Injustice basically).
- FINALLY A POPULAR FIGHTING GAME ON PC THAT ISN'T STREET FIGHTER. Now we just need Tekken and Guilty Gear Xrd Sign and I can die happy.
Cons:
- At the moment, there seems to be a fair few issues with the netcode causing lag. I can't comment much on this, as my internet at University restricts a lot of multiplayer games, so I get lag the majority of the time. Still, I imagine these are problems they will iron out in future updates
- Fatalities can get repetitive, especially the more drawn out ones. This is only really an issue with online play, or if you're finding the final boss difficult.
- If you play online, 8/10 fights will be against a Scorpion or Sub-Zero player. the remaining 2/10 fights will be against Takeda in the Lasher variant.
- They still have a block button. Why. Why.
Overall, I'll give this game a solid 8.5/10

- Test Your Might. Who mashes the buttons the fastest?
- Test Your Luck. Random character and random modifiers. Good for a laugh or two, but you can't do Fatalities in it *sadface*
- The Krypt. My most absolutely favourite part of the game. It's almost like a game within a game, where you explore the Dead Woods Cementery and get new skins, fatalities, brutalities and many other stuff. But watch out, monsters are lurking in the shadows. At least the QTE events in it aren't annoying but they scared the **** out of me.
Cons:
- While the game is good overall, the netcode still needs a lot of fixing. I succeded playing only one online match and almost all others ended with a "Game desynced" message or couldn't connect at all
- Some characters are OP (like Scorpion)
That's it. If you are a type of an offline-player (like me) you'll enjoy this game (although, unlocked & DLC characters are avaliable online). I'd give it a solid 9/10.

Spelunky is one of those games that can only really be recommended to players with a very specific mindset about the games they play. Before I get to the good and bad of Spelunky, ask yourself the following questions:
If you answered "yes" to one or more of those questions, Spelunky is probably not a game you would enjoy. It is frustrating, getting to its conclusion is a difficult feat, and death is the player's constant companion. It is a game that I love and hate in equal measure, simply by virtue of its design. It feels odd that my first review is a "not recommended", but this game had so much potential and i believe my expectations got the better of me.
I should preface by saying that I dont hate the game at all, but god it felt like it was testing me at some points.
I'm going to start with the biggest issue i had with this game right off the bat. The characters, namely the protagonist. I actually took a liking to Rufus at the beginning of the story, they had given him some poor, yet relatable qualities like being messy and carless, yet ambitious. That ended very quickly. It didnt take long for me to realise how utterly infuriating his whole charater was, in fact i didnt even leave the house before realising.
But not only is he completely irredeemable, he continues to have everything go right for him in a way that feels almost like some sort of fever dream. Everyone in the town dislikes him, if not hates him, and yet they just let it slide. I understand the angle that they were going for was a loveable prankster who dreams of a better life, but it really just comes across as an entitled deadbeat who has no empathy for anyone around him and is only interested in his own wellbeing. Maybe a bit harsh, but i was happy to let that slide for a while. besides, the best part of an story driven game is the growth of the characters in better or stronger people. NOPE. Rufus remains insufferable through many great potential points of growth, in fact he almost seems to acknowledge that he should have developed from some situations but then just brushes it off with some flatline quip. But enough about Rufus, i think i've painted a vivid picture of him. The rest of the cast in this game are actually pretty good, I enjoyed the fact that most people felt the same about Rufus as i did and they did feel reasonably immersive for the world that they lived in. It was a pity that most of them were only there for Rufus to pester occasionally with his rudeness.
Now, appart from the above mentioned, i really liked the world design and the voice acting, but it was not enough to make me stay for long. The puzzles and the minigames always felt extremely convoluted and i spent most of my time walking back and fourth trying everything on everything just to look up on a walkthrough that there was 6 more steps that wasn't even really necessary.
This review quickly turned into a rant, but it pains me to see such a great game be ruined by the simple pitfalls.
TL;DR
The protagonist will probably make you want to jump off a cliff. but if not, you might enjoy this game

I have 12.4 hours registered in the time of this review.
4 characters unlocked and 2 still locked and all available stages at the moment finished with the first girl.
And I'm having a blast.
In short It's a beat'em up, hard as ol beat'em ups used to be, with lots of personalization and some rpg strokes.
Choose your Soda Girl (tm), choose weapon skin, character skin, stage and fight!
From fighting you'll be getting caps, with caps you can buy and choose upgrades for your girl (+hp, +damage, faster attacks, faster movement, hp recovery, inmunity, more exp, more caps, ....... SO MANY COMBINATIONS). You'll also get sometimes gifts, gifts can contain huge amounts of caps, weapon or character skins, +hp or +soda upgrades.
Each girl has a max of 27 attacks, you'll choose 5 in the order you like to create your own combo.
you'll have 4 main buttons: Attack, Jump, Dodge and Drink Soda to heal.
You may think, then all I have to do is hit Attack all the time and that's it. But no. This game is hard. Each enemy is different in it's own way and attacks. You'll need to know their patterns and best way to hit them without dying in the process. And you'll die, a lot. There's a death counter in your save file so you can see how much of a noob you are. #goodtimes
As I said you can level up and upgrade yourself and there will be a moment you'll be a lil overpowered. BUT you also have a section to upgrade your freaking enemies ((NGH~ YES HARDER PLEASE)). They change aspect with each upgrade, thing I find really neat.
So, with all this said. Right now it's an Early Access Game. And I'll probably play more than 25hours as it is right now. The devs are working hard in the UI, combat, solving bugs and adding new characters and stages. (you also have challenges, really unique ones).
so, PROS:
- Art and character design superb, graffity/panty&Stocking style. 10/10
- Different levels, a sinking port, being chased by a tank-train, Elevator, moving raft, ...
- Customization everywhere. Main characters, weapon skins, upgrades, make enemies stronger one x one
- lots of unlocks that keep you motivated on going and going.
- Variety of enemies, each one with their own strategies
- Good number of playable characters each one with a unique fighting style. Maze, Mecha/robot dog, katana, laser, knives, fists,...
- The right ammount of difficulty, making you sometimes farm a little to get stronger and beat that boss.
"CONS" (most of them because, you know, right now IT'S EARLY ACCESS, you know what u're getting into, will update when it's finished):
- You'll find some bug here and there. They're getting fixed.
- Lacks a little explanation about things, you need to figure out by yourself what "X" thing does.
- It would be nice to have some story between the characters, when rescuing/unlocking them and such. Would give them more personality/lore. And psst, that sells.
- Using a controller, inputs get a little laggy in some stages. With keyboard they don't. But you can get thorugh it upgrading your attack speed. It needs fixing though.
So, if you are like me and loved the simpsons arcade, golden axe, streets of rage, turtles lost in time, captain commando and Gekido. And even more if you like cool designs, you're gonna love this game.
This one deserves more attention and I'm glad I'm supporting the devs into making a great finished game.

This week we take a look at Soda Girls,
Soda girls, a side scrolling beat em up that will only offer you nothing, but one combo that you’ll will do over….  and over again. A game that will also offer you platforming elements with the ability to upgrade the enemy’s and even unlock new ones. Soda girls brands itself as a quote on quote “different game” which is true, but for all the wrong reasons and this disappointed me. The game has so much more to offer, as it looking great and the idea of the different characters style is incredible. Unfortunately for Bomber Studio’s they did this all wrong.
Now then let’s take a look at Soda girls and experience a game where you play as a girl who lives in a can of soda then shall we?
Pros
- Challenging Bosses
- Fantasic Comic Design
- Upgradable Enemies
Cons
- Same 5 Hit Combo
- Short Levels
- No Customization
- Others You Nothing For Leveling Up
- Boring Gameplay
- Terrible Enemies
- You Move From Left To Right Pressing The Attack Button
In Conclusion
The game isn’t all that bad, for example I love the great comic art style of Soda Girls and the hard boss battles, unfortunately that’s it. I can see what soda girls are going after as it’s in early access after all. However, what I believe they’re trying to achieve is a side scrolling beat em up with fun and challenging enemies with harder bosses. A unique way to customize your soda girls with presents and challenge modes that would offer a challenge. However, the game doesn’t do it right… at all. Instead they offer you a beat em up where you just move from left to right pressing attack over and over and Unfortunately for soda Girls that's all they will offer you!
So like always should you buy this game?
Like always that's down to you! Do you want a challenging boss battle? Do you want to be a soda girl? Do you want to do the same 5 hit combo over and over? Do you want to do multiple short levels? Do you want to play a game with a great comic art style?
Well if so then soda girls is for you!

I will echo many other reviews and start by saying: If you liked Diablo 2, you should really enjoy Torchlight 2.
In fact, at times I felt this game was almost too derivative. Both games have 4 Acts. Each Act has its own hub town, bosses, unique geographic setting and a narrated cinematic at each Act's beginning. Even the storyline has a lot of similarities.
With all that said, Torchlight 2 clearly wasn't designed to be novel. Instead they set out to do the dungeon crawler genre really, really well. And they succeeded.
The gameplay is fast paced, addictive, loot filled fun. Everything about this game is user friendly. It's easy to get to and from town; your pet can easily be sent to sell off your unwanted spoils while you keep adventuring; even playing on the Veteran difficulty I almost never had to buy potions or magic scrolls; quests are clearly marked on the map, never leaving you wondering what to do next; when you die you have the option to respawn in town for free or lose gold but respawn near where you died.
My main criticism is likely to be experienced differently by each person who plays Torchlight 2. I started to get bored with the game about 3/4ths through the story mode. This is common for me with games of this type. I should note that I played to the end of the game fully in single player. Your mileage may vary particularly if you plan to play online with friends.
I'll close by saying if you did NOT like Diablo 2, or other highly rated dungeon crawlers, do not be swayed by all the positive reviews this game has gotten. Trust your gut; I suspect that the type of person that will enjoy this game already knows that they will enjoy it.

As an RPG game, it's not so great, and only stands as a simplistic Fallout parody.
As a FPS rogue-like, combat-focused, score-oriented game, it's among the best I've played.
It seems that most people come looking for the former, and get frustrated that every level has what amounts to a time limit - a machine-gun wielding Brotherhood of Steel wannabe dude, slowly walking from the beginning of the level towards the player. But it's a time limit that can easily be dealt with: you can kill him (albeit hard), hide or run.
People also get frustrated about the limited inventory, it's not your endless fallout backpack that you throw everything in and hoard stuff until you sell them to a vendor.
I think these limits make you think strategically and focus more on survival and combat, which I found very fun.
On the other hand, comparing it to other games of the genre, like Ziggurat, it's actually very forgiving. There is "perma-death" of your character - when you die you lose everything on your backpack, you get to play with a different character, and inherit every item left in your house. You get many opportunities to send items/money home from the "dungeon", and you get to buy back important items you lose after death, so there's always a sense of progress and you rarely feel like "wasting time".
The game has some great and original mechanisms of randomization, it keeps the game fresh and exciting.
Also, the music is amazing if you're into 80's music. The writing is very funny with the witty NPC dialogues and a lot of 80's references.
Overall I think it's a great pick if you are into the genre.

wasted is a very specific homage to the dungeon diving of fallout 3, complete with replicating very specific feel of navigating a bethesda game in first person (rummaging through containers, scooping objects off the game world, stripping bodies bare). being a roguelike-like, every death is a farewell to your latest randomly generated wastelander, but there is enough persistency to take the sting off losing your current inventory. extra gear can be stashed at a communal hideout, and certain npc's will let you recover particularly valuable items, for a fee.
the actual dungeon-diving throws you into coolers (read: vaults) randomly assembled from pre-fab room parts, filled with various enemies that may require different tactics. there is a timed element: linger too long and an extremely tough but slow enemy appears from the entrance and sloooowly starts making his way through the level. this is a bit of a point of contention for many people, but i feel that this serves the same function as the ghost in spelunky: a bit of background pressure to encourage you to keep moving, to scavenge as much as you can from the environment but, perhaps, forcing you to adjust a strip-mining mentality to a smarter, more efficient one.
i don't really see the comparisons to borderlands: just as in fallout 3, loot properties are static, not randomized. enemies carry a semi-random assortment of gear and weapons, but any given uzi has the exact same properties as any other. this predictability works fine when you're low on resources and not feeling particularly risk-averse.
i'm honestly most amazed at how well wasted replicates the really specific feel of a bethesda game in the moment-to-moment gameplay. it's just very lovingly done that longtime players will probably appreciate.
if you want to just dive into some modern fallout dungeons without all that pesky rpg getting in the way, wasted is pretty fun for that!

For a lot of people, exploring vaults in the recent Fallout games was the best part. They had interesting stories and secrets, as well as plenty of lockers and wastebins to rummage through. Well, some genius took that specific gameplay element and made an entire game out of it, looting and mutants and groin shots at all. Not only that, but they added some clever ideas and hilarious writing of their own to make something way more fun than just hunting for bobbleheads.
So the bombs fell and the world looks like an English gravel quarry now, and the best and brightest that survived ended up being a bunch of booze-swilling idiots. That's literally all they do now, they go spelunking in the old vau-I mean, coolers in search of irradiated brews to get good and ♥♥♥♥ed up on. There are a bunch of factions duking it out over who gets to drink what, from the feisty Cervezmen to the hard♥♥♥♥♥♥♥S.O.B. soldiers. And you're no better than any of them, descending into the underhalls to gather janky guns, stretch pants, fanny packs, and all the swill you can swill.
In gameplay terms, it's a first-person sci-fi dungeon crawler. Each cooler is a labyrinth of nearly a dozen randomly-generated floors to shuffle through, full of strange enemies and stranger loot. Most of your time will be spent scouring lockers and containers and fighting against your limited inventory space. The rest of that time goes to finding your way through the maze-like levels and killing any weirdos you meet. Managing your resources like different ammo types, healing items, and unlocking tools will be key to surviving the deep dives into each cooler.
If this sounds like Fallout boiled down to just exploring vaults, you're right on the money. However, there are a few key features that add a level of urgency to your jaunts. For one, it's a one-way trip. You can't return to previous floors, and the only way out if you don't think you can go the distance is to find a bottle of radioactive booze and chug that ♥♥♥♥♥ 'till you black out. This returns you to your home base where you can stash gear, and depending on the booze you can get a permanent buff or debuff for future runs. You'll definitely need to consider this if enemies get too tough or you keep getting caught by the S.O.B., an absurdly deadly hunter that starts stalking you if you tarry too long on a level. Your time limit is pretty strict too, so you'll have to be quick about your looting.
There's a wealth of junk to find in the halls of WASTED, and very little of it useless. There are weapons divided into melee, pistol, rifle, revolver, and other types, each with their own damage and armor penetration and other attributes which will be important when battling the varied raiders and mutants and robots in your way. You'll find head, chest, and leg armor that boosts your character stats, along with fanny packs and other terribly 80s storage solutions to expand your paltry inventory. Then there are food and medicines, throwable objects, crafting materials, and so on. With limited space you'll need to consider your options carefully, both in what you need to survive and what you should escape with to stash at home or sell in town. A handy mailbox system also helps you get useful junk out without having to bail or lug it around forever.
I was enjoying the game just fine while looting and killing, but reaching town elevated it to a whole new level. The kooky 80s wasteland vibe comes alive in the characters, who have some of the funniest dialog I've ever seen in a game. They're brash, they're rude, they're foul, and they're absolutely endearing about it. There's a Richard Nixon knockoff, a terrifying weeaboo, a valley girl shopkeep, and a mail clerk that's all too happy to philosophise on fart metaphors. Even the incidental characters have laugh-out-loud moments, and the item names and descriptions fit right in with the insane atmosphere of the retro apocalypse.
With plenty to see, plenty to loot, and plenty to kill, WASTED is extremely gratifying to progress through and build a deadly wasteland adventurer with. And then they'll eat a spectacular crit or a devious trap, and they'll be gone forever. Poof, all your buffs and weapons and gear, gone. That's because WASTED is actually a roguelike, and a pretty wicked one at that. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but you need to be prepared to lose hours of loot and character building at the drop of an ugly hat. Thankfully it's designed pretty intelligently for this, with scads of loot to replace lost goods, the home base and mailbox systems for saving stuff, and shortcuts you can pay for in town to get back up to speed. It means you need to be careful and you need to pay attention, and you always need to prepare for the absolute worst.
I had kind of an odd experience with WASTED, because I beat the first cooler on my first try. I don't think that's supposed to happen, you're probably supposed to ♥♥♥♥ up a few times, then learn to booze out for buffs as you assemble a solid set of gear, then get to the bottom a few hours in. It gave me a skewed view of the game that made dying halfway through the second cooler sting a lot more than perhaps it should have. But I put in the time to work out the cadence of the game, and now I can do quick runs in cooler 1 to gear up a fresh waster for cooler 2, and attempt it as many times as I want. It's still hard as hell, and I die a lot, and sometimes it feels like forgetting to save in Fallout and having to re-do 30 minutes of exploring, but once you warm up to the random levels and crazy combat it provides hours of entertainment. Coupled with the excellent aesthetics and hilarious writing and characters, I would encourage anyone to give this wild adventure a serious try.

Played it for about a hour and got it refunded. Just couldn't get myself to like the experience. Why?

Surprisingly not because of the S.O.B. (a kind of time limit per level, where a super OP "hunter" appears after a short while and starts chasing the player down). Most people really dislike that feature, but I actually get it - the game would be too easy without something motivating the player to move fast. A bit annoying, but manageable.

What put me off, was all the stuff that probably caused the devs to add the S.O.B. to the game in the first place - absolute lack of gameplay that would feel fun by itself. Forgetting the timer constantly running out for a moment, the whole rest of the game seems to be shooting totally inaccurate "spray-and-pray" guns at absolutely brain-dead enemies at absurdly short ranges. Rooms are super small (and visibly repetitive, despite the supposed random generation, which really changes the layout of the levels a little but very little else) and the enemies just rush you, killing one another in the process most of the time or stepping into traps that almost never seem to be aimed at the player for some reason.
While that state of affairs is explained in the intro by a joke that all the people left are total morons, it seems more like a cop-out by the devs, trying to explain away poor AI and lack of real gun-play, which is kind of a bummer in a run-and-gun game.

There is no interesting story or background and on top of that, the loot (the game's progression is done via looted equipment and random one-time bonuses gained by drinking a radioactive booze, which ends current level run) felt boring and the interface was very clunky making the overall gameplay simply not very fun.

While the premise - loot as much as you can, weighting the risk-reward balance to decide if its time to drink and get back to the base or loot a short while longer, the unfun mechanics and general lack of polish fell short of making that an enjoyable experience for me.

The biggest defining feature in Torchlight 2 is the pet system.  It can carry stuff, buy stuff, sell stuff, and transform to better attack enemies.  There are 4 different classes with tons of playing styles between them, though they are not as varied as one might think with just four classes.  Its other great features are also its flaws.  You can choose any difficulty from the get go, but the game remains at that difficulty when you start new game +.  Another issue with new game + characters is that for multiplayer, it has to be the same number of completions,   That is, players who have completed the game 3 times (new game +++) cannot play with players who never finished the game.  Freezing and therefore crashing does happen during loading screens.  There's a great modded community and there's tons of great mods, but if you want to play in multiplayer with mods, everyone has to have the same mods and in the same order.  Thankfully, the modded game is separate from the vanilla version.  A PVP option is also available.  Players who declare themselves hostile are game for PVP.

This game is one of those rare gems you find in the modern sea of "meh" games. A true diamond in the rough, it starts with a simplistic appearance, but quickly pulls you in with surprisingly complex (but easy to learn) mechanics, a subtle but neat background lore, and a sense of real time effect. There are measurable relations between yourself and characters in the game.
The gameplay and fighting are fairly simple, but allow you to choose an approach to combat. Want to charge headlong into the enemy without a plan? Go ahead. Want to station archers atop a hill to rain death on those who dare to advance? Feel free. What to hold the enemy in place with Infantry and flank them with Cavalry? Do it. Each faction in the game plays differently due to having different focuses. The same strategy doesn't always work for every enemy.
Politics add a new layer of depth to this game. Most RPGs are open-world, but contain a linear story. For instance, you can complete quests in Skyrim and end up choosing one of maybe four endings, but you have no real impact past that. You can't truly take control of your own path, it's all pre-determined by a linear narrative. In Mount and Blade, you can do as you damn well please, instead of staying on rails the whole time. If you want to sieze a city and hold out against the inevitable counter-attack, you can. You establish relations with other characters through your actions. Each choice you make holds actual depth to it, and different lords have different responses based on personality. This system makes other games feel shallow. It's cute and all that you can execute this guy or that guy, but you'll never be able to conquer Tamriel, because that would hurt the narrative. For the record, I'm not trying to bash Skyrim, it's a good game, it's just a good example of a semi-linear game.
Choice is a big part of this game. You decide when you're ready to take an action, not the game. You can stay on the safe road, building up a fortune, renown, and a right to rule, or you can hire a small army, and begin a campaign of death and destruction across whatever lands you desire. Your playstyle is actually factored in, and every action elicits a reaction. This is not a casual game, this is a campaign where your end goal is set by you and you alone.
Mods make this game. The best overall are in the workshop. Due to this game being coded in C++, it's extremely mod friendly.
Calradia is a wonderplace, with a mix of jovial fun and dark undertones. Will you pledge service to a Monarch and aid their conquest, or will you decide to take Calradia for yourself? Do you wish to make it as a famous adventurer, or will you become the most infamous raider ever known? Will you act as a benevolent warrior, or a bloodlusting conquerer? Your experience is your choice, down to the last detail. Calradia will continue to change without your presence, as she waits for no one. Whether or not the reins of fate are pulled by your hands is determined by you.

This 'review' is only to tell people to TURN OFF MSAA and either put Volumetric Lighting on On or Off. Do not set it to Ultra. Contact Hardening Shadows should also be set to On instead of Ultra as well. These settings are HUGE performance killers with very little noticeable differences ( Mainly Volumetric Lighting and CHS )
Volumetric Lighting and Contact Hardening Shadows are hard to notice on Ultra unless you compare two screenshots side by side and look for the differences. Save yourself the trouble and leave them to On or Off depending on how much of an fps boost you want.
Do the above and watch your FPS jump. I'm currently getting 50 fps average ( using the provided benchmark ) with a 980ti @ 1440p on Ultra with MSAA Off and Volumetric Lighting + Contact Hardening Shadows set to On.

Been a long time fan of the Tekken series since T2 back on the Ps1. I'd say I've owned most Tekken games apart from 4 and the Gameboy & DS version. Tekken has evolved just like most fighting games like DOA and SF however Tekken has been my main fighting game in my life.
How the characters have come to life and evolved and some taking on a comical niche, some more serious and some less serious but it balances out well.
I would always say the old Tekken system is better as it is more balanced and more simple. Now its more Korean/Japanese hyper skilled air juggles. Not saying its a bad thing but sometimes people just want it balanced and not whoever gets launched up in the air loses basically.
Now onto Tekken 7
T7 has been around for a couple of years now and has been getting tweaked and tuned as it launched on the arcades, most like every other Tekken machine I can imagine. IMO I would say it took a long time for the console/PC release to say the assets and game is already available but I can imagine this was Namco trying to get as much money as they could on the arcade machines which is understandable.
I was skeptical about T7 as IMO T6 wasnt all that great and TTT2 was more of a spin-off spoof (what-if) title. Was incredibly surprised that Namco decided to crank out a PC port. Tekken has NEVER been on PC apart from maybe a modified T3 version and SFxT. But like most Japanese devs they see a growing market in the PC Gaming world, like all they realise not all of us go for consoles like we used to (or never have)
Tekken 7 Pros/Cons:
+Solid PC port, 4K ready, possible mods, works on extreme settings with an old i7 and 980Ti. Rarely stutters
+Re-designed characters looking flashier, sexier and sleeker with more flare and pollish
+Big rooster (though some popular characters absent)
+Nice graphical settings to work with many weak/strong systems
+Gallery showing previous Tekken footage, clips & artwork
+Addictive (just one more match, just one more match)
+RAGE System
+Some movelists, added, tweaked and changed
+Fluid and detailed animation
+Customization
-OST is too hard dubstep and doesn't fit with the Tekken series (some tracks are okay)
-Air juggling is very hit and miss and requires a lot of time per character
-Akuma. I understand Capcom and Namco are respectable long time rivals but the SF character just doesn't sit well in a Tekken game
-Short arcade and quite a breeze even on the highest difficulty. Doesn't seem has hard as previous Tekken titles
-No graphical filters like vibrant, bloom, Winter etc
-No interactive photo-mode. I was expecting a photo-mode with moveable camera, frames and filters. This should be added
-Story mode. Namco's first time at story driven plot with cutscenes and backstory. Overall very short, explains Kazuya's past and how Heihachi & Kazumi met. Jin completely sidelined from the plot, story fight scenes quite scripted, Akuma's goal quite linear and just vanishes without a trace, questions still not answerred on how Kazumi is a demon (deity?)
-Side-Stories. Side stories is a texted opening scene of the said character, ONE battle and a quick ending scene. Very short and unrewarding. It should be a standard arcade style with an opening scene similar to T5/6, a short scene in the middle and an ending scene per character
May change as I play more but so far this is possibly the Tekken we've been wanting since T3

Playing this briefly to as much extent as I could, The game does have promise and positives, and yes, as we're all saying, early access means theres still a lot of work to be done. For an early review however, there are a number of pros and cons.
The game styles as a hack+slash fan-fest for all Rwby fans. Be your favourite character, grab some people with their own favourite characters, go from there and co-op like crazy. Yes this is a great idea, yes there is a lot of possible ideas, and yes, I do hope they put more characters in. Paths are linear, monsters appear, kill to progress, carry on. The scenery isnt barren, but it's not exactly rich in awe-amazing backgrounds to reflect on while running to the next objective. Attack styles are unique to each character, with a basic levelling system, and a host of grimm to fight that play some sort of tribute to the one's shown already in the show.
The pros I can find really are just the potential. It has a basic structure, it has a frame which it can build on. That's it at the current.
For the cons, ohohoh....
The game has a tendancy to crash, On three occassions have I tried to make it to the third act, all of which the game died on me. Until some sort of an update, I just cannot committ to playing it
The levelling system in the game is seemingly not saved. Your progress, your hard work, all you need to do is stop, and you start from the beginning.
There is no Single player, nor is there a pause button. Yes, you can cheat and make a private lobby, but oddly no, you cant leave the game running. Any sort of mid-break you take from the game will "kick you from the lobby due to inactivity". A kick voting system would be more appropriate.
Yes, running downhill will freeze the running animation and make it wierd.
The grimm attacking invincibility frame rates are jsut annoying
The boar grimm roll too frequently. Its the only time when actually making distance on the enemy is a good thing. You valiantly charge in to fight it, its gonna roll, and unless you're near it where it stops, its gonna roll again, and again.
The smoothness of running the game is still patchy. For a decentish computer, its gonna seem like it's struggling to handle it at first.
Im sure there's a lot of other points, but those are jsut what I found. If you have faith in the game to improve, you will buy it. If not, then I would not blame you for waiting until later. Early access yes, but not the finest of fandoms to reach our hands.

Portal Knights is a simple game with Zelda-like combat and Minecraft-like worlds. It's more platformer than builder but relies on a heavy resource gathering mechanic for game progression. Levels start off pretty and exciting but soon become samey and the dungeons are basically just templates used over and over again. It's not a bad game at all but it lacks any real diversity in it's gameplay to keep my interest past the 16 hours I've played, barely making to the second boss before I gave up on the resource grind, which gives you scaling armour and weapons but at the expense of having to grind materials for far too long to make them worth while. I'm giving it a positive review because multiplayer is really fun and would carry this game much much further in terms of hours played and if you like building, there is plenty here to allow you to experiment for many more hours. In terms of value for money, it has plenty to offer, but I just find it too samey to continue for myself.

This is my top game of all time.  It should be treated less like a game, and more like a movie that you get to take part in.  The best way to play it, in my opinion, is to find a time where you can sit down for 4-5 hours and play it from start to finish in one shot.  The controls to the game are unique.  They make sense, but don't expect yourself to control your characters flawlessly.  Your left thumb stick controls one character, your right controls the other.  Actions are executed either by using the corresponding triggers or by rotating thumb sticks.  I found myself getting the characters switched and running them in the wrong directions at times, but this isn't damaging to the gameplay.  The strongest point to this game is the story line and the way the controls make you feel like each character is important.  By the end of it, I teared up.  In my mind this game is a 10/10 must have.  It goes on sale quite often, so you can usually buy it at a time when it costs less than a dollar per hour to play.

Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! You wont be dissapointed.

Not as good as the stick of truth, but still a lot of fun along the way.
The game plays with a somewhat unique grid-based RPG. you control a small party of your chosing (usually) that all have their own unique identity and powers, and they are quite inventive and really nicely put together - such as Stan's alter ego toolshed and his various power tools, the coons sharp claws making enemies bleed, and so on. The requirement of careful positioning and such keep it interesting and fresh, and i never got tired or bored with the system.
Your own character is basically any class you damn near please, and you can switch whenever you want to try other ones out after a certain point in the game. You can focus on one or two stats or go nuts and pick whatever the hell you want, its up to you which i really like.
The overworld exploration is fine, set up to give you glimpses at things to come in the future as you slowly unlock more powers and teammates. It has a few puzzles here and there involving your "powers" and overall the game is well executed. It's only real weak point was the side quests seemed incredibly pointless, with next to no rewards for doing them, and the "selfie" system is just annoying and i found it forced and unneccessary.
but overall, the humor in it is well executed, and the game itself is a lot of fun and easy to recommend!

Aah, Spelunky. A classic among classics. This remake of the 2008 student project Spelunky by Derek Yu (which you can download for free by the way) adds a ton of content and game modes.
So what is Spelunky? It is a 2D randomly generated rogue-like, with permadeath. You start your descent into dusty old mines, slowly filling your journal with knowledge about all the creatures and traps you encounter. After a while, you find yourself becoming better at jumping, fighting, using the various items, avoiding traps etc. This game offers not only a lot more depth than you'd initially expect, but also a completely different playing experience every time. And while the learning curve is not very high, there is a lot to learn over time. And you will have to accept a lot of spectacular deaths in the run-up to it.
Personally, i would say Spelunky is THE defining 2D Platforming Roguelike. The simplicity of its objective (climb down to the exist door without getting killed) is what makes it so brilliant, because you have a multitude of ways to traverse the randomly generated levels. If you have the bombs to spend, why not blast your own path to avoid enemies and uncover burrowed gems?
On top of that, this game probably set the standard when it comes to interactions with Shopkeepers in modern Roguelikes. You can buy their wares, or attempt to murder them, but they'll be guarding your exit doors to get revenge for the rest of your run. Which might also happen if a random trap causes an explosion in their shop. You're at fault anyways, so you have to play with the cards you're dealt.
However, 99.9% of all Spelunky runs CAN be won, maybe not in spectacular fashion, but it's always possible. No bossfights with indefinite HP that you cant beat because you're choked for resources in this game. It's all about your skill and will to study the enemies and counter their attacks. Only once have i ever seen a glitched map spawn causing two pushing rocks that would individually be moveable to trap a player who had no bombs left at the beginning of the stage. And believe me, i have watched and played a LOT of runs of this game.
The Artstyle certainly helps the game along nicely too. No objstructing particles, clear enemy and trap shapes, very distinct colors, you will never die because you looked at a threat and were unable to identify it as such.
To add even more Value to the game overall (a concept that seems to have gotten lost on newer games) there are multiplayer co-op modes for up to 4 players simultaneously which can lead to complete chaos (SADLY only local multiplayer) in cooperating spelunking as well as PvP Deathmatches, which can become REALLY fun, chaotic and explosive within seconds of taking off. The PvP in particular seems to have inspired a series of new games, you could describe it as a predecessor to Duck Game and it's incredibly fun to do. To top it off, it also was the first roguelike game to add daily challenge runs which can only be attempted once and are identical for all players, allowing you to REALLY compete for the better score with everyone in your steam friends list.
With a lot of secrets to discover and multiple whole new layers of unlocking hidden places to explore and score attack techniques to maximize your looted cash, Spelunky has so much value it's hard not to recommend it to anyone who likes 2D Platforming. And while a Controller allows for finer motion control, i was perfectly able of beating it with a Keyboard before i even owned a Controller.
The only things holding the game back are the lack of online multiplayer and the sometimes slightly jumpy difficulty (getting an amazing item in an early random crate might make your run a LOT easier than the average run). Either way it's still a solid 9/10 and in my opinion a must buy for anyone who likes roguelike games.
One last advice, this game is insanely discounted in almost every steam sale, sooo if you're not buying it now, add it to your wishlist and grab it when it's on sale ;) And it's also a good contender for a bunch of the steam awards

Playing this briefly to as much extent as I could, The game does have promise and positives, and yes, as we're all saying, early access means theres still a lot of work to be done. For an early review however, there are a number of pros and cons.
The game styles as a hack+slash fan-fest for all Rwby fans. Be your favourite character, grab some people with their own favourite characters, go from there and co-op like crazy. Yes this is a great idea, yes there is a lot of possible ideas, and yes, I do hope they put more characters in. Paths are linear, monsters appear, kill to progress, carry on. The scenery isnt barren, but it's not exactly rich in awe-amazing backgrounds to reflect on while running to the next objective. Attack styles are unique to each character, with a basic levelling system, and a host of grimm to fight that play some sort of tribute to the one's shown already in the show.
The pros I can find really are just the potential. It has a basic structure, it has a frame which it can build on. That's it at the current.
For the cons, ohohoh....
The game has a tendancy to crash, On three occassions have I tried to make it to the third act, all of which the game died on me. Until some sort of an update, I just cannot committ to playing it
The levelling system in the game is seemingly not saved. Your progress, your hard work, all you need to do is stop, and you start from the beginning.
There is no Single player, nor is there a pause button. Yes, you can cheat and make a private lobby, but oddly no, you cant leave the game running. Any sort of mid-break you take from the game will "kick you from the lobby due to inactivity". A kick voting system would be more appropriate.
Yes, running downhill will freeze the running animation and make it wierd.
The grimm attacking invincibility frame rates are jsut annoying
The boar grimm roll too frequently. Its the only time when actually making distance on the enemy is a good thing. You valiantly charge in to fight it, its gonna roll, and unless you're near it where it stops, its gonna roll again, and again.
The smoothness of running the game is still patchy. For a decentish computer, its gonna seem like it's struggling to handle it at first.
Im sure there's a lot of other points, but those are jsut what I found. If you have faith in the game to improve, you will buy it. If not, then I would not blame you for waiting until later. Early access yes, but not the finest of fandoms to reach our hands.

It even made me reconsider the whole big-evil-coming-to-get-you-if-you're-too-slow mechanic, i.e. the SOB Purifier. The game is more fun if you play it fast and loose. If you REALLY want to do something while being chased he can be avoided by running around circular rooms or by distracting him with a brick and sneaking the other way.

Been a long time fan of the Tekken series since T2 back on the Ps1. I'd say I've owned most Tekken games apart from 4 and the Gameboy & DS version. Tekken has evolved just like most fighting games like DOA and SF however Tekken has been my main fighting game in my life.
How the characters have come to life and evolved and some taking on a comical niche, some more serious and some less serious but it balances out well.
I would always say the old Tekken system is better as it is more balanced and more simple. Now its more Korean/Japanese hyper skilled air juggles. Not saying its a bad thing but sometimes people just want it balanced and not whoever gets launched up in the air loses basically.
Now onto Tekken 7
T7 has been around for a couple of years now and has been getting tweaked and tuned as it launched on the arcades, most like every other Tekken machine I can imagine. IMO I would say it took a long time for the console/PC release to say the assets and game is already available but I can imagine this was Namco trying to get as much money as they could on the arcade machines which is understandable.
I was skeptical about T7 as IMO T6 wasnt all that great and TTT2 was more of a spin-off spoof (what-if) title. Was incredibly surprised that Namco decided to crank out a PC port. Tekken has NEVER been on PC apart from maybe a modified T3 version and SFxT. But like most Japanese devs they see a growing market in the PC Gaming world, like all they realise not all of us go for consoles like we used to (or never have)
Tekken 7 Pros/Cons:
+Solid PC port, 4K ready, possible mods, works on extreme settings with an old i7 and 980Ti. Rarely stutters
+Re-designed characters looking flashier, sexier and sleeker with more flare and pollish
+Big rooster (though some popular characters absent)
+Nice graphical settings to work with many weak/strong systems
+Gallery showing previous Tekken footage, clips & artwork
+Addictive (just one more match, just one more match)
+RAGE System
+Some movelists, added, tweaked and changed
+Fluid and detailed animation
+Customization
-OST is too hard dubstep and doesn't fit with the Tekken series (some tracks are okay)
-Air juggling is very hit and miss and requires a lot of time per character
-Akuma. I understand Capcom and Namco are respectable long time rivals but the SF character just doesn't sit well in a Tekken game
-Short arcade and quite a breeze even on the highest difficulty. Doesn't seem has hard as previous Tekken titles
-No graphical filters like vibrant, bloom, Winter etc
-No interactive photo-mode. I was expecting a photo-mode with moveable camera, frames and filters. This should be added

While I know this game flies under the flag of Adult Swim Games, its nothing like you would expect. A wonderful piece of first person "roguelite", WASTED is if Fallout didn't have any "reliable" people survive nuclear fallout, and now everyone is just dumb bar crawlers who are trying to get as drunk as possible. Each cooler is a maze-like murder fest of raiders, mutated animals and creatures, robots, and the ever popular Syndicate of Buzzkills, or the SOB. Take too long on a floor murdering your way through and stealing fanny packs, ammo, junkfood, and whatever fits in your tiny pockets and youll get a nasty minigun toting SOB Badass to murder you in a few seconds flat. However, find your way through enough floors and you will find one of the fantastic boozes, radiated and ready to give you a mutation hangover. Maybe it'll be good, like health back when you kill people, maybe it'll be bad and you'll take more knockback from attacks but move way faster. Which will you chug? Will you get wasted? Or get wasted trying?

Fallout + Borderlands + roguelite FPS
WASTED puts you in the shoes of a string of disposable characters that share a permanent loot stash. Try your best run and make sure to leave good stuff for the next character to use, because you'll be dying a lot.
At first sight it may remind you of Borderlands, but the similarity is visual only. WASTED is a roguelite, though it does not have the wealth of loot and items that Borderlands or roguelikes usually do. Instead, you will be encountering the same pool of weapons and armour and consumables on every run. This is a game where you won't spend any longer than 2 seconds comparing similar items to choose which to keep.
This is a conscious choice because for better or worse, WASTED is meant to be a lot more fast paced that your average dungeon crawler (or is it?). On every level of the bunker, if you stay for too long, an overpowered NPC starts hunting you, spurring you to rush the rest of the floor and find the way down or out. It's not too unforgiving - as long as you keep moving at a steady pace, this "purifier" won't catch up to you. Unless the level's random layout throws a couple dead ends and you need to backtrack. Personally I can't stand this forced time limit. Especially since the game keeps encouraging you to deploy traps and use stealth, both of which require time to do right. It's like it can't decide if it wants to be fast paced or not. If we were able to hide from him or trap him, it would make sense - but the purifier just moves inexorably towards you.
Aside from the dungeon-bunker itself and your ramshackle house where your stash is, there is an outpost where you can pick up a few quests. This aspect of the game surprised me. There are several quest givers with fully voiced conversations.
WASTED doesn't take itself too seriously. It's got a fun, violent, foul-mouthed edge to it.

Really fun! Great aesthetic! Holy crap the forced pacing and cheap shot deaths via the Purifier suck!
The hunter mechanic is a festering boil on an otherwise excellent game. Seriously, I know the developer feels confident in leaving it there but if anything makes me set this thing down for good it'll be that. 90% of the time you can just deal with it by throwing down a mine at the start of a level and maybe pillar dancing it if you get cornered. The other 10% it's a BS death you could do nothing about and is concentrated, weapons grade anti-fun.
With the bad out of the way, lets get to the good. The aesthetic is great, feels like a cartoonier Borderlands in all the right ways. The UI while a little primitive feeling is overall smooth and doesn't generally get in your way. The combat is fast, fun, and in spite of the limited AI will keep you on your toes. Weapon balance and ammo scarcity feel really good, I'm consistently forced to use weapons that aren't my first choice, but am also rarely disappointed by them. It adds a lot of variety that you wouldn't be organically pushed towards in other games. The lore isn't exposed to a great degree, but what's there is funny and thoughtful and I wanna know more.
Bottom line, I'd recommend picking this thing up if you're decent at FPS games and like dungeon crawlers and/or run and guns. It's got excellent bones, and I really hope mod support ends up being finished so this excellent foundation can be elaborated upon and expanded.

The short: It's fun to pick up and play for an hour or two, then put it down again, though it lacks any kind of depth at all. It parodies many elements from the Fallout series and has great dumb humour. Play it like you were going to play an arcade FPS like Doom and not expecting it to be much like a roguelike at all beyond perma-death, procedurally generated levels and permanent bonuses/maluses. The weapon selection and equipment in general is kind of lackluster, with a handful actually looking like the developer really tried to make them function differently from the others in interesting ways. Buy this on sale if you're tight on cash. If you have the disposable income though, feel free to give it a shot, it's a decent time waster but nothing spectacular.
The long: The game is fun in general, but the developer did not do nearly enough with it and at times feels outright lazy. You will see the majority of types of rooms that can potentially show up in your game within the first half hour or so of play, the other dungeons of the game having one or two unique rooms (as far as I can tell). If I had to estimate, I'd say there are roughly 30-40 rooms altogether in this game (this includes connecting hallways, but not boss floors or administrator rooms, which are large, single room floors). After the first couple of floors in the second dungeon of the game, I started to become incredibly disappointed that yes, all of them were going to have the same type of rooms generate in them, with one or two types of rooms unique to each dungeon.
The weapons are pretty lazily done as well, with there being very little difference beyond a few numbers differences. There's usually one in each category of gun weapon that is automatic and then one or two odd ducks that are pretty fun to use, but at the same time are too few. Like the majority of pistols do the same thing except better/worse, with one that fires in a 3 round burst and two fully automatic ones. The melee weapons are worse, since they all attack roughly the same way, just with different swing speeds, though with how knockback works in this game, melee is more of a last resort than an actual choice of weapon (knockback prevents you from taking any action except going into the menu to use an item).
The inventory system in this is absolutely horrendous, you can hold very little to begin with and your equipped armour + weapons take up slots as well. With this, you're pretty much restricted to carrying two weapons of different types + their respective ammunition and one or two slots for healing items. There are multiple items that give short term buffs that you can carry, but at the same time their duration lasts for a very short time and their uses are situational at best, so there usually is no point in saving a slot for them and saving them instead for the assorted gear you'll find and want to stockpile. Oh, also you can only hold 5 of each healing item/short term buff item, so if there was room for them and they weren't such mild effects (barring two) you would still be very limited in how often you could use them. The other problem with the inventory system is the fact you can only carry 100 of each ammo type (which also takes up a slot of your inventory), which forces you to scavenge and use weapons off of enemies, dumping them as they run out. Why not unload them for their ammo? You can't! The developer actually gave a decent reason for this, it being that it'd allow you to get around the ammo limit with high capacity weapons, but at the same time it's such a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥system to manually switch between these weapons (since there's not point in hotkeying them if you're going to drop them 10 or so shots later) that I'm surprised the developer didn't add in unloading weapons anyways or some alternative.
Oh, also the only way to increase the amount of items you can carry (until mid-late game when it's practically won) are with 3 differently named fanny packs which effectively increase it by 2 each (it's 3 each, but since they take up a slot each..). Without them, you're even more restricted in what you can carry with you into dungeons, which can make things very frustrating when rolling a new character after dying.
Finally, what really disappointed me the most was that the hub town and first dungeon were actually really good introductions to what the game had to offer. It made me think that things would continue being this rad throughout it, with its silly toilet/stupid humour, with quests here and there to pick up that poked fun at assorted aspects of Fallout and the community and a fun boss battle at the end of the first dungeon, which paid tribute to another great game series.
After that though, the game goes downhill something fierce, or not so much downhill, but rather goes nowhere. It's like the developer ran out of money and pretty much had to can a ♥♥♥♥♥on of planned assets and quests that would have fleshed the game out more and made it more interesting. After what was a decent amount of humorous voice work and quests, there's very little of either. What was a good boss fight that got the game going on a good note is soured by the second one just circle strafing to win and two others that simply don't happen if you pick the right convo choices (always the ones that rely on your stats) that give you uninteresting rewards for doing so (which affect the town hub in a boring way). Oh, also there's no final boss battle. It looks like it was building up to one, but nope. Whether this was intended to be a jab at Fallout 3's terrible, anti-climatic ending or not doesn't matter, since it still hurts the game and again, feels like the developer was too lazy to design one, or ran out of money for the project and just wanted to shove it out the door.
The game has its good points, but overall it will disappoint you if you expect it to keep up the pace past the first dungeon of the game. There's so much more I could rant about what's wrong with this game and how I can see bits and pieces of an awesome game that it wanted to be, but I've already put in over an hour writing this for people that likely will only read the first paragraph or two then skim through the rest of it. (not that I could blame them)
Actually, one last point based around laziness: The music. Seriously, you could make a new song for the first 3 floors of each dungeon, but reused the same ones for the remaining 6 in each one? Like come on man, really? I know it isn't exactly easy making music, but at the same time it's just making people see more and more how lazily some parts of this game were made.

The controls aren't the best considering this is only a point and clicker. You often have to click multiple time to select something from your inventory, I had to click 7 times before I could pick up the damn parrot. The characters are fine and I think the art style is nice but the game starts to get generally frustrating after a while. It sends you on a load of convoluted fetch quests that are generally boring and take far too long because of the speed of Rufus. The fetch quest style of the game is made extra infuriating by the fact that you have next to no clue about where you're supposed to be going/what you're doing. Your only options are to grab a walk through or talk to every single person, using every single dialogue option.
Navigating the world is a pain too. To go from The Crane to The Tunnel, you have to click down from The Crane, Up to the platform and then click The Tunnel, and that's all on one screen. Half the time you either walk to the place you're going but don't actually enter the room or you don't move at all. The music is fine at first but generally gets very repetitive and annoying after a little while, and it took 2 of us half an hour to pack the suitcase so you can imagine that you'd be listening to it for a while. Hearing the dialogue repeat constantly gets physically frustrating and playing the game becomes a task with all fun removed either because you're endlessly confused or you're annoyance at the bugs is greater than the tiny feeling of accomplishment you get from the Steam Achievements popping up at odd times.
I'll admit, the animated cutscenes are quite good and some of the jokes aren't too bad but if I knew this game would start out with packing a highly unlikable main characters suitcase and 2 hours of confusion before they make a "oh, the one thing you didn't pack" joke, I probably wouldn't have bought it. I will continue to play though incase my judgment is changed and because I refuse to be defeated by this game

I love Spelunky. I find it to be hugely addictive, partly because it taps into the simple, colourful pleasures of the arcades and the 16-bit era of my youth, and partly because the game is so beautifully and precisely polished mechanically. But behind the simplicity and the chunky little graphics there lies a nest of evil and cunning, designed to torment your soul and turn your hands into sweating, controller-shaped claws. Each game of Spelunky is an exercise in unpredictability and randomness, and beating it does not mean that you have mastered it, or even really completed it, only that you beat it on that particular run. It’s OG gameplay in the old-skool playground, and your knees are going to get scraped.
I would recommend this to anyone who likes games that are easy to pick up but hard to master. The different modes and randomisation mean that Spelunky has almost infinte replay value, and at 15 Euros you just can't argue with that.

So. As far as I've played, the game is pretty okay. I only played it with a gamepad, haven't tried the keyboard. Anyway, it's an early access game so should be accounted as so. First things first: if you buy it, make sure you have three other friends who are going to buy it as well. It's decent. But still far from an excellent game.
What I've noticed is that it oscillates between surprisingly easy and damn ♥♥♥♥ing hard. Pretty much all you have to do is mash your attack button in the right direction. But then again you die pretty easily. Your HP gauge is Aura, and when it gets depleted, you still don't die, you're just in an in-between state wherein you can take a little bit more damage before dying, or you just wait for it to recharge. The problem is, this mechanic makes the game surprisingly easy, yet you take so much damage it's very welcome. I would say you should need to make the HP gauge go down less fast, but would also regenerate slowly instead of in one go. And so, make the "bleedout" mode shorter before death. Secondly, there is a cruel lack of variety in gameplay. All you do is pretty much mashing your button, with the occasional use of a spell.
Basically, you smash and smash and smash. The monsters smash back, end your combos and put you in bleedout, but you still rarely will die. Another problem is that when you die; it's such a ♥♥♥♥♥torm around you that your friends simply can't help you up. Finally, the four characters don't have enough differences in their playstyle. Grimm Eclipse uses MOBA-like mechanics (just a few spells + non-persistent levelling per game), well I think it should apply the same to the characters. Ruby, Weiss, Blake and Yang are too alike. The only differences in their playstyle are their spells, but you can rarely land spells, because you're too busy mashing your attack button to be the MVP. And you'll use them a few times so they can help you, but spells still cost a lot to use: special points. You have only a few of them, and some of the spells cost even two of them. Now, how do you recharge your spells? You land a 12-hit combo. So okay, I've had a few 60-hits combo with Weiss, but still, most of the time your combo will be broken by the Grimm moving away, or another player taking down your target. This is quite problematic to say the least. The fighting system ought to be a little more polished, with different types of hits, parrying and stuff. And the spells. Just make it a mana gauge with cooldowns and it'd work much much better. Now that would be MOBA-like, and probably not bad. Oh, and if the spell trees were more interesting, with choices to make and ways to build a character, it could give interesting replayability and mechanics.
For the moment, the game also quite lacks content. The campaign is quite short, it's about as long as a L4D2 easy campagn (which is not a problem in itself) but there's only one campaign. Of course, the story is unfinished, so I know there's bound to be more content to come for that. I'd like to see more characters, more campaigns to start with, some different ways to build as I've mentioned earlier, and all. Then again, it's in early access, so I hope this is planned.

Otherwise, the game has potential to be good. It just needs some improvement. Oh, and get three friends to play with you, seriously. So now, I'm not going to decommend the game, since it could be far worse, but it deserves to be far better.
