Just played through the entire campaign with all four characters and here's my thoughts. I'll breakdown each character's gameplay further down.
FIRST THOUGHTS:
Starting off, it's aesthetically very much like the anime. The voice acting is very good, as expected, but can easily be drowned out by the chaos of battle. The controls are easy enough to pick up to start bashing away at things. Though, in order to survive, you'll need to learn how to time your dodges effectively [Shift]; otherwise you'll be on the ground very quickly. Sounds can be a little repetitive and overbearing at times (I'm looking at you, Blake), but it's still early access.
PROGRESSION:
Yes, there is a progression system. Well, more like an in-game achievement system with in-game rewards. As for those claiming there is no progression system, that's half true. Your character LEVEL does not save. You'll be starting the campaign over again at level one. However, your talent unlocking progress DOES save. For example, 0/100 kills needed with a specific ability with a character can be built up through multiple playthroughs.
Achieving the level cap of 10 in a single playthrough to unlock their 'master' talent can be tough, and may require multiple playthroughs after unlocking some talents to help secure kills. That's where the urge to keep playing comes into play. Once talents are unlocked, they are unlocked for good, and can be purchased with attribute points without needing to unlock them again. Not a bad system, but may not be for everyone. I was only able to finally get to level 10 as Yang due to my allies dying while I cleaned up the battlefield, on multiple occasions.
MECHANICS:
It's very much a hack and slash, and does a very good job at it. Aside from there being only one button to attack with, the combat can get dull rather quickly. That is, unless you tie it together with dodges in-between, which resets the combo, or pressing right mouse-click during the combo to interrupt it with some sort of knock-back or finisher. There is no visual 'lock-on' as of yet, so its hard to stick to one target unless your pointing your camera directly at them and/or using your WASD towards them. But, it's very easy to "get the hang of it" so it's not much of a negative once you understand how it works.
Your Aura meter is your health pool. You can take damage until its depleted and a little bit more until you collapse completely. Stop taking damage for awhile and you'll regen it automatically. Easy enough, just run like a coward while watching dem booties. Some character abilities grant invulerability, so it is possible to remain in comat and still regen. I.E. Ability -> Dodge -> Ability -> Dodge, etc. Seemed a little more exploitable on Yang than the others. Sometimes a little too exploitable to be called broken.
The experience is my biggest pet peeve about the game. Whoever last hits, gets the experience. Doesn't matter if I've been bashing away at very tough monster - another player can swoop in with an ability to swipe the experience. This leads to a bit of a sour and competitive experience if you're trying to achieve level 10.
REPLAYABILITY:
So far, the only campaign is pretty short. About 45 minutes to an hour long. I did feel the desire to play with everyone, so there is some replayability there. If you're a 100%er, and want to unlock every talent for every character while enjoying the hack and slash RWBY style, there's quite a bit of time to be spent here.
I sure hope to see more characters from the other teams, more campaigns, more monster types (only about 8 so far, and they look very similar), and perhaps some more modes. But for what there is so far, it's a toss-up. If you're looking for a quick hack and slash while playing with your favorite RWBY character and don't mind the price point - pick it up. If you'd rather wait for more content than just a single campaign that lasts an hour at most - hold off.
In this next section, this is a purly SUBJECTIVE opinion of my experience playing through the campaign with each character. Edits to the review after multiple playthroughs are below the initial impression.
Possible SPOILER ALERT: Don't continue to read if you want to find out how these characters work for yourself.
CHARACTER MECHANICS:
RUBY
She's very fun, and one of the more polished characters to start playing around with. Her ability kit out-shines everyone else's in my opinion. Extremely powerful AoE, single-target, and ranged AoE abilities gives her an edge over everyone else. Her damage is above average, and flows very well without losing a lock-on. There's no need to dodge-cancel a combo to stick to a target. Her ranged attack is a long-ranged rifle shot that has huge kickback. Great for first starting out in your first campaign to get rolling on how the game works.
Further Playthrough Edit: Her kit is still solid, and has the hardest hitting melee AoE ability from what I've seen so far, especially when talented. Her linear melee ability is frustrating at times when you finally charge it up only to have the the enemy go invulnerable. Not as reliable as other characters' "big-hitting" abilities. Dodge-cancelling her ranged attack after two clicks reduces the delay significantly.
________
DIFFICULTY: Novice
SKILL CEILING: 5/10
WEISS
Her quick rapier attacks force you to play a little different than the others, here. I had to dodge-cancel her combo to repetitively use the first half of her combo to stick to a target effectively. Her abilities can be game-changing. She's the only one with a [talented] heal, and the only one with an AoE that [talented] freezes the enemies which helps immensely on tough targets. Her other two abilities, however, are mediocre at best. The dash is nice for tying into combos, but the ranged ability has absolutly atrocious targetting. Don't expect to hit anything with it unless you're in point blank range. Not to mention her ranged auto-attack will only hit about half of the time with this same targetting - or lack of targetting.
Further Playthrough Edit: Once talented, her dash attack is the hardest hitting ability in the game, from what I've seen so far - and can be used in quick succession. So there's that.
________
DIFFICULTY: Intermediate
SKILL CEILING: 6/10
BLAKE
Quick and nimble, you'll find yourself all over the enemy - quite literally. Simply put, she needs work. In my opinion the least polished of the four with her current playstyle. The second half of her auto-attack combo puts you over the top of enemies, making it miss every enemy shorter than herself. I had to dodge-cancel her combo every... single... time against short enemies. Granted those aerial autos are extremely powerful, they're only reliable against the taller enemies. Her ranged attack is a light-hitting pistol with little-to-no kickback. As for the abilities, only two of the three are reliable, in the sense of maximizing your damage. Most of her kit seems bent on maneuverability rather than damage (although her ranged ability does massive damage if used at point blank) - but prepare your ears if you're going to play Blake with headphones. You have been warned.
________
DIFFICULTY: Advanced
SKILL CEILING: 10/10
YANG
Feels the most polished of the four, and feels great playing her. Her auto-attack lock-on mechanic is the best out of all of them. She hits hard, and hits fast - especially if you dodge-cancel and utilize the first 3/4 of her full auto-attack. She can remain invulnerable for a long time if you time her abilities and dodging correctly. All of her abilities have their uses. Powerful AoE ability, powerful single-target ability, and a hard-hitting "dash-in" ability. Her ranged attack is a short-ranged light-hitting shotgun spray - great for cleaning up enemies that aren't worth another combo. Solid choice for bashing skulls in.
________
DIFFICULTY: Intermediate
SKILL CEILING: 8/10

You play as Rufus, a sarcastic, egomaniac, who’s one goal in life is to escape the ball of sewage he calls home and live in the floating city of Elysium. Now that description of the main character may though you off. And I will admit Rufus is a bit of an♥♥♥♥♥and you could easily dislike him. But he’s funny and a little sympathetic to. So I found myself eventually warming up to him. Plus he does start to show signs of change by the end. And this is only the first game in a trilogy so he’s bound to get better. Oh and quick side note, since it is the first game in a trilogy there is a lot of set up but little pay off. Not a deal breaker though, since there was enough to make me want the next one. Now back to Rufus. If you still hate him by the end don’t worry because there’s always another character to pop his ego balloon, leading to some very funny moments. The only negative I have to give this game is that it has a very odd train of thought for some of its puzzles. But a good walkthrough solves that problem. All and all this is a great game with funny duologue and a set of challenging but absurd puzzles.

Time Rifters is a futuristic, colorful, and FREAKING FUN FPS game. Not only does this game look totally awesome, but it's so fun to play! It's hard to explain the gameplay but here it is: When you enter a game, you start on your first "trial". You go through whatever stage you are on, but when you complete it, you play it AGAIN but with a clone of yourself with a different weapon. You then not just play with that current player, but it saves what you did your LAST trial, and your past attempt fights along side you, which is crucial to win in this game. You can also upgrade a variety of different weapons at your disposal. This game has a nice mix of strategy and fun. My only complaints are that the player models don't look very good and that there isn't a whole lot of content...
recommended!

Time Rifters is a single-player co-op blast! The game is a bit on the short side (consisting of 3 episodes, each with 5 levels that can be completed in ~1hour overall), but because of the nature of the game, there is plenty of free workshop content to download in the form of arenas/score attack levels.
The basic game mechanics are simple. It's a first-person shooter where, at the start of the level, you will select what weapon you want and you can purchase upgrades for the weapon using gold earnt from killing enemies. Then you enter the level and destroy as many enemies (which are basically coloured cubes that move - sometimes they form a shape such as a spider or a crab) as you can before the time runs out. The really cool thing about this game, though, is that you then play the same level again alongside yourself from your first playthrough (a recording of your previous actions). At the end of a level you can have up to 4 copies of yourself all contributing towards destroying the cubes! So basically the game is as I said before, a single-player co-op first-person shooter.
In addition to the gameplay, the music is really cool too (mainly dubstep music) and the graphics are not bad either (there's only so much you can do with shooting cubes - though some levels have a nice cave design or an underwater theme). Gladly these were not done bad as nothing takes away from the base gameplay which is really good fun!
Overall, if you're a fan of first-person shooters, time attack games, or playing with yourself, this game is for you! If you don't think you will get much out of the workshop content though, maybe wait for a sale.
Enjoy! :D

Here's a fair review from an avid hardcore gamer with a fairly unbaised opinion.
MKX is pretty great. To sum it up, easily an 8/10. But I'll break it all down here.
Pros:
The games graphics are great. The X-rays are brutal, the fatalities are twisted and gorey, and the gameplay mechanics are solid. To be honest, it feels a little dumbed down for new players, but then again I've been playing a lot of Marvel vs Capcom and Killer Instinct lately, so I guess I should have expected that feeling. There's quite a few good modes (Your towers, some online modes like King of the Hill, and Faction Wars), but don't expect there to be a ton of modes like your stupid Call Of Duties because this isn't that type of game...or genre. There are also modifiers to make matches unique, annoying, challening, or ridiculously fun. There's 25 characters and I've seen people ♥♥♥♥♥ about that, but it's fine. I just wish they had brought out some of the older ones and made em playable, even if it were in their "revenant" form, but whatever.
Cons:
Ok, I'm gonna start out by saying most of the negative reviews are by idiots who expect things to be perfect. In this day and age, that's just not possible because games are either Ports or there's so much hardware that they just can't test on all of it, and have to take their best guest on the machines they built it on or the testers that played. That's why the majority of games have bugs these days. They can't test on EVERY piece of hardware or configuration. It's just too costly and not possible. So, that's why they fire out patches, like they are right now. For the record, I hate ports. I wish it was♥♥♥♥♥backwards where the ports were to the consoles, not from them. The game feels finished, just not polished. Anyhow, I digress.
1) The game still has some FPS issues, which they've addressed and are working on. The only other graphic issues I've see are A) Green Blip screen between cinematic starts B) Fatality glitched out and the dude stood their dazed, nothing happened, and it still awarded my fatality. Seemed like it just didn't launch the cinematic. I dunno. That could also be programming.
2) Because of being a port, the Netcoding is still in need of work.
3) Some noticable issues with skins not changing during cinematic scenes
4) No animalities, friendships, stage fatalities or bablities.
5) Needs to be more alternate costumes. At least 3 for each char anyway.
Not Cons, But Not Pros:
1) Some fatalities are awesome, others are....lacking. (Erron's Six Shooter is dull. He could have thrown three bottles in the air, then when they got near the person's face, shot them so glass exploded in their face/eyes, and then flipped a coin up, rapid fired 4 bullets, and then slo-mo could show each bullet hitting the coin to make it spin faster, and then have the coin plow in between hands covering their face and drill straight through their skull. I dunno, something like that).
2) Brutalities could be more brutal
3) There's 14 stages. I've seen people complain about this too. I honestly don't care and they don't repeat enough for me to notice it or have it become an issue. MK9 had 26 stages, so I guess they could have at least added a few more stages, but I'd rather they focus on more characters than stages.
Anyhow, that's my thoughts after 20 hours. It's not a bad game, and since it recently got released, it's still getting some polish work done (which it needs in some areas). Regardless, the issues don't ruin the gameplay or enjoyment of the game for me (at least until I start playing online, but I need to get better before I even consider that lol).

This is basically a Diablo clone.  To me, that makes it also quite similar to Dungeon Siege and Titan Quest.  I did not like Diablo 2 and have not played Diablo 3, so keep that in mind for reference.
This game wasn't as good as I'd expected.  After reading a few other reviews, I guess I expected something better.  Still, it was quite fun overall and when I got to the end I was still left wanting more.
It has all of the magpie attributes of picking up every possible piece of loot and spending all sorts of time comparing what you just found against what you already have to slowly upgrade your character.  It's a bit like Borderlands (1 and 2) in that way.  Some items have "sockets" which allow for further customization and upgrading.  They have solved the problem of selling all of that loot by giving you a pet who can go back to town and sell your gear for you while you continue to adventure.  Your pet is also a very useful combatant as well.
Death is not permanent.  Depending on where you are, you can either come back for free in the last town (which can be quite a hike back to where you were when you died), pay a certain amount of gold to come back at the entrance to the current map, or pay quite a bit of gold to come back right where you died.  No experience loss which was quite nice.   Basically, death costs you time or money and most of the time I found myself spending some money.
Once thing I did not like about the items is that some are part of a set.  If you collect more members of the set, the items give you bonuses above and beyond what they already have.  The problem is that such items are few and far between so getting more than 2-3 items in a set is quite unlikely over the whole course of the game.  Never mind that by the time you find the next item, you may have found better equipment than the first item, so your incentive to hang onto a set is not as high as it should be.  The bonuses you get just aren't good enough to make it worthwhile.  Also, there are many different sets, so the next item you find might be part of some other set which doesn't help you.
Overall, I did enjoy the game and if you like Diablo, Dungeon Siege or similar games, you should enjoy this a lot.

WASTED is a rogue-lite that's a mix of games like Fallout, Binding of Isaac and Zelda.
The gunplay is good, the writing is good, and the overall experience is pretty good. The only thing I don't really like is that there are these tough enemies called S.O.B's that will hunt you down on a floor if you take too long exploring. My problem is that they spawn too quickly, leaving a sense of urgency that kind of defeats the purpose of having a stealth system.
Other than that, it's a pretty fun game.

WASTED is a rogue-lite shooter that tasks you with finding booze in a post-apocalyptic world where only stupid people survived (they even use toilet paper as currency).
You are going to search vaults (as in Fallout, yes - there are plenty of references to Fallout in this game) for booze, loot, guns and more booze.
Mechanically this game is pretty amazing - shooting feels very good, all guns (or at least gun types) can be easily distinguished, your character stats influence combat quite significantly. Enemies act stupid as they should, which can be hilariously abused to make them fight each other and trigger their own traps.
Since that's a rogue-lite game - when you die, you lose everything. There are various ways to pass your items to your next character, but, let's just say, those are not very consistent ways. It might be that you'll end up with amazing loot that you will lose to the pure nature of randomness. Sometimes this might infuriate even the best of us.
Interestingly enough, the world is full of lore and quests - which is quite unusual for rogue-lite games. And that lore and quests are just as silly as the rest of the game.
In addition to normal progression with unlocking new levels and quests, there's also a daily dungeon run that doesn't affect your main character. But if you can find and extract cool loot - your main character might actually receive it. And daily dungeons do have significantly better loot than your normal levels.
The game is also relatively bug-free and updated regularly with dev being super responsive on forums. Always a good thing.
Now, with all those good things said, I want to talk a bit about the most infuriating mechanic ever - S.O.B. merc with a minigun. When you take too long exploring the dungeon - he will appear and start marching towards you. Once you meet him, you are dead in 99.9% of cases, his minigun is just too powerful and can stun-lock you, so you can't really run away. The only option to deal with him is either to quickly exit the level or to use side rooms and corridors to evade him. The problem here is that you don't always have those side rooms. "Corridor of death" was a thing until one of the last patches, but I personally don't think it's much better now. I have died (and lost all my shiny loot) so many time to that damn minigun I'd lost count. It infuriated me immensely, especially when I was on the deeper dungeon levels, getting lost in the direction opposite to the exit just to get mowed down by the minigun.
The big problem here, in my opinion, is the fact that by rushing you through the dungeon, the game essentially restricts you from using all the cool mechanics it has. You no longer have time to sneak around, plant traps, plan on how to make enemies kill each other, etc. You just have to find exit really fast. And that kills a significant portion of fun for me. Up to the point where I actually quit the game for a week. I do return every time I see a patch in the hope that this mechanic will be tweaked even more ("casual" mode without it? pretty please?). Or maybe because I like to suffer :E
Nonetheless I would wholeheartedly recommend trying this game if you like rogue-lite shooters. I have an incredible time with it. And hoping to have more, when S.O.B. thing is somewhat easier (I know, I'm bad at games).

An FPS/RPG hybrid with a tongue-in-cheek sense of humour, WASTED Is the best roguelite shooter to date. If you played the newer Fallouts, you will feel right at home.
Combat is highly enjoyable. The knockback system works well with different types of weapons, allowing rapidfire guns to stunlock and shotguns/melee to fling enemies away. It applies to the player too, so watch out! Because of it, the guns and melee weapons feel very enjoyable to use. And the sounds and visuals make blowing off crotches and heads very satisfying, with enemies exploding in a shower of blood and TP. The enemy variety is good too. Melee and ranged humanoids, robots, mutants and they can have champion modifiers, which make them tougher.
The levels themselves are randomly generated and filled with a plethora of traps, enemies and goodies. It's overwhelming at first, but once you start seeing the patterns, it's hard to get lost.
Character progression is done through gear and hangovers. Gear can be looted from dead enemies(who drop everything they wear), crafted, recieved as quest rewards and taken from bosses. Said gear can then be modified. Hangovers are similar to perks in other games and you get them by drinking radioactive booze found in the dungeons. Gear provides mostly S.H.O.T.S(stat system) boosts and a few unique perks. Hangovers provide S.H.O.T.S boosts as well, but also unique abilities, such as slowing down time midair and boosting your damage during multikills.
You also have a house, which you can upgrade as a reward for completing dungeons. There are both aesthetic and functional upgardes and you can't get them all in one run.
Graphically, the game is unique, while clearly drawing inspiration from the Borderlands. The art style is quirky and endearing and since it's so stylized the game looks great even on low settings.
The sounds are great. The weapons sound meaty, you can use the sounds to detect enemies and the voice acting is great. Oh and the soundtrack is absolutely phenomenal.

WASTED, a game heavily inspired by a large number of post-apocalyptic franchises (like Fallout and Wasteland), is branded a "post-apocalyptic pub crawler". I must admit that it took me a while to understand why would it be called like that, as there isn't much in terms of pubs in this game. And then it dawned on me. The pub-crawling is actually the dungeon-crawling, as you go down, get wasted, pass out and go back for another swig like a real addict. In essence, that's what the game is playing at - your addiction to dungeon crawling, "just one more level" mentality, and your unvawering conviction not to give up as the going gets tougher and tougher. This what it makes it the right game for me. I like dungeon crawling, engaging action, and good puns that put a smile on my face.
Let's look at the good and the bad.
THE GOOD:
1. The game is extremely atmospheric. It plays the post-apocalyptic card just as well as the games it has been inspired by.
2. The music score is great, albeit a bit repetitive.
3. The gameplay is extremely engaging. The game is tough as nails, but by no means unfair. It lets you decide how to play, as there are many ways to approach the game.
4. To address the elephant in the room - permadeath is indeed an issue, but if you play the game the way you are supposed to, your "successor" can start with ample supply of goods and pick right where you left off at no loss of progress, apart from some hanovers that give you some positive and/or negative buffs. This is a good thing, as it keeps you on your toes and makes you think for the future, not just the current "cooler" run.
5. Gear makes or breaks your game - there is no real RPG progression involved, unlike Fallout, where you put points in stats and skills. I thought I was going to hate this feature, but it actually ends up working for the better. Loot is extremely plentiful in the game and you are able to store and stash it for future characters - in essence allowing them to pick up exactly where you left off - if not stronger. And about that...
6. Your toon has a number of stats that gear items boost. They are referred to as S. H. O. T. S. (clever) - Shoot, Hit, Oblity, Tinker and Stealth. Apart from that you also have armor (flat damage mitigation), critical chance and critical damage procs based on chance or actions. This allows you to focus on gear that would suit your playstyle, and stast gear that would fit a different one, in oder to try it in the future, which I find quite cool.
7. Puns, jokes, jabs, pokes at anything that exists, smiles, laughs, and so on and so forth - it is an understatement to say that everything in this game is a joke. From the character interractions to the item descriptions, from the enemy taunts to the way everything is so jovially put together - you will feel challenged, but also entertained every step of the way as you discover the plethora of easter eggs or read the consoles about how people in the coolers descend into insanity and mutate in all manners of ways.
8. Accepting the game for what it is and playing it as intended makes for a pleasant experience - WASTED plays the "success is not guaranteed" trump card to its fullest. As such, you can really help your game if you refrain from attaching yourself to a toon, and focus on stashing stuff, ammo and gear for future runs, and just plainly enjoy the ride.
9. Action never lets down - the game keeps you contstantly on your toes, regardless whether you are bum-rushing a level or sneakily taking out enemies.
10. The voice-acting gets the job done - it is nowhere near stellar, but it works to convey the idea of people dumbing down in general.
The BAD:
1. While the levels are randomly geneated, the game is repetitive. You will not find yourself in the same area, doing the same thing, fighting the same enemy, looting the same item from the same place - but it will sure as hell FEEL that way, as your goal is inevitably to reach your goal, or be forced to abort early or just die. And speaking about aborting and dying...
2. If you abort by drinking booze (and getting a hangover) or die, you need to drive back to the cooler and start from the very first level of it, not where you left it. And if you die, anything you haven't stashed or put in a courier box is lost - apart from unique items or ones maked as "important" - a stamp you craft later on in the game that forces that item to reappear in the "lost and found" and you get to buy it back.
3. Dungeon levels are randomly generated each time you go in, and have similar loot that only changes after a certain spot. This means you need to wade through the same pistol or melee enemies during the first few levels until the game opens up a bit. And speaking about randomly generated levels...
4. The random layout of a dungeon can make or break your game. You may find a good dungeon layout and make off with tons of bullets, money (toilet paper) and cool items and hangovers, or you may find yourself stuck in a long winding path and take way too long to reach the next level. And about that...
5. If you take too long to reach a level, a big bad wolf, send by the Brotherhood of Steel (BOS), whoops, sorry, I mean Syndicate of Buzzkillers (SOB) Purifier will start hunting you down. If you are forced to retrace your steps, you will inevitably run into him, and likely die. There are ways to get past him by exploiting the environment or the time he is forced to reload, but if the dungeon layout doesn't allow it, your run is over, along with all the sweet loot you gathered.
6. If you don't play the game as intended (stash stuff, deposit your cash, don't get attached to your first toon, etc.), you will tear your hair out and throw a ton of expletitives at your screen. I know I did...
7. Sadly, you don't get to customize your successors. So if you do get attched to your toon, Alt-F4 on death might be your option, as many do now. This way you will have to redo the cooler, but at least get to keep your dude... This is why I keep on saying that you shouldn't get attached to the characters and just play as the game expects you to.
Conclusion:
I really, really like WASTED. It is tough, but not unfair. It aims to kill you, but gives you so many options to hold your own. It lets you buildcraft (or should I say gearcraft) and change playsyles on the fly. If you play it properly, it allows you to progress even through death. The models are cool, the enemies are fun, and the easter eggs and jokes will put a smile on your face. If you enjoy fact-paced dungeon (or should I say "fungeon"?) crawling action, this game is certainly the right one for you. And to repeat myself, anything (or anyone) that can put a smile on your face or make you laugh and feel happy is priceless.

This doesn't continue the Anomaly "story".  It's more of a re-hash of the same story, abbreviated, for those who haven't seen the story before (in the full "Anomaly Warzone Earth").  Which is understandable as the "...Mobile Campaign" was likely introducing the story to the mobile market.  However, perhaps being a mobile-targeted app, the campaign is short.  I was able to complete the entire 12 mission campaign in approx 2.5hrs, not defeating
turret on every map, but nearly so.
Anyway, I got used to the massive sized-for-smartphone buttons (having also played "Anomaly: Korea" which is also a smartphone-targeted game) so that part of the controls weren't too annoying for me.  Quality-wise, to me, this game seemed a little better than Korea.  In fact, this was almost as good as the full "Anomaly: Warzone Earth" game.
On the plus side, I liked not having the separate commander run around and get lost in all the action on the screen.
There is absolutely no reason to play this game on PC if you have played the original Anomaly. Mobile games usually not suited for mouse+keyboard and this one is no exception.

Firstly, I would like to mention that I personally enjoy the Anomaly Series and I would definitely recommend it to my friends. Anomaly: Warzone Earth Mobile Campaign is a Tower Offense game, instead of the traditional Tower Defence games. This makes the Anomaly Franchise stand out of other games.
With that said, the original intention of creating Anomaly: Warzone Earth Mobile Campaign is to be played on mobile devices, rather than on a PC. As this is a game meant for mobile devices, it is pretty much the same as the original Anomaly: Warzone Earth, just that you would realise that there are no keyboard shortcuts, making it unfriendly for PC gaming.
For PC gaming, my recommendation would be to get Anomaly: Warzone Earth, instead of Anomaly: Warzone Earth Mobile Campaign as I find the PC version more enjoyable and with keyboard shortcuts, making the overall gameplay more convenient rather than having to use the mouse all the time.

Deponia is weird and quirky and Rufus is indeed a jerk, but in a good way. Suffice to say, he'll grow on you towards the end, like that fungal infection in your right toenail that you left untreated for too long. But in a good kind of way. It's hard to explain.
The game is good, it's hard, and the story is very well developed and told. I have to say I'm not a big fan of what happens with the dowsing rod, but I'm also not sure whether the authors made that choice intentionally, as a nod to old-time adventures, or whether they just thought it was funny to play with the players like that. Either way, it's not the hardest enigma. It's in fact quite obvious, and that makes it even more infuriating, but hey!
I played the game almost entirely in German, with Italian subtitles because I don't understand much German. Now, I know and appreciate very much that there is an Italian dubbing, but it's… erhm, let's just say it's wonky. The acting is most of the times lame, and I can't say the same for the German -- or event the English -- dubbing. Still, I appreciate the effort!
Overall, I enjoyed almost every bit of the game. The character animations could be better. The team clearly put a lot of effort in the art -- it's beautiful! -- and the cut scenes -- amazing! -- but in the end you are stuck watching the same 6-frames walk cycles over and over, and even other occasional animations aren't that much better.
My girlfriend hated Rufus -- but that's kind of the point, I suppose. She left the room and didn't come back until I stopped playing. Oh, well. I'm just glad that people are still making well written and engaging graphical adventures these days!
Absolutely recommended if you are a fan of the genre.

This may just be the single worst game I have ever played in my entire life.
By God, where to start?
Oh of course, let's start with the accuracy system. This has to be the single most INACCURATE accuracy system to be implimented in a shooter. It's actually very simple: I pick up a Hunting Rifle, and it functions basically like a shotgun, so the spread is wide, and highly loose. However, the enemy with the Hunting Rifle can snipe me from about thirty meters away, with zero spread. Every. Single. Time. That's not of course limited to that weapon, no no... in fact, just about any weapon the AI has can snipe me from thirty meters away.
In other words, my bullets from my gun have about a one-eighty degree spread, and can't hit a single thing (unless RNGesus takes pity on you) while the AI headshots me with an AK and sends me flying like a ragdoll.
Still on the subject of guns, I can load a full pistol clip into someone like a Military soldier's unarmed head, and barely even stagger the man. With their inhumane accuracy, it hardly takes a clip in my head to eat the dirt over, and over, and over again.
Another tedious thing is the prices in the game. I can't say I know if it's any different later on (because I lack the patience to waste another moment of my life with this), but obtaining healing items is distinctly painful due to the fact that every trader provides them at a price that for a beginner, is pretty unreasonable. Farming them off enemies is practically impossible for the main reason of the previous paragraph, and I've consistently found myself stuck at the fact that I'm broke, and can do nothing about it, because I can't go fight, because I don't have the medkits or bandages to make up for the amount of times I'm going to get my head blown off by a shotgun from some guy a million kilometers away.
The fact a medkit lacks components to bandage wounds is beyond stupid. That's just a terrible mechanic. Why on Earth would bandages have to be a separate item, for a separate purpose, when medical kits exist in the game to provide healing? I don't think I've ever played a decent game which such a thing.
I've already had so many moments of: "OH MY GOD, WE FINALLY DID IT BOYS!"... and then mere moments later, I'm doomed to a situation of where even if I save, I inevitably die, because I ran out of bandages.
I think one of the most annoying parts had to be reaching Cordon, where the first thing I encounter is a machine gun turret of the military, with an unlimited clip of ammo, and the sights of a bloody NightForce NXS... and of course, the accuracy of an AWM. I certainly had no chance whatosever, other than to duck and run, because God knows I'd never be able to get close, nor pick him off with my constantly jamming curveball shooters. It must've taken me at least thirty minutes to get ten meters thanks to that.
Unfortunately for me, the small distance I made it rendered me to pass Steam's available refund time limit. I cannot recommend this trash to anyone who wants an unmodified, vanilla playthrough. Frankly, I'm quite surprised it can be physically completed with how poorly designed it's combat system is. I'll have to find something that reduces spread by at least ninety percent. Kudos to those who actually did it back in the day.

NOTE: REVIEW MAY BE SUBJECT TO REVISION UPON FULL RELEASE
This is an amazing game, it's an FTP first-person shooter that's set in the European Theater of WWII. You start as a standard infantryman, but as you increase in rank you can unlock new classes (like tank crewman, fighter pilot, recon, and paratrooper). The game also allows you to unlock new weapons and vehicles through both rank and by earning combat ribbons (basically an achievement system). There is also a place to get together with friends of the same class and form a squad so you can all play together (number of friends in you squad is dependent on your class, i.e. infantry can have six, while tanks can have three). You can also have multiple soldiers, so you can have a variety of classes to play with (I have an infantryman, a tank crewman and a fighter pilot).
There is also a place where you can pay to unlock vehicles and weapons early (although for tank crewman, if you buy a heavy armor off the bat you will not be able to use it very often until you get to a rank where there are heavy armor squads).
Another neat feature is you can unlock upgrades for your weapons, like a hair trigger for your guns that will increase ROF but decrease stability. Or for tanks and jeeps you can get infantry support crates (ammo and health, or anti-tank weapons).
All in all, this is a great game and it's only in beta form. It has a great diversity of classes, weapons, and vehicles. If first-person shooters are your thing, then you should definitely try this game, and since it's free, it can't hurt to try it.

As a huge RWBY fan I had high hopes for this game. I played the alpha and was blown away by the amoothness of the combat.
On day one of early access I was blown away by the story and even more fluid combat. I was not let down. Rooster Teeth delivered.

As a diehard fan who loves RWBY more than anything (including Harry Potter) I enjoyed the game but it needs a right bit of work, even in early release some of these issues shouldn't exist (in my opinion).
CONS:
-The characters slide for a bit before they start walking and then continue walking in place after they stop moving.

-The time before logout due to inactivity is too short, as a suggestion let the host be able to determine inactivity time before log out.

-There's no attack animation for the Grimm when they attack the control servers you defend and such.

-There's no offline single player, which while unnecessary, would be a nice addition so it can be played in locations without online access.

-While the difficulty of such is understandable, it would be nice to have Arryn voice all of Blake's lines in the full release of the game.

-There's a lot of weird invisible walls that prevent the player from making small jumps across gaps and/or entering areas that look like the player should clearly be able to enter.

-There should be a level select and the game should save the character's individual levels and skills (like how borderlands does) while allowing the player to create and delete different character saves (again like borderlands).

-There seems to be no shading on any of the character which would be a nice addition that would make the characters look better.

-The majority of the characters (Ruby, Weiss, and Blake specifically) all seem to move relatively the same in battle animation, understandable in this state of the game however.

-None of the characters have any sort of shadows and lack depth (which while not easy, the hair at least should have some static shadow to provide depth).

-While I've only played through the Emerald forest and some of Mountain Glenn there have been no rewards, achievements, or special unlocks.

-The special meter shouldn't be filled by combos that can get broken in all of two seconds and instead should be filled up over a period of time.
PROS:

-Fun as hell and sticks well to canon.

-The transfer of the weapons from melee to range is quick and seamless.

-The voice acting is done well.

-The combat controls are smooth and flow well (both on controller and keyboard).

-The graphics are look great.

-It holds well at very high resolution (1912 x 1080 @ 60 GHz)

-Frames drop rarely and lag doesn't last long when it occurs.

-The fast pace of the characters hold together well.
As of now the only reason I would recommend it is because, as I said earlier, how much I love RWBY and I see A LOT of potential for an outstanding game.

This game is really quite excellent!  The basic concept is that it's sort of a virtual reality shooting gallery.  You buy a gun, upgrade it with some gold, then hop into the level and kill as many target cubes as you can.  The cube patterns are fun and clever, sometimes even forming giant monsters that walk around the arenas.  After your time-limited run, you start again as a new character, buy new guns with the gold you earned from the last run, and then try again.  But there's a twist!  The 4 lives stack on top of one another and play out synchronously, so on your second life you'll see your first life playing along with you and you'll want to choose targets and weapons that compliment previous runs.
It's a bargain price (even full price of $10 is great) and provides a very unique and fun experience that combines some good FPS challenges with a clever and interesting single-player time-based co-op mode that works extremely well.  The presentation, music, visuals - they're all slick and polished making for a great overall package.  I want to give a special shout-out to the HUD UI - all of the menus are presented in a sort of helmet-based augmented reality that feels natural and keeps you in the game; it's very clever and I want to give a high-five to whoever on the team came up with it.  I can't *wait* to get an Oculus Rift to try this game out in (which is apparently has native support for!).
The amount of built-in content is admittedly low (only 3 "episodes" of 5 levels each, each episode takes about 20 minutes to play through), but if you work on trying to optimize and go for high scores you'll be replaying the episodes multiple times.  Additionally, it has full support for community-created levels, and I suspect they will eventually be adding more level packs if the game sells well enough to warrant it.
There's also a demo, which you should definitely try out.  The only thing that's not clear from the demo that was a really pleasant surprise was that as you go through the 5 levels of an episode you get to keep spending gold upgrading your weapons.  This means that by level 5 your guns are doing crazy amounts of damage and effects on the targets, which is a great sense of progression and strategy.

Very unforgiving to the point of insanity. The only less forgiving titles I know of are the Kaizo Marios.
Most games tend to let you live more than five seconds before deciding to kill you.  Most games I've played (yes, including rogue-likes) tend to start out a little slow, you know, to ease you in, let you get used to how the game controls, that sort of thing.  For instance, in FTL, the enemy ships are weaker, and there's a tutorial that explains all of the game's mechanics.  In Risk of Rain, the enemies start out weak, and slowly become more powerful as time goes on.
This game, though?  Here's a brief tutorial that tells you what buttons to press in very little detail (you could have figured that out just by going to options and looking at the controls)!  The only real compelling mechanic it introduced was that you can sprint across one tile wide gaps.  If this mechanic is ever used in the actual game, I didn't make it that far before getting too frustrated to continue.  It introduces that the Idol and the damsel are present, and the controls for dealing with them, but it doesn't tell you what the damsel is there for.  Knowing that saving the damsel heals you for one heart (and that it can go over the initial 4 you start with) could potentially be useful, but apparently it's not something the tutorial felt the need to mention.  It just tells you that you could potentially receive a kiss for saving her.
The random generation is fairly poor:
If you run out of ropes/bombs you CAN and WILL get stuck.  The random generation can generate holes that you can't climb out of on your own, so you'll need either enough ropes to climb back out, or enough bombs to blast your way out.  Otherwise, hopefully there's something in there you can use to kill you.
You'll also find yourself faced with leaps (or in this case, falls) of faith - you'll often end up in situations where you can't see where you're going to land.  Did I mention there's fall damage?  This is another thing that the tutorial didn't really think was important enough to mention.  It tries to be too realistic about it too, by stunning you when you hit the bottom, letting the enemies finish you off.  While you can look down, it's slow, and there's a time limit.  Also, since you've probably been running from enemies because your whip is terrible, you are probably not in a position to safely perform said looking down action.
The whip sucks. It's very slow (so you'll often get hit by what you're trying to attack), has pathetic reach (so you'll probably get hit by what you're trying to attack), and it can't attack things that are above you for some reason.  No weapons in the game that I am aware of are capable of shooting up, which is a problem because most of your enemies either fly or spawn on the ceiling.  You CAN deal with them Italian plumber style, but that only works well for enemies that die in one hit.  Seriously, the largest single improvement that this game could make would be letting you attack upwards with the whip (and preferably diagnally as well).  Because of this, you're best off just running past the enemies, because attacking them is super risky.
Arrow traps are a load of BS.  They spawn as early as the first level, often in great quantity, and, once fired, are almost certainly going to hit whatever triggered them.  You can throw/drop objects in order to trigger them, which will allow you to safely pass, but there are so many of them and they have such large range that it's very easy to miss one, and it will take away half of your life and stun you, leaving you open for enemy attack, which in your stunned state will almost certainly prove fatal.  Oh, and the strategy of disabling them that I mentioned?  Also not mentioned by the tutorial (which does in fact contain an arrow trap in it).  It also requires that you have something to throw at them anyway.  It's possible to have to just tank it (and your character is really bad at tanking, and besides, you can only do that once).
Bone piles are usually destructable/pickupable but can be enemeis, and you won't discover this until it's too late, because the enemy will appear and instantly damage you.  This also can happen if you break pots with the whip rather than throw them.  This wouldn't be a big deal if you had health reserves, but you don't.
Items are clunky to use, and if you need to set off a trap, rescue a damsel, or collect an idol, you have to put down your tiem.  There are a few guns, which at least have range, but you can't shoot up.
If there is a giant spider outside of the shop, preventing you from leaving the shop, you can't kill it without angering the shopkeeper, whose solution to his anger management problems is to murder everybody in existence.  I think you might be able to use the whip in the shop (keyword: might) but you can't shoot up, which could potentially be a problem if that's what direction the shop exit is.  I am not making this up.  This legit happened.  Other reviews I've seen have mentioned that apparently even if you do manage to escape the shopkeeper by going to the next level, which is an impressive feat, he won't forgive you and will continue his murderous rampage next time he sees you.
If the shopkeeper is angered in any way by anything (including the randomly generated environment and giant boulders whose trajectory cannot be controlled or contained or influenced in any manner), he will go on the aforementioned murderous rampage, blaming you for the RNG being a jerk.  I'm not certain, but I think he might be capable of one-shotting you.  If he isn't, then he can deal damage fast enough that he might as well be one-shotting you.  He's got a pretty large range and high movement speed in addition.  You probably won't escape.
All in all, if you're looking for a good roguelike, I'd suggest playing Binding of Isaac, Rogue Legacy, Faster than Light, or Risk of Rain instead,

Wasted is a neat little "Fallout" inspired FPS shooter with roguelite elements mixed in.  It's not perfect, but it's certainly worth a look.  It basically reduces (modern-era FPS) Fallout to a series of randomly generated vaults to explore.  There's a total of 5 vaults, and it took me around 15-20 hours to survive all of them, although I was far from optimal about it.
I liked the shooting and exploration elements of the game, and the Fallout parody is well done and generally pretty silly.  The elements of progression are a mixed bag - your character doesn't so much as level up as they gain mutations from exploring the vaults, and these are lost if you die.  On the other hand, there's a player house that persists where you can store loot so that you've got a better chance at surviving a future run.
The difficulty is somewhat uneven.  I had real trouble with the second vault, but then it was a downhill slide to the final cutscene from there.  There's a divisive "hurry up" mechanic in the form of a difficult optional boss enemy that chases you if you linger too long in a level.  I didn't mind it, but that's mostly because the benefit of additional loot plateaus early.  Past the second vault, I changed very little of my gear, and most of what I did change was quest reward related rather than exploration related.  There are also a few bugs and exploitable game mechanics.
Despite simple graphics, I was unable to play the game on my machine.

Have you ever wanted to play a roguelike, but it's actually Fallout with big heads? This is pretty much that.
The game starts out very hard and it ushers you to not sit around and try to explore every nook and cranny because of the impending doom of the S.O.B. Purifier. Everything hurts you in one way or another (like standing on a brick) and you will have to learn what traps/obstacles to look out for as they can end your game quickly (I'm looking at you trip mine next to exploding barrel that one-hit kills me). After you get a few positive brews, especially things that increase your suvivability, the game actually gets pretty easy and I blew through the last 2 coolers.
I feel the game could use more content, I found myself memorizing all of the possible room layouts and there wasn't a lot of variety between coolers other than the color of lights and different enemies. After I beat the game, I was not really compelled to do it all over again, but the daily challenge run is pretty intense as you spawn with randomized gear and random enemies with the addition of level variants like "no lights", etc. I just wish the ending levels were a lot harder (not bullet-sponge enemies) as I could just sneak-crit enemies into oblivion.
I know I gave the game a lot of crap, but it's very fun (as you can see it took me 22 hours to beat it). I feel it's worth the 13 bucks and I presume the developer will add more room types and maybe even guns or something and refine the difficulty.

Gameplay:
You've probably seen Wasted being advertised on Adult Swim recently. If you're like me, you probably hold a stigma against games coming from Adult Swim. I've always had the misconception that the games advertised were shameless cash grabs, but Wasted has turned that assumption of mine upside down.
Everything Wasted does oozes style and humor. On its surface it seems like it's ripping off Fallout's setting, but where it sets itself apart is how it takes any given idea from Fallout and twists, stretches, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥izes it to the most absurd satire. Caps have been replaced by toilet paper as the currency of the post-apocalyptic world, reasoning that it's the most valuable commodity since no one wants to wipe their♥♥♥♥♥with their bare hands after all.
The gameplay feels like the perfect blend of Spelunky and Fallout. You start with only the shirt on your back and a dinky pistol that any card carrying NRA member would be embarrassed to be within the same zip code of. You're shoved into a dungeon, a "cooler", essentially the analogue of the vaults of Fallout. Your goal? Reach the bottom floor. Alternatively you could find some of the radioactive booze in the cooler to chug and receive permanent buffs to your character, though doing so will cause you to black out and wake up back in your hideout.
If you manage to find your way back to town, you can stash any of your belongings and your TP in containers peppered around your home in case you die in the cooler. Death in the cooler results in all of your loot being lost and starting over again with only the items you started with or things remaining in your stash. When in town you also have the opportunity to take your TP to one of the three shops in town. One shop will let you purchase special booze emulating those you would find in the cooler, though you can only have one of these special drinks each run. Another shop will let you purchase random items though they are a bit on the expensive side. Lastly, there is the Courier shop. During your gameplay you're going to run across items whose names are colored purple. These items are not lost on death, but are instead collected by the couriers who place them in a lost and found inventory for you to repurchase, though they are much more expensive than other items.
Inside the dungeon, you're going to want to explore the randomized layouts thoroughly to better equip yourself and earn as much TP as you can, but be warned. You're heavily encouraged not to linger around long, or else some S.O.B., a member of the "Syndicate of Buzzkills", is going to show up at the beginning of the floor and slowly pursue you. S.O.B.s are very dangerous and impractical to fight, sporting over 500 hp and a minigun that will stunlock you until you're Swiss cheese. They are not impossible to defeat but until you acclimate yourself to the game you'll want to avoid them, as killing one involves guerrilla tactics in a circular path, and probably a concrete brick or two.
I've already clocked 14 hours in the game and have just now made it through the first cooler. I plan on many more hours to come. If I had to point out a few flaws with the game, one would be the hit scan nature of the enemies. If an enemy has line of sight to you and is aware of you, you're going to eat a few bullets. A second issue I have is the amount of stun that the enemies can cause. Being hit by most bullets will stagger you. While staggered you're not able to move or return fire. This means there are going to be situations where you round a corner and are immediately held in place while numerous enemies take you out with no opportunity to fight back without being outright killed.
To sum things up, this game is a definite purchase, and at $12.99 (6/21/2016) it's a steal.

Having played through the Fractured But Whole in full, here's the simple reality: It is Stick of Truth, But Bigger.
That is a universal throughout the game. The town is larger. The Fights are more complex. The Cast is more diverse. There is simply a little bit more to do in every 'theatre' of this game. The unfortunate consequence of that, however, is that the game sometime aches under it's attempt to do a little bit of everything 'more'. The Crafting system is barely needed, and lacks much depth. The UI for having characters assist you in the open gameworld got even more complicated. The running gags of the last game show their age.
Sometimes, TFbW picks up on this and avoids it. If you recall the "Jimmy stuttering for 2 straight minutes" joke that was present in SoT, it's gone. Sometimes they rub their damn noses in it. Case and point: The repeated mocking of the silent protagonist trope was fine and good in SoT, where you were by no means the star of the show. However, TFbW has chosen to invest in letting the player have a Gender, a Sexuality, a Racial Background, an Alignment, Fears, and so much else... And yet they are trapped being completely silent. It contradicts itself for the sake of continuing the joke.
But /is it a fun game/? Yes. Absolutely. It's a smart little RPG with enough strategy (Especially on Mastermind Difficulty) to keep your attention. It's jokes hold up if you enjoy South Park humor. It manages to fill about 20 hours without issue, and the plot reads like a longer episode of South Park.
If that sounds good to you, you should buy it.
PS: Didn't buy the DLC. Didn't effect my gameplay at all. Perfectly full of content as-is fresh out of the box.

Time Rifters provides simple, but compelling game-play in a pretty package.  The lack of a tutorial causes a little confusion at the beginning, but it doesn't take long to figure out what is going on.  You have four runs to complete the level, with all prior past runs combining with the current one (i.e. you are playing with yourself).  Play smart and start with an area effect gun for maximum damage (e.g. missiles), then on the second and third run stick to a section of the screen (left or right half).  Finally on the last run use an accurate weapon (e.g. laser) to cleanup.  With a good selection of weapons and upgrades, this game is definitely worth the asking price.

Story mode was pretty good, I like the roster and the variations, fatalities are sick, but netplay leaves a lot to be desired.  Latency, memory leaks, connection issues, all of that good stuff. While admittedly I don't have issues practicing in training mode or single player mode, the whole point of a fighting game is to play against other humans.  Also, note that I'm leaving out a lot of other issues I've experienced.  Even after a 15 Gb (yes, giga) update, we still need more fixes.
If you have a PS4 or Xbone, buy MKX for that instead.  I had read bad things about the company responsible for porting the PC version, but I gave them a chance.  I had hopes that fighting games could be given a chance on PC with this game.  Unfortunately, this port did no favors for PC fighting games and I'll understand if other fighting game developers shy away from porting to PC after seeing this.
I am willing to update my review if the devs provide fixes.

Mortal Kombat. A sweet indulgence of ripping people apart and smashing bones. When it comes to fightning games, I tend to have a distaste for them. The only fightning style games I tend to enjoy is the Mortal Kombat series. This game did not fail to give me that same joy.
The story line to MKX was a huge improvement from other games in the genre. Mostly story in a fighting game are stale to nonexistant, which I understand its more about the fightning then the actually story for those hardcore fighter players out there. This story was amazing. Making me wanting to keep playing and not put the controller down. There where areas that could of been more explored, more background into the new characters being one area of interest.
The gameplay was as you would normally have; combos, uppercuts, x-ray explosions of testicles. They made it more enjoyable for non fighter experts to slightly (for lack of a better word) dumb down the button sequence for the Fatality and a more clear line of what needs to be accomplished for a Brutality
Outside of the story mode, mulitplayer, faction war and everything else going on there was they Krypt. Where you spend your bloody koins on unlocking skins, more fatalitys, and concept art. You did this through a maze of a hidden mini game with jump scares and a a need of finding certain items to unlock more areas. They did a incredible job on the krypt.
At the time of writing this review, the game did seem to have a unfortunate glitch with the steam cloud and I lost all my game data. Losing 14 hours worth of progress. Everything lost, that whole krypt I just about had finished....gone...

The game is a little rough around the edges but it shows a lot of promise for what it can be. The hack and slash aspect isn't as straight forward as one may think. Charging into a group of enemies will get you mowed down. Tactical retreat, hit and run, and attacking with your allies is the way to survive. The action and use of source material makes this the best in my books. I understand this is an early access we have so far but here are some things I've noted while playing thus far.
The settings menu doesn't seem to like saving the previous session settings. I toned down the resolution and quality for my first time playing. I have an older machine so I didn't want to stress test it just yet. When I went to change the video quality, the resolution also changed to 1920x1200 without my input. The second time I opened the game, it forgot I turned on subtitles.
There are certain gameplay aspects that I found to be lacking. Whenever static artwork like a speaking characters face was shown, it was a low resolution but blown up image. I hope this will be resolved in the successive releases. The fighting audio seems to overpower speech audio. Perhaps you can have all sound lower slightly when a character is talking?
I know animation work is difficult and doubly so for a gameplay where the models are at the player's whim. The animations are pretty good for walking on even ground and jumping but there was an odd falling animation and sound when going down a gentle decline. It also prevented additional movement input like jumping.
Is there a way to include mutators before the match? Perhaps having the option to prevent people from selecting the same characters. I also suggest a way of changing characters when changing levels.
These are probably the major issues that I have encountered. As for suggestions… the opening credit scene plays for too long, the main menu screen lacks a help option to see the button mapping, perhaps allowing button mapping in the settings menu, an extras menu option for tracking stats, concept art, artifacts found, stats on how many kills, and achievements, aura recharge upon leveling, and perhaps a UI upgrade to have a transparent backing to make it look similar to the phones or screens as shown in the series.
I’ve rambled on long enough. Good game so far but with a bit of polish, it can be great!

This is one of those rare games that come every once in a while that you love and hate at the same time. For me a lot of the elements of this game frustrate me to death, the S.O.B, the lack of decent loot or ammo, the room full of enemies with automatic weapons and the high knockback leading me to basically be stun locked and more. But for every frustration there's something that i love about the game, like this game being one of the few games that REALLY nails the look of the old scholl fallout in a campy goofy 80's kind of way.
Gameplay-wise the game feels great to play for the most part, turn up the FOV and you feel as fast as can be and it runs pretty smooth and you feel like a god when you get the right amount of loot and perks, even if death is only a bear trap away.

If i had to be honest, I love playing this game but at the same time I hate a lot of elements on it, maybe that's just the roguelite way, but a lot of the randomness can really weigh the game down, one run you can be sitting here breezing though, the next you're in a hallway full of exploding enemies, and others with automatic weapons while the S.O.B is looking for you and you're running low on healing items.
All in all I like the game, but as i said, the frustrating elements really weigh it down to the point where it's enough to get in the way of me progressing personally, i'm no stanger to difficult games, I love them even, but when it's all based on chance or luck i can't see myself progressing much further having all my progress thrown away in an instant, essentially wasting time.
I'll reccomend this game only because I like it more than I dislike it, but I reccomend it to people with patience, and  a lot of time to spare.

TLDR; Best in the series. Amazing soundtrack.
Long version:
What can I say about this fighting masterpiece? I've been playing Tekken since it's first game though I've only gone through 1, 3, 5 and now 7. I'm by no means a pro, I know the basics, know a few combos and have fun.
Having only just returned to Tekken I must say that this is easily the best in the series.
Not messing with a winning formula, we get the same familiar technical gameplay though with some new additions.
A new rage system which is essentially a despair move with flashy animations. Some special characters like Akuma and Eliza also use a resource system of their own which allows them to use special moves.
Also, without dumbing down the gameplay they managed to lower the entry bar for newer players.
The soundtrack is yet again the best in the series and includes those of previous games as well.
Fighting a certain someone under the sound of Heat Haze Shadow 2nd as the fight transitioned was absolutely epic.
The game is powered by the Unreal Engine 4. For it's insane graphics and animations the game runs surprisingly well on PC.
It doesn't feel like a port at all.
We also get character customization now (though I'm not sure if this was present on previous games in the series). This comes in the form of unlocks, like sunglasses, clothes, effects, etc...
As for the story, it's very short but it gets back on track into the interesting part of the Tekken lore bringing a degree of closure the Mishima storyline.
Side characters also have individual story missions, but they're really only one match and one video. This part was somewhat disappointing if we compare it to the likes of Tekken 3. But by no means does it hinder an otherwise amazing game.
I've tried the online mode briefly and so far I've had no issues with connection stability or latency. I'm used to fighting games having plenty of online issues so this was a pleasant surprise.
Tekken 7 is a very well polished game and having already been out in Japanese arcades for awhile one can also say it's balance also had time to mature.
For those already familiar with Tekken, this is the best in the series and definitely a must have.
For those unfamiliar, this is good time to get into it. The entry barrier is lower and it allows new\returning players to build up their skill on their own by trial and error without looking at the moves list too much.

Tekken 7 is the best fighting game on the market for people who have been playing them for a long time and even new comers alike.
The reason I think it is the best FG on the market currently is because it invokes the feelings older fighting games had where it is actually difficult to play at even a decent level. Improving in Tekken 7 feels 100x better than improving in a shallow watered down FG like Street Fighter V and if capcoms current track record is anything to base it on Marvel Infinite will be the same.
I've been playing fighting games in a casually competitive way since Capcom vs Snk 2 was released and I haven't had the sense of fullfillment like I have in getting gradually better everyday like I do with Tekken 7 since CvS2. It's a deep engrossing game for those looking to challenge themselves and improve.
Now I guess I can comment on the single player content which is fairly weak. The story is not good, I only got to chapter 2 before I decided going back to training mode and learning another characters move set in order to properly punish them with my main online was a better use of time. Treasure battle is a slog that at least can be cheesed if you have a controller with a turbo button and choose Katarina. There is an arcade mode but the AI is atrocious and it's only 5 fights. The best feature is the customization, I just absolutely love how many outfits I can come up with for my characters and not have to spend a dime to do so unlike nearly every other fighting game currently out.
But with that said the real meat of a fighting game is playing against other people and improving your game gradually over the course of many days/weeks/months/years however long it takes and Tekken 7 excels greatly in this regard. Buy this game if you want a thorougly fulling experience that will never stop challenging you to get better.
I also happen to own this game on consoles as well and this version is by far the most superior in terms of input lag and netcode. Only thing I wish it had was juke box mode as I'm not a huge fan of the music.

I think the game itself is fun, but I can't recommend the pc version in good faith.
The main plus for this game in my eyes is the character variations, with each character having 3 styles which can change special moves and mormals, to choose from. Some of these variants can feel quite homogeneous e.g. D'Vorah, where the differences between the styles may seem subtle and only really reveal themselves after some time spent honing the character, whereas others such as Takeda allow for almost different characters due to the differences between them.
Whilst still allowing someone to pick up a character and learn them, the variations allow you to potentially cover macthups which your character would normally struggle in. That's probably the intention behind it, and whilst it almost certainly doesn't succeed in every case it definitely feels like it can help some characters be played in a way which better suits how you would like to play a matchup with them. I can see it adding a bit of lifespan to the game as well, as players try to determine which variants are the characters optimal styles, and then which ones should be used as counters to other characters.
I don't really have much to say about the single player content; the story seems as shallow but well presented as I'd expect, as good a way of shoving in your face the reasons the character you want from the last isn't there as I can think of. Krypt is still an annoying way of unlocking things, possibly moreso since it's been turned into a poor mans first person maze game where you'll inevitably waste half your in-game currency unless you check a guide online, also ♥♥♥♥ spiders. Pretty much any time I've spent on single player has been in training mode.
So the negatives:
Even after several patches the game is still suffering from performance and stability issues fairly frequently, and the netcode still leaves quite a bit to be desired ( granted there's only so much you can do with such a variety of network conditions, in a genre which relies on precise frame windows for inputs and reactions ).
In terms of performance, pretty much any stage with particles is going to cause you problems unless you're a nice machine. Even once the settings have been turned down you can expect <20fps on some stages on lower end machines or laptops. Seriously, if you're in a lobby and someone actually picks the Sky Temple as a stage; kick them, they're a♥♥♥♥♥♥
Stability-wise I've had several crashes and hangs, even after the aforementioned patches. There seems to be a real fragility whenever the game struggles to make a connection with some of the servers, notably the Faction server which seems to be almost permanently down. On some occasions you can end up with a hard lock if you attempt to access the Faction page or Living Towers and the game client doesn't receive a response, which will happen at some point. Similarly I've encountered quite a few issues after matches online, either hangs or crashes, when the game seems to be trying to update standings etc. I haven't encountered as many ( though I have had some ) of these issues when playing training or single player mode, so you may have an ok experience if that's largely what you're going to be playing, but expect some issues if you plan to play online.
The streaming install has to be mentioned as well. It screwed over anyone who actually tried to pre-load the game. That may not be an issue anymore, but the fact that the game cannot be benchmarked initially, and that you won't be able to play even a training match until several of the install packs have been downloaded ( due to the first pack or two not actually including a stage, so the game will crash when you try to load up any match ), seem absurd. I don't know specifically whether the fault lies with Steam or NRS/whoever did the port job, but it is not a good experience.
In summary; pretty much the first line again. If you have access to a PS4 or Xbox One, get the game for that instead. The game seems to run smoother due to fixed hardware specs and also being an NRS inside job, rather than a porting job by whichever sham-merchants did this pc version.

Before I start, I have no knowledge of the RWBY series and know nothing of its Universe. I played this game only because I saw it was a hack-n-slash that could play up to 4-players in online co-op, not minding it was in early access.
I don't know in what stage of development the game is in, but from what I played, it felt very much like it was still in its alpha stages. It was very apparent with how the game was thrown together with mostly its core aesthetics and mechanics, making the game still playable, but of course rather bare-boned.
The game has huge potential and felt fun to play, that's for sure, but I'd definitely wait for the game to be more polished. It's quite buggy still but I haven't had very annoying bugs encountered...Although I died in one of the stages, and the checkpoint I respawned at was slightly altered, the path I took when I died was blocked and another was shown, so it felt like I accidently skipped a part of the game? But oh well. Oh, also, if you don't care much about the game being in alpha and buggy and all, well, the online 4-players co-op is already up and working, so you can hop on that and enjoy that right now.
My main problem with the game is not really a bug, but rather a feature that was included in the game deliberately...The auto-targeting. You see, holding a direction or even turning the camera in a specific direction won't matter on where you attack. You could easily be trying to focus on an important enemy, and for no reason, it would make you target another enemy. It can be annoying when you know some enemies can have their attacks interrupted if you attack them or if you have a huge enemy that is more dangerous, but the auto-targeting system seems to do things of its own. There's no option to disable that, neither there is a button to change which target you are "locked-on" to.
But as I said, this is my only concern with the game. The game doesn't have much yet, but I definitely would play it a LOT when more polished. Even if the auto-targeting system pisses me off and that I would wish for that to change or being a toggle option, I genuinely would play the game some more anyway. (And don't use that as an excuse to not include the option. I'm talking to you, devs >_>)
I'll eagerly wait to see how the development plays out on that one.

Spelunky is a roguelike platformer that manages to be very difficult, but always completely fair, despite its procedurally generated levels. The difficulty may seem a bit offputting at first, but if you keep at it you'll get the hang of it and experience all the thrills and depth Spelunky has to offer.
Let's look at what makes Spelunky great:
-Huge replayability. The procedural generation works great; each run is full of surprises and challenges and is never missing any sort of key element from the game.
-Lots to do: There are a lot of goals for you to set for yourself, depending on your skill level. There's also a lot of ways to play, with something to suit almost anyone's style.
-The art and sound aren't anything extraordinary, but are still quite good and suit the game's style very well.
-LOCAL co-op and free-for-all deathmatches, if you're into that. (NOTE: Haven't tried these features as of this review.)
-Games are typically quick, making this game a good choice if you need something to kill a few minutes, but can't stay too long.
-In my experience, the game ran perfectly with no noticeable bugs.
-I've played this game with both a keyboard and an Xbox 360 controller (No, not both at the same time), and I can say that both control schemes work great. Both keyboard keys and 360 controllers ARE rebindable.
-Success is extremely satisfying.
Now, let's look at what makes Spelunky not so great:
-Can be frustrating, especially if you were really close to accomplishing something significant before you died. But try not to get too frustrated over this; you can try again as much as you want.
-The default HUD is very much opaque and can get in the way of seeing important things in the top-left corner of the screen. The game offers a "Pro" HUD option that I strongly recommend you use once you get the hang of things.
-The earlier levels (The Mines, which is the starting area) feel pretty mundane and repetitive once you've played on that tileset a lot.
I bought this game for $2.50, and I can safely say it has been well worth the money. I'd say it's worth its full price if you can't wait to get it.
Thanks for reading.

WASTED is one of the most surprisingly addictive FPS rogue-lites I've played, full stop. Combining elements of Borderlands, Fallout and (IMO) TimeSplitters / Goldeneye, WASTED throws you into the merciless corridors of the Coolers, failed bomb shelters riddled with radioactive booze and the various factions competing for it.
The story and aesthetic are immediately charming, and the difficulty offers a suitable challenge for players skilled at balancing speed and caution along with health and inventory management. While beginners may find themselves desperate to drink every last bottle to stack multiple buff-inducing Hangovers, a skilled gunner can deftly clear the game sober-- in alignment with S.O.B. beliefs.
WASTED's most pressing challenge is becoming familiar with the threats that can instantly end your run if left unchecked. Purifiers, Spewmen, or a surprise Sod Off / Ratatat Trap upon opening a door is all it takes to drain your Waster's precious 100 HP with frightening speed. That said, these challenges are not at all difficult to play around so long as you know the solutions that counter them, which makes learning those methods to conquer these newbie-killers all the more enjoyable.
Before the Giant Bomb quick-look of WASTED, this game was not anywhere on my radar-- and yet, I've since cleared the game three times and still find myself coming back for more. WASTED is without a doubt my gaming highlight of Summer 2016, and I hope that this indie gem can be yours too.
