There are some other games mixed in there, but I can't quite put my finger on what they are at the moment. The odd part about this game is that there aren't really permanent upgrades so much as you just save good loot for the next run. That part is dissapointing for me. There was controller support which was great, but the game was too dark to play from the couch (and there were no sliders - maybe that will change). The core combat/runs is quite 'meh' to me. The game urges you to be quick about your runs by adding time limits governed by tougher-than-nails mobs that hunt you. Its fine, but I always hated time limits (even in
). The gear felt very repetitive. The traps in the level didn't feel all that useful, but maybe I just needed to git gud. During combat, I felt like I had to just take a lot of shots due to the level design. Lots of narrow hallways with little to really dodge behind.
+More ambitious than the average roguelite. I think this is a great thing. I really like the base and open-world feel.

Wasted is a rogue-lite that draws heavy inspiration from Fallout. Imagine a randomly generated vault filled to the brim with raiders, mutants, robots, and loot. Now imagine that instead of the world ending in the 50's, it ended in the 80's. There you have Wasted. Adult Swim, in my experience, tends to publish unique and well-made games. This is no different. Wasted is a highly addictive rogue-lite where you explore randomly generated vaults, killing enemies and hunting for loot so you can, of course, go deeper into the vault, so you can move to tougher vaults.
The game features perma-death, meaning that anything on your character when you die is lost. You can, however, store things at home so your next character can use them. You might think this would mean you'd have to play carefully and slowly, but Wasted doesn't want you doing that. Take too long in a dungeon and a powerful enemy will begin hunting you. This enemy has a TON of health and is armed with a powerful minigun, meaning getting caught can be deadly. To avoid this, you have to play rather quickly. Unfortunately, even the enemies can be deadly! Raiders, mutants, robots; all of them can end you in seconds if you sprint carelessly into a room. So, cleverly, the game requires you to balance playing fast to avoid getting caught and playing slow to avoid bungling into traps or foes.
What's more is that you can only leave a dungeon by either dying or drinking booze. Hence the title. Booze is found, generally, every three levels. Drinking gives your character a permanent hangover that confers bonuses that can either help or hurt you. You might lose speed, max health, or aiming ability. Conversely, you might up your carry capacity, gain regenerating health, or double your melee speed. Booze that affects you positively, however, is found deeper within the dungeons. This adds a nice risk/reward system to the game. If you're injured, you might want to bail early and take a penalty so you can keep gear you've found, but if you push too far you might lose everything.
Over all this is a story about the apocalypse and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ being used as currency. Wasted doesn't take itself seriously, poking fun of modders, gamers, games, and even Richard Nixon. The humor is generally juvenile but written well enough that it brings laughs instead of cringes and even the requisite computer logs you find scattered about the dungeons get a good laugh or two. Some of the dialogue you hear from generic raiders is repetitive (If I hear 'Welcome to the own zone!' one more time..) but the scripted stuff is really nice. The soundtrack is also more than serviceable, providing a small but catchy number of tunes that really have an 80's vibe.
Overall I highly reccomend Wasted and have almost nothing but praise for it. Highly reccomended!

It's like a streamlined version of Fallout with a lot more comedy and a good amount of replay value.
The gunplay feels good, the weapons are pretty well designed and melee, while more challenging, can be fun to pull off. There's also a nice variety of enemies most with their own special abilities.
The only gripe I have is with the permadeath mechanic and the booze mechanic. They don't mesh very well.
The equivalent of a skilltree for the game relies on you drinking different Booze flavors to permanently increase your character's abilities, but if you die, you lose all those abilities. Whenever you gain an ability by drinking a Booze you're forced out of the current dungeon (Cooler) you're in and have to restart it, which leads to it being pretty time consuming if you want your character to gain abilities, but at the same time, if you die, all that time spent "leveling up" your character, goes to waste.
So, I made it a point to always play it safe and never die and thus was able to enjoy the game and beat it after spending 22 hours farming abilities and items. I definitely spent more time than necessary on just one playthrough but was actually able to level up my character pretty well by doing so. I definitely got my $13 worth and will probably play it through again. I definitely recommend it.
(It's also one of those games that you can easily play while watching Youtube videos or binge watching Netflix, which definitely can make the grind not feel so grindy)

I can forgive spending full price on this because I thoroughly enjoyed the previous game, The Stick of Truth, and this direct sequel does a great job of improving and expounding upon the mechanics of SoT. The movement-oriented turn-based combat is definitely fun, if a little weird to get used to if you haven't played a game with similar mechanics (the one I'm most familiar with is the GBA game, Megaman Battle Network).
I can forgive dual (even triple, if you count Steam itself) DRM because the process of logging into a Uplay account doesn't necessarily bother me (plus, I feel, under pressure from gamers, Ubisoft would remove this or at least minimize its importance in rgeards to playing the game).
I can forgive small hiccups in performance in a brand new game. Some kinks just can't be ironed out completely and require real world use to make apparent.
Hell, I can even forgive day one DLC since I don't buy DLC unless I really want to. And I usually don't want to.
I can't forgive a major loss in progress due to the game just not responding after a basic combat function (the TimeFarts). I had to completely redo Dr. Mephisto's Genetic Engineering Ranch because during the Cousin Kyle fight, I used the TimeFart to revoke an enemy's turn, and after it finished, it just... didn't continue. I waited a good 10 minutes before I finally just quit the game and had to take some time to myself because I wasted a good while going through that nonsense. As of writing this, I still haven't rebooted it up because the desire isn't there, and I fear it's just going to dwindle if this continues.
I can't forgive a substandard story. South Park's major strength to me is the level of storytelling. They follow a very good and very compelling ideology of "therefore and but." This sort of storytelling method creates interesting, fascinating stories through saying "this happens, BUT this happens, THEREFORE this happens," instead of "this happens AND this happens AND ALSO this happens," which just continuously adds to the story and bogs down the pace, making the experience worse overall for the audience. The Fractured But Whole seems to take from both methods, more from "and" and less from "but, therefore." Some events happen in the story that I don't really follow WHY they happen. SoT had a very interesting cadence and lent a lot of its humor and tone from how purposeful everything felt. Sure, it went from "kids playing Lord of the Rings in their backyard" to "fighting Nazi zombies and the government for a stick," but that ridiculousness was proper. It had a good reason to go there. Playing FBW, I forget why I'm doing something halfway through the mission. In SoT, I remembered exactly why I was doing something.
In all honesty, if you're a fan of SoT, this could be a good continuation for you. Maybe you can overlook what I can't. If so, by all means, grab this. It's fun when it needs to be, but be prepared to get grabbed a little ways in instead of immediately.
However, if you're like me and just can't ignore some of those glaring problems, then maybe stay away until a sale comes around or just don't bother entirely.
TL;DR - if you can handle the problems, then grab it. If you're looking for a clean experience, wait or don't bother.

So looking through the comments it looks like this game is pretty divided, so why not throw my hat into the ring. Keep in mind this is just a review and is how I feel about this game. It's mostly subjective so you're welcome to disagree with me if you want. I won't be talking about bugs in this game because I personally have not encountered any of the bugs that several other people seem to be having so I can't say for or against it really.
So let's dive into the game itself and then I'll talk my piece on the whole Uplay/DLC/DRM stuff afterwards.
PROS:
-
Compared to the previous game the combat is just more in-depth. It's a lot more strategic and imo a bit more fun.
-
If you're a fan, then you'll probably like it. It kinda feels like an episode of South Park.
-
I think they did a great job with the music. Different enemies had differently themed music that I felt fit well with who you were fighting.
-
Unlike the first game, you can pretty much change your playstyle whenever you want. This can be good or bad depending on how you feel about class changes. I personally like it because it allows me to test fun builds without having to start a new save file and re-unlocking all the classes.
CONS:
-
If you don't like South Park or are in the middle ground about it, there's a high chance you won't like it.
-
I was a little disappointed that my choices didn't make as big of an impact on the game itself, but hey in all fairness I was expecting less. I'll still mark it as a con but it's more of a neutral point. I was just hoping for at least a different ending cutscene where everyone else finds out I was a girl this entire time.
-
For something priced at $60 USD, it's a bit short. I think I beat it in about 26-28 hours? And that was with me going through and doing most of the sidequests. It was an entertaining 26 hours, but still kind of short for a $60 game.
-
Just like the first game, there really isn't any replayability. I started going through it a 2nd time as different classes so I could fight some bosses again but differently and it's kinda fun, but most people will probably just play a different game.
All in all, I'd personally say I achieved $60 dollars worth of enjoyment out of this game. I would still recommend this game to anyone else who's a fan of South Park, but keep in mind that a game's enjoyment to money value ratio isn't something someone else can gauge for you. How much you enjoy a game is subjective. It's literally whether the good parts of the game subjectively outway objectively bad parts and vice versa. Even if it's the world's objectively best designed game both mechanics wise and story wise, you probably still won't like it if you hate that genre and the same goes for the reverse (assuming the flaws don't make the game unplayable).
Now there's a lot of complaints about Ubisoft and Uplay, day one DLC and Denuvo. So how do I feel about this? (If y'all even care, if not feel free to just stop here and thanks for at least reading this far):
First and foremost I think that these are valid points to bring up since these are all things that could degrade the experience of playing the actual game (Not including the DLC argument). Kinda like if a company decided to use super glue to seal every bag of chips and made you tear open the bag from the middle in order to eat it. It's going to annoy you and make you like the product less.
Now going over these individually.
Uplay: I think it's pretty poorly done platform, but it's not the worst thing in the world. I haven't had any issues with steam and uplay fighting each other when I try to start up the game so I'm not entirely sure what that's about. I mean I guess I use Uplay for R6: Siege kinda often so maybe that's why? But I can understand people's frustrating with this and how it degrades their experience with the game. I'll just point back to my bag of chips scenario from the paragraph above this.
Day1 DLC: I mean at this point it's weird for a AAA title to not have this, which in itself is telling to what this industry has become. Denuvo: I mean DRM will always be a thing as long as big corporations are spooked by piracy. It won't ever go away and it's pretty much a futile point but can you blame them for implementing anti piracy stuff? I personally haven't had any issues with it, so I can't speak to the gravity of the situation but to me right now it feels like a situation where people are getting mad at someone for trying to protect their own stuff.

It's basically Minecraft, but with a lot of improvements - at the cost of size. There's Zelda-lite combat and a somewhat goal oriented incentive for exploration. There's also a lot more furniture and vanity items to find and craft. You go from island to island, exploring for loot and resources that you carry back to your home island, where you're free to construct a base for yourself whatever way you'd like. In the end, though, for my playstyle, it's essentially the same game as minecraft. Getting the resources to use on crafting a cozy base for yourself takes about as much time as in minecraft, and I just don't have the patience.
The game starts with a brief tutorial which reminds me of WoW's questing system, but it's not seen again afterwards. Since every level (or island) is pre-made by the devs, they could have populated every level with a handful of quests to incentivise excursions out of my base, so it's not just mere resource farming I explore for and just make things generally interesting. Without quests, everything just feels pointless. There's no public multiplayer either.
Ultimately, why do anything in this game? Just to get to the last island? I don't need to build a nice home island for that, at all. And if you ignore base building, then you're left with a shallow game.
But I guess that's sandbox games for ya'....

Bridge Construction Playground is another ClockStone's remake (first was Bridge Constructor) of old Chronic Logic's Bridge Builder.
Aim of all those game is simple - you have to build a bridge that withstands trains, cars or trucks, with resources like wood, metal bars, stone pillars and lines.
Despite being very similar to Bridge Constructor, Playground offers more flexibility. Instead of a strict caring about a budget, you can freely build any bridge in any way you like. Every level has also few tasks which requires building a bridge in some specific way - without some resources, with some strict budget or with keeping stress of the bridge under some level.
In comparision to Bridge Constructor, physics is not that hilarious as it used to be. It improved a lot.
Graphically this game is bad. But it doesn't matter at all. Music is nice and not disturbing.
Playground is way less challenging than Bridge Constructor, though it is still fun.
The most annoying thing in Playground is inability to move once set joints. You literally have sometimes to delete whole bridge just because you can't move one damn joint. And it was possible in the previous version.
Also in some camera positions it is impossible either to place parts of a bridge or to delete them. You get used to it, but it is very irritating at the beginning.
And the game still lacks a speed up button.
Anyway, it's a very funny and addictive game. Not the best one of the genre of building bridges, but not bad either. But if you like the genre, it's a game just for you.

Saw Mixed reviews for this game so I feel obligated to write a review since I quite enjoyed it. It's exactly a more simplified version of Bridge Constructor and Bridge Construcor: Medieval, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. I'd highly recommend this game for newbies to the bridge construction genre, as diving straight in to a game like Poly Bridge can be frustrating and lead a person to quit. That's not to say this game is easy. This game teaches you the very basics of bridge building without any hand holding after stage 3 or so. If your primary objective is just to pass each level and move onto the next, sure this is a quick 2 hour game. There are added challenge badges for each stage though which will put even your best bridge construction skills to the test. Use only wood and stone while keeping the cost and bridge stress under limits, that sort of thing. If you're not worried about the challenge badges the game is somewhat easy but that can also make it fun depending on how much creativity you put into the game (take a look at people's solutions to the "Storm Warning" achievement for an example - trucks launched into the air).
In short this game is as easy or as challenging as you want it to be, and it's anywhere from 2-6 hours long. Value the game accordingly, I'd say around 2 to 3 dollars is the right price, but it's a lot of fun for that price.

The look of the game compared to the established world of RWBY is pretty spot-on, which is the best thing this game has going for it, to be honest.
Gameplay is solid and pretty much bug-free as far as I can tell, though combat does get old VERY fast. It basically boils down to left clicking, occasionally hitting shift to dodge, and using a special move when the crowds get thick.
Movement animations are a bit awkward, mainly noticeable when you go up and down slopes.
My biggest issue so far with the game is the replayability/value for your money. As of right now, the entire game consists of four levels that you can go through in about an hour, depending on how many people you have and how often you die. Outside of that, there isn't any sort of external progression system or achievements to give you motivation to continue replaying. Unless you're bored, have friends playing, or just want to use every character, odds are you won't be playing this over and over for a while.
I know this is early access, but right now I'm not sure if there's enough content and value to make this worth a $15 purchase. The devs have said that the price will go up in the future, so if you're on the fence right now, I'd pick it up, if only to save money down the line once this game is more complete and more worth it to buy.

Super Crate Box Review -Detroit0127
This is a free to play, 8 bit, 2D shooter and it's used in such a way that makes it creative and mostly definitely difficult.
Basically the whole objective of the game (in each level) is to collect crates (which will give you a new gun) and then to dodge or kill enemies while doing so. There are a total of 3 levels and to progress to the next level, you need to collect 10 crates. Now, this sounds incredibly simple but it's not... matter of fact, it's insanely difficult and I just recently beat it.
Technically, there are 4 levels including the tutorial and that will teach you what you need to know but not enough to guide you for what you're about to play.
The Guns are really fun to use, my favorite is the Revolver, a one shot amazing weapon and every time you get a crate, you change your weapons. Now, each weapon is a little different, you start off with a simple pistol, and you can get dual pistols, a machine gun, and what is the world's worst gun: the disc gun. Now, the disc gun literally shoots discs, one hit for the small guys and two hits for the big guys. This weapon will go through the enemies, bounce off the wall and then shoot right back at you, this is going fast... and you can die super easily and it gets annoying. There are even mines which actually work well.
There is a character select, but that's not much of a feature (which is kinda of a down-side) you get the same character but basically you just get a bunch of different hair styles. It is cool to have the normal hair flipping around when you're jumping from place to place but it's not much of a selection. 6/10  An indie game that deserves a look, but lacks enough to fall short of being a gem.
First off i would like to state that the game has a solid base, but it lacking in many ways.
The graphics of the game are nice and the environment and monsters are well made, but it does not make up for the lack in gameplay and bland storyline progression/representation. The pet system is a nice addition in torchlight games, but minion managment beside the pet is non-exsistant.
The cutscenes besides the ones between acts are similar to diablo series but are barely captivating enough to watch through them. I understand the game is indie made and lacks the money for voice acting but the current representation is much like a mmorpg that gets boring and bland very quickly. Even a few voice acting clips or character interaction cutscenes would have made a heavy impact, along with static and never changing maps makes replayability that much less appealing.
The gameplay gets boring quickly and the skill system althou balanced, leaves much to be desired dynamically and interactively. Skills are all independant of other skills and are only level locked making the choices at low and mid levels very boring.
The good side is the easy access to modding and the ease of using them, alas, many of them do not function properly with all difficulty levels and often upset the balance the developers have tried so hard to create.
overall Torchlight II achieved a good overall difficulty balance and graphics but is lacking in gameplay and storyline representation.

Great game. A solid RPG with better story than some AAA titles and an enjoyable combat element.
TFBW feels like a small season of South Park. There's enough length to it to be satisfied by the end of the game and want to come back for another playthrough. Character customization is similar to TSoT. Graphics is typical South Park, but handled with care and genuinely feels and looks like an episode of the show. It doesn't feel like a knock off handeded down to some off-shoot developer.
Story: Not a typically deep or engaging story, but it does enough to keep you invested. Pacing was impeccable. I felt no lulls during progression of the main story. It's like experiencing a comic, the story is written to have the player experience the content going "What's going to happen next?". Much like TSoT, the characters around you interact with the silent protagonist in a way that feels organic to the story. I left the main story feeling very satisfied and wanting to replay TSoT and come back to TFBW.
Combat: There are enough mechanics at work here to make combat feel engaging. It's not incredibly deep. The combat statistics are integral enough to consider what your equipping and why, but not enough to require you to break out a calculator and min-max. Movements and actions are animated well and retain South Park's signature humor. Attacks feel and sound impactful. Whether it's Call Girl's selfy sticks smashing against a 6th grader, or Captain Diabetes' 1-2 punch, the button prompts help keep you engaged in the combat. The grid based movement system adds another level of strategy to the game, and it's often a mechanic that's well integrated into several boss fights. The game does a good job of keeping it JUST deep enough, to the point where I found myself tactically evaluating the usage of my abilities and placement, completley forgetting that the "Time Fart" mechanic I was coveting is still in fact a fart.
Graphics & Sound: I experienced no graphical hiccups or bugs of note. I played this game on a 1440p monitor and the menu's, characters, and animations felt buttery smooth. The lack of visual fluff helps keep the game moving and feeling like a premium experience. Background music keeps the tone of the game feeling epic, until you look at your character and his surroundings and realize it's just a kid playing with a bunch of other kids. The aesthetic of the game always brought a smile to my face.
In conclusion: If you're a South Park fan or are familiar with the series, you know what you're getting into. With the humor and character the show is well known for, those of us already exposed to the je ne sais quoi of the show are in for a treat. If you aren't familiar with the show, I encourage you to try this game out. Get out of your shell, let go of any expectations, and just have a good time. The game isn't the type of game for min-maxxers or people that desire a level of depth akin to Disgaea or any stat crunching game. It's not a loot hunting game, or a grinder. The best way to describe the game is an experience. If you allow yourself to experience the game for what it is, you're in for a good time.
Verdict: 8/10

I played this game on my friend's computer, and I was shocked by its art style & gameplay. So I rushed home, bought this game and wrote this review. I've already played it for hours.
This game was in my wishlist in days. I have to say its art style impressed me, but it's not enough for me to gave it a try since it's terrible gameplay trailer: This video only showed some shooting scene, but the game's core mechanics -- you co-op with 3 other yourselves was not shown in the video! I feel lucky not miss this game, and for developers: you really need to learn how to make a trailer to help your game sale better :)
After the trailer "disaster", everything went smooth. You have to shoot down every cubics in the level to have a 100% completion, but time is limited, there's no way for you to shoot all of them down in 60 seconds. But you have 3 other "yourselves" to help you! When time's out, you will become the next "yourself", and you will play along with the last "yourselves", they will perform EXACTLY what you have done just like back in time! This makes game pretty interesting: you have to find correct steps, combine suitable weapons, remember your past moves, and decide the best strategy for 100% level completion.
The game's art style is simple but elegant. GUI system is the most innovative I've ever seen. I don't know how they implemented that in Unity, but it's better than what I've thought. The starting scene is also a "wow" moment, you have to include this in your trailer :)
For me, I will give this game a 8.5/10. 9.99$ is a fair price, worth buying.

This is a really great game with a few minor shortcomings. But before I even mention them, I should point out that it's absolutely worth getting. I have a couple of minor nitpicks, but overall think it's a fantastic VR experience.
Firstly, the aiming mechanics are somewhat ill-considered. Because of the look acceleration as you get further away from the center point, accidentally swivelling your chair while playing basically makes aiming impossible (which can be frustrating at best, neck-straining at worst). I imagine with a decoupled gun controller this game would be even more outstanding.
Secondly (and perhaps more importantly): the gun balance is very poor. Several guns (specifically everything except the laser and the particle cannon) are completely useless. After a bunch of experimenting, I'm pretty certain that it's completely impossible to get 100% on all levels without using exclusively the laser and particle cannon. Perhaps you could also use the instant-rifle thing, but that's about it. The upgrades are also somewhat poorly done, with acid and punch being far, far more useful than any other upgrade.
For a game where the majority of the replay value is in experimenting with different loadouts and upgrade combinations, this is slightly disappointing.
However, those two minor faults aside, I love Time Rifters. Of all my VR games, I've perhaps put the most time into this one (although that's probably just because my PC can't run Elite:Dangerous!)

Sniper Elite III est un jeu de tir tactique développé par Rebellion Developments et édité par 505 Games, sorti en 2014 sur Windows, PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, Xbox 360 et Xbox One. Il s'agit avec Sniper Elite 4 d'une préquelle de Sniper Elite V2.
Le scénario de Sniper Elite III se déroule plusieurs années avant les événements de Sniper Elite V2, retraçant les exploits de l'officier de l'Office of Strategic Services arl Fairburne, qui participe au conflit Nord-Africain, durant la Seconde Guerre mondiale, où il apprend le secret du développement d'une « super-arme » par le Troisième Reich le projet du Landkreuzer P. 1000 Ratte.
Scénario[modifier | modifier le code]
Le scénario de Sniper Elite III se déroule entièrement pendant la campagne Nord-Africaine de la Seconde Guerre mondiale.
En juin 1942, durant la bataille de Gazala, le tireur d'élite de l'Office of Strategic Services (ou OSS) Karl Fairburne est envoyé pour assassiner le Général allemand Franz Vahlen et découvrir son projet secret. Il prête alors main forte aux soldats britanniques afin de repousser les forces du Général Erwin Rommel. Cependant, le port de Tobrouk est malgré tout perdu et tombe aux mains des troupes du Reich le 21 juin 1942 et Rommel et nommé maréchal . Fairburne se rend à l'oasis du Lac Gaberoun , en Libye occupée, afin de subtiliser à plusieurs officiers des renseignements sur Vahlen. Il découvre un document révélant le nom du projet de Vahlen, le « projet Seuche » (Litt. « Projet Peste » en Allemand). Peu après, le Long Range Desert Group sollicite l'aide de Fairburne afin de détruire plusieurs 88 mm FlaK dans la passe d'Halfaya.
Le seul espoir de localiser Vahlen semble résider dans le sauvetage d'un informateur britannique détenu au Fort Rifugio par les allemands. L'homme, nommé Brauer, indique à Fairburne que plusieurs officiers susceptibles de détenir la localisation de Vahlen sont réunis à l'oasis de Siwa, en Égypte occidentale. Fairburne, dont le talent au tir de sniper lui a valu le surnom de « Wüstengeist » (« L'esprit du désert » en Allemand) par les allemands, se faufile dans la ville et découvre que les officiers envisageaient de trahir Vahlen en donnant son journal intime à Hitler. En effet, Vahlen semble prévoir de supplanter le Führer à l'aide d'une super-arme. Fairburne assassine l'officier chargé de porter le journal à Berlin et subtilise la preuve, qui détaille les plans de Vahlen, consistant à conquérir l'Europe après la prochaine victoire de l'Afrika Korps en Afrique du Nord, depuis une base d'opération située quelque part dans le col de Kasserine.
Fairburne et Brauer, qui se sont liés d'amitié, infiltrent la base et découvrent la bobine d'un film secret indiquant que le « projet Seuche » est en fait le nom de code d'un nouvel engin de guerre en production, la forteresse mobile « Ratte » (Semblable au Landkreuzer P. 1000 Ratte, dont les allemands ont véritablement créé des plans avant d'en abandonner le développement). Malheureusement, Brauer est abattu par un obus de char Tigre, que Fairburne finit par détruire. Ce dernier enterre le corps de Brauer et fuit la base. Il rejoint alors le Long Range Desert Group, et met en place un plan consistant à prendre d'assaut l'aérodrome du Pont du Fahs, aux côtés des britanniques, où il trouve une carte menant à l'emplacement de production des Rattes, qui est niché dans le canyon de Midès. Il pénètre seul à l'intérieur du complexe, et prépare des charges de démolition destinées à faire s'effondrer la base lorsqu'il prendra fuite. Fairburne place un explosif sur la tourelle du Ratte en production et fait tomber plusieurs obus dessus afin d'amplifier l'explosion. Vahlen est mortellement blessé tandis qu'il tente de s'enfuir du complexe, et Fairburne l'achève avant de s'enfuir.
Fairburne, en voix-off, déclare à la fin du jeu que les renseignements qu'il a acquis sur le Ratte ont permis à l'USAAF et à la RAF de lancer la Bataille de la Ruhr dès mars 1945, et que les effets de l'Opération Chastise sur les ressources en acier des allemands ont forcé l'abandon des travaux sur le Ratte.
Système de jeu[modifier | modifier le code]
Sniper Elite III a été créé grâce au même moteur que l'opus précédent. Il en reprend ainsi un grand nombre de caractéristiques, bien que celles-ci aient été quelque peu améliorées. On constate ainsi l'ajout d'une mini-map, qui facilite le repérage spatial des ennemis. Toutefois, au contraire des deux premiers épisodes, Sniper Elite III se déroule en Afrique du Nord, et non plus en Allemagne.
Le fusil de sniper est l'arme principale du joueur. Ce dernier se voit proposer une palette d'armes et d'accessoires différents, aux qualités et aux défauts distincts, au début de chaque mission. Ainsi, le joueur peut faire son choix en fonction de ses préférences de jeu, s'il préfère la discrétion ou l'offensive directe. En plus du fusil de sniper s'ajoutent une arme secondaire (fusil mitrailleur, panzerschreck ou lance roquette), un pistolet silencieux ou un colt ainsi que plusieurs accessoires tels que des trousses de soin, des grenades à main, des mines antipersonnel ou antichar, du TNT.
Les fusils de snipers peuvent eux-mêmes être modifiés. Au fil de la progression du joueur, qui gagne de l'expérience (Exp) selon des facteurs d'élimination divers tels que la précision, ce dernier se voit débloquer plusieurs améliorations, modifiant les caractéristiques du fusil (Visée, recul, dégâts...). Une dizaine de réticules de viseur différentes sont également débloquées, permettant une personnalisation poussée de l'équipement choisi.
Sniper Elite III propose quatre modes de jeu : Campagne, Multijoueur, Défis ou Stand de tir.

*Note: Every aspect of my review (especially improvements!) takes into consideration the fact that this is an early access game and that the developers are working on changes continually.*
Things I like about the game:
-Cooperative play: This game is pretty fun playing solo, but playing with friends on any game makes it that much more enjoyable. Plus, the more people you have, the more enemies that will spawn for some crazy encounters.
-Leveling: While I usually prefer the permanent leveling skill-tree setup found in games like DMC, this game makes the MOBA-style leveling system work in it's early access stages since it lacks many maps.
-Graphics: This game is a lot more aesthetically pleasing than I was anticipating. I am not the kind of gamer to prioritize graphical quality, but I do appreciate solid graphics.
-Combos: The fighting system is very similar to DMC where you left-click for a normal attack and right-click to fire your weapon. When stringing together left-click combos, you can throw in a right-click to add a heavy attack. This works during aerial combos as well.
Suggested Improvements:
-Bigger character selection: While I am sure this is highly requested among the community as it is and I am sure they are currently working on this, I thought I would include this in my review as well, seeing how much it is currently limiting the game.
-More maps: Another aspect that I am sure is highly requested is additional maps. While this game is considered a MOBA, the map pool is currently small. Instead of adding more maps to the branch of maps that is currently playable, Making different branches of maps for players to choose to run through would not only solve the problem of the small map pool but keep the MOBA feeling as well.
-Improved combos: I know I said the combos are great, but I do feel that there are improvements that could be made concerning them. For instance, whenever you right-click for the heavy attack in a combo, it's the same strike no matter when you use it. While this is not a major issue, it does sort of burn players out faster viewing the same animations repeatedly. Different heavy attack animations for each combo would reduce this monotiny.
-Customization: Adding the option to change the appearance of your character and their weapon would be something that could benefit this game, too. For example, alternative costumes, changing the color of your weapon, maybe even create a character. While I fully understand that create-a-character for a game like this is very ambitious, it is possible and would definitely draw a wider player-base.
-PVP: While this is not the most necessary addition, it could draw a larger player-base if it was included. The Vytal Festival arena with randomized terrain would be a fantastic map for it.
-Bigger skill-tree: Fully understanding that this is a MOBA, I would like to see and extended skill tree. Not necessarily more skills to use, just more upgrades to the existing ones. Maybe the addition of an "ultimate skill" where the player unleashes a massive strike on the enemy at the cost of all special points and a cooldown.
Bugs I noticed: Sometimes when I am sprinting, the character's legs will stop moving mid-stride. When running across uneven terrain, the character will be performing the running animation for one second and be doing the landing-from-a-jump animation the next. This is especially apparent when running down an incline. The game volume seems to overshadow the characters' vocal volume most of the time.

When I first finished this game, I thought it was cool and fun and interesting. After thinking about it for the last 24 hours, I've decided that this game is really nothing short of a masterpiece. It is everything I want to encourage in video games. It has innovative ideas and controls and marries them PERFECTLY with the environment and narrative. It is narrative-driven, but it's not a movie. In fact, the game never TELLS you anything - there is no dialog. Every word is in a fictitious language (like The Sims).
I have liked and even loved some games which were basically a movie with some gunfire mixed in to make it technically a game (looking at you Bioshock Infinite). This game is not that. The mechanical controls for the game are interwoven perfectly with the story.
And the story is great. This game is the true meaning of an adventure. The set pieces are gorgeous and will take you from feeling like two boys in a small town to feeling like a tiny fly on a grand stage.
Now to the downsides... First, you must have a controller to play this game. TECHNICALLY you could play it with a keyboard, but it will not be as enjoyable. The game was clearly designed with a controller in mind. I would not recommend buying it if you do not have access to a controller with which to play it. Secondly, it is very short. We're talking ~3 hours with virtually no replayability.
That being said, overall this is a fantastic game that innovates in many ways and shows what video games could be and how they could uniquely present a story. If you have access to a controller, you simply must play this game. It is excellent.

I played and enjoyed it for a while, regardless of the things i was annoyed about at the start, the whole dying was no big deal to me until i later noticed, but that story is something i write when im done.
The positive parts about the game is that there arent many Roguelite shooters. This one is fast and gives you a handful ways to play the game. May it be sneaky, loud or if you want to go full Melee, you can do that.
Unlike many other Roguelites, this one had quite a moderate story, which surprised me at first.
Lastly positive thing i can say is the combat is approached the way you want, you can literally let enemies fight, place mines or use your envoirment to  get rid off your enemies.
Now for the bad bits..
Unfortunally.. no matter how many Coolers (Dungeons) you visit, they are all the same aside from maybe on or two rooms the RNG generates in your randomized dungeon. This includes placement of traps which sometimes get lost inside walls or are placed extremly weird.
No matter how deep or how far you are in the game, the new stuff to loot stagnates quickly, often coming to a sudden stop of offering you new toys to play with.
For a Roguelike that is this fast paced it is sure grindy.. the way to advance in this game. Giving you essential boosts and survivability for later levels. That said.. once you take one boost, you are put back home.. requiring you to do all you archieved up until that point against, with just one boost. Which seems fine, but is very little in the long run.
As for my story, and my last bad point about the game. While i understand its a Roguelite game, dying is part of it. However as for your gameplay experience AND your patience, dying with a long living character is extremly fatal. You can store guns, ammo and outfits  at your home to have a new character take up on it, but non-quest related items cannot be retrieved from the one you died with. Which for me was very good and essential equipment. Unfortunally i had about 40~ Hangovers which gave me all i needed, spent alot of time to get those. But died somehow, despite of my full hit stat and high armor to a ye-olde sod off trap, which normally has nowhere near enough damage to scratch me.
After that i lost all my interest to even pick up the game again. I did not want to visit old coolers again as its just tedious to go from generic room to generic room just to hope for the right Hangover to be at the end...
Which would be not so bad, if physics and odd glitches wouldnt be too common of a stupid death situation.
Too grindy for a Roguelite with Story and Advancement, there is no enjoyment at attempting old Dungeons.

This is a game I bought after seeing TotalBiscuit say he had no idea how to review it. I've loved the Souls series and games in that vien (oddly hated fallout for everything except it's narratives which I never really find that interesting.) I have isaac and never really enjoyed it. This game however I've loved. Thirteen hours of fun and Seven hours of Pain. That "Pain" is what everyone seems to hate. The Purifier in CA-1 seems to be a game breaker for some people. I love it.
Purifiers
This is one of the biggest complaints. I can see why people don't like it but at the same time It's something that exists to make sure there is some punishment behind dawdling and taking everything extremely slowly. After a few minutes a BUZKILL PURIFIER will appear. Total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ him. Existing to ruin your fun and destroy you with a minigun. Except he's really weak for what people say. Almost any melee weapon or gun with an armor punchthrough of two is just fine for dispatching him.
. The irony being you need a *lot* of patience to kill him. About two minutes for me using weapons from the first cooler and a lot of cat and mouse.  If it sounds annoying it is, however his gear gives you a -10% to all damage if you wear the full set, and +1,+4,+3, to certain stats. It's really good and you *always* get it along with seventy bullets and his gun.
Knockback
When hit by a gun the knockback is basically moon gravity multiplied by a million. You can't access your inventory, reload, shoot, or move while this is happening. *It is annoying* but you *can do it to the enemies as they do to you.*  An enemy with an SMG will destroy you as fast as you destroy them. There is a stat system like fallout, armor however is a direct *you take this much less damage* and can be negative. I don't believe it makes you take Zero damage, but it does negate the problems you'll have with enemies that will juggle you. Unless of course there are multiple in which case have fun seeing "Turned to mush" on your screen.
*Pro tip : ALT+F4 allows save-scumming.* Again , you can negate fall damage, there are hangovers which do so,  and some buzzes which do.
Buzzes + Hangovers
Possibly the best/worst/WHAT THE F#$% inducing part is definetly the hangovers and buzzes. A buzz is a temp. buff that lasts as long as you are in the Cooler, they can be as bad as Halfing your health, to subtracting a stat by Five. To as good as dealing 1.5x more damage, Plus  Five to a stat, take -75% to damage from X direction, Regen 5 HP every three seconds.  They are the BEST. You can get a "daily" (In game) buzz from a barkeep, it's just one you take knowing what it is and you have the choice of doing so or not.
*Hangovers* are the run resets, the rouge-like part of this game. "Reset" for a free buff/debuff, keep all your gear and "aquired" loot. There is no way (other than an optional thing in the first cooler) to remove these unless you Die. So taking one like 'Splosive Sidecar (BOOM whenever things die about 50 damage) or Bruised Brandy (+10% To all damage taken) is SERIOUSLY a bad idea.
Bugs -
AI have an annoying thing as knowing where you are at all times and tend to walk towards you, which can be abused
It's funny but the dev should find a way to prevent exploitation of the AI by jumping on beds, or by standing in a corner, causing the purifier to spaz out trying to decide between two doors.
TL;DR
It's a great game, however if you don't like GOING FAST or STRUGGLING ONLY TO WIN eventually, you'll hate this. It'll be another ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game to you.

This is an interesting mix of game. It's like Fallout 3, time trial edition: the roguelike. Character death is permanent, though player base upgrades and stored loot are kept. But it's also a blast.
You will die several times in to your first couple of dives. But that's okay. Don't be afraid to die. Take some bad hangovers, store some good loot, learn how the game works. Soon you'll be burning through the game at your own pace, enjoying what you want.
Character build wise, don't be afraid to try to specialize. It's hard in the first dungeon, but going entirely one way for your stats, while it might seem unfeasible, is what will ultimately teach you how you'll want to approach things.
Don't be afraid to go back to old coolers, once you've advanced through the game a little, to take the best hangovers from the lower floors. Once you have stats from armor you like, and you grind a few good hangovers, you'll be more or less unstoppable, barring a very unfortunate encounter with traps, red barrels, and the S.O.B. purifier.
All in all, recommended.

My play time that steam lists for this title is not really indicitive of how much time i have put into Mount and Blade. I actually bought into the open beta of the original game back in 2009, and from then until now it could very possibly be my most played game.
Mount and Blade is a bit paradoxical (pun intended) in that every part of it feels just kinda janky, the graphics at their best are lackluster and at their worst downright wierd, Combat animations are strange, and some gameplay mechanics just dont really work or seem pointless.
And yet all of that doesnt really matter at all because Mount and Blade offers so much freedom and excitement that at many points i've found myself wondering how this game could possibly be this good. Traveling around the map fighting bandits and slowly leveling up your character, equipment, and troops is a great feeling; and slowly building up into a small mercenary force and then into a lords army, and from there possibly a king, is a smooth and dynamic transition. Overall the Campaign mode is extremely ambitious, but fun and rewarding.
Combat is also extremely fun, and very well balanced in the sense that you can become very skilled at it but you're never a god on the battlefield no matter how high your skills are, and how good your equipment is, you can still get taken out in one shot by a couched lance. That being said high skills and good equipment will allow you to wreak havoc on untrained armies.
Multiplayer is also very fun, the game has some really unique game modes, and the online community is fun to interact with.
One of the biggest factors in this game's replayability is the mod support. This game has a legendary amount of good mods ranging from basic changes to massive overhauls of the entire game. I only know of a handful of games that have ever had better mods than this game.
To wrap things up. Mount and Blade is probably one of the best Action Adventure games ever made. If you can look past some polish issues there is an immense amount of fun to be had.

In the vast sea of Minecraft clones it can be hard to find a game that stands out but Portal Knights does a nice job of doing so. With it's cartoony looks, simple controls, and relatively easy combat it makes for a game that anyone can get into. For those looking for a more challenging/grindy sandbox type of game there's something for you as well when it comes to the higher end items with some requiring larger amounts of materials and rare drops. While the main 3 bosses are not too tough, as of the current update (Update v 0.7.0) there are now much tougher bosses you can face which require help from others to take down.
The classes are an interesting touch to the genre but don't really feel like they are fully fleshed out yet especially given the fact that no matter what you choose to play as you can still wear any of the gear in the game or use any of the spells. They should either remove the classes or adjust it so that the gear/spells can only be used by the specific class.
The team seems small so updates/new content tends to be a bit slow at times but they appear to be attempting to implement player suggestions such as: larger worlds, a vanity tab, pets, and recently attribute points and water (added in update v 0.7.0) to name a few. A heads up to those reading, using large worlds can make it difficult to locate the portals and may lag you out so using medium worlds is advised.
Overall it's a nice game but still has a way to go

Great game. A solid RPG with better story than some AAA titles and an enjoyable combat element.
TFBW feels like a small season of South Park. There's enough length to it to be satisfied by the end of the game and want to come back for another playthrough. Character customization is similar to TSoT. Graphics is typical South Park, but handled with care and genuinely feels and looks like an episode of the show. It doesn't feel like a knock off handeded down to some off-shoot developer.
Story: Not a typically deep or engaging story, but it does enough to keep you invested. Pacing was impeccable. I felt no lulls during progression of the main story. It's like experiencing a comic, the story is written to have the player experience the content going "What's going to happen next?". Much like TSoT, the characters around you interact with the silent protagonist in a way that feels organic to the story. I left the main story feeling very satisfied and wanting to replay TSoT and come back to TFBW.
Combat: There are enough mechanics at work here to make combat feel engaging. It's not incredibly deep. The combat statistics are integral enough to consider what your equipping and why, but not enough to require you to break out a calculator and min-max. Movements and actions are animated well and retain South Park's signature humor. Attacks feel and sound impactful. Whether it's Call Girl's selfy sticks smashing against a 6th grader, or Captain Diabetes' 1-2 punch, the button prompts help keep you engaged in the combat. The grid based movement system adds another level of strategy to the game, and it's often a mechanic that's well integrated into several boss fights. The game does a good job of keeping it JUST deep enough, to the point where I found myself tactically evaluating the usage of my abilities and placement, completley forgetting that the "Time Fart" mechanic I was coveting is still in fact a fart.
Graphics & Sound: I experienced no graphical hiccups or bugs of note. I played this game on a 1440p monitor and the menu's, characters, and animations felt buttery smooth. The lack of visual fluff helps keep the game moving and feeling like a premium experience. Background music keeps the tone of the game feeling epic, until you look at your character and his surroundings and realize it's just a kid playing with a bunch of other kids. The aesthetic of the game always brought a smile to my face.
In conclusion: If you're a South Park fan or are familiar with the series, you know what you're getting into. With the humor and character the show is well known for, those of us already exposed to the je ne sais quoi of the show are in for a treat. If you aren't familiar with the show, I encourage you to try this game out. Get out of your shell, let go of any expectations, and just have a good time. The game isn't the type of game for min-maxxers or people that desire a level of depth akin to Disgaea or any stat crunching game. It's not a loot hunting game, or a grinder. The best way to describe the game is an experience. If you allow yourself to experience the game for what it is, you're in for a good time.
Verdict: 8/10

Spelunky is the best game I've ever played. I've written so many reviews for this game, but never taken the time to write an official one on the store page.
Spelunky is the fairest game I've ever played. If I died, it's because I was greedy, or I wasn't careful, or I was rushing. Out of the thousands of runs I've played, I'd say less than five of them were unfair.
It is procedurally generated in a way that there is always a way to the exit without using bombs. Again, out of the thousands of runs I've had, I've only had three that were completely closed off, but those are on the levels that have certain events like "Wet Fur" or "Fourth of July", because of the way those levels are layed out, they are different from normal levels. Speaking of events, there are a lot of those levels with their own events. "Wet Fur" is random and spawns a giant yeti. It only happens in the ice cave section of the game and is not guaranteed. "Snake Pit" spawns a guaranteed pick axe in the mines but the event itself is not guaranteed. Those are just two examples, but there are many more in the game.
There are many secret levels. There are several secret runs. You think you beat the game and you're done? Nope, go back and finish the secret run. You finished the secret run and you think you're done? Nope. Go back and finish the even secreter secret run.
The iconography is great. Each monster has bright different colors so you can easily tell them apart. Blue frogs only jump. Orange frogs jump and have gunpowder in them and will explode if you hit them. If they jump in water, they turn blue and they can't explode anymore.
You always know what items you're looking at, and you can easily guess what they do even if you're an early player. Climbing gloves let you stick to walls, glue makes your bombs stick to things, jetpack lets you fly, etc. All very clear and easy to understand.
The cultural, myth, and monster references are great. This games references monsters and culture and myths from all over the world. The Egyptian references are part of one of the runs, so they play a role in the game.
I highly recommend this game. It's the best game I've played in my years of gaming.

If you've ever wondered what a Fallout-style roguelike would be like, then this is probably the best place to look. It requires a fair amount of patience and trial and error, as is the case with many roguelikes. If you're expecting to build up a powerful character and be able to breeze through the game with some lucky drops then this might not be the best choice.
There is a lot that you slowly pick up on as you play, and player experience is the best way to make your character stronger. It can take many runs and many deaths, but you'll eventually reach points where you get to know the AI and how to get through certain situations that might have seemed like instant death before. For example - The large enemy coming out with a machine gun to hunt you down if you dawdle too much intially seems like an invincible push towards the exit (one way or the other), but over time you'll find yourself being able to look out for his cooldowns and dodge his gunfire. Eventually you'll figure out a way to kill him and even use him to pick off more annoying enemies.
There is quite a bit of looting to do, but there's very little space to store anything. Equipping certain items increases the number of item slots available, and you get an additional few semi-limited ones once you unlock the courier boxes. You can still stockpile items here and there in your base as you go, but it takes a fair amount of grinding before you can build up much of an arsenal. It's somewhat annoying, but I guess it's a fair way to add to the challenge of the game, keeping your supplies limited and making you decide what's really worth toting around.
A lot of work has obviously been put into the game and the developer seems really dedicated to updating it and staying active. If it seems a challenge that you'd enjoy then I'd say it's definitely worth the asking price, just don't expect an easy ride.

First Impressions:
An interesting twist on a game that advertises itself as a co-op shooter even though the gameplay is strictly single player.  To sum it up, you'll be playing alongside with either the ghosts of yourself or the ghosts of others from previous play sessions via Steam Workshop.  The menu itself really impressed me in that I could move around and interact with it, something I don't often see in games nowadays.  Some might be put off by the simplistic art style, but I found it to be colorful and eye catching.  I also like the fact that you can use gold to upgrade your weapons in your play sessions, though your gold only lasts for those arena bouts only.  Once you return to the main menu, your earned gold is lost.  Overall, a pretty fun FPS that worth a look or two.

Time Rifters is a single player coop shooter. You stack your performances throughout 4 playthroughs to blast all the cubes that are strategically placed throughout the level. You must balance your zone control, weapon upgrades, and skill in order to achieve 100% completion.
This game rocks my socks... 4 times in a row. The music is rock hard, the level design is both spot on mechanically as well as visually. Seriously, the amount of aesthetic diversity in the levels is immense. For those who have this game already, take a close look at the wall in the tree level. There's a pixel matrix style effect that is so subtle I doubt many will notice it but the fact that it's there speaks leaps and bounds about the love and care poured over this game.
Content wise, there's 3 episodes consisting of 5 levels each which will take you about 30 minutes each. But if you actually want to beat them aka 100% them you'll be going back a few times. And then if you really want to push yourself you'll try to 100% the level before you've used all your guys.
When you've had enough playing with yourself there are online replays that you can either upload yourself or download to play with. A handful of youtubers have already posted their's up so you'll be able to play alongside them right off the bat.
Downsides? Well even after coming back a few times to up your score, the content feels a little on the short side but in my opinion it's still well worth the $10 price tag because of the immense polish around the game and you'd regret not having played it more than you'll ever regret having spent the money on this rather than something else.
Lastly, a quick note about the VR. If you're a virtual reality developer this is a mandatory buy for you. Buy it and see how to do VR implementation correctly. You don't have to copy it but atleast take a deep look at it and see why it works wonderfully from the autocorrecting camera depending on where you walk with the joystick to the UI they use to the menu and even the level design itself. Look at it and feel intimidated because they're setting a high bar to measure up to.
For those of you who aren't VR developers and wonder if this game is as good without an oculus rift, OF COURSE it isn't! EVERYTHING is better in VR but that doesn't make it a bad game outside of it. In the case of Time Rifters it works just as good and still is worth your time and money.
4/4 Time Lords, would rift again.
Edit: They've just released a daily challenge mode/level editor as a way to offer more content. No excuses now, get buying!

Full video review:

A lot of people know, that playing with yourself can be reasonably fun. Only a few know, that playing with yourself in an fps style TD - like game can be so entertaining and addicting. I would call Time Rifters a fps self-coop TD-like game ;) I really enjoy playing it and can only imagine what a blast people that own OR device are having.
The goal of the game is to destroy cubes of different color, bundled in different shapes, as efficient as you can - aiming at that 100% destroy ratio, and you have 4 tries to do it. For each try you play a differently colored character, that can choose a weapon and upgrades, that are character specific, but not exclusive - you can have all your characters run around with the same weapon. The only thing that's common between your characters is your money - you get those by destroying cubes and picking up the coins they leave behind. Upgrades are character specific - so you'll need a lot of coins to upgrade all of your character's weapons, as upgrades get progressively expensive. Once you've completed an episode, the game gives you the ability to choose and replay it again with free upgrades, so you can test and see, which weapon + upgrades is the most efficient way of achieving the goal.
The game uses unity engine and gives you a satisfying number of options to play around for your best gaming experience. The graphics are reasonable with some really beautiful backdrops. The "combat" is fluid and increasingly satisfying, once you wield a well upgraded weapon and melt cubes left and right ;)
The soundtrack is mostly dub step ( I think), and even though I'm not exactly fan of the genre, I found it fitting with the gameplay.
Judging by the highscores, there is a way to achieve >100% destroy value by completing levels earlier - so yea, it's nice to have a competitive incentive to keep you optimizing that efficiency.

This is a fun single player FPS co-op game that uses replays of up to 3 of your ghosts simultaneously to join you in a timed arena match and It brings a new intense experience.
Watching my ghosts come to life, move around, load up, test their equipment, and get to action was so much fun. I got to learn more about how I play from another perspective.
The point of the game is actually simple. You run around FPS style, shooting cubes and cube monsters that move in a set pattern and you have to destroy them all within a certain time limit before the round ends to achieve the full 100% completion. But this is where you can really enjoy the game because you can create a tactic and then switch it up on the following arena round leaving your ghost to do what you prepared it for like flanking one way while you go the other to shoot down cubes and cube monsters to try to achieve higher completion points. And if one tactic doesn't work then you can think of many different ones to use and have your ghosts perform them while you try different ones.
There are a lot of Steam achievements to earn and even some achievements that have you find intentional arena escape glitches and some cool features like being able record and upload your replay ghosts for others to download and play with them or you can download theirs as well.
The controls are very smooth and the game supports Keyboard & Mouse, XBOX 360 controller as well as the Oculus Rift VR headset. This game shouldn't have a problem running on older systems. I even tested it out on a gaming notebook running a GTX260m with a Dual Core 2.93GHz Intel processor and 1920x1200 resolution with all settings maxed except for AA and got a fluid 60 fps throughout the game. And the cool thing about the options in the game is that you can access and configure them right from your point of view in the main area by walking up to them.
This is an awesome game and once you get your hands on it you will have a lot of fun and try your hardest to get those 100% completion points. :D The only downside I found was reaching the end and wishing there was more. :(

Lengthy text review below video:
Gameplay:
In a sea of generic FPS titles Time Rifters does something different. You are tasked to enter an arena destroying as many targets as possible in a set amount of time. One attempt is not enough to get the job done. Luckily, through some kind of futuristic science, you are morphed into a new avatar and time is rewound so you can play alongside the first avatar. In the end you will be controlling the final vessel while 3 previous Time Rifters simultaneously play alongside you.
It takes strategy and planning to destroy all of the targets. A variety of weapons are available to choose from and collecting gold allows you to upgrade them in between each round. A little planning on what and when a specific firearm is used and how it is upgraded is an important decision that affects the final outcome. The thinking does not stop there as you must also plan on how you will navigate through each arena destroying the square blocks. Shooting random areas commando style will net you a low score with previous avatars attacking the same targets that are no longer there.

Graphics/Sound/Performance
Time Rifters runs fantastic on the Oculus Rift. No screen tearing, no jitters, and a consistent high FPS count resulting in a wonderful motion sick free experience. The graphics really come alive when looking through the Rift and the art style is well suited for a VR experience. The menus are superb and easy to navigate while giving a fresh style to the game. It also looks and runs great on a standard monitor though I would prefer a wider field of view. The soundtrack is also worth noting as it provides a catchy upbeat tempo that matches the play style.

Controls
Controls are a breeze whether using, a controller, mouse and keyboard, or the Oculus Rift. Everything feels just how any quality FPS game should feel. Aiming with the Rift is done by simply looking at where you want the reticule. It works perfectly and I cannot detect any delay in movement. I would like to see more FPS titles using this control method.

Multiplayer
This title has been billed as a multiplayer game where you control all the players yourself. This means that a traditional online multiplayer mode is not included. It does offer what is called “replay mode”. This is accomplished with a player playing the first two avatars and uploading to Steam Workshop so a second player can play the second two avatars. In an age where a majority of online multiplayer games are dead before they even get started, I think this is a fantastic idea that works perfectly with the gameplay. It sure beats hanging around in an empty lobby in the hopes that somebody might join.

Conclusion:
My biggest gripe is that Time Rifters is a bit light on content. The Steam Workshop is a novel idea that hopefully will catch on adding some additional entertainment value. I would have also liked to see a proper scoring system with leader boards and more than one difficulty level as the game seems a bit on the easy side. These two things would have gone a long way.
Still, the low asking price for the content available is fair. It’s well polished and has fresh ideas. Time Rifters is enjoyable using a standard display but simply a must buy for anyone owning an Oculus Rift. Since the launch of the Oculus Rift most of the available "games" fall into one of three categories. It is either a small snippet of a demo like Dread Halls, a shallow novelty experience like Riftcoaster, or a previously made game with Rift support shoe horned in. I have had tons of fun with all three categories but I have been left wondering when we will start seeing "real" VR games. And now we are. Bravo Proton Studio.

Well, unlike most of these negative reviews for the game my game actually works, and you aren't missing anything.
I have beaten 150 games in the past few months, just going through my steam list, and there are about 20 in total that I cannot bring myself to finish. This is one of them unfortunately.
This game deviates much from sniper elite 2, where it turns into more of a 3rd person shooter than your traditional stealth sniping game you've come to know.
Let me begin by saying these aiming controls are not very good, mouse acceleration is in full effect here, no matter what you do, and this is typically a big no no in shooting games. This makes it very difficult even with the percision of a mouse to kill an enemy without pumping him full of 10 or so rounds.
The issue here is that once you do kill an enemy about 10 more know where you are and advance on you, and the enemies in this game are VERY keen. TOO keen. They know where you are if you just so happen to put a pinky toe in their periphery. Let me say, I do enjoy the relocation function, and the 62 minutes i did spend on this game did have me consider continuing many times, which I may still do, alas, there are roughly 20 other games that I have left that require my attention and I feel as though 8 more hours of this type of game play is not something I am interested in doing at this time.
Keep in mind, I did complete sniper elite 2, once alone and once with a friend, and most of sniper elite 1 (even though you feel like you're ice skating.)
Let me also say that yes, while the xray kills are entertaining, it does simply become an old tired gimmick. Unfortunately I cannot recommend this one unless you are a die hard fan of sniper elite and can trudge through about 45 minutes of gameplay between gems (actual sniping and fun) which is what i imagine this is all about.
overall, I dislike giving games a number score, but this is a 5/10, TL;DR  its generic in a way and its gimmick gets old fast. You will find yourself not sniping more often than sniping and running to relocate while ignoring enemies (since there is a vast number of them) in order to find new cover. The mouse acceleration is a big issue and makes aiming a chore I do understand there is an empty lung function, but with the running you're doing good luck with that, and the pay off is that you just get more enemies to bombard your position since your sniper rifle is the loudest thing that man has ever created.
If i come back to this one and possibly lower my DPI on my mouse and give it another real go and complete the majority(or all) of the game I will also come back to this review and update it/change it. This is a first impression over the course of 3 separate tries (20 minutes to finish the 1st level, which is the tutorial/first mission and 40 minutes on the second mission.)
I know it isn't much time, and I understand that, but for a casual gamer that doesn't have much time, youll be hitting F6 more than you care to, and if you forget, may the lord have mercy on you.

Wait for a steam sale.
Is the game worth playing? Maybe.
However, it didn't live up to my expectations. I enjoyed the stick of truth since it was a fairly simple RPG with some good southpark humor. I felt that the fractured but whole was a regression on humor and without that, the actual RPG aspects are not worth the cost.
Maybe I am getting old, but modern southpark is funny to me because they tend to be relevant with some sort of topical/political satire. The show has evolved a lot from the original bathroom humor -- however, the designers of the game seemed to not realize this.
Mild Spoilers Below (nothing super specific to the story line)
There is a whole game mechanic based around using toilets, time farts, etc that I found really dumb and added no value to the actual gameplay. When I saw the electrical boxes that needed to be hacked, I assumed "Call Girl" would be able to hack them somehow. I didn't expect that I would be farting hamsters into them - that was really stupid. Same thing with farting on Captain Diabetes to make him flip over objects or doing "Fartkor" to get on roof tops. It seemed really lazy.
As for the RPG aspects...
The combat system was mildly interesting - it is grid based and your attacks hit at various angles on the grid.
However, the class progression was incredibly lazy. You unlock 1 class archtype, then later a 2nd, then a 3rd, then they just give you access to all of them. This doesn't actually modify your abilities at all though -- it just gives you access to different ones. So instead of Blaster + Psychic combining to be some new archtype, you are just a Blaster + Psychic and can chose 3 abilities + 1 ultimate from those 2 classes. Then if you regretted a decision, oh well, you can access to everything at the end anyway.
Same goes for the gear system. You unlock costumes that are nothing but cosmetic. The only "Gear" you get are the mutagen type items -- but they are all the same. They all give you a flat boost to all stats based on their item level -- sorry "might" level. Again, lazy design.
Then the quest system - really dull again. I felt like I spent more time walking in circles in this game than I did in a massive open world game like Zelda: BOTW.
So would I recommend the game? Sure. Would I recommend you buy it now? No. Wait for it to be 50% off on sale, its worth $30 to get a weekend of mild enjoyment. Not worth the current $60.
