2016-06-17 - WASTED: A Post-Apocalyptic Pub Crawler is an interesting foray into the world of first person shooter Roguelites / Roguelike-likes. It offers a fairly humorous and reference-filled take on what the world would be like after it had ended in a Fallout-style nuclear fire. The down and dirty of this title is that its a first person shooter with permadeath and some RPG and inventory management elements. A persistent world waits for you between characters who will inevitably die, allowing you to re-arm and delve into the dungeons ("coolers") in search of fortune and fame. Well.. no, thats not entirely true, what you're really looking for down there is a good hangover. You just want to get wasted, without getting wasted by the others who live down there.
In WASTED you explore the Cooler looking to find yourself a good buzz or hangover and maybe a little bit of loot and some spare toilet paper to bring back home, ya never know when that stuff will come in handy! Buzzes and hangovers provide temporary and permanent buffs (and debuffs) to your character, with the better ones seemingly found the deeper you go. The trade-off is that if you're having bad runs or running out of resources to keep yourself going, you can choose to drown your sorrows by downing a tall glass of irradiated beer. These are scattered throughout the coolers, but theres also a fairly well stocked bar at the end of each section too so if you're feeling a little weary, just knock back a cold one and before you know it you'll be back at home safe and sound, albeit with a hell of a hangover.
Drink or die is the unofficial motto of the game for inexperienced players, as there are quite a few dangers that lie in wait for you down in the depths, to include some random heavily armed S.O.B. who's on a crusade to cleanse the cooler of its filth.. or just raiders like you actually, and believe me hes brought the right tools to do it. If you find yourself trying to explore every nook and cranny of the Cooler for that one good drink or as much TP as you can carry, you'll undoubtedly have a run-in with the scary S.O.B. who will clean the floor with you the first time that you bump into him. Keep moving and dont dawdle too long if you want to get what you came for; A bad hangover is oft-better than going home wearing a bunch of bullet holes and body bag as an accessory.
-
All fluff aside, WASTED is a pretty competent and compelling first person shooter which seems to realize the vision of the world its going for. Its built on the Unity engine though you wouldnt know it at first glance as the implementation is fairly well done. All is not roses in this game however and there are a few things that stink a bit, but if you're willing to put up with the smell of Unity, theres definitely a gem to be found buried in its mess.
I'm not terribly hip on all the funnies and references out there, and yet I managed to get quite a few of them, from the subtle wordplays to the more overt and in-your-face jokes that the game makes. Don your rubber gloves and be prepared for poop jokes and you will have a fairly good idea of what to expect from this game's humor. The game is published by Adult Swim, and if you're familiar with their shows you kinda know generally what to expect here. Admittedly I think WASTED has vastly superior and more intelligent jokes than most of Adult Swim's stuff on TV which I typically dislike. Its still definitely a game made for a more Mature audience however.
The theme of WASTED feels cohesive and coherent and the AI is competent but not terribly bright (which is explained away in the lore.) The game-mechanics of WASTED are unique, varied, and interesting, but are perhaps not fully thought-out or realized in some areas. Given the wide range of playstyles and people who will be playing the game, that is both a good and a bad thing. I like many of the systems in place, but feel that they could use a bit of tweaking to prevent exploit or unnecessary pace-breaking, yet at the same time I also realize that you can poke holes in pretty much any system and that there are no perfect solutions which fit everyone's needs.
I currently play pretty slowly and find that this leads to a slightly less rewarding experience.. but I'm also not a typical player either and seem to have an affinity for breaking things and systems. Because of this, my runs tend to last a very long time and dont always get very far, which sometimes puts me in the place of needing to save/quit when there are no options to do so. But adding in the options to save and quit anywhere would also open the game up to exploitation and would encourage more people to play the way that I do, which is contrary to what the developer intended I suspect. (Im a hoarder and spend way too much time managing inventory, as I get better I realize its less and less necessary to do so but its still hard to stop.)
-
Pros:
- Permadeath adds a sense of tension to each and every turn, no saving and reloading here!
- Inventory based FPS-RPG. (Not many good games in this genre, WASTED feels fresh.)
- Good variety of weapons and items, including uniques and mods later on.
- Replayability. (Randomized layouts and loot locations mean that exploring is rewarded.)
- Roguelite with a story. (WASTED actually has a bit of story and lore, and its not half bad!)
- Daily-challenge. Compete on the daily leaderboard to see who can get the furthest in a pre-seeded 'Waster's tale.'
Cons:
- Built on Unity. Unfortunately, Unity is not known for consistent or great performance.
- Radeon users have reported framerate problems and some minor graphical glitching.
- There are a few objects in the game which cause dangerous interactions in the physics.
- Limited ability to save and quit without losing progress. (S/Q at end of floor might be nice.)
- Level generation is currently a bit repetitive, room variety needs quite a bit of a boost.
- The level-timer mechanic might not be for everyone, but without it the game would suffer.
- Inventory space is -very- limited for new players. 10 slots upgradeable to 16-18 usable.
- Some game stats and mechanics are not fully explained or worded very well. Ambiguity and uncertainty ensues.
Conclusion:
I went into WASTED without knowing much at all about the game, so it continually threw surprises at me from the persistent (if small) overworld, to the ability to upgrade your house, to the daily challenge mechanic. Theres a bit of a crafting system in place, although it does not feel fully fleshed out and theres also a 'daily drink' offering a different and customizable buff or debuff each in-game day. WASTED tries to do a lot of things, and it succeeds in many areas though they dont always feel like they were perfectly implemented.
At the end of the day, WASTED is a pretty good game and I've definitely enjoyed my time with it on the whole. Yes, its got a few bugs and could use multiple 'usability/interface/keybind additions.' And yes, unfortunately has a few performance issues which might not be solvable for some people. But with that said, at its core is a game that brings a fresh perspective and fun take on the whole post apocalyptic RPG/FPS thing, and if you like first person shooters, permadeath, and dungeon crawlers, you'll probably find yourself a happy home in WASTED.
-

Windows 7 x64
Intel i5-4670k
Radeon 7850
24 gigs ram
Game resolution: 1280x720, with reduced graphics options to (try) and maintain 60fps. Typically have 60fps in the coolers, often have less in the overworld. A fluid 60 at 1920x1080 would increase my enjoyment of the game unquestionably.

The game is a first-person shooter that focuses around "dungeon-ing" (dungeon crawling? You know: you go into a "dungeon" kill people, get loot) although it has no traditional leveling system , it's reminiscent of fallout, but with much different art style, also it's not open-world, the story is linear.
Anyways I'll sum up my experience:
+ The gameplay is very enjoyable, easy to learn hard to master kind of thing.
+ The characters are funny and the dialogues well written.
+ Many weapons to screw around with.
+ Original "Hangovers" (kinda like "quirks" from fallout) which can change the game and your approach radically.
+ Daily "courier runs" (daily maps so to speak) that allow you to get better gear and compete for highscores.
· The game is hard, specially at the beginning.
· The dungeons (coolers) are filled with traps (landmines, bear traps, rigged guns, explosive barrels...)
· There is perma-death, when you die you get a new random character.
· Until you unlock new recipes you don´t really have much to craft.
· After you hang around too long in a floor a guy with a minigun comes to kill you.
- The gameplay can get repetitive, specially if you try to farm stuff (which is not necessary).
- You will probably end up memorising the rooms that you go through, and where is which loot.
- The first time you boot it you get a character creation screen, which matters not since after you die, he/she is gone.
- Basically it lacks a bit of variety, there are some side-quests but not much more to do besides dungeon crawling.
What you do in Wasted is basically enter underground dungeons filled with enemies, you gain loot and hangovers, which are bonuses to your character adquired by getting drunk on radioactive booze, which also make you exit the dungeon (it's either that or death).  The rooms are the same, what changes is the layout of the floor and the placement of the traps, which makes you, after you get better at it, basically breeze through the first three floors of the coolers nonchalantly, after some experience you can perfectly get through the first three floors of the first one with just a melee weapon, get the loot that you want (since most of the lockers in certain rooms always contain the same) and just keep doing it to farm some good booze and upgrade your character, also the AI is pretty dumb and mobs sometimes kill each other , and walk into all of the traps which makes it slightly more interesting and lowers a bit the difficulty when facing harder to kill enemies.
The game gets harder after you manage to get far enough, and the "time limit" (guy with a minigun) makes it so that you don´t have the pleasure of looting calmly and composedly but rather forces you into going faster in order not to be pinned between the purifier  (the minigun wielder) and a hard place; I think that makes the game kind of unique and gives it a faster pace which I personally enjoy.
The game is kind of addictive because of that, you strive to make your character better with the right hangovers, sometimes you get destroyed by a well placed trap and have to begin anew, it's the dark souls kind of thing, the right mix of difficulty, frustration and occasional grinding, mixed with the pressure of the purifier right behind you and the many traps waiting behind every corner.

My play time that steam lists for this title is not really indicitive of how much time i have put into Mount and Blade. I actually bought into the open beta of the original game back in 2009, and from then until now it could very possibly be my most played game.
Mount and Blade is a bit paradoxical (pun intended) in that every part of it feels just kinda janky, the graphics at their best are lackluster and at their worst downright wierd, Combat animations are strange, and some gameplay mechanics just dont really work or seem pointless.
And yet all of that doesnt really matter at all because Mount and Blade offers so much freedom and excitement that at many points i've found myself wondering how this game could possibly be this good. Traveling around the map fighting bandits and slowly leveling up your character, equipment, and troops is a great feeling; and slowly building up into a small mercenary force and then into a lords army, and from there possibly a king, is a smooth and dynamic transition. Overall the Campaign mode is extremely ambitious, but fun and rewarding.
Combat is also extremely fun, and very well balanced in the sense that you can become very skilled at it but you're never a god on the battlefield no matter how high your skills are, and how good your equipment is, you can still get taken out in one shot by a couched lance. That being said high skills and good equipment will allow you to wreak havoc on untrained armies.
Multiplayer is also very fun, the game has some really unique game modes, and the online community is fun to interact with.
One of the biggest factors in this game's replayability is the mod support. This game has a legendary amount of good mods ranging from basic changes to massive overhauls of the entire game. I only know of a handful of games that have ever had better mods than this game.
To wrap things up. Mount and Blade is probably one of the best Action Adventure games ever made. If you can look past some polish issues there is an immense amount of fun to be had.

Finally played this game after its been sitting on my library for a while. Can't recommend this game in it's current state which is 0.7.0. They call it portal knights but I've spent almost an hour unsuccessfully looking for one on the first island. A little better than Dragon Quest Builder's combat at least.

First off, the devs for this title are wonderful. They consistently listen to suggestions from the community, acknowledge their player base on multiple platforms, and make worthy, thoughtful improvements to the game regularly.
Portal Knights is a solid, well-made game especially for its current state of development. While you have the ability to build at your leisure, you also get a robust palate of RPG elements. With separate workstations for each class (Ranger, Mage, Warrior), as well as new sets of armor with each upgrade to your workstation, the class immersion is well in place. On top of that, there are six unique attributes as of 0.7.0, and a talent tree with a point available every five levels. There is also a lengthy but exciting progression, with the max level currently being 30.
The lock-on (many say it is akin to Legend of Zelda) combat system in Portal Knights, considering its genre first and foremost, is unique and well executed. Fights with various enemies become increasingly difficult as you step through each newly opened portal, giving a great sense of gratification for every island discovered and successfully explored. To top it off, there are currently three excellent boss encounters with unique maps, mechanics, and loot.
Overall, Portal Knights has an exceedingly high potential for being one of the best titles of its kind. The community and devs continously work together on ways of improving gameplay, ideas for completely new content, as well as bug fixes. The game is well worth its price, and there is only more great content to come.

I first bought this game in December of 2013, about two months after it's release date, for $7.49; a price which I, by no means, minded at all. The game looked promising, and I was genuinely excited to watch it's development regardless of any bugs, glitches, or lack of music that plagued it's early release. Hell, the account I first purchased this game on has nearly 20 hours of play time.
I stuck with this game for a long time despite their frustratingly slow update schedule, during which the decision was made to make this game free-to-play. Instead, a premium currency and content paywalls were added. I'd assumed that since I had backed the game for so long and purchased a copy during its early stages of development, that I would have access to these features. As you can probably assume, that was not the case.
Is it a good game? Sure. The controls are a little sloppy, but they're easy to look past. The music is nice, and its a great game to sit down and relax with for a few hours. The amount of content you get for a free game is nothing to sneeze at. But after paying for this game just to be treated like any other free-to-play player after supporting this game until now, nearly the 5 year anniversary of my initial purchase, it truly saddens me to recommend against getting this game.

Gory, bloody, and just plain violent gameplay typical of the Mortal Kombat series makes an incredible return so we can test our might further! Despite one of the worst PC launches I have ever experienced, Mortal Kombat X is one of the best fighting games I've ever played.
So despite the fiasco that was the game's launch in which people who bought the game on day 1 couldn't get access to any of the content for nearly a whole day, once the actual content was unlocked you were in for a treat. Mortal Kombat X takes the gameplay that was refined in MK9 and reinvents it in a new way to keep the game interesting. Object interactions and character variations keep people on their toes as new ways to beat down your opponent are presented to you.
Story mode is completely cinematic with a few QTEs thrown in. I was a bit mixed about the actual story itself though. Although visually it was presented incredibly, there wasn't really much to it. Big bad guy appears. Good guys have to go stop him with a load of character cameos thrown in the mix. That being said, compared to most story modes in fighting games (I'm looking at you Soul Calibur V) it was quite impressive and takes roughly 6 hours to complete so there is a lot of content there.
The gameplay itself is tight, smooth, and an absolute joy to play. The character variations offer different combos and abilities depending on which variation you choose. X-Rays make a bloody return and a new feature called Brutalities which are as the name suggests brutal finishers you can do upon last hitting your opponent with a certain move. Test Your Might and Test Your Luck are back as well. Tag Team matches are gone though.
Factions are a big feature in MKX that tries to center around pretty much everything you do. You pick one of 5 factions upon starting the game. When you complete matches, win online games, you gain experience for your faction. After each week the faction with the most point wins the faction war and you unlock a fatality called a Faction Kill.
As of writing this review, there have been a few patches to fix various issues with the game. Online play is mostly alright now and lag seems to be minimal. The link between the mobile game though is still atrocious. Even if you have a valid ID it is touch and go for a lot of people. I still haven't unlocked most of the rewards for either game depsite me fulfilling the unlock conditions. The game is also poorly optimized for PC. It is incredibly demanding and if you have anything less than the recommened specs you're gonna have a bad time. I actually have the recommended specs exactly and I still need to turn down a few setting including resolution to get a playable experience.
Technical problems aside Mortal Kombat X is an amazing fighting game with tons of replayability after you finish the story. Competitive online play, living towers, faction wars, unlocking skins, the Krypt, and much more. The game offers a gratifying gameplay experience that other fighters would find tough to rival. MKX is a must own for Mortal Kombat fans and fighting game fanatics alike.
PROS:
-Excellent Gameplay
-Tons of stuff to do
-Engaging Story Mode
-Lots of unlockables
-Great character roster
CONS:
-Poorly optimized
-Occasional out of sync voices in story mode
-Online connections can be dodgy

Update 6/1/2015 - Netcode is still trash. Updates still erasing saved data. Just to add to the frustration, the game is attempting to reinstall itself. Yes, you read that right..the ENTIRE game is reinstalling itself..all 29 or whatever parts. Do not buy this port. It's a catastrophe. I feel like I lit my money on fire - though that may have given me a moment of amusement..which is more than this game has given me.
I loved Mortal Kombat 9 on the 360 so much that I bought it on the PC and played it again, alas, I cannot recommend MKX. I am not a hardcore fighting game person, so take the following criticisms as you will. I will divide this review in to sections - Story, Graphics, sound, gameplay. Game play will be a bit split-up as I don't want it to just be a wall of text. Note: I am playing with an Xbox 360 controller.
Story- The story mode is basically pointless. I didn't find it engaging, or interesting. The best way to describe it would be as an introduction to playing some of the characters. It's also quite short. But hey, who plays Mortal Kombat for story, right?
Graphics- You need a really, really good rig to run this maxed out. Yes, I can run it maxed out. That being said, I didn't find the game to be anything spectacular graphic-wise. It looks nice, but the characters and stages feel dull and washed out - lifeless. Don't get me wrong, I don't expect a Mortal Kombat game to be vibrant and sparkly, but, I expect it to feel..well, alive. Particle effects are ok, again, I wasn't really "wowed" by anything graphics-wise. X-rays are a bit laggy as well, and not nearly as brutal as I had hoped..and they don't look that great. Essentially, it's not really that noticeable an improvement over 9 when it comes to graphics. Also, don't expect as much damage to character models as you saw in MK9, it's just not really there to any great degree from what I have noticed.
Audio - They sound nice, especially the sounds for breaking bones when doing an x-ray. I realize "nice" is a vaguely descriptive word, but I am not sure what else to call it. Everything sounds fairly crisp and how you would expect it to sound.
Gameplay - I was lucky and had no installation issues (barring when it was released at midnight and that whole mess). The game is not really impressive when it comes to pulling off combos..there's no sense of "woah, that was awesome." The combos are not much to look at visually, either. Further, I haven't really found this game to be one that lends itself to fluidity when it comes to switching from one attack/combo to the next. They feel somewhat delayed/sticky. I can throw a punch, then try to pull off another move, and it will work...but the way it looks reminds me of a poorly edited film where it looks like your character stops for a moment, then goes on to the next attack despite your input being fluid. If you notice my repeated use of the word "fluid" it's because I believe a fighting game should look and feel seamless when changing from attack to attack. I do not get that from this game. Really, what I am looking for is that feeling of satisfaction after I pull off a multi-hit combo but that's missing here.
Online - I haven't played it much. I tried one match against a Steam friend and it lagged..a lot. So much so that it was nearly impossible to play. I have read about other players having mixed experiences with the online, as well. So I guess they haven't fixed the netcode up sufficiently, yet.
Fatalities - That's what we all came here for, right?! Well, they're not really too impressive or brutal. Kitana's is down right  laughable. Throw fans in to a guy, open them and cut his fingers off and head in half - nice..but then she swirls him away on a cloud of fan-air. It looks excessive, in a dumb roll your eyes kind of way. Now, I know Mortal Kombat is all about excessive, but give me excessive brutality that makes me go "Daaaaaaamn!" not "Oh please.."
So what's new in game modes? You can pick a faction to join and engage in the faction war. A faction victory awards you with Kombat Koins. How do you participate? Fighting an "invasion boss"(basically a character from the roster with tons of health that you chip away at until he beats you down), or partaking in invasion towers. This mode was a bit wonky for me(as in, an error with the invasion servers or some such), so I have not played it extensively yet.
Aside from invasions, invasion towers etc., you'll find modes like the Challenge Tower (where you pick your favorite fighter and kill everyone else in the face until you reach the top), a local versus mode, test your luck, test your might..standard fair from MK9.
Roster- It is large and offers a variety of 3 different fighting styles for every character, so if you are in to that, then you'll probably enjoy this aspect. The styles add different techniques and even stances, such as Sonya's Military Stance.
Stages - Remember the stage-outs and such in MK9? They are not in here as far as I know. What they have added is the ability to use certain aspects of a stage during a fight. So, for example, you can bash your opponent's head in to a stone fixture, throw a pan of coals in someone's face, swing on an overhanging vine, and even use a bystander as a club. I love these aspects of the stages as they make the game feel more 3 dimensional and interactive. After the first few times of using them, though, they may get a bit stale as the set few interactions for each stage remain the same.
Costumes - I hope you're not expecting anything. Yes, anything. There are very few costume variants currently. What variants there are, are rather mediocre and uninspired.
Krypt - Not sure what they were going for here but DEAR GOD IS IT TEDIOUS. It's in a first person view, and you have to wander from section to section - through a  graveyard, winding corridors, scary spider caves etc., What makes it tedious? Well, certain sections are set up in such a way where you have to find an "artifact" lying somewhere, god only knows where, in those winding passages. Now, I don't know about you, but I want to use my damn Kombat Koins and I DO NOT feel like wandering around aimlessly looking for a claw, or sceptre etc., Aside from that, there are fairly lame attempts at, what I guess I should call "jump scares." I don't want to spoil when/where these occur, but basically you're wandering and will be prompted to mash a button when something jumps out at you. I was not at all impressed by this and after it happens a few times, it is, like the whole Krypt experience, tedious.
Overall, I was, am, disappointed with this game and would not recommend it in its current state. Perhaps if they add more costumes, polish up the gameplay a bit and step up their game on the netcode..it will be an easier recommend. As for now, it's not worth $60.
Addendum: "Pay $19.99 to unlock the Krypt. All of. Nao" I laughed.

The game plays kind of like a cross between Project Temporality and Sanctum. Movement is fairly quick, jumps are floaty, and gunplay is pretty arcade-y. The goal of each level is to destroy all of the blocks before they disappear either through a time limit, or out a specified exit.
The gimmick is: you play cooperatively with yourself. You get 4 chances to destroy all the blocks, and each chance runs concurrently with the previous ones. So, by the third iteration you're working with two versions of yourself in the past to destroy the blocks. This means you have to remember what your strategy was previous rounds, and also have to adjust your current tactics to make up for prior runs failings, weaknesses, and strengths. The six available guns each have different specialties as well, and sometimes it takes a lot of planning to get the order and upgrades up enough to clear a level at 100%.
Time Rifters takes it a step further, and lets you record your own gameplay to share with other people. This way you can work with your friends to clear puzzles even if they aren't there. This feature is also set up for Youtubers to record themselves with commentary, so you can play along and have them talk to you as you play. It's a really clever feature.
The game itself is very pretty (kinda like Mirror's Edge), and has pretty great music (EDM/Dubstep- but they're not overwhelming at all.)

I've included a link to my video review, below you'll find some quick bullet points and following that is a short but more in depth review of Time Rifters.



Time Rifters is a beautiful game that has a unique spin on the “playing along with recordings of yourself” style of shooter. While ham-stringed slightly by a lack of overly challenging levels Time Rifters packs a fun and exciting punch, ramped up but a great soundtrack.  Your mission is simple, shoot every block and let none escape. Each arena you play in will have blocks that either move about the level or remain static, and you have a certain amount of time to destroy as many as possible. You will play a challenge four times, each time adding the previous recordings of yourself to your current play through, giving the game a faux-multiplayer feel by the fourth attempt.

If you're a fan of puzzle based shooters, or the types of mechanics popularized by raiding in MMORPGs (or Destiny) you'll find a lot to enjoy here. Each member of your team will need to have a specific role and execute that role flawlessly in order to reach perfection.

The levels are beautiful, crisp, and accompanied wonderfully by the electronic soundtrack. Diverse weapons, each with a particular use, will force players to make smart decisions about when and how to use them. Upgrades deepen the diversity by introducing enhancements like more damage, more accuracy and acid, which causes damage over time on blocks. These interesting upgrades can change the weapon significantly, but not always for the better depending on how that weapon is used. Players won't be able to afford every upgrade for every weapon, so they must make smart decisions and maximize the potential of each weapon . Acid tends to feel overpowered, it causes damage over time but doesn't appear to wear off, hitting a block with it means you can immediately move on as that block with quickly be destroyed. Once you discover the potential for acid you'll to never be without it.

Blocks spawn in beautifully synchronized patterns that make each level feel like a work of art. Blocks take the shape of butterflies, bats or snakes, and sometimes form geometry and architecture. Each level has a unique feel and requires a tailored approach to succeed in destroying every block. Perfecting a level is satisfying as it requires you to work together with your previous recordings and be smart in what each character is doing on each playthrough. If you overlap shooting the same blocks as a previous version of you that block will be destroyed faster, but while your current character will move on, the previous version will continue shooting at empty space.

Though thoughtful and surreal, Time Rifters could do with more challenging content. It will only take a few hours to perfect all but a few levels. With that said, this is partially a compliment as well as a complaint, Time Rifters is so enjoyable you will likely be left wishing there was more.

The leader board system feels unnecessary since levels are finite challenges with a cap on how well you can do, so setting a high score isn't really possible. Furthermore, the levels tend to be on the easier side so achieving 100% on most isn't much of a challenge. The Let's Re-play mode is creative and interesting, it allows you to create a recording and upload it to the Steam Workshop for your friends/fans to download and play with, but ultimately relies on people being interested enough to participate with it.

Overall, Time Rifters is great fun and worthy of the price. It's a unique game that you'll go back to just to experience the zen feel of shooting colored blocks and sinking into the vibrant soundtrack.

It's time to put that waffle iron languishing in the back of your cabinet to good use. These airy, delicate and crisp-edged waffles are so fabulous, yet so simple to throw together, they're destined to become part of your weekend breakfast routine. Freeze leftovers, if you have any, in Ziplock bags and serve them during the week. You can pop them in the toaster to reheat (use a light setting) and they come out nearly as well as freshly made, maybe even slightly crunchier.
For a lighter, fluffier waffle, separate the eggs, beat the whites until stiff, then fold into the batter. For whole-grain waffles, use 1 1/3 cup all-purpose flour and 2/3 cup whole-wheat flour. You can also substitute brown sugar for the granulated.
// Ingredients
- 6 tablespoons unsalted butter, more for waffle iron
- 2 cups/240 grams all-purpose flour
- 1 tablespoon/15 grams sugar
- 1 teaspoon/8 grams baking powder
- 1 teaspoon/5 grams fine sea salt
- ½ teaspoon/3 grams baking soda
- 1 cup plain yogurt (or see note)
- 1 cup milk
- 4 large eggs
// Preparation
Melt butter either on the stove or in the microwave. Set aside.
In a large bowl, whisk together flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and baking soda. In a separate bowl, whisk together yogurt, milk, melted butter, and eggs. Fold wet ingredients into dry ingredients. Preheat a waffle iron and, using a pastry brush or paper towel, lightly coat with butter. Cook waffles (using about 1/2 cup batter per waffle) until golden and crisp. Butter the iron in between batches as needed. Serve waffles immediately as they are ready, or keep them warm in a 200 degree oven until ready to serve.

Grand Theft Auto V was one of the greatest starts for the franchise. Bundling a more-or-less "full" multiplayer experience, as had been desired since the days of GTA 3. I have sadly yet to explore the main story, as I'm sure most have as well, but as I understand it, it was fairly true to the genre, and was enjoyed by hardcore fans.
This game also had one of the greatest falls from grace, due nearly entirely to greed by the developers. A "Pay to Win" system was introduced, and was widely disregarded, as most players had no trouble enjoying a game balanced for a non Pay-to-Win model. The developers soon realized this issue, and quietly set to work devising a way to increase in-game sales.
An incredibly popular update came out at first which included heists and a number of "luxury" items and properties to purchase. The heists gave enough money to buy the new features. This was the last balanced update.
From this point on, the ability to give a friend some of your hard-earned cash was removed, supposedly to stop "hackers". Along with this, new updates came out adding minimal features, a few really cool new toys, and a huge in-game pricetag to pay in order to enjoy them.
The game becomes a grind at this point, running the same 3 or 4 missions over and over, to make tiny amounts of cash. Every new feature costs more and more money, and the options for making money become fewer and fewer.
At this point, the multiplayer experience is an expensive one, spending hundreds of real-life dollars in order to try a single new feature in-game. All that is left is the relatively solid Single Player game.
The modding community had been hard at work since release making the single-player more chaotic or interesting: or showing off technical examples that would be later used to create fairly sophisticated mods.
This avenue of enjoyment has been ended as well.
This game went from an exceptional multiplayer experience to a fairly average single-player experence. They axed 2/3rds of the game.

Heroes and Generals holds a special place in my heart, so I'll try to write an un-biased review on it.
The game over all out-weighs cons with pros, so after stating that; we'll start with the pros:
Pros:
Society -
The society / community of H&G players varies, though speaking from my experience with the German army throughout a few months of play was quite nice, the players were polite, we played somewhat strategically, and overall we didnt have that many complainers or team-killers
Gameplay -
The game controls beautifully, couldnt ask for better. Planes, Vehicles and Infantry all control as if they were created for a high budget, professionally developed game.
Sounds -
Oh my god, the sounds are ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful (Excuse my french). The guns, shells and bombs are the most amazing and / or most terrifying thing to listen to while running through a forest sneaking up on an enemy soldier.
Visuals -
Personally I can only play this game on medium, so speaking from that stand point, the visuals are pretty good too, I prefer the foggy maps purely out of ambient gameplay; and the game does the fog so perfectly (aside from it being in buildings).
Currency -
Currency could be improved on a little, but otherwise its pretty good. A player might get roughly 1000 credits per match, if they play well, and about 300-400 will be spent on repairs and re-arms. Overall this is a nice currency system aside from a few problems that arise, see con section for those.
Pay to win -
There is no pay to win in this game, despite people saying so. My version of a pay to win game is creating items of over-powering regular items that are only available via playing real money, for example making a regular gun have ~200DMG and offering a gun for ~300DMG, but you can only get it by paying $5.00. So this game allows everything to be bought via credits, including premium membership (This is an awesome idea and I love it), though to get enough credits it will take a long few days of grinding.
And now we move on to the cons:
Menu -
I have a big issue with this one, the menu (In which you customize graphics settings) can only be accessed in game, so you have to deal with the whole cursor-moving-at-5-FPS-trying-to-turn-down-the-graphics thing for a few minutes after launching into the game. I think it would just be a bit easier to put the menu in the match-selector screen.
Currency issues -
The currency, whilst being relativeley balanced, also has the issue where if you use a Sniper class / Pilot / Tanker and you arent very good at it (._.) you end up losing almost all of your credits repairing and re-arming, meaning that you get no where progression-wise.
Reto -
Reto has stated that they are working on this, but I havent heard anything about it so far so Im putting it in for the hell of it, Reto has a tendancy to update or upgrade their game, but not (what I assume to be) tidying up their code and assets, meaning that after an update there will usually be a long section of time in which the server is taken offline to fix some error that arose due to their lack of organization. This is a small issue, but when you play on AU servers and there is already a lack of players, and then the servers go down, it can get quite irritating.
Overall I love this game, the Pros will outweigh the Cons any day and I will tell anyone that asks to play the crap out of it despite its few flaws.

There was a time when I would have wholeheartedly recommended this game based on its singleplayer and multiplayer alike. It has a pretty solid story and base gameplay, and initially the multiplayer provided an interesting environment for both running missions and screwing around with friends. Since then, however, things have changed significantly.
Many complaints in the past were centered around the abysmal hacking community that surrounded this game, but every day I find it harder and harder to hold their actions against them. While many laud 2K for releasing many "free" additions to GTA Online, it's become increasingly clear that the pricing of these additions is specifically tuned to push players to purchase real-money "Shark Cards," requiring sums of in-game money that are nigh-impossible to acquire for anyone that doesn't treat playing GTA Online as a day job. Clearly this strategy has paid off, with 2K raking in incredible profits off of these microtransactions, and giving up on any plans to release single-player DLC for the game.
This is fine. I don't like it one bit, but it's a fairly common business practice and all I can do is expect people to vote with their dollars. What isn't fine, however, is the increasingly money-centric strategy that 2K has been pursuing with regards to its community. They have taken to aggressively shutting down any group or service that they fear may negatively affect their profits, inclding modding tools, private servers, and so on. This comes across as nothing more than an attempt to funnel more players into GTA Online, where the money is, at the expense of hurting their community.
Conclusion:
I can't approve of this practice, and I can't recommend GTAV as a fun experience anymore. It still has a solid singleplayer campaign, but the singleplayer experience is now relatively limited with the shut-down of the OpenIV modding suite. The multiplayer experience, while fun at times, is hopelessly grindy for the purpose of enticing you to purchase real-money shortcuts. The community is...pretty bad. Lots of angry, slur-spewing kids with the occasional helpful player willing to lend a hand. Overall, I just can't find much reason to play it at this point.

I'm one of those people who is returning from all the way back in the Tekken 3 era. I had a Playstation 1, ps2 was released and I bought a PC, and I've stuck with PC ever since. The game surprised me, I recall having pretty bad experiences with Tekken 5, Tekken 4 felt subpar compared to 3 as well to me, so I was a bit worried Tekken 7 just wouldn't be able to live up to the feel of Tekken 3. As it turns out, I had no reason to worry, this game is awesome.
If you're new to tekken (or better yet, fighting games), I'll tell you what probably the most important feature to me is. Call me a casual n00b but, I think one of the biggest reasons why I like tekken and not street fighter is because the control schemes aren't crazy difficult. I mean street fighter is cool and all, but spinning around the analogue stick 3 times (exaggeration) and pressing X to execute a double punch just isn't for me. I prefer the Tekken way, where you press X twice for a double punch. In street fighter you will press ---up,left,down,right,down,left,x--- to perform one super cool move, and you need to be autistic enough to get that first part right to be successful in street fighter. In Tekken however, press ''X+Y,X+Y''  to perform a super cool move or even you know, the really cool moves "Up to the right, X+Y" (on Yoshimitsu this makes you fly using your sword as a helicopter blade, I'm not joking) so yeah, I don't know about you but it's just a lot easier for me to press one movement button and two action buttons, than to spin my analogue stick around as if I'm having a seizure and then pressing one action button to do cool moves.
Fair word of warning: Play this with either a playstation-like controller or an arcade board thingy, don't use the keyboard or an Xbox controller like a scrub, it just doesn't work as well. Logitech Dual Action or Rumblepad 2 are good choices. I'd say the xbox controller layout is sub-optimal for this game (would explain why Tekken 6 failed to take off on Xbox) I know I used Xbox button examples above but that's just because my rumblepad has em. As for the steam controller... Also sub-optimal (It's difficult to press sideways down or up on the D-Pad so you need to use the analogue stick) use the D-Pad for movement, it works better in this game than an analogue stick (even if it was designed for arcade sticks originally).
Cons:
- I don't like the idea of crossover characters from 2D fighters like Street Fighter. There's only one in the game right now, Akuma, and playing against him just feels silly, he doesn't fit in. I could say the same about Eliza but she's only a near
miss. (If they wanna do crossovers so desperately, try Soul Calibur, but honestly... why not just add more of the old characters? Where's Julia? Where's Anna? Boskonovitch? Mokujin&co? Gon? Jackie Cha... . . Lei Wulong? Kunimitsu? (Guess we have master raven instead of kunimitsu?) There's plenty of tekken characters left out, why add characters from outside the series when you haven't even finished adding all of your own characters?)
- Arcade mode is basically pointless, you play against 4 or 5 characters, then you get a credits list, that's it. To replace what used to be cinematics at the end of arcade mode on each character, there is a single fight side-story for all characters outside of the main story in the story menu (this too feels kinda pointless, the old system was more "tekken")
- Rage Art, this new mechanic is sort of a hit and miss thing, in tekken usually you either had skill to beat your opponent, or not, but with this new mechanic, even if you lack the skill to beat your opponent, once you are beaten within an inch of your life and rage is activated, in many cases you will only need to land your one (rage art) hit and you will take half the HP off your opponent, meaning that if you're in a fairly narrow fight where two players have low health, the one who drops into rage first has a better chance of winning than the more skilled player who should be winning in that scenario.
- The Netcode sucks, matchmaking in ranked matches takes a while and you will very VERY commonly end up finding a match, requesting a fight only to have it say "Connection to opponent lost", not only this but there's also this 'syncing' thing they have going on when two players are connecting to each other, sometimes this syncing takes a very long time, and sometimes it simply times out "Connection lost". Also in tournaments, spectation is completely broken, I've sometimes spent ages syncing to spectate the finals to eventually end up with the fight being over and me not getting to see anything.
- The Tournament system design is broken two ways, the first way is that when the tournament is started, the reward pot will increase based on the amount of players playing (2 million for 8 players, 500k for 4 players), the problem is that if someone gets beaten in a fight and they decide to leave, the reward pot drops for everyone else (even if that person wasn't gonna fight again anyways) that person is also stripped off their reward (there's usually a 300k money reward even for 5th place) I don't know why they'd try to force beaten players to watch the tournament, that's just silly, they clearly don't know gamers very well if they think they'd stick around for that instead of playing. The second way in which it is broken is that if the tournament host leaves, the tournament is canceled and nobody gets their reward (so if a host is beaten at the start of a tournament and decides to bail cus he wants to fight more, tournament is over and nobody gets their rewards).
- There are some gimmicky character customization items you can add to your character (like assault rifle) and then actually use in combat, it's a bit unorthodox for games like this.
Pros:
- There are a lot of classic characters in the game, mandatory Heihachi Mishima and Yoshimitsu included, there's also Xiaoyu, Eddy Gordo, Hwoarang, Bryan Fury, Jin Kazama, Kuma/Panda, King, *Jack, Nina Williams and Paul Phoenix to name a bunch, and they all seem to have their old moves (although some may have been refurbished (yoshimitsu's half hp stab move is now only quarter hp stab move :( (and yet the game has regular moves that take half hp on other chars) and the button combination to do some of them may have been altered) so if you want nostalgia, you've got it.
- Rage art, yes, I said it's a con, but it's not all bad, it adds an extra layer of difficulty to defeating your opponent, you can't simply keep hitting them until they die because if you get careless, you may be the one who ends up dead. Rage arts can easily be blocked so you can throw in a few faints to dupe your opponent into using their rage art when your guard is up.
- Tournaments are pretty damn cool when they're not busy being broken.
- To make up for the now pointless Arcade mode, we now have Treasure Battles which is basically survival mode where you will fight and fight and fight as many battles as you can until you go down last I did it I went for 70 consecutive wins and I still didn't lose, so next time I want to do it I can pick it up where I left off since your win count doesn't reset if you take a break. In treasure battles you get a reward at the end of every fight, a treasure chest or two (with customization items usually) and cash money. The more consecutive wins you have the higher your money reward and the better your chances of epic lootz.
- Character Customizations (yay!) and that assault rifle you put on your♥♥♥♥♥doesn't have to be just for show either!
- Online play! Despite the netcode issues, it's pretty fun, I've spent most of my time in this game beating the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of my little brother who lives a 15 minute drive away over the internet. (The good old Versus mode where you play locally on the same screen is still there, don't worry!, but you do not get any rewards for it which sucks)
And that's about it. Buy it, have fun! Money well spent!

Wasted is a humorous satirical adaptation of the Fallout universe. The art style is akin to Borderlands or comics and works well for the setting Mr.Podunkian wanted to create. All of this helps provide the face for what is otherwise a great and testing roguelite experience.
You start as a lost "Waster" who stumbles upon an abandoned house, where you setup shop, and your first "Cooler"! The Coolers function as the Procedural dungeon system for the game and creates a good path to expand on content later without excessive effort. The procedural system is continually being updated based on feedback to prevent bottleneck or trap scenarios from occurring.
The main theme and titular claim is, of course, Booze. Your whole journey and foray into the Coolers initially is driven by the drive for those sweet, sweet glowing bottles. The "Booze" are the key power-up in the game and are also your safety net to escape the Coolers. They carry over between dungeon dives but not between characters and since this is a Roguelite, you may die a few times.
- Great Gunplay - Different guns have proper accuracy and bullet spread to make them feel different
- Urgency - That S.O.B. Purifier lends a sense of Urgency that most roguelite do not have. This causes great focus on shifting priorities.
- World Development
- Musical Score - The 80's retro track is great.
- Enemy Factions/Variation - For such a small project, the variety and theme of enemies was well thought out.
- Daily Challenge and Leaderboards - Everyone loves a little competition
- Lack of Indicators - While I support the S.O.B. Purifier, his random nature is a bit unnerving even for experienced players.
I.E. Sometimes he will spawn as I finish a floor, Other times, he will spawn 1 room in. There is definitely a variable timer for    his spawn but it would be good to see more consistency. This would let new players start a floor and KNOW how quick they need to be instead of guessing.
- No full map - The minimap is available and can be used but later levels get bigger and no full map option exists.
-
All in all, I am quite pleased with my purchase of this game and am glad I went back to give it a second look after the initial launch.

So here's another review about how the so-called SOB ruins the fun of the game. You've probably already heard about it, but if you haven't: on every floor, there is a killing machine enemy that spawns after a certain time. And it's very boring.
You've probably already noticed or figured out that this is a roguelite type game, where you make dungeon runs through a certain set of floors (the first dungeon has 10), while collecting loot and gear upgrades along the way. There are other roguey features like random potions and, of course, permadeath. It has a fun take on permadeath that's similar to Rogue Legacy: if you die, that specific character is dead forever and you get a new, randomized one.
The gunplay is pretty good, even if the "aim down sights" is of that really weak mobile variety where it just zooms in a little and your character doesn't actually raise their weapon. The loot is pretty good too. The graphics are decent for what they are and there is crafting, trading and little side quests. None of these features are very deep, but it's nice that they're there.
The humor is, in my opinion, rather low brow but most of all it's way too wordy and takes too long to get to the punchline. Dev needs to look up the phrase "brevity is the soul of wit", because it's true and he seems to have no idea because the NPCs will just prattle on and on repeating the same joke like 10 times. It's long-winded poop, fart and beer jokes. If you think a 5 minute joke about farts sounds like the height of hilarity, you will adore it.
Overall, the game comes together well and is a very fun entry to the roguelite genre. I unfortunately haven't played Ziggurat yet, but Wasted is probably the best roguelite FPS I've personally seen. If it wasn't for the two things that really bring it down for me.
Let's start with the short one: the random potions I mentioned have various effects, some good and some bad. Raise attack, lower defense, you know the type of stuff. Typical RPG potion stuff. My problem is that there's one that removes your crosshair, which is just devastating for me. This isn't the type of game that has a FoV and gun model that allows you to just point with the barrel, at least not for me, so losing my crosshair essentially means that I'm dead. Since that potion is in there, I can't drink them at all. Risk is too great for me. Kind of a boring potion to throw in there, isn't it? Sort of like if Spelunky had a potion that stops you from jumping for the rest of the game.
Onto the big problem. The infamous SOB Purifier. He's like the ghost in Spelunky, except massively annoying and not at all easy to deal with. Once you get over the initial shock of the ghost showing up, it's actually pretty easy to lead and dodge. Just gotta make sure you're not running into a dead end, and you should know where those are if you spend long enough on a level in Spelunky. The ghost takes his time to come out. I don't know the exact numbers off the top of my head, but in Spelunky the ghost maybe shows up after maybe 3 minutes in levels that a decent player can easily beat in 30 seconds or less. In most runs, you have to force the ghost if you want to jewel farm for score.
The SOB works in the exact opposite way! He shows up incredibly quickly, knows exactly what you are at all times, and chases you from the floor's starting room to wherever you happen to be. This stops you from looting carefully, using the game's built-in stealth mechanics or the trap mechanics. There simply isn't any time to be messing around with all of that. All you can do is rush as fast as you can through the rooms, open as many containers are you think you have time for and sprint to the exit. This problem is exacerbated by the fact that the game generates exclusvily linear floors that can and often do have dead ends. If you're not equipped to kill the SOB, you can lose a run simply because you weren't psychic and didn't know if the left door or the right door would lead to a dead end. If you guess wrong, you'll end up in a dead end that's so long that you won't make it back to the fork before the SOB cuts you off.
But wait, there's more! There's even more levels of exacerbation in the knockback effect and the visual effects that occur when you take damage. You see, the SOB carries a fast-firing minigun, but the visual effects are obviously designed for regular fights with regular enemies and their comparatively low rate of fire and damage. When they hit you, you're dazed for maybe a second and it's fine, but when the SOB unloads... In short, you can't move or even see a ♥♥♥♥ing thing. Your screen is literally just one giant blur, and the knockback effect from every single shot will stunlock you in a corner.
It feels like the developer of the game is one of those people that has misunderstood what "rogue" is supposed to mean. It's supposed to mean "tough but fair" and "requires experimentation and player knowledge", but some people think it means "dying over and over to frustrating things". The developer seems to be in the latter camp and refuses to change his mind about his designs. It's too bad, because this could've been a gem.

Love it, love everything about it. I've been waiting for a roguelike/lite FPS that actually plays well for longer than I care to recall, and this is the one. The hangover/perks system is solid and you can make some pretty diverse builds, the gunplay feels right with a range of weapons that actually differ from one another outside of DPS, level generation is pretty good, and the humor even got a few chuckles from me. Honestly, I have a hard time coming up with something that I have a serious problem with.
My two cents on the divisive SOB topic: he's fine. Usually I'm the type to explore every square inch of a level and open all the drawers and horde all the junk but the SOB thankfully saved me from myself since doing that usually leads to burnout on a game since 80% of my playtime turns into pointless, compulsive gathering. The sense of urgency is great, leads to some genuine exploration decision making with the challenge rooms as well as some top-notch risk/reward situations (I'm looking at you, Fallout 4 - no risk all reward), and the timeframe isn't so tight that you absolutely must sprint to the exit. If you need to mindlessly gather garbage to have fun, there are plenty of games that let you do that, stop weighing this game down with bad reviews because you have a monkey on your back and let it be itself. The knockback reduction was appreciated, so baby doesn't end up in a corner after one hit and you can make a messy escape if you're not good at stealth. You know what you're doing, guy.

I really can't sing the praises of Torchlight 2 enough.  A lot of people I know describe it as "Diablo 2.5" and to be fair, it kinda is.  I maintain, however, that it's not a bad thing.  Graphically, it's as pretty as anything I've seen Diablo 3 produce.  Its interface will be instantly familiar to you if you've played Diablo 2, unlike D3 which looks like I'd have to learn all over again.  It has a quest system overworld-and-dungeons combo you'll be familiar with from D2, a potion and scroll system reminiscent of D2's, an item transmutation system that's a very simplified variation of D2's, even tiny atmospheric critters you can squish underfoot, just like in D2.
That's pretty much where the similarities end.  For one, your inventory is far more convenient.  Gone are the days where you have to juggle space for every item - now everything takes up a single inventory block, and furthermore, consumable items and spells (more on those later) have their own inventory tabs.  Gone are the skill trees, where you have to take
skill in order to take
skill.  Now if you meet the level requirements, you can level the skill.  You can even freely mix skills between various trees without feeling like you're penalizing yourself.  Gone is the irritating stamina system - you can move at full speed, full time, instead of being forced to walk unless you guzzle potions.  Gone are the complicated extra rarities of stuff - there's normal, there's enchanted, there's rare (which includes some sets), unique (also with some sets), and at the highest end, legendary.  Everything drops, eventually.  No need to jump through complicated hoops of requirements to get a particular item - if you're at the right level range for it to drop or appear in the Gambler Shop's inventory, you can get it, if you have the patience and gold.
New to the genre are permanent pets.  They're more than just there to look cute.  For one, they have their own inventories, which are as robust as yours.  Load 'em up with everything you don't want to carry, like all those trash items you'd never bother with otherwise.  Then, send them off to town to sell your loot.  No need to stop adventuring or use a town portal scroll just to clean out the garbage!  Your pet can even go purchase supplies for you while you're in the field.  Just a brief one or two minute wait is all it takes to get whatever basic amenities you need to keep adventuring.  More than just pack mules, all pets can fight, possessing a basic attack.  However, you can also teach them skills, too.  Ever wanted an alpaca that could spit fire and ice?  How about a bulldog that shoots swarms of bees when it barks?  Or maybe a necropanther - a panther necromancer, summoning skeletal archers and exploding zombies?  Find the right spell scrolls, and your pet can do just that!
Speaking of spells, these little gems are throwbacks to the days of Diablo 1, where all the magic you own was found in the dungeon and learned the hard way.  Spells exist in addition to your class's skills, and you can have a maximum of four spells.  They're not unique to any class - any class can learn any spell, with the only restriction is having the required level or better.  They range from passive effects to buffs to direct damage spells.  Your berserker, in addition to his horrific melee combat ability, can supplement his murderous rampage with fireballs, or buff up his attack and movement speed to get him into the fray faster.  It all depends on what spells you find and learn.
Finally, Torchlight II does away with the slowness and stodginess of Diablo 2's gameplay.  Characters are fast and dynamic, enemies are slightly fewer but more brutal, with many, many more enemies having special attacks and abilities, not just champions.  You need to think on your feet a lot more, and use your skills intelligently and in good combination to dominate your foes.  There's less a focus on the stats you fight with and more on
you fight, and there's always numerous ways you can approach a situation with every class.  As an engineer, do you charge in with melee attacks and rely on your armor and defensive buffs to survive?  Or do you hang back with a cannon and blast crowds of enemies while your various killer robots do the grunt work?  It's up to you, and both approaches are completely viable.  In addition, enemies and the world feel more 'alive' - they don't just approach you in random themed hordes, but instead appear dynamically from the environment.  Ezrohir ambushers will burst from the sands of the desert underfoot.  Sturmbeorn raiders will leap from the cliffs overhead to challenge you.  You'll encounter zombies and ghouls devouring a corpse, and when you kill them, the flesh-stripped corpse rises as a skeleton to fight you as well.  Vile mystics will be found performing rituals upon desecrated tombs or will be trying to sacrifice innocent captives, and you can draw the attention of a lich by disturbing its grave.  You can rescue slaves from packs of slaver-bandits, and be surprised when you fight a horrid monster, only for its even-more-horrid mate to show up and join the fight!
All in all, I consider Torchlight 2 to be a worthy entry to the action-RPG dungeon-crawler subgenre.  It strips the BS out of Diablo 2, keeps what Diablo 2 did well, and then improves upon the whole formula without being as wildly experimental as Diablo 3 is.  And hey, if you
like what Torchlight II does, vanilla?  Well, it's mod-friendly, and has Steam Workshop support.  If you don't like it, change it!

As someone who loves stealth games, but is inevitably bad at them, I found Sniper Elite 3 to be a very mediocre experience through and through. While the sniping felt excellent, which is exactly what it needed to do well, it doesn't really do much else particularly well, though some are notable.
Let's start with the good: the sniping. There is a clear sense of momentum (if that even makes any sense), and the accuracy of your shot is dependent on your heartbeat/breath and the distance you are from the target. It adds challenge to the experience, and is welcome to stay. However, I cannot get over how cartoony everything looks. Even the environment, and down to the character models - it all feels like a cartoon! It's hard to take Karl Fireburn (or whatever his name is) seriously when he looks like an action figure. Anyway, the graphics didn't bother me too much except for about 5 minutes whenever I would boot up the game.
Atmospherically, I think the game did pretty well, but it wasn't very immersive. The music accompanies the tense gameplay very well at times, but soldiers seem to have superhuman hearing and seeing abilites sometimes, and sometimes you could be in plain sight and the soldiers wouldn't see anything. Rather disappointing and immersion-breaking. Killing them only feels good with a sniper or the little silent pistol (similar to the one in Metal Gear Solid V - a much better game than this; actually, I mostly bought this because it reminded me of MGS.). The automatic weapons are terrible, and it felt horrible to use them.
The game also gives a pretty foul impression that this is an open world, though the game feels much more linear than it was supposed to be. There aren't many options to take down your targets, or whatever you have to take out, and the sluggish gameplay made the game feel like a crawl. Adding insult to injury: the game was pretty damn boring. So overall, we are left here with an experience that is nothing to brag about, and sometimes may actually be a pain. It got frustrating many, many times throughout.
All missions end in a pathetic tank battle which not only feels forced, but annoying! Unless you have a rocket launcher, these tanks will kill you. A lot. And it's not really that a tank battle is a problem, it's just that it happens WAY too much. And ultimately you are left expecting them throughout the whole experience, making it feel rather dull since you always know where it is headed next.
Not sure if this is a spoiler or not, but there is no final tank battle, which is a HUGE shame because the Ratte is constantly described through the experience as ruthless, and the final mission revolves around destroying it, but not in a battle. Very disappointing, and while some would say: "Well, tank battles are boring. No more would be a relief!" but we're talking about the ♥♥♥♥ing RATTE! An amazing plan that would have been insane to be carried out - honestly, I think it would have been cool if we fought the Ratte. Like, there's really no way to describe this whole experience as other than SHALLOW. It just kind of SUCKS. You can have fun, that is for sure, but there's just little payoff. The ending is a simple: the war is not over yet. And leaving it on to further sequels. Wonderful.
So, as you can tell, the whole experience is a very mixed bag. The gameplay can sometimes feel satisfying, but it comes off as hugely underwhelming and sluggish, and I would much rather have you play MGS 5 instead. The game may LOOK like MGS 5 (only reason I bought it) but it's far from it. I can recommend this to you on a sale, but even then it's not a great experience. 5/10 - This review is much more negative than my experience. Just go in expecting little and you may be surprised (or not).

Pros: Cute layout, cute characters, and fairly decent graphics that can run tolerably on older graphics cards.
Cons: Not much story, no real death penalty (though this could be a 'pro' feature, and worlds sometimes generate with holes in them).
Long version: Upon reading up on and sitting through the intro to Portal Knights, it seems to come off as a more plot-driven Minecraft. Randomly generated worlds, little islands which are linked together with portals that have to be repaired, sounds fun! Boot it up and you may need to tweak your graphics settings a bit if you are running on an older machine, but you are still up and running in no time!
However, you hit some of the downsides just as quickly. For example, falling off of/out of you islands because of a big gaping hole. The movement and combat also feel a little clunky, mostly because of the environment. Everything feels.....almost too small. A steep hill feels like a sheer cliff, enemies hiding in grass that doesn't look too tall but comes out to be chest-high, and don't get me started on how useless it is to set up a base. If you are going from portal to portal, what purpose does it serve to create a home?
So, it's a cute game, and I still say it's a decent creativity toy. But I can't bring myself to overlook its flaws for the sake of what amounts to a cute miniature, combat-Minecraft. Clear Sky has been the black sheep of the series for a long time.  Its reputation was such that I actually hadn't given it much thought or time until very recently, when I decided to give it another shot on a whim.  Turns out, it's a fine entry in the series, on par with both Shadow of Chernobyl and Call of Pripyat.  But it has its own identity and feel that sets it apart, and I think the fundamental dislike people have for the game is based on unfounded assumptions and a failure to understand this identity and take it on its own terms; I intend to try to explain why it's worth playing, and clear up some misconceptions.  It's my belief that Clear Sky's commercial failure and its harsh judgement by fans resulted more from the timing of its release than anything else.
In order to better explain Clear Sky's tone and gamefeel, it's helpful to contrast it against SoC and CoP.  SoC, being the first game in the series, was rough.  It had many beautiful, expansive environments and a lonesome, wistful sort of feeling in between brief bursts of action.  It is a difficult game, but its shooting mechanics are relatively straightforward for an FPS, leaning a little bit toward realism, but not taking into account the full extent of ballistic physics.  Call of Pripyat, on the other hand, had much smaller and fewer environments, but with more densely-packed content.  It contains many quality of life improvements over SoC, and its narrative and progression is much more focused.  Much of what CoP improves over SoC was taken directly from Clear Sky, however, the ballistics model was toned down to be more like SoC again.
In Clear Sky, we have something of an experimental game.  It has the big environments of SoC, and much of the same level design, but with a much greater emphasis on local tactical choices, with many small locations packed with bits of cover, with several approaches and angles of attack.  The ballistics model is highly realistic, taking into account acceleration, drop, and scatter.  And the overall game flow is centered around an ongoing war between factions, which the player takes part in.  At the time the game was released, nothing like this had ever really been seen before.  Hyper-realistic military shooters were still a very niche product, and most FPSes had hitscan weapons where you click on the enemies to delete them.  Games like Rainbow Six Siege, which demands hyper-awareness of your surroundings and lines of sight, and taking into account bullet drop and other factors, were still about a decade away.
Players just coming from Shadow of Chernobyl, who you would think were better equipped than Call of Duty plebs to handle a realistic ballistics model, were nevertheless endlessly frustrated by the ballistics in Clear Sky, leading to rumors that (for instance) the game would randomly make your bullets disappear, or that combat was "all luck".  I've watched video reviews of people making this complaint, and it's often over top of footage of them trying to plink away at people with a pistol or SMG from long range, too scared to get closer.  Other reviewers have complained that enemies are bullet sponges, because apparently they're aiming for the torso or using flechettes on heavily-armored targets that can be dropped by a single pistol shot to the head.
Guns in real life, particularly old and/or poorly-maintained guns, are not point-and-click devices.  Bullets don't go exactly where you point the barrel every single time, no matter what video games have trained you to think.  They take time to reach their target, and they're constantly buffeted by physical forces like wind, air resistance, and gravity on their way there.  If you're spraying and praying from mid-range with a submachine gun, you might as well be shooting straight up into the air for all the good it will do.  You have to protect yourself, move carefully, be aware of sightlines, and make every shot count.  This reality is reflected in Clear Sky.
The tone and core game loop of Clear Sky is also different from the rest of the series.  The faction war, especially in the first area where your faction is at an extreme disadvantage at first, has you running around much more actively than SoC, which encouraged you to take lots of downtime right from the start.  Once things click for you with the combat, Clear Sky is akin to a MOBA or an MMO FPS, with you running to the aid of whomever needs your help, analyzing the local tactical situation and jumping in for surgical strikes with care and precision, then running to the next objective.  There is still downtime, the Zone will still blow you away with its beauty, but it takes place while waiting for counterattacks or reinforcements, or in the times when your faction has locked down an area, or before you join up with a faction in a given area and are wandering around trying to get a foothold for yourself.
Combined with the extremely realistic ballistics model, I think a lot of players simply didn't know what to make of the game when it came out.  They were frustrated that they couldn't hit anything with their usual careless tactics, or that the enemy used grenades to flush them out of cover (how dare they!).  Veterans of the Zone cranked the difficulty up to Master (knowing it makes the game much better), and would die even more quickly than in SoC.  People were running around carelessly, feeling buffeted by the constantly-shifting landscape of war, unable to grasp the larger strategic picture.  They felt powerless and ineffectual, and concluded that the game was flawed or made up excuses as to why they were having a hard time.
I want to urge you to give Clear Sky another shot.  It is a beautiful, expansive, gloomy, intense, ruthlessly difficult, and extremely well made game.  It richly deserves its place in this venerable series.  I only really have one complaint about it, and that's that they removed the hunger system for some reason.  It was re-implemented in CoP, but in Clear Sky, food is just for healing small amounts.
That's it.  Get out of here, Stalker.

South Park: The Fractured But Whole is a decent rpg, but a rather bit of a letdown when compared to The Stick of Truth. That's all I could think by the ending credits of the game.
I feel like, The Fractured But Whole should have came out before Stick of Truth, as its significantly less funny, less shocking, and less enjoyable then Stick of Truth was. In their attempt to tone down the offensive fun of south park, the game makes up most of its comedy by relying on even MORE fart and poop jokes then the first game, and significantly less on other forms of comedy.
Furthermore, the game plays more like a marathon of CNN. While Stick of Truth had it all...Abortion babies, Nazi Zombies, Aliens and Government Officials, Retro Canada, and Underpants Gnomes (taking you through a fun and wild ride that left you laughing and looking forward to what will happen next); Fractured But Whole mostly hits on the last years controversies like Cops and Racism, PC shenanigans, and other SJW crap like Microagressions. (though there is a bit of utherworld cthulhu tossed in) The whole game felt like it was holding back on being the in your face funny, creative, and offensive that one expects from South Park.
You also never really get as much option or control like Stick of Truth offered. You can't choose sides, so you are pretty much Cartman's goon even if you were hoping you could side with Professor Chaos or The Freedom Pals instead. And you hope by the end credits you get that chance to hit the button to say something, like telling the boys to f off, but unlike Stick of Truth...you are completely silent to the very end and beyond.
The ending battle was also a bit anticlimatic, hardly holding a candle to Stick of Truth's final boss. Still, if you liked the first game, its not bad to pick up the game and play. Just be warned that you may love it, or feel a bit empty by the end.
(also, all this focus on defining gender, sexuality, and race....yet there were no Ethnicity options like British, German, or French? Really? There were options for Dane and Czech and Slovakian and Russian...but no British? Bleh.)

Scratches an itch I've wanted scratching for a long time. It's a dungeon crawler/rogue like first person shooter. An obvious love letter to the Fallout series, and it's an Adult Swim game, so expect that type of humour.
You have to make your way through randomized "coolers" (think Fallout vaults), fighting other wasters (wastelanders) on your mission to find better loot, and ultimately, BOOZE!
Booze gives your character either a negative or positive perk (perhaps both, I haven't gotten far enough to say for sure), and will also cause your character to pass out, spawning back at your base with all the loot you had on you. This mechanic can leave you with some interesting decisions to make: Do you risk having a permenant(?) gimp stat so that you can get yourself out of a sticky situation? Or do you keep on going. It is a tad annoying to have to restart a cooler run if you want to get a nice perk though.
I can't wait to see what the rest of the game has to offer, and I hope it continues to get updated.

A lot of people will say that if you don't enjoy this game, it's because you lack the skill to play it. Maybe they're right, maybe they aren't. I'm leaning towards it doesn't matter, because honestly this game is not well designed. The randomization feature is often not as random as it should be, resulting in levels that feel only slightly different from each other, allowing almost-memorization to speed you through the game. The enemies are interesting looking, and that's about it. Either they leap at you, shoot something at you, or wiggle about in place. There's no variety, and their hit boxes are questionable at best. The addition of one hit kill traps honestly feels extremely out of place in this game, as it's the only real danger you face. After everything else does one heart of damage, running into a spike trap and dying instantly feels out of place and jarring. This game does not follow the tenents of game design, as in, 'Do not attempt to trick the player into dying, merely give them a challenge.'.  Well, the game isn't challenging, and it attempts to trick you too often, so, in closing, it's mediocre at best, garbage at worst. I don't feel too bad though, I bought it for like, fifty cents on a steam sale.

This is a pretty fun and addictive game. It's a rogue-like platformer that boasts some serious challenge and randomly generated levels so each playthrough is different. Armed with a whip, bombs, and rope you must traverse a trap and enemy laden dungeon while filling your pockets with treasure along the way. The gameplay is pretty standard 2D platformer fare, with the added fun of a fully destructible environment. Shops where you can buy items and hidden goodies you can find throughout your adventure helps ease the difficulty and makes the dungeon run more manageable.
The game is primarily split up into four zones, with a few hidden areas to unlock as well. Each has their own unique set of enemies and monsters, with each zone being overall more difficult than the last. I have yet to finish it myself, which is a testament to its challenge, but I keep coming back for more. The hidden items and areas give it some pretty high replayability as well. Highly recommended.
