Love this game. Grew up with Tekken. Been playing the Tekken games since Tekken 2 way back in 1998 when I was child. This is literally one of the only fighting games besides Soul Calibur and some of the DBZ titles that I actually really enjoy. The combat is very fluid compared to the old Tekken games from the late 90's, doesn't feel much different than 5 or 6, just a little faster and/or polished if that makes any sense. They added something called Rage Arts in this game, which I personally feel was a brilliant decision to incorporate in this game because now the game feels more balanced and fair, if you're dying it'll activate and you can use a special move on the opponent to even the odds, where as before.... if you were at the mercy of your opponent and their bullsh*t combos you were pretty much f*cked. With Rage Arts you actually have a fighting chance, this is great for all players, pros and noobs.
Aside from that there doesn't really feel like there's much in this one though compared to Tekken 6 and 5. Just a Gallery mode to view all the Tekken videos from all the Tekken games, an arcade mode that only has 5 battles, Treasure battle mode.... which is like Ghost Battle from the past Tekken games, you beat the computer and win fight money and rank up. The story mode is REALLY well done but it's extremely short I think, and the other characters stories after you're done with the main one is also extremely short.... like 1 or 2 battles and you're done type of short. No team battle, survival, or time attack like the old games.... not sure why they removed those.
The character customization is better, not by much, but it gives enough variety to choose from and edit that it feels like you're own personal character. F*ck the online mode, man.... the combo jugglers on here will drive you insane if you're not on the top of your game, one mistake and you're suddenly suspended in the air and at the mercy of their bullsh*t, and trust me.... it's going to p*ss you off, I promise lol. Even with the Rage Arts, it's still not enough to avoid a brutal az whooping sometimes. This is one of those games you get really, really good at... you're dominating the computer and dominating all your friends, and then you go online and suddenly you realize how much of a failure you are. I'm pretty decent at the game, reached the rank of Mentor in Online ranked matches, but man.... some of these Tekken Veterans on here will straight up stomp you and make you feel worthless, and then it will fill you with endless rage XD.
Other than that, this is really great game, and I have had no issues with the game either, it runs perfectly, no crashes at all and is very smooth. Only complaint I have is with the online mode when trying to connect to another player it's usually always telling me it couldn't connect with the player, and I know it's not my internet because I have the Blast service from Comcast, which is the best net you can get from them, insane speeds and barely any DC's, so the game has an issue there. It's not just me either, it happens to a lot of players it seems. Hopefully it gets fixed because it's annoying a/f.
And hopefully Soul Calibur 6 makes it's way to PC too, I'd love that.

Story: You are a spelunky (spelunker?) and you have discovered Olmec's caves, a place where death has lost it's way and your soul will literally not be put to rest if you die (so you just come back to life basically), in Olmec's little home lies treasure. You want that treasure. However, there are many foes! Bats! Spiders! Giant Spiders! Snakes! Tiki People! Frogs! And much more. Sounds simple, yes? WRONG. Olmec will be sure to break you. Want to prove him wrong? Then play this game if you dare.
Alright onto the real review. The game is absolutely fantastic. You could play the game "the normal way" and honestly miss A LOT of extra things you probably didn't even know about. You carry a whip, a few bombs, and some ropes. You can acquire more from boxes, purchasing (or stealing if you're feelin' lucky) some from shop keepers or finding some underground (sometimes). As I said before there is a "normal" way to beat the game which consists of 4 stages. The game is also VERY difficult for (most) newcomers. So don't feel disouraged if you're not doing very well.
The enemies. Oh boy, are there a lot of these fu- I mean suckers. They all do more than just touch you to do damage mind you. They will leap, fly, shoot, spit, crush you, use psychic moves, charge at you, throw boomerangs, throw you, and the list could go on. Trust me. It's a lot and brutal. But for all the right reasons which adds charm to the enemies and much of a challenge.
The lovely, lovely items. There's TONS of items. Ranging from your whip and bombs to an ancient knife found in the belly of a giant worm and an incredibly dangerous high tech alien rocket launcher. There's more than just weapons too. There's items that can make you run faster, climb walls, hover, fly, see through walls, and even an eggplant!
The events...oh dear lord I'd cry inside every time I encountered one of these. So basically an event is when you enter a level and something "unusual" is happening like the room being entirely dark, the room may be ridden with giant spiders, or even an alien lord may be nearby. Each stage has it's own set of events fit for it's own stage so certain events will ONLY happen in that stage.
I don't want to make this review too long (though maybe I have), but this is a must play game if you're one who enjoys a challenge.
Just fantastic.

I played Deponia a number of years after it was released, at the time there was a considerable amount of talk about it, perhaps it was even heralded as a return to form for point and click adventure games. So as a fan of the genre I was quite excited to play it. However I must say the game is certainly a bit overrated.
My main issue with it is that it doesn't really do anything what other adventure games haven't been doing for a while now, especially the games from the same developer. So the main draw here must be story, which does have a nice premise and an interesting world behind it. But other than that it's pretty cookie cutter.
The main character is intentionally portrayed as annoying and self centered, so there's lots of room for character development here. However we don't really get that much of it. Perhaps it's because this was conceived as the first game in a trilogy so they left that for the other installments, it's just a shame that this game suffers for it. There is also less interaction with other characters than in other adventure games, which makes the world feel really small. And when you do interact with someone you don't really learn much about the plot or the game world. It could be that this is also another casualty of being the first game in a planned series.
As for the puzzles themselves, in true point and click adventure game fashion, some of them can be annoying to figure out as they require a different line of thinking. In general though they aren't too difficult.
I have to say though that Daedalic managed to build an interesting world with this game, and with some interesting characters as well (not so much the main character though). So I am looking forward to playing the sequels as there is a basis for a good adventure game series here.

This has to be the funniest point and click I have played in ages. Not only is it hillarious from start to finish. It is also incredibly challenging. You really have to think outside the box for some of these, but at the same time it makes sense, just like in Sam and Max. So you will find yourself explaining your reasoning for solving a puzzle to someone who doesn't play this, to only get a facial expression thrown back at you that says "What on earth are you on??" Lol. The mechanics are very old school, which is great, and definately hark back to the early DOS days. Being able to bring the items menu up and down via the mouse wheel is pure genius, and gives me a great sense of pleasure every time I do it.The visuals are gorgeous. Every landscape and character you see is very sharp and clean, with loads of colour and detail. The script, storyline, characters, songs, music and voice acting is phenomenal! The humour is very adult so I'd steer younger kids away from this (It's not Deadpool or anything but there's the odd bit of language and double entendre and it can get a little dark in places). This game had me hooked from start to finish. Even though I had to break away from and come back to it occasionally when I got stuck. Getting stuck was definately the most frustrating thing about this game, because you'd get a real head scratcher, not be able to solve it for a while, but really want to know what happens in the story. Still I don't think I would change anything about this game. Amazing. Would definately recommend it and am looking forward to playing the next installment 'Chaos on Deponia'.

While I have really enjoyed MKX, it is not without its problems.  All in all, I recommend the game, but unless you are a die-hard fan it may be worth waiting until the glitches are fixed.
Pros:
Each fighter has 3 variations, each with their own special attacks, brutalities, etc.
Story mode is fun and gives you the chance to play several of the characters (twelve chapters, each chapter is one character, and you have 4 fights per chapter.
The graphics are incredible.
The fatalities and brutalities are really creative and also very gruesome.
Faction Wars are interesting and give you new challenges every day.
Cons:
Online mode seems to be down every day.
When online mode is up, it is very laggy.
Game often crashes or freezes.
Invasion events (bosses, towers, etc.) sound fun, but few people have been successful in actually connecting long enough to play them.
tl;dr
This is a great game, but was released unfinished.  Assuming those things get fixed, it is worth buying.  If they don't, it's not, at least at full price.

This is a short, yet beautiful game I just can't recommend enough. It plays a bit as a graphical adventure, or a co-op game where you are both people.
It tells the story of two brothers who go on a journey to find some medication for their ailing father, finding many an obstacle among the way they need to work together to sort out. The gameplay twist lies in that you control both of them at the same time - the left controller stick controls one of the brothers and the right stick the other one.
Besides the gameplay, the other two draws of the game are it's storyline, which is quite good (We're not talking Tolstoy levels of narrative here, but this is quite decent in its own way), and the graphics which are just beautiful.
Honestly, if you have a couple extra bucks and are looking for a short, beautiful and kind of relaxing game go for this one. You won't regret it.*
* This statement is not a legal binding. You might actually end up regretting it, particularly if you're looking for a shooter or if you're stingy enough that spending $3 during a sale on a game that's under 5 hours long bothers you.

This is simply one of the most beautiful, charming and touching games I have ever played. The graphics and artwork is beautiful, the characters are beautiful, the soundtrack is beautiful and the story is beautiful. I know I just used the word 'beautriful' four times in the same sentence, but it really is the best word to describe this game.
Though the game isn't very long or difficult, the gameplay is unique in that you control both brothers at the same time with the same controller (or keyboard, though I imagine that would be a tad more difficult) - one thumbstick for each. The puzzles themselves aren't terribly hard, but having to control both brothers (often doing two different things) adds a nice bit of spice.
The story, well, I don't want to spoil anything, but basically two brothers must go on a journey to find a cure for their dying father, who I affectionately called Jorgen. It may sound simple, but it is really much deeper than that, and explores issues like coming of age, love, trust and death. It does so in a refined, elegant manner, avoiding stereotypes. Perhaps the only thing I could have wished for
Also, if you are looking for an easy game to get 100% achievements in, this game is ideal. None of the achievements are hard, and are more like rewards for exploring everywhere and interacting with everything. You can get them all in one playthrough if you like, or if you miss any, you can just load up the individual chapters without having to replay the whole game.
I highly recommend playing this game, even if you only play it once. It will touch your heart and you won't be able to forget it for a long time.

I spent about half an hour getting into the game, which in my belief is the most important aspect. If you can't get dragged in at the start, you may not enjoy the rest.
Anyway, I took my time making and naming my character, fiddled around with it, and went through one of the 'dungeons' the game has to offer, only to find out that if I spend too much time on one floor, you become hunted by a very strong NPC. The timer seems to be about 3 minutes, so if you're not on the next floor by then, a small icon will appear on your map.
There's barely a warning for when you're being hunted other than that icon. The only time you'll notice is if you're close enough to the hunter, that the music changed to a sinister tone, telling you how close he is. And he is EXTREMELY powerful for just starting out. After he ruthlessly murdered me in the corner of the ceiling, a small cutscene plays out with a girl running down a road. Come to find out, that girl is me. My old character is now dead. Gone. Completely eliminated. I'm unsure if there's something you can do later on to change it, but when you die, you're dead. This seems a bit strange to happen just at the start of a game. No save point or checkpoint? This bothers me for a few reasons, which I'll list now!
This game is, at first glance, just another crappy cash grab. Honestly, I don't like the character models, but I can look past that for the most part. My only issue with them is they don't seem to fit the area they're in. The characters are all bright and colorful, while the zones are dark and gritty.
That note aside, the gameplay is smooth and fun. You can loot boxes, enemies, anything you want! Think of this like a mix between Borderlands and Fallout. It's based in a post-apocolyptic world, with a silly little story detailing what happened, and it has a good bit of childish humor and fun jokes. One my personal favorites is the "Sod Off" shotgun. On top of that, if you have a stackable item in your inventory, such as bullets, simply opening any loot box will automatically add those items to your stack, along with any cash that was in the box, making it nice and simple to get what you know you need.
Over-all, I do recommend this game, especially since it's free! If you can get past the idea of behind hunted down and obliterated by someone far stronger than you, then by all means, go ahead and do it. I haven't explored past the first area it throws you in yet, but as a rogue-like exploration game, I don't think there's much of a reason not to play it!

Wasted is an action roguelite and it is already my favourite roguelite, hands down.
It is from the first person perspective and the controls are pretty tight, although you have a shoot stat that does affect your aim at early levels.
The graphics are downright beautiful for a roguelite. The voice acting is extremely well done as is the music, production for everything is way above par for what we've come to expect with first-person roguelites. I think that it might have the best voice acting in the history of roguelikes/roguelites.
This is a humorous game and everything in it is silly, and the comedy is a mix of (literally) toilet humor, satire and parody, I find the style to be charming and well above what I normally accept for a 3d action roguelite.
There is a lot of satire and parodying in this game, especially in the graphics and the dialogue and "lore" that you may find.
As for the gameplay itself, it's not a "go deep in dungeon, get amulet, get out, done" type of game.
Instead, you can get a persistant buf that stays with your character for its life butwhen doing so, you are taken out of that dungeon.
Also, it is possible to stash items when you return to your "home" in between  dungeons, and to unlock different locations so there can be progression from character to character even though the game has permadeath. But you do NOT keep the buffs if you die, you (mostly) only keep what you've deliberately stashed.
This is very much a game of choices. Do you take a buff and start the dungeon over? Or keep going and risk it all for a better buff, or even a chance at taking down the boss to unlock a harder dungeon with better stuff in it? Do you take a buff you don't even want so you can go stash the items you've accumulated or maybe escape a bad situation? Do you unlock a side route that may have better loot, but may see you getting caught by the purifier (a relatively tough but slow moving npc that spawns if you take too long)?
RNG does play a role but I've found it to be a fair game that rewards risk assesment and brutally punishes carelessness.
Also, the monsters/idiots in the dungeon can get mad at eachother and fight and even run into traps and hazards, this can be very advantageous to you, but it can just easily cause a chain of events that ends in your demise.
It's also really funny either way.
This IS a roguelite, you will die, a lot.
If you've never played a roguelite/roguelike, this might be the game to introduce you to the genres though, the actual combat is slick and fun and the game and its mechanics are easily accessable; it's hard but not so complicated that newbies to the concepts will be totally lost. It has the inherent replayability of a roguelite, and also a daily seed (a dungeon/character that everybody plays the same version of, and you can even sometimes take an item from it and give it to your own character).
I have not had this game for very long but it is already one of my favourite indie games, there has been a lot of work put into this, it is the best action roguelite that I have played, in my opinion.

This game really is an indie gem with so many endless possibilities. It combines strategy, third person combat, and RPG elements that come together to form a wholly unique and fun experience. You start out on in campaign sandbox map in which you are left to do as you wish. Join up with one of the game's factions, gather local farmers to train into epic knights, raid close by villages, or take on mercenary work for a city's guildmaster. This game is a true medieval simulation in which their are many different choices for your character. Inside and outside of combat you are faced with a lot of choice to your style of play, and you can experiment with each.
Within combat the game plays rather similar to Chivalry, although with more depth. The basics are that you control your swing and block directions via mouse movement. However beyond that, there are hidden mechanics that will get me beaten in a duel server everytime. It's a simple concept, that is easy to learn, but difficult to master. You also have ranged weapons and horse combat as an option if you so choose. Either way, you can hone your skills through combat or an RPG style character panel.
The feeling of progression is given with your troops as well. It's such a cool feeling to gather 10 farmers from a village on the strategy map, see them fight against bandits with pitchforks, and slowly progress into a team of full plate armored knights. You can constantly be increasing your army size and ranks through the renown you gain in victories, as well as your own level. You never are put in a sitatuation where you feel stagnant, you always have something to work towards that is within reach, and that really hooks you.
The world you inhabit is also constantly changing. The factions dynamically wage war with one another, and take new land. Lords will defect to other factions and will be given fiefs by the King. Something you can partake in should you hold his favor. You can take land for yourself once strong enough. You can besiege castles and make a claim to the throne yourself. This will differ in effectiveness based on your relationship with other Kings and your "right to rule". If no one respects your claim, you can be put in your place rather quickly when every faction wants you dead for your warmongering. I will say, although the politcal system is not particularly deep, it is servicable and enough to keep you entertained.
This game is not perfect however. It does show its age. Combat animations and animations in general can look rather janky. The game does not go very deep in certain areas, though enjoyable, sometimes you just wish that it had more to it in areas. Also graphically, it's far from perfect. Most of these problems can be solved by mods though, and the mods for this game are nothing short of incredible. There are mods that add to the depth of politics that stretch all the way to total conversions for this game. If you've ever wanted a Game of Thrones RPG, you can make this game into one. They really do vary to every era in history, and to other licenses in film and other video games. In fact, the other week, I managed to play a Star Wars themed mod, that was surprisingly functional.
This game is just the gift that keeps on giving, and for the amount of times this thing has been on sale, it deserves a place in your library. I have 200 hours plus in this game, and for less than the price of a Subway sandwich, it has most definitely earned my money.

I wanted to say first, that I'm a huge fan of the STALKER franchise. I loved every single game in the series. I replayed ShoC twice, CoP almost thrice. I adored every moment of those games. Except for this one.
Now, I see what the devs wanted to do with this game. They tried to introduce alot of new stuff, however most of it wasn't really 'polished'.
Pros:
Factions:
I really like that they kinda introduced a new faction. Clear sky has a pretty interesting structure, story, and 'style'. I like that at the start they really want to keep their base location 'private'. I like that you can befriend the bandits.
I like that they fleshed out the faction interactions. You can participate in wars, defend camps (optional), attack camps (optional) on behalf of you faction, you can even fight with them. The new 'statistics' tab in your PDA shows your rep with all the factions. In the 'Faction Wars' tab, you can see your group's armaments, how many people you have, how many places you captured. Same goes for the enemies.
Combat:
Combat in this game is pretty.. well.. mediocre? Now for some reason you need to bandage multiple times, depending on the seriousness of the wound. (Maybe this is a bug, maybe a feature, I really don't know.) Can't say much about actual 'shooting' because I used AO w/ sky reclamation project. You can upgrade your weapons and armor, which is a very welcoming addition (Not as fleshed out as in CoP, but still, pretty good).
The Zone:
Atmosphere is there. The whole zone is pretty large, and you're free to explore, just like in ShoC and CoP. Random patrols/groups of Duty, Freedom, Bandits, Renegades, Clear Sky, Loners, and other can be found. Mutants also roam everywhere aswell.
Misc.:
[con]This game is VERY buggy. Not sure why, maybe they didn't have enough time or something. Anyways, if you want to enjoy the game, you will need a bug-fixing mod (For example, Sky Reclamation Project, or the COMPLETE mod.)
I like that the character isn't a loner, but is a merc. I know it really doesn't 'matter' since our character is still running around doing things for various rewards, but still, pretty nice. There are various 'quality-of-life' additions that I love, but I probably couldn't fit them all in this review. But trust me, there's alot of them.
Now onto the cons... oh boy.
Story:
Some parts of the game feel like being there JUST to extend the playtime.
Very dissapointing that in the main quest, you don't have many choices. This is especially shown when talking to other people. For example, once I had to intimidate a captured military officer, however I couldn't choose what I was going to say, so it ended up in me completing a quest killing all his buddies. (Would've been nice to have so that you can just intimidate him really well by choosing the right sentences, or be able to kill him, maybe try and sweet-talk him and offer him goodies, maybe release him completely to escape. In ShoC, you mostly were able to do all these things when talking to someone, or just completing a quest in general.)
///SPOILER ALERT/// THERE MIGHT BE LIGHT SPOILERS IN THIS SECTION OF THE REVIEW, CONCERNING THE ENDING.///
The Ending:
This is my biggest dissapointment. It is HORRIBLE. DISGUISTING. BAD. At the end, you get a boss fight. The 'boss' is a very generic bulletsponge that can withstand about 10-20 shots with a gauss rifle. The whole 'boss battle' doesn't make sense. At all. None of it does. Now, after the VERY frustrating bossfight, comes the final cutscene. The cutscene is two mintues long. TWO MINUTES. TWO ♥♥♥♥ING MINUTE LONG ENDING. It is very vague about what's happening, and incredibly short. You have two choices. You either defeat the boss, or let him go ( this choice is hard to notice since the game never mentions it, all you need to do is not shoot the boss.) this is understandable since if there'd be more choices, the things happening in ShoC wouldn't make that much 'sense', however the TWO MINUTE (or less) length ending is unforgivable, the terrible, TERRIBLE bossfight isn't forgivable aswell.
Conclusion:
I understand what the devs wanted to make. I really admire what they wanted to make, however those ideas were mostly executed poorly. I do not know why, since ShoC, the first STALKER game this studio made, was brilliant. If you really want to experience the things that happened before ShoC from another perspective, sure, give this game a try. If you are new to the STALKER universe/games, get ShoC, then CoP, then if you want to, CS(this game). Get this on a  sale, give it a try, if you dislike it, refund it.

Ahh, the familiar loop of Dead Rising: leaving the safehouse, fretting about the finite time you have to rescue bizarre civilians, panicking when their braindead AI leads to them being eaten by actual braindead zombies, and picking yourself up and doing it again. It's a love-it-or-hate-it affair, with some players hugely turned off by the time limits and the constant anxiety they bring with them. I've always loved them for that exact reason; most games that deal with the undead quickly become power fantasies, and though you're practically a demi-god who can do suplexes in this series, time constraints and stupid survivors make for highly memorable high-stress scenarios that I relish.
Despite my love for Dead Rising, I had never played the sorta-sequel sorta-expansion Off the Record, which brings the protagonist from the first game to the Vegas-themed playground of the second. Since I prefer smug ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s (Frank West) to father clichés (Chuck Greene), I figured I was in for a good time.
I would have been right if it weren't for all of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ technical problems.
I won't explain the nitty gritty of Dead Rising 2 to you, seeing as how the game has been out for ohmygod six years. All you need to know is that Off the Record is a "What If?" type of riff off of the second game, where Frank is the hero instead of Chuck. Since his successful exposé in the first game, Frank is now a washed-up has-been everyone calls fat and ugly, who wants a second shot. He finds this in the Terror is Reality game show, which pits him against live zombies in Fortune City (Vegas, basically). Things go awry, a new outbreak occurs, and Frank sees his opportunity to become relevant again in the form of unraveling a conspiracy.
Thing is, this conspiracy isn't hugely different from what Chuck experiences in Dead Rising 2. A couple of story beats deviate -- especially the ending -- but you'll still mostly be doing the same exact sidequests and fighting the same psychopaths. This gives the whole game a bit of a cheap feel to it if you've played both games. Since it's been six years, I enjoyed myself the whole way through, but I imagine if I had played it directly after 2 I would have been annoyed.
The new stuff that is there is great, though. With the return of Frank comes the return of his camera, which means you can take horror, drama, erotica, and comedy photos for extra experience points. Some of Frank's exclusives missions involve the camera, but just running around with it feels so right. I associate some of my best memories of these games with trying to line up the perfect shot (like a psychopaths's charging tiger leaping towards me, toothy maw open and ready), so I was happy to see the mechanic return. There are also new combo weapons, one of which involves connecting a fake escape pod with a fire extinguisher to make a small UFO that freezes and shatters zombies, so I was a happy little sadistic man. A space-themed amusement park area that wasn't in Dead Rising 2 debuts here as well, and it ties in so well that I had to double-check that it was new.
A sandbox mode is also included for those who want to play without time limits, and it can be played cooperatively just like the regular game. You can run around with a buddy to complete challenges that net you cash in the game proper, but since you have to defeat a certain number of zombies first, repetition should be expected.
But mostly, I'm just happy to have Frank back. His brand of sarcastic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ makes for a somewhat unique character. Most protagonists fall in either the heroic goody-two-shoes or grimdark categories, so I'm happy to play as a jerk who knows what the right thing to do is, and will (probably) do it. His quips are great too, like when he bemuses stuff like "Sure, I don't need my own expensive♥♥♥♥♥zombie medicine or anything" after handing it over to a survivor. Capcom Vancouver broke the fourth wall just enough to be amusing here, and I dig it.
This all would have been great if it was running competently on hardware that's more than capable of acing it at this point. My game crashed six times: twice when I was looking at the included DLC costumes (so save before using this menu!) and four times at random. The "locked at 60 frames per second" should actually read as "swings wildly from 20-60 depending on the size of the area you're in and how many zombies there are." On the Silver Strip, the biggest area of the game, I even did the classic trick where I'd stare at the ground or the ceiling to improve the frame rate.
These problems are extra frustrating, because when Dead Rising 2: Off the Record functions properly, I have a blast with it. The story is nothing memorable, but the toybox that is Fortune City allows for all sorts of emergent storytelling that I'll remember for some time. I'm hoping that Frank's return in Dead Rising 4 fares better.
And by the way. The fruit of the cake.

Quick Summary: Dead Rising 2 Off the Record is a Third Person hack and slash game with some light gunplay thrown in for variety. It’s sort of a revamp of the original Dead Rising 2, with the main character changed to Frank, the hero from Dead Rising 1. If you’re deciding whether you want to play Dead Rising 2 or Dead Rising 2 Off the Record, I’d recommend Off the Record simply because it adds more gameplay options, such as a new map area, new weapon combos, and a Sandbox mode. The storylines of the two games are mostly identical, with a little switch-up at the end.
In Off the Record you play Frank West, a washed up reality TV star who has been coasting on his fame from surviving the original Dead Rising zombie outbreak, but fallen on hard times. Frank finds himself in the middle of a new zombie outbreak, this time in Fortune City (kind of like a mini Las Vegas). Being an intrepid photojournalist, it’s your job to find out who/what caused the outbreak and reveal it to the world, while trying to avoid getting chomped.
In terms of gameplay, the zombies in Dead Rising are more of an annoyance than a real threat, especially after the first couple hours of the game. They are quite slow moving and do very little damage, but there are so many of them that you need to hustle wherever you go, or you’ll be grabbed. The real threat comes from “psychopaths” who are aggressive human survivors that appear throughout Fortune City, armed with a variety of weapons. These guys are the “bosses” of the game, and while you can skip most of them, what fun would that be?
One of the things that really sets Off the Record apart from other semi-open world games that I’ve played is that the game has a fixed timeline. You’re told from the beginning that “rescue” is coming in three days, so you have until then to survive and explore the city. Game time seems to run at around 5 real time minute = 1 game time hour, and the clock is always running. New missions and psychopaths become available at certain times (for example main quest #10 may open at 11 pm of Day 1, or a psychopath may appear from Day 1 noon to 8 AM on Day 2). This means that if you really wanted, you can sit in a safe area and just chill until main quests are available, then run out a complete them before hiding again.
Reasons to play Dead Rising 2 Off the Record:
+Huge variety of weapons to play with. There are a ton of items laying around all over the city to be picked up and club zombies with (guns, pipes, wrenches, chairs, etc) and most of them can be combined with other items to create “combo weapons.” For example flashlight + gem = laser sword, and laser sword kicks a lot more butt than a stupid flashlight or gem. This is where much of the game’s fun comes from, because there are dozens of combos for you to experiment with.
+The game is built for replay with a character level cap of 50, and you’re not going to reach it in one playthrough. At any time during the campaign you can restart the story with your current level, money, and combo recipes (you do NOT need to beat the game to start a “new game+”). In fact, a number of the psychopaths are very tough and you’ll have trouble with them on your first playthrough. Playing in Sandbox mode to level up or grab cash also carries over to the campaign.
+You can play the entire campaign in co-op mode with a friend. The co-op has its problems (only the host saves story progress, disconnects when reloading checkpoints, etc) but if you’re playing with a specific friend rather than internet strangers, you can make it work.  Not too many random players online nowadays though.
Reasons you might skip Off the Record:
-If you’ve already played the original Dead Rising 2, this will be mostly the same. I mentioned before that the storylines are mostly identical, and this includes the side quests and psychopaths. The final boss is different (more fun) and there’s more to do in Off the Record so if you’re only going to play one of them, I would pick Off the Record as the one to play.
-Frank is a chubby middle aged man who runs pretty slowly (at least for the first half of the game) and there isn’t any “fast travel.” For the most part you need to walk/run all over the place with zombies groping at you the whole time. This can be annoying when you’re racing to get to the next story mission before your time runs out.
-Not a big deal to most people, but just a word of warning. If you really care about your Steam achievements %, it will take some time to max out in this game. It’s doable but we’re talking 50-60 hours and several playthroughs. Since the game is “timed” you can’t just run through the main quests to finish the game. You’d actually have to wait for them to unlock.
Overall I enjoyed the game and am looking forward to playing Dead Rising 3 in the future. With Off the Record being low priced recently you may find an influx of new players to go through the campaign with in co-op.

I truly think that this is an enjoyable train simulator but it falls short in so many aspects. One of the issues is that the controls are pretty much set in stone which, for instance, makes it frustrating to control acceleration/brakes because you can't hook up a throttle controller to have more fine-gradined control over them.
But by far the most frustrating aspect is the harsh scoring. After completing a level that goes beyond 45 minutes, the game might tell you that you failed because you either didn't end up on the correct platform or were speeding slightly too long. And even if you mastered all other aspects of the scenario, it still awards you with zero XP.
While I can understand that this might be an intentional design choice to make the game more challenging, it is being made even more frustrating by the fact that the map is pretty bothersome to read and use and that the speed limit can suddenly drop significantly without a warning.

I "completed" one of the high speed missions, for example and I could not get credit for finishing as the track itself ended 0.5KM before the mission endpoint.  I certainly tried as I nudged the front of the train to the end of the line.  I certainly was not going to "Silver Streak" the train through the station.
Also, for the last few years, you cannot alt=tab out of the game while driving a train...Soon as you try to get back into the game, it crashes due to a vertex buffer failure.  If you are not driving (as in the menus), this bug leaves you alone.
Biggestr beef:  There are far more missions for points than missions to do for fun!  When 6-% of the missions are not allowed to be played for fun or practice, one cannot be aware of any pitfalls...like potential collisions or derailing.
Second biggest beef...Why are there oddly placed speed limits?  IE: a 60 KM limit, then a 110 KM Limit, followed by a 60 KM limit, all within the length of the train and given that an increase in speed is only permitted when the last consist has passed )or in this case a few KM away from the destination) and the lower speed limit is right there, no sense in even trying to speed up regardless of where on the line you're at.
However, I will recommend this despite the flaws as it's a good way to kill some time.  If you have a powerful computer, one can get full FPS out of it, but, a budget PC is below minimum specs.  Any I7 or FX-6300 + a 4+ GB GPU will get you reasonable frame rates.  Anything below this and you might as well run it on standard def and medium settings, turning off the additional eye candy.  If the game clock has a 5:1 ratio for advancing time, time to reduce settings, and, turn off dynamic lighting.

First off, I love the art style in this game, it's fantastic. The gameplay is extremely enjoyable, though people comparing this to Minecraft are very mistaken, IMO. Being a voxel game doesn't make it Minecraft, nor does having mining and crafting (Guild Wars 2 has mining and crafting, is it Minecraft?) make it Minecraft. The combat is different, reminds me a lot of Zelda in some ways. Except for the fact you have more abilities and weapon choices than in Zelda games. The biggest flaw to me is how the game practically tries to establish itself as a dungeon crawler yet feels like it's restrained by the constant need to grind for materials. And as you advance throughout levels the grind continues to just increase.
Example would be I need 2 copper bars for such an item at this level of the game, but once I find iron I will need 4 iron bars to get the same tool. Not an entirely accurate example but it's pretty much what the game does. Now I find myself needing 6 portal pieces to make just one block and I just find it hard to play anymore because of the boring grind. I feel like this game would be a lot better if they offered and alternative gameplay type that is more fitting to this game. All this considered though I like the game, it's very unique and it is only Early Access currently. I look foward to what the devs have in store for this game.

One of my all-time favorite games, and I don't say that lightly. Perfect mechanics that are easy to learn and difficult to master. You will die hundreds and hundreds of times, and 99% of those deaths will be absolutely your fault. It doesn't get easier, but you will get better.
Fifteen dollars is a steal for this game. I've gotten more playtime and enjoyment out of it than I have out of most AAA $60 games. If you're on the fence, don't wait for a sale - if you have even an inkling that you will enjoy this game, GET IT, because you will.
Don't be too intimidated - yes, it IS difficult, but I've had more fun losing in Spelunky than I have winning in other games. The "bulls---" factor is very low, so dying isn't frustrating because every death is an opportunity to learn and improve. I've probably sunk more hours into trying to beat Spelunky than I have Dark Souls.
Keep in mind, too, that through the freeware "Frozlunky" extension, you can create, share, and play customizable maps and challenge maps. You should ABSOLUTELY buy this game if you're at all a fan of platformers. A near-perfect game, absolutely.
I also want to mention that my >120 hrs played in the Steam version is paltry compared to the hundreds of hours I sunk into navigating the pre-Steam version of Spelunky.

This game is a rouge like which scratches that Falloutesque itch. With a snazzy 1980's soundtrack, humour and nods towards other pop culture references, all the while providing a challenge to the player. The combat is entertaining due to the challenge of stronger enemies which can keep the game entertaining on your first few runs. The pacing of the game can stumble in the first few hours if the player completely forgets to push through the first area to the last floor and instead focuses on collecting Hangovers in the game. These boons can also have disadvantages to the player and this can mutate the style of game play unexpectedly.
When you die your character is gone for good and it can happen so suddenly if you are not paying attention that the first time is a little jolting. All your Items/Hangovers/TP (currency) are gone and aside from the Purple ones there seems to be no way to retrieve them. This can be frustrating at first however upon death your new randomized character will coincidentally stumble across your persistent house where you can store any items you escape with from your journey. You can also upgrade this through game play with permanent changes which can further benefit your next incarnate which will unwillingly stumble to their demise in the depths of a Cooler. The maps are randomly generated using set pieces and random item placement so certain room layouts become familiar however the actual floor plan changes each time, leading to a different and sometimes frustrating experience. This can be due to following a long trail leading to a dead end and to find you have spent too long on that floor. As a consequence you become hunted through that floor until you reach the exit which can turn a good run into an exercise of painting the walls with your own insides as you try to escape. This unforgiving pacing can put off some however I personally like this as it keeps me moving and stops me trying to loot every single piece of worthless junk I see.
Pros:
+ Initial Character is customizable
+ Humorous pop culture references
+ Falloutesque themed environments, enemies and weapons
+ Snazzy 1980's soundtrack
+ Challenging Combat
+ Persistent House Upgrading and Storage
+ Voiced Characters
+ ♥♥♥♥ and his friend.
Cons:
- RNG maps can lead to your untimely death
- Completely losing all your stuff can be disheartening
- Difficulty spikes after respawn if you have no replacement equipment
- The soundtrack of the Cooler can become repetitive if you die enough
- Easy to forget to progress through the Cooler and get caught up with Booze

As many others have, I received a copy of this through Humble Bundle's Monthly subscription. I have never heard of the game before then and I had no idea what I was getting into. Out of the monthly's I've had, this is easily the best surprise I've recieved. This game is pretty much a 80's themed roguelike Fallout 3 with a hint of fallout 4. You have your own house where you can store and craft items as well as sleep. You can fast travel via your car outside to (so far) two locations, the Cooler (vaultish) and Suckrimento.
I'm not a huge roguelike player though I have played a handful of them but this game, from my experience, has by far the most unique mechanics. Once you enter the Cooler, there is no turning back. There are three ways to exit: Death, Making it to the end, or drinking Booze. If you die, you lose everything you had on you and start a new character from the begining with very basic equipment. I haven't survived through it so I don't know what happens there. Booze is somewhat rare to find but if you find it and drink it, it will send you back home with a hangover. The catch is hangovers will either give you a negative or positive debuff. The effect it has on you greatly depends on how far you made it in the cooler. The further you get, the more likely the booze is to benefit you. There are also flasks that rather than giving you a hangover, give you buzz which can result in a helpful, detrimental, or hilarious buff/debuff.
There was a lot of discussion pre-release over this and a lot of people were upset about this mechanic. How it works is a SOB purifier equipped with heavy armor and a minigun that will literally ♥♥♥♥ you up the wall if he finds you will spawn after a certain amount of time, depending on the complexity of the floor. This adds a Risk/Reward system where the longer time you spend looting, the higher the chance you have of dying. At first I agreed with the many complaints that it should either be removed or rebalanced. However after putting a few more hours into it he's not nearly as hard to avoid as I previously thought after learning how much time I have and how to tell whether or not I am on track to the exit. Another good strategy is to make a bunch of small runs for ammo/meds/food/crafting items and stock up so that you can later go in fully equipped and prepared to deal with him. You are able to kill him but he will respawn the next floor. It's more "Be prepared for him" than "Be able to assault him."
The main cons to this game, depending on what you're looking for, are likely going to be the SOB purifier, the default 10 slot inventory space (it is expandable) and the relatively small item stack limits (100 pistol ammo, 5 food/meds). At first I disliked all of those but after more time in the game it feels balanced and fair, you just have to adjust your playstyle. This isn't a game you can take your time in. If those don't turn you away I highly recommend this game. The gameplay is pretty polished. It's fairly well optimized, the combat feels nice and fluid, the UI is basic but well made, and the looting system is optimized for speed and the dialogue and general atmospher is hilarious. All stackable items are automatically stacked. It's a ton of fun, has a good amount of content, and I find to be a complete steal for the price.

This game is amazing. It's a roguelike where you can actually make a lot of progression, even if you die.
First off it's a first-person-shooter that takes after Fallout and Borderlands. There's a humorous tone to the game, but don't let the visual fool you: it's brutal. Your character is on a quest to get to the end of the dungeons, called "coolers," and drink "booze." A "booze" is a buff (or a debuff, in some cases) that, once drunk, ejects the player from the dungeon with their inventory to their home, allowing them to restart the dungeon from the beginning. Boozes are modifiers for your character that persist until death that add modifiers like increased inventory space, increased ammo capacity or even increased damage when killing enemies in a chain. Along with this, players equip armor, weapons and bags to improve their utility. Upon death, you lose everything and get a new wasterel that stumbles upon a common sight: your abode.
So, in being a roguelike, death is final. However, your homestead is infinite. The homestead of the player character is something of a progression hub for your gameplay. It acts as a giant storage chest for the characters that end up owning the building. As you go further into the dungeons, you'll unlock new functions for your homestead. Regardless, building up a cache of weapons and equipment every time you egress is a cornerstone of the game. It's an interesting system, in both mechanics and story. You still might lose a powerful character, but your new explorers will benefit from the fruits of your last generation's labors.
The game is randomly generated, so dungeon layouts tend to be varied in a limited way (tilesets, etc). Your character will have to make their way using stealth, melee and ranged attacks, and some RPG-lite lock-picking. There's a ton of loot, and there's plenty of had choices to make in the game, such as taking unknown "buzz" buff/debuffs, or if drinking a "booze" bonus is appropriate.
This game is both excellent and genuinely funny. All "downsides" I could list are purely preferential issues and some minor nitpicks over animations. The gameplay is solid, and I've found myself coming back for more consistently. An excellent roguelike for the increasingly eclectic rougelike collection.

Can you survive a zombie outbreak? This game mixes comedy, survival, crafting and more to create a unique style but many minor issues make it frustrating to play. Single player lasts around 16 hours.
You play as Frank West, a photojournalist, who is caught in a zombie outbreak in not Las Vegas. It is a difficult game to categorise, I guess it is primarily a survival game, but it has many other elements. You have an open world to explore but have a strict time limit. There is crafting as well as mini games such as poker. As upgrades to the original dead rising 2 there is a photo mode to earn extra experience points and a sandbox mode that removes the time limit.
Having different paths through the game sounds fun but in reality you won’t miss huge amounts if you answer all the calls for help. The survival gameplay and settings are both novel and provide some enjoyment. It looks good for it's age and the environments are detailed and interactive. The main problem is that the gameplay just feels like a chore.
You can create wacky weapons but unless you find killing endlessly respawning zombies fun this quickly becomes dull as you stick to the most efficient and easily available weapons. After this the game boils down to running from point to point following the world’s most useless navigation arrow.
The experience system doesn’t really fit in a game with a strict time limit. Essentially you become faster, stronger and can carry more as you complete missions. This creates a problem where the optional psychopath bosses are balanced for co-op as well as high level characters so they are really tough if you don’t play this way.
In combat everything has really long animations and there is no lock on so melee feels really clumsy especially when you are constantly surrounded by zombies and debris. The inventory system also suffers from only having 1 button to pick up, good luck trying to pick anything up out of a pile in a hurry. You have survivors who you can escort for a good chunk of experience. But they have virtually no survival skills, can be grabbed by zombies, can’t shake free and can take friendly fire. Thankfully you can pick some of them up and carry them. Finally in the last third of the game you have fast spitting zombies which make you barf if you let them get you which may be the most annoying thing ever.
I hope all this whining makes it clear that this game is a recipe for frustration. It constantly feels like you’re being beaten down which just isn’t much fun for more than a few hours.

I'll qualify this review by saying that I'm not a railfan.  I snagged this one as part of a Humble Bundle, because I enjoy simulator games.  I also haven't played very much, only completing a good chunk of the "academy" levels and doing a few short runs along simple tracks in an electric train.  However, since Train Simulator is pretty much exactly what it says on the tin, I still feel qualified to review it, because I can already grasp both what's going on in this game as well as why some people might become railfans.
As the hilariously badass Serious Voice in the intro video informs us, trains are about PRECISION and PERFECTION.  Train Simulator accurately represents the interiors of various kinds of trains, puts you at their helm to pull levers and such, and tasks you with getting to stations on time.  The level of interactivity and complexity on offer here is really compelling, and I find it far more interesting and challenging than I might have expected.  You're free to drive however you like, of course, but you're gently encouraged not to accelerate too quickly, to speed, to brake too quickly, or to be late to your stops, by a system of point penalties that don't really affect your gameplay but will bother you psychologically if you have any kind of sense of responsibility or professionalism.
You have access to a wide variety of trains to drive, including an antique steam locomotive (which I find particularly cool) and several varieties of diesel and electric trains.  You can tow passengers, or cargo; you can work switches, you need to ask for permission to pass red signals, you have to pay attention to weight and grade and the weather.  You can turn on headlights and windshield wipers, you can honk your horn.  You can interact with the controls directly (my preferred method), or you can use a kind of overlay with abstract representations of the controls that is easier to parse at first but, in my opinion, slightly less cool than laying your mouse pointer on the actual levers themselves.
You have a similarly large selection of tracks to run around on, from simple passenger runs from one stop to the next, to longer circuits, to branching paths involving backing up to connect to cargo cars or grab other locomotives for repairs.  There are free-form driving scenarios as well as a "campaign" with lots of premade situations for you, and you're free to design your own as well.
I can't speak for the truly hardcore, but to my untrained eye, I found (and continue to find!) Train Simulator 17 a very thorough and accessible introduction to the concept of driving trains, and one I plan to put a lot of time into in the future.  There's something really compelling about that PRECISION and PERFECTION, about accelerating up to the right speed and then just coasting along checking out the countryside, checking your instruments from time to time to make sure everything is under control, making minor adjustments.  There's something reassuring about the way the train moves down the tracks, like a well-trained (har har) but powerful beast that you have a loose leash on.
Very very minor nitpick: it would be nice to be able to customize the little avatar that shows up in the cabin when you're in other camera modes.  This ultimately doesn't really impact my experience much, since I spend most of my time in first person mode inside the cabin, but it would be nice.

This game really is an indie gem with so many endless possibilities. It combines strategy, third person combat, and RPG elements that come together to form a wholly unique and fun experience. You start out on in campaign sandbox map in which you are left to do as you wish. Join up with one of the game's factions, gather local farmers to train into epic knights, raid close by villages, or take on mercenary work for a city's guildmaster. This game is a true medieval simulation in which their are many different choices for your character. Inside and outside of combat you are faced with a lot of choice to your style of play, and you can experiment with each.
Within combat the game plays rather similar to Chivalry, although with more depth. The basics are that you control your swing and block directions via mouse movement. However beyond that, there are hidden mechanics that will get me beaten in a duel server everytime. It's a simple concept, that is easy to learn, but difficult to master. You also have ranged weapons and horse combat as an option if you so choose. Either way, you can hone your skills through combat or an RPG style character panel.
The feeling of progression is given with your troops as well. It's such a cool feeling to gather 10 farmers from a village on the strategy map, see them fight against bandits with pitchforks, and slowly progress into a team of full plate armored knights. You can constantly be increasing your army size and ranks through the renown you gain in victories, as well as your own level. You never are put in a sitatuation where you feel stagnant, you always have something to work towards that is within reach, and that really hooks you.
The world you inhabit is also constantly changing. The factions dynamically wage war with one another, and take new land. Lords will defect to other factions and will be given fiefs by the King. Something you can partake in should you hold his favor. You can take land for yourself once strong enough. You can besiege castles and make a claim to the throne yourself. This will differ in effectiveness based on your relationship with other Kings and your "right to rule". If no one respects your claim, you can be put in your place rather quickly when every faction wants you dead for your warmongering. I will say, although the politcal system is not particularly deep, it is servicable and enough to keep you entertained.
This game is not perfect however. It does show its age. Combat animations and animations in general can look rather janky. The game does not go very deep in certain areas, though enjoyable, sometimes you just wish that it had more to it in areas. Also graphically, it's far from perfect. Most of these problems can be solved by mods though, and the mods for this game are nothing short of incredible. There are mods that add to the depth of politics that stretch all the way to total conversions for this game. If you've ever wanted a Game of Thrones RPG, you can make this game into one. They really do vary to every era in history, and to other licenses in film and other video games. In fact, the other week, I managed to play a Star Wars themed mod, that was surprisingly functional.
This game is just the gift that keeps on giving, and for the amount of times this thing has been on sale, it deserves a place in your library. I have 200 hours plus in this game, and for less than the price of a Subway sandwich, it has most definitely earned my money.

Guns, Countless Bullets and an almost endless wave of Zombies.
There is something strangely satisfying about playing this game with your favourite playlist playing in the background. That feeling of leaning back in your comfy chair and unleashing a wave of molten metal justice into the unsuspecting horde of zombies. I'm not usually one for such mindless carnage (although now I think about it I enjoyed the hell out of Carmageddon all those years ago). Yet, I found myself turning to this game when I had no idea what else to play.
I'm not going to sugar coat the game at all, it 'says what it is on the tin' to be fair to the developers - It's  Zombie Shooter. That's all there is to it, yet there feels like there's more.
It has a Campaign and a Survival Mode, both of which are pretty fun, although I did find myself enjoying the Survival Mode more. In Survival Mode you have survive as many Zombie Waves as you can in a small confined area. There are a selection of maps (each with their own unique element), a wide range of guns and a collection of power ups to use as you see fit. Interestingly there's a perk system too, which allows you to customise your character as you level up from killing the Zombies and surviving the waves.
Campaign mode was OK for what it is, a isometric 'corridor' shooter, and doesn't really try to be anything else. However, it does suffer from some environmental clipping, which is perhaps the most danger you'll find yourself in as it's easy to become trapped/stuck (forcing you to restart the level).
Much like the Survival mode you can upgrade your character, but you have to find the guns to unlock them (rather than the guns falling off of Zombies and into your lap).
I think what I really liked about the Campaign was that there wasn't a half-arsed story tacked onto it to try and justify the mindless onslaught against the Zombie Hoard. It just plonked you into the game and allowed you to go. It makes me realise that I'd actually like to see a Zombie Movie based on that idea - no poorly written story with terrible actors, just a person or two killing endless zombies before the zombies kill them.
The controls are basic and use as WSAD approach with Mouse aiming, sadly no gamepad support (that I could find). There are no real options to customise resolution or graphics, so you'll have to make do with what they offer. The sound is OK, but not amazing. I do feel as though this game is missing out on a killer soundtrack to support the carnage.
If you have low expectations, and are perhaps just looking for something to sit back and waste a few hours on this game is ideal - it might even surprise you.

This game is a super tight platformer with rogue-like elements. I first encountered the game from it's humble beginnings December 2008 when it was a GameMaker-made game.  Even with the limited tool set Derek Yu, the developer, put in a lot of great work into the release creating a fervor on the forums I posted on (SomethingAwful) at the time.
What led this game away from other similiar platforms is that if you died, it was because you were not using the tools provided to prevent that death.  People would complain about rocks randomly coming from explosions hitting them in the head until they were told not to be in the same room when any explosions was going to expected to happen.
Derek Yu took this and brought it new life with the addition of great new features but keeping the onus of staying alive on the player.
The roguelike nature of the game gave the player and enemies a world they all need to try their hardest to live in.  Yes, I said enemies.  The players can use the world to fight back against the enemies such as knowing a player can enter spikes from the side while the spiders only know how to drop onto players but spikes will instantly kill anything that drops on them.  What you get is the player being protected by spikes while the spider throws itself into the needles.
The world is fair and it's up to the player to find out these patterns and use them or avoid bad configurations.

Who ever thought it would be addicting to die this much? Spelunky is a great rogue-like game that is just as addictive as it is frustrating. It can take a little bit to get used to, as runs can range to fairly easy to ridiculously hard depending on what you have on you! Getting through the levels and finding treasures become that much more rewarding though. The artwork is fabulous, as is the charming [although sometimes stereotypical, they add to theme] character designs. If you're a fan of fast-paced, adventurous, rogue-like games, you definitely will not regret the purchase. I wouldn't recommend it for those who get frustrated easily, or prefer casual relaxing games.

A decent racing-themed car brawler where the aim (in the main game modes) is to blow up opposing racers as many times as possible within a time limit by picking up bonuses from the track which enable you to use one of your three combat abilities, which for multiplayer purposes seem pretty unbalanced between the cars, but for single player interest there is a fair range of different preferences catered for - you have cars (trucks, ice cream vans) whose best weapons are laid like mines ahead of the enemy racers, others that need to be adjacent to the target for best (or only) results, and others that attack from behind, with a couple with a mix of options.
The racing, particularly single player isn't too great, the controls aren't the smoothest and most of the time where you placed in the race is irrelevant compared to how much mayhem you inflicted - racing far ahead is usually easy, even on the tougher difficulties of most tracks, but means you will have no one around to attack, thus guaranteeing a loss, so the main advantage is first choice of which bonus to pick up before moving to the appropriate position to use it.
The tracks have a reasonable variety, which a strong preference for lots of jumps and other risky locations to crash and burn, either unaided or with some help from your friendly competition, but the directions are well signposted so the learning curve of new tracks isn't too steep in most cases. The graphics are servicable enough but not amazing, and audio does the job well enough.
So overall it is a bit of fun, but be aware the multiplayer side of things is sparse (if that) unless you bring your own, and even if you do don't expect a fair fight, but nevertheless it is a reasonable game.

In many ways this game was very fun and an upgrade from the Stick of Truth. That being said, this does not meet the expectations of Stick of Truth -- at all. This game is filled with Matt and Trey's brilliant humor, yet the story itself is predictable and not very entertaining. It has it's moments. Stick of Truth explored the entire South Park universe whereas FBW offers very little. No farms, Girls bathroom council, Cafeteria, Canada, places like the UFO, or any special areas; everything you see on the map is pretty much all you'll be exploring in this game and maybe a few surprises -- that don't actually contribute to the plot.
Sadly, expectations were set very high and the product failed to deliver anything above a decent game.
TL;DR
Fractured But Whole is well worth a buy, just DON'T expect it to exceed the Stick of Truth. You need to have very low expectations to enjoy this game. This is not an Obsidian game. This is a triple A Ubisoft product.

WASTED is a fantastic game about getting drunk in a post apocalyptic wasteland.
*scroll down for pros and cons
This is a very very creative and hilarious game where you dive into a dungeon (called the cooler) to find booze and get a perk. The only way to exit the dungeon is by dying and losing all your items, your character and past hangovers (previous upgrades recieved by booze) or finding booze! Drinking booze early on usually hurts u by giving u a -10% accuracy forever on that character but waiting until later results in you possibly facing harder enemies and dying.
Taking too long on one specific level and you will start being "hunted" and lemme tell you right now, you are going to want to GTFO when that starts and DO NOT go back. This is a great feature as it makes you think quick on your feet and try not to get lost in these maze like levels but I find that it comes a little too quick as I frequently get lost in the levels and have to back track a minute or two which sometimes results in death.

But this game is quite different as permadeath is not complete permadeath, you keep everything that you stashed in your house as well as whatever currency you stored (Currency is toilet paper HA!).
There is also a special game mode that you unlock that pits you against super hard enemies with a set character and dares you to go as far and last as long as possible. It's very random and very hard. This is where there is a multiplayer component, wellllll not multiplayer as much as leaderboards. After your run is done you see how you stack up against other players.

TL;DR: WASTED is a fun, if occasionally infuriating dungeon crawler that I recommend
for its charm, ease of play, and depth of strategy required to be successful
Adult-Swim Games has done it again! I don't know what exactly is in the water over there (maybe 'booze'?) but they make pretty damn good games, and this is no exception. WASTED is not shy about its fallout references and inspirations, but they are used to enhance the game, and not as a crutch that it falls back on.  At its heart, WASTED is a rogue-like dungeon crawler that takes place in a post-apocalyptic 80's tech wasteland. There is no free-roaming like what is in the Fallout series, instead a variety of set locations that you fast travel to and explore when you aren't dungeon crawling in the Cooler. Sounds pretty typical so far, nothing fancy. However, once you enter the dungeon, you cannot leave unless you die or drink booze, and this is where the strategy comes in. Booze in this game are bottles that bestow upon you a permanent effect, and it can be either beneficial or detrimental. Some booze may make your attacks ignore enemy armor, while others may make it so that your attacks do no damage unless you hit enemies in their heads. Once you drink booze however, you exit the dungeon and return to your home, so often it becomes a risk versus reward scenario. Do I keep exploring to try and get a better booze buff, or better loot? Or do I cut my losses and take the hit, returning home with plenty of spoils, but now I take more melee damage? However, once you do inevitably die, you do not need to despair, for you respawn as a brand new character in the same world using the same safe house, so any loot you left behind can be used by them (however, you lose any items you did not stash away and your hangovers). I would have liked for there to be customization options for the characters you respawn as, but I guess that is just another incentive to stay alive as long as possible. All in all, I highly recommend this game!

Their lack of fixing known bugs and how often they listen to the community makes the game sometimes frustrating. Yes, they do pay attention, such as how they added medic packs, something the community wanted, but things like fixing fps and such took too long.
An example of something inbalanced is that without a vehicle, the game becomes a 'walking' simulator (In 'Assault', even if there are bikes and trucks placed around the map, it is not enough, so you will usually rely on movable spawn points. Not sure what exactly pet peeved some people into disliking this particular one in the trilogy, but I believe that of the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. franchise, this is an amazing ´sequel´ to the Shadow of Chernobyl.
I use the term losely in this concept, as Clear Sky takes place prior to the events of SoC, yet is the 2nd installment in the trilogy (red.)
CS brings in the familiar tone and setting from the SoC and along with it, a shít-ton of new features (and bugs).
Right off the bat; this game is not perfect, however it is damn near perfection when modded properly for more realistic lighting, shadow, texture and sounds - however I suggest newcomers to experience the vanilla game beforehand.
The story - which can be read/summerised in the wiki-page - is nothing unusual. In fact, SoC had somewhat of a more interesting angle to the protagonist than CS. Nonetheless, it´s still manages to draw you in.
As someone who´s obsessed with snipers, CS offers a even larger variety in the gamplay, with the added feature of modding your weapons! From a simple reduction in recoil of your guns, to more accuracy and flatness (projectile speed) and undermounted grenade launcher, you can customize almost any given weapon to fit your needs/style. Add the choice to attack a scope to nearly any rifle, you can turn a full automatic AK into a mid-range sniper rifle. Granted, I wouldn´t go with an AK due to their terribly low accuracy, but just as an example.
NOTE! Most first tier modifications are available at nearly any weapon smith. To unlock the 2nd and last tier, you´ll need the blueprints/schiematics in form of USB-drives (that´s right, bítches, it´s USB sticks).
These can be obtained from loot spots (backpacks, boxes, supplies or others), which you can learn about from either PDAs on enemies or buying the info from bartenders or other NPCs.
Another option is doing missions - main or side, they will reward you occasionally with a USB, unlocking mod possibilities for various weapons - and even armor!
Artifacts, bítches! Get em while they´re hot!
The enemies vary from a simple bandit in Addidas track suit, taking pot shots at you with a 9mm well beyond it´s accuracy threshold, to SVD Dragunov wielding bullet sponges in exoskeletal armor to psy-enhances mutants, with the power to debilitate and kill even the most hardened veteran of the Zone, should you be unlucky enough.
NOTE! I found shotguns to be particularly useful at point blank when dealing with almost any mutants. Thanks to the spread, it made zig-zag´ing dogs and bloodsuckers(!) easier to deal with. Bloodsuckers are even tougher than in SoC. At least in my experience. They seem to be circling around you in an effort to distract and avoid gunfire more frequently than the SoC-variations.
The factions and their disputes are on much larger scale than SoC, meaning you´ll have plenty of oppertunities to either push or prevent a certain faction to advance or retreat. Ultimately you can wipe out entire factions, should you be so bold. (still not certain if it was intended as an option in the game or not. Could be part of a mod. Might edit if any news should present itself)
The locations are almost identical to the SoC with a few improvements and changes in the direction of progress. Still that eerie and gloomy tone and ambience to really make it more fun plaing all alone in complete darkness. It´s called immersion, I´m told.
Conclusion: Outstanding game which deserves every praise and attention it gets!
