Train Simulator is a constantly-improving simulation of what operating a train is really like. Now that it works again with the "Rail Driver" accessory controller, diesel and electric operation feels a lot more like reality than just pushing buttons on a keyboard or XBox controller. However, these things also work.
The positive reviews are correct. Most routes include all the track and visible scenery--buildings, roards, bridges, even seashore--along about 100 miles of track. For example, with the "Pacific Surfliner" DLC, you get everything you would see looking out the windows during the 3 hour ride from San Diego Santa Fe Depot to Los Angeles Union Station. SoCal fans can also choose to purchase the very different experience of Cajon Pass between San Bernadino and Barstow.
As others have noted, NONE of the DLC's are necessary to play the original "Train Simulator" game--they don't help you "win" or something like that.
Train Simulator DLC's are NOT "PLAY-TO-WIN" like in many other, more competitive, games.
All the DLC do is give you more experiences. If all you want to do is run trains on Caltrain to San Francisco or up the North Wales line from Crewe, experinces you can have with the most basic "Train Simulator 2018," you don't have to spend another cent!
In addition, "Train Simulator" includes all the tools you need to add or delete track, modify the railroads you buy (or download for free-more on that below), or you can even build an entire new railroad of your own. "TS" also includes the tools you need to make new "schedules," including all the other trains the train you are operating happens to pass. So you can have a lot of fun without spending a penny more after you buy the original game.
You can also create your own cars and locomotives, if you have the right graphic tools. I haven't done it, but obviously many others have.
One last thing: There are NO good physics if you derail (wreck) your train. That's because this game is about operating trains, not wrecking them. Buy GTA5 if you want a "smash-em up!"
If this sounds boring to you: DON'T BUY THIS GAME!  - Respect the people who enjoy it.
Now back to "Pacific Surfliner" DLC
I live in Oceanside, CA and I travel by rail (and sometimes car) to Los Angeles, San Diego and Orange County often. So I know this line well, and I can recognize many key landmarks the designers incuded. Most of the buildings are generic ones substituting for the real ones, but this game is about trains, not architecture. The Train Simulator version is now "historic," because a lot of new double-track has been laid, and new bridges built, but some TS railroads--like the Pennsylvania R.R. Horseshoe Curve (Altoona-Johnstown) DLC--reproduce a line as it existed fifty years ago, or earlier.
How accurate is the "Pacific Surfliner" DLC? Well, I have traveled the Oceanside-San Diego section dozens of times, and driven it along Interstate 5, and I was convinced they just ommitted a few miles between Encinitas and Solana Beach,one of the fastest pieces of track along that segment that includes a town with no station called "Cardiff-on-Sea."
I WAS WRONG! There are only four miles between Encinitas and Solana Beach---I checked the Amtrak schedule that lists the mileage--it was just my impression that there was more there. Yes, the designers incuded "Cardiff," but the buildings they used are really generic-looking compared to the riot of color and light at the real place. They also made the San Clemente Pier neighborhood look more blah than it really is. Like I said, this game is about trains and track.
For "Pacific Surfliner" DLC, there are two additional for-pay DLC's. One covers the San Diego commuter rail (Coaster), and the other is Los Angeles Orange Co. commuter rail (Metrolink). You get the trains, all painted up accurately, correct locomoties, plus several realistic scenarios that include the Amtrak trains from the "Pacific Surfliner" DLC railroad, along with the Coaster or Metrolink trains you get in these DLC's.
Note that, although the LA Commuter rail (Metrolink) DLC scenarios have no San Diego commuter (NCTD Coaster) trains, and vice-versa, now that I own both, I COULD create scenarios that include both Metrolink and Coaster trains. There wouldn't be too much point, except that Coaster and Metrolnk share the same maintenace and storage yard north of Oceanside. The "Pacific Surfliner" DLC includes the entire facility, and it always contains both Coaster and Metrolink trains side by side--plus both railroads run their trains up to their joint yard after dropping off their last passengers of the day at Oceanside. As a result, for several miles of track, you can see Amtrak, Metrolink, Coaster, and BNSF freight trains running by each other.
None of these DLC's are very expensive--$19-$39 or so--and they help make "Pacific Surfliner" run a lot more like the real railroad.
However, if you didn't want to pay a penny more, you don't have to spend another cent!
Furthermoere, "Train Simulator" has a "Community Workshop" where people have uploaded additonal cars, locomoties, scenarios, and even entire new railroads. Most are FREE.
In the case of "Pacific Surflinter," some kind soul has uploaded a FREIGHT (Goods) train package so you can also run freight trains up and down the LA-SD route. Being much heavier and longer than passenger trains, freights respond much differently to acceleration and braking. The LA-SD line includes one significant hill just outside San Diego which is challenging in the game -- AND in real life. Railroaders call it "Sorrento Grade." The designer of the Freebie freight scenario also added more information about the geography, like all the "Control Points" along the track that the "Pacific Surfliner" DLC designers left off. You can add your own geographic data to any scenario you want, thus effectively creating a new scenario, with the tools already in "Train Simulator."
BTW, since the LA-SD track is so busy during the day, essentialy all freight trains from Fullerton to San Diego operate only at night. The Workshop DLC scenarios should be night-time. However, that is easy to change. You can change the weather--from California Sunshine--to Seattle Rain Squalls--to a Wyoming Snowstorm--aas well as  the time (with the sun and moon changing naturally from day to dusk to night) on any scenario, almsot at will.
The Workshop does get complicated, because someone can upload, say, a new scenario for one of the DLC railroads that requires you to add a few other locomotives and cars you have to search and often pay for. However, this is a hobby.
Bottom Line: I love model trains, but I don't have the time or space to build any now. "Train Simulator" gives me an experience that is unlike model railroading, but doesn't cost the thousands of dollars one can eventually plow into a well-detailed model railroad. It provides an experience that is even better than model railroading because I can run my train for hours without coming back to the same place.  ALL ABOARD!
P.S.: My biggest criticism: The audio is still not really realistic. Why oh why doesn't the the game say something logical like "Highball Metrolink 608!" instead of "O.K. to Proceed"? Basic railroad talk.
Well, "Train Simulator 2018" represents the culmination of almost two decades of work, and things can only get better.

It is made by 3rd party companies that specialize in simulator content and is then PUBLISHED by the developers of this game. You are not being nickel and dimed by the devs.

It features a decently big open world map in which you fight your way through literally thousands of zombies to complete a story or to play at your own pace in sandbox mode.

To make this game look even better, I fiddled around in Nvidia Control Panel, setting Antialiasing, Texture Filtering and other options I could find for the game, to On. This made the game look really amazing without the need for any major graphically intensive mods. The only extra mods I used for the game is an FoV file modification and the use of a program called Flawless Widescreen which fixed some hud elements and tweaked some other graphic options.

DEFINITELY. Wether you pick this up for full price or on a sale, you won't be disappointed.

Zombie Shooter looks and is extremely low budget. It could easily have been a DOS game from the mid 90s, but it was actually released in 2007. With that said, it is an enjoyable DOS game from the mid 90s. The level design is basic, linear, and straightforward. Animations are the bare minimum that one could expect from an average game from that era. Each mission involves doing very similar actions, like reaching certain specific areas of the map a couple times in order to proceed. There are several items and upgrades that could be purchased between each level, as well as upgrading skills from your character, which makes for an interesting and fun addition to the upfront running and shooting. The AI has very serious problems, and at times you may use this to your advantage. Zombies will often get stuck behind walls or other objects, and many times they will also spin in place and not move, without doing anything else. Besides the campaign, there are two additional game modes, but they are much less interesting and do not provide for a true extension of replay ability. Zombie Shooter is a short and basic game, with very simple game play mechanics. It is plagued by severe AI path finding issues as well as general AI problems. There are also various bugs throughout the game, and the final boss is not challenging at all, in comparison to the massive groups of non-boss zombies that will come at you almost non-stop. Also, the small amount of text found in Zombie Shooter has some grammar errors. There is very little variety to be found in Zombie Shooter, and the short lived amount of game play will not keep you very interested, and it will not last long. For an unintentional DOS game from the mid 90s, this is a small gaming distraction amidst the abundance of better, more polished games out there.

Spelunky is hands down one of the best platformers on Steam, and probably ever made. I've completed the vast majority of the game, but even in 120+ hours of play, I haven't been able to beat the super-secret, ultra-hard final level.
Positives:
>The physics are tight, and the controls feel intuitive, whether using Keyboard and Mouse or controller.
>The gameplay is extremely challenging and also rewarding -  you will die often, and you will fail often, but it almost always feels "fair" and you can easily see your improvement as you learn the tricks the game throws at you.
>The ambience and charm of the game are undeniable. The characters are adorable, the enemies are (ferociously) adorable, the art-style is great.
>Replayability: 10000%. Every game is different. Replaying over and over for favorable item drops so you can have an easier time doesn't feel like a chore. Replaying over and over even in a standard way because you die so often doesn't feel like a chore. Some runs will be easier, some will be nigh-impossible (until you level up your proficiency at the game).
Negatives:
>The multiplayer isn't great. Which is fine, this is a single-player masterpiece.
>The level of difficulty is probably a shade too high. For someone who wants to obsessively complete games, this was great, as I always felt challenged. For a casual gamer, it might be a tad bit frustrating.
Overall, I give the game a 9.5/10, it's basically a perfect game. It has essentially no gameplay bugs and the bugs it does have, add to high level strategies that most players will never encounter. Pick up Spelunky if you're looking for a challenge or a game you can play over and over and over!

I received this game as part of the Humble Bundle and what a pleasant surprise it was. It is an FPS / dungeon crawler with a quirky Borderlands-esque art style and a wicked sense of humour through-out.
One thing most other reviews haven't mentioned as yet is that the mechanics allow for shorter gameplay sessions to still be rewarding. To explain, each run into the dungeons (known as coolers ingame) can end in several ways. You can be a boss completing a whole dungeon, be a heroic statistic (die horribly) or choose to drink some radioactive booze which causes you to pass out and wake up at home with a 'hangover' which can be a permanent buff or debuff. Part of the game is deciding whether to press on and try for more loot or even completing the cooler, or taking a drink in order to escape the terror that is the S.O.B. Purifier who hunts you down if you take too long reaching the exit of a level, or taking a drink because it'll add a useful buff to your character for the rest of his or her short life.
Items stored and upgrades to your house persist through character deaths and hangovers persist through dungeon runs (both buffs and debuffs). This rogue-like progression helps improve your chances over successive runs as the challenges keep getting tougher.
Did I mention how incredibly fun the game is? Pretty sure the dev has an indy hit on his hands with this one. 9.5/10
This game is basically a Rogue-like mixed with fallout in the best way. Feels really good to play and definetly a go-to when I am bored.

GAMEPLAY 9/10
The gameplay (as advertised) is a mix between Borderlands and Fallout, with more of an airy feel. Your goal is to find Booze, a substance that you can only find in giant underground vaults (called Coolers). This Booze will give you special abilities that can vary from having every enemy you kill explode, to increasing your characters base stats. These special effects and abilities are permanent and are never detrimental. The gunplay is very reminiscent of the last generation of Fallout games, where your shooting skill severely affects your aim and damage. The inventory system is a little weird, and might take a little bit to get used to. Also important is that you will have VERY little space for items. You need to find a fanny pack. One more important thing would be that this isn't a fully open world, you travel to certain areas then you are confined to that area.
STORY 6/10
From what I can gather from the opening cinematic, as well as a little exposition, the world ended in 1980 due to nuclear war between all nations. Because of this, the wasteland is stuck in constant 80s mode, where big hair rules and fanny packs are in. The "story" doesn't just follow one character though, after you start a new game and create a character, dying becomes commonplace, and every time you die, a new character comes under your control and gets whatever your last character left in your safehouse.
GRAPHICS 7/10
This is where the game gets a lot of inspiration from Borderlands. The graphics are very cell shaded and cartoonish. In my opinion it's a very smart decision from the developers. It gives the game a timeless feel, and gives very good replayability.
HUMOR 8/10
This isn't a normal category, but because of this games major studio I feel it's somewhat necessary. This game is hilarious though, from the dialogue, to the item descriptions, to the world itself. It's all incredibly stupid and fun, and honestly, it's a great way to just relax and ♥♥♥♥ around.
OVERALL 7.5/10
This game is incredibly fun and just a really easy going game that you aren't going to have to invest a lot of time in if you don't want to, if you do want to invest time in the game, the challenge is there. This game has everything you could want and I recommend it.

I was skeptical about this game when I looked at it time and time again in the highlights. The trailer seemed simplistic and  didn't show much despite it showing a lot. However, after playing heavy triple A titles, I started longing for a lightweight adventure story, packaged in a nostalgic point and click genre... at least that's what I thought I was going to get... and with the release of a 4th Deponia game, I decided to try it out. I have not visited an adventure point a click game genre since I've played the Neverhood when it came out back in 1996... speaking of which... didn't the studio make a new game in the same style? .... anyways... Deponia - a refreshing and seemingly lightweight adventure title made by an indie studio who have definitely delivered the best of the genre in this game. The protagonist is an egocentric, narcissistic, self centered and industrious nut job with a clear goal and a heart in the right place. He's the village idiot with a genius twist and although there were a few moments when his written dialog pushed the utmost boundaries of his character type, I still noticed my own reflection in his persona and was able to relate and see myself in his shoes. The story features a full character development arc and harbors within it's cartoony look a serious adult topic with a strong dilemma. When I started this game,I thought I was getting a lightweight comic time passer and boy was I pleasantly surprised when the game really too me for a ride.
The puzzles were ok, there are a few minigames that seemed a tad over-complicated for my taste but the game offered a skip button for those which was a fantastic feature that let me get along with the plot. Progressing with the gameplay was not too hard and there were only a handful of parts where I had to consult a walkthrough but I'd honestly have to blame myself for not figuring out some of them as they were fairly straight forward. Comedy consists of a mix of adult and childish topics. The songs and gameplay music were phenomenal which, being a composer myself, is something I pay extra attention to in games so kudos to the composer. The voice actors did a great job, only complaint was the mix job on the Organon characters voices but it's a minor nuisance, and the artwork along with chosen character and environment concept styles were an absolute perfect fit for the idea that the developers wanted to depict. Only other complaint there were the cutscene animations gags, the automated movements that you get with After Effects (or software alike) is really mechanical and sometimes missed the mark on the timing where the gag would have been perfect (as said in the Max Fleischer biography, he'd sometimes spend hours at a editing station cutting and pasting frames since he believed perfect gags occur only at the right time)
Needles to say, I just bought Deponia 2 and 3 and will be playing that for a while, although it's been a while since they came out, I hope for the same and even perhaps improved experience. Definitely looking forward to what these character are about to go though.

If you are a big fan of the South Park cartoon and The Stick of Truth, you'll probably have a great time drowning yourself in the South Park universe and it's satrical quirks. It also ties in with the show as well (S21E04). With all these being said, I would recommend you getting it right off the bat.
But if you are just looking to explore another RPG title, you might want to consider getting this during a sale or a few months down the road. As a video game, there are tons of hand-holding moments (even on the highest difficulty) which takes a chunk out of challenging its players. But it is also a refreshing take on games, you probably need not worry about making mistakes and that is what playing a game is all about -- enjoying it without taking a beating. It WILL NOT give you that sense of satisfaction as you would beating a game but rather laugh at the butt load of jokes / twists right till the end.
I did not encounter any game-breaking bugs but felt that the minigame controls could be further improved or optimized. Otherwise, it feels pretty polished even though some may argue that it is blatantly a console port.
The game carries on the same ol' formula that they have built upon the first game, one that is worthy to be referenced as a sequel. Some kinks they have to work on is the comedic shock value and issues touched upon could be bolder and crazier than the last game. Some mechanics will also feel redundant and repetitive as you summon your superhero buddies to overcome an obstacle that you couldn't otherwise pass until you progressed through the story (i.e. like Link able to move heavier boulders).
With that being said, I think the 70 bucks will be well-spent if you are a big fan and as an entry fee for a South Park experience for the next 2 days.

NOTE: (edited for clarity).  This review is broken up into three parts:  1)  addressing the issue of DLC and the anger people feel about it; 2) those things I liked about the game (and why I voted yes as a recommendation) and 3) those things that are still an issue in the game that have not been resolved.  It is a long read with additional comments in the comment section.  I invite you to read it all to see my point.  THANKS.
A lot of the anger about this game is being misdirected for several reasons.  The ongoing assumption is that when you buy this game, you should have dozens and dozens of routes and simulations to play.  Many people will not be happy unless there were 20, 30, even 50 routes for you to drive.  If that is your assumption, this is not the game for you (Let me be clear - if you are purchasing this game with the idea that you are going to have 10, 20, 30 routes, lots of engines and assets to choose from - you will be disappointed - its not there).  In real life, there are hundreds of trains, thousands of different cars, locos, assets and countless routes all over the world.  In real life, you will never get to experience all of them.  This game is no different - you will not get to experience all of them.  However, you are FREE TO CHOOSE those routes and settings that are of specific interest to you.  YOU ARE NOT REQUIRED TO BUY ANY DLC AND PURCHASING A DLC WILL NOT FUNDAMENTALLY CHANGE ANY GAME PLAY.  The DLCs just represents extra game play if you are so interested.  With that said, would I like to see the base game contain at least 8 to 10 routes instead of 4 or 5 - I COULD DEFINITELY ARGUE FOR THAT - but then again they are here to make money - not to make cheap games for us to play.
Now are there some actual concerns that should be addressed? - A DEFINITE YES.  Do some of the routes still contain bugs, physics issues and environmental concerns?  - YES.  Do I wish the game had more "environment" - more natural sounds of urban city life, people on the platforms, cars on the road, etc? - YES.   Is some of the scenery rehashed and some of the loco sounds used again and again? - YES.   Like any product, do your homework to find out the quality DLC that are good value and buy them.  Those that are not, don't.
There is a lot to like about the game and a lot that I have enjoyed.  The trains (both inside and out) are realistic and detailed. Driving trains are fun and can be challenging.   The scenery on some routes is a joy to see.  Meeting timetables, hauling cargo - if that is your kind of thing - you will have fun with it - warts and all.   I know I have.  But to down vote this game because you don't understand how the DLC works or to scream I have to spend thousands of dollars to enjoy the game or to say that the DLC price should only be one dollar or five dollars is simply not accurate or appropriate.  I won't argue the fact that a few more routes would be nice and a better value (I tend to agree with this) - but if price is a concern, wait till it goes on sale.  The sale price is worth it.
Keep in mind, the base game cost $40 USD not the typical $60 USD.  That is a good start.  If this game was a typical AAA title costing $60 or more - yes, I would be groaing and fussing about it.  On the surface, $40 USD is not a bad price.  But as I keep saying, steam sales are a dime a dozen.  If $40 causes you angst, wait for a sale.  ON SALE, IT IS WORTH EVERY PENNY.
In the end, buy ONLY what interests you, ignore the rest and enjoy the ride.  I hate DLCs just like the next guy but folks we are stuck with them.  The industry is falling over itself to do it this way.  And the simulation market is re-pleat with hundreds of DLC choices (i.e Trainz, A New Era, Euro Truck Simulator, Farm Simulator, etc).  You just have to be wise in your choices.

The King of Iron Fist is Back!
Tekken 7 Returns to the landscape of Fighting Games with their first console release since 2012's Tekken Tag Tournament 2 with the added bonus of releasing a very competent, arguably superior PC port in their first foray into the PC Market.
The console/PC port of Tekken 7 is a faithful translation of the arcade version of Tekken 7: Fated Retribution which is itself a version update of Tekken 7, released in arcades in 2015, adding a robust story mode that elaborates on some of the finer points of the Mishima Saga and introducing the wildly popular Street Fighter character, Akuma/Gouki ( present in Vanilla T7 as well.)
First thing I noticed upon booting the game up is how much the visuals pop out at you. Even on my Low-Mid range rig ( i5 4670k, 8GB Ram, Radeon  R7 360 ) with graphics settings at a mixture of med/high options the game looks and moves beautifully at 60 FPS, which is essential for any serious fighting gamer.
The game also natively supports 4k resolutions for all the tech-nuts out there so you should have no problem pushing the visuals to the limit with the right rig.
Tekken also is well regarded for their strong catalog of music, and this entry is no exception with Akitaka Tohyama and company delivering another strong soundtrack that perfectly matches the flow and feel of the Tekken universe in every way. From the main menu theme to the battle music you'd be hardpressed to find much if any music that seems out of place here.
Gameplay wise there is a noticable amount of new things introduced in Tekken 7, notably the Rage Art system which is similar to the Critical Edge system in another fairly recent Namco fighter; Soul Calibur V.
Simply put, once your health meter reaches a certain area, your character and life bar will flash red, increasing your damage output and giving you access to the Rage Art and Rage Drive techniques.
The "Bound" system of previous Tekken Titles is gone as well, replaced with a mechanic known as "Screw Attack" which instead of staggering an opponent to open them up for more combo opportunities or bouncing them off of the ground, sends them spinning sideways through the air for more juggle possibilities.
The usual customization options are still here as well, so you can create your crazy renditions of your favorite characters with a sizeable amount of wardrobe options although to my memory it seems like Tekken Tag Tournament 2 had more items to purchase with the in game Fight Money, especially when it came to the hair options.
Hopefully this will be addressed later in the games life with a customization update of some kind but it is not a deal breaker personally.
Online netcode seems really solid so far, a big improvement over Tekken Tag 2 on console as far as how it handles lag as well as how playable 3 bar matches are compared to 4 and 5 bar matches.
Player lobbies seem to have a problem with the time delay causing the next player in the queue to be skipped because they are still spectating a match that has already ended. This will probably be fixed soon and is not a big deal as much as it is an annoyance.
The character roster is robust as expected but is also missing some fan favorites such as:
Lei Wulong
Armor King
Anna Williams
and a few others, but as I said before it shouldnt be a deal breaker if you are looking for a solid fighting game.
The Lack of a proper tutorial mode cripples the games accessiblity a bit, since the Tekken series has a reputation for being notoriously difficult at an intermediate/high level and the lack of in game explanations for terminology and fundamental techniques could have less knowledgable players who may want to take their game to the next level poking around in the dark for a bit while trying to figure out some things.
With all that said, I think Tekken 7 may be at the top of the PC Fighting Game mountain along with the recently released Guilty Gear Xrd Revelator 2 and is a must buy for any fighting game fan whether casual or competitive.
Big ups to Namco Bandai for not being lazy on the PC port and giving us a full robust product which shows much promise and polish in their first PC release from this series.
Pros:
-Great Sound Design

- Very well optimized for PC
- Nice singleplayer features ( Story, Arcade, Treasure Battle )
- Improved netcode over the previous online enabled entries in the series
Cons:

EDIT: I'm changing this review to a big, fat thumbs down (sorry triggerers). The developer abandoned the PC version leaving those of us who spent $100 on the title out to pasture. Do NOT buy this unless you like the idea of having a neutered game. I still stand by my enthusiastic review below about the gameplay and performance --- clearly I was still on my honeymoon with the game but I never had any of the technical problems that so many people complained about. However, I've been dying to play as the Baraka/Xenomorph Alien merge for about 11 months now and right before it comes out; we hear it's abandoned for PC? ♥♥♥♥ that and ♥♥♥♥ everyone at Warner Brothers and Neverrealm, I was one of your biggest fans.
All right, I'm going to start this review on a technical note by listing my specs because I know some people are having major technical problems with the game while I've had ZERO. The game runs at a gorgeous 60fps during gameplay but it's designed to drop to 30fps during menus, x-rays, fatalaties, and other cinematics. To be honest, I wouldn't have even noticed the dip if the Steam FPS counter wasn't on because there's no choppiness or tearing when it falls. Perhaps it gives the x-rays (etc) a more "cinematic" look but the transition from gameplay is flawless on my system.
Specs:
i7-4790k
EVGA GTX 970
16gb RAM
Game installed on WD Black 1TB mechanical drive
Win 8.1 on Crucial SSD
Playing on a DualShock 3 controller using "SCP DS3 Service" Xinput Wrapper (first time using this, works awesome!)
The graphics really feel "next-gen" and the gameplay is a touch slower than MK9 but feels more refined. I have only practiced with a few characters so far but there seems to be WAY more depth to personalize your style (due to 3 "variations" each character has).
The story component is a major upgrade over MK9. The budget was certainly bigger and the fight scenes are like a Yuen Wo Ping choreographed martial arts movie. Props to the animators/mocap people.  The actual storyline is still, thankfully, beyond ridiculous but perfectly self-aware. There are plenty of old and new faces throughout.
The fatalaties/brutalities/quitalities are the best from a Mortal Kombat ever. They're brutally violent, often funny, always creative, and certainly fullfilling when you pull them off.
I was worried on Day 2 about online due to lag but they released a patch (or patches) that improved it dramatically.  Every now and again you'll run into someone with a poor connection and the lag will be terrible but, more often than not, I've had lag-free games that feel very similar to playing locally. No matter what, you'll never be able to truly mimic the local 2-Player experience due to the limitations of bandwidth and server nodes on the internet. When I played a friend who lives close to me, it was pretty close though. Very smooth.
For those of you who like unlocking stuff, well The Krypt will be your dreamboat. I'm intentionally choosing not to look up Krate locations/unlocks to keep them a surprise. There is SO MUCH extra content (art, music, costumes, fatalaties, stages, etc) that it seems like it will take me a year to get to them all.
On a scale of 1 to 10 I would very easily give this game a 9.5. The only reason it doesn't get a 10 is because they took away TAG VS from MK9. I'm not entirely sure why because who doesn't have a ton of fun teaming up with a friend to fight others? That being said, it's the best MK game ever made by a long shot. They've raised the bar to a height that won't be easy for them to surpass with MK11.

I really like the design of this game. I love the multiple variations of characters,the living towers, the story, and the faction system. That is, I would really be enjoying the faction system if I could ever connect to the faction server. The graphics optimization is pretty bad, with twin 780 TIs not even being able to run the game in 4k with everything else at minimum settings. For these two reasons, I can't give the game a positive review. Fix those two things and you'll win me over.
Edit: Recent update (Tanya) made the single GPU performance a lot better. I can almost play the game in 4k at high settings on a single 780 TI now. Unfortunately, due to the lack of a working SLI profile, the only way to get SLI working is to use some hacks which introduce some artifacts. I would imagine at this point a single gtx 980 or r290x could run this game at max settings in 1440p but I don't have either of those cards to test. I still need to test for a week to see if the faction server availability has improved much. Hopefully they add an SLI profile at some point so I can turn this review into a recommendation.

I think PAM gives a simple short & fast paced punch of fun, and though it's not particularly special, if all you're looking for is a simple car combat racer then you'll come back to play this time and time again and it wont leave you disappointed.
Simplicity is rarely a benefit, but this game pulls it off well. It's succinct and straight to the point. Everything fits and makes sense and the controls serve it well. This is a problem as well as a benefit because it may lead to boredom from lack of variety for some, but the fact that the developers have a complete package with few flaws and tight gameplay holds value.
The most severe problems with PAM are the same universal problems that the vast majority of multiplayer racing games suffer from: the lack of persistent mutliplayer. After a certain amount of time all multiplayer games will suffer from this, and that's just part of the scene, but for a game who's best enjoyment comes from the multiplayer combat and blasting and racing with and against your friends, it's sad that it's pretty much dead just a few years after release and the absence of local mutliplay is definitely a black mark.
Steam groups like
may help to alleviate this and find people to play with, and the single player is still strong enough alone to have plenty of fun, but it's a big loss and may be a deal breaker for you, especially when compared against newer releases with similar mechanics and more players. If you have friends with the title or you're happy to blast around racing against the AI in single player then this probably isn't an issue for you.
Lack of content, specifically tracks and game modes is also an issue. With just an arcade racing mode, a slightly extended Challenge mode and only 7 tracks you can expect to explore all this game has to offer in a couple of hours. Yes, the game is simple chaotic fun, and the limited variety of vehicles and power-ups mean that every play will be slightly different, but it's still very much a one trick pony. The question is whether that pony is fun enough for you to ride on long enough to justify the price.
On Steam at $9.99/£6.99/9,99€, Post Apocalyptic Mayhem is good value for money for a game you're likely to come back to time and time again. There's also a 3-Pack option on Steam, which offers a negligible discount, and two Next Dimension packs which offer their other less positively reviewed game I, Gladiator which should probably be avoided. There's also the Chaos Pack DLC which offers 3 additional vehicles. This isn't much, but the price is so low that it's a fair buy for those who have played through the game and still enjoy it enough to pick up some extra vehicles.

This is one of the games I play when I feel like having mindless fun. Post Apocalyptic Mayhem is a racing game, except honestly the racing doesn't matter. What really counts is the level of destruction you cause on the other drivers while racing.
The game comes with a variety of cars (ranging from an ice cream truck, police car, and more cynically, a mobile meth lab) that all play differently. Each car gets three weapons, which are activated by finding colored barrels.
Gameplay is pretty straightforward. Literally. You just drive down the track, collect weapons, and make it hell for the other drivers. If you can wreck another car, you get a point.

One thing that strikes me more than any other aspect of this game is the creativity. Everything in this game is very unique and stands out from other racing games; from the vehicles to the tracks, and of course the weapons. It is so much fun. This is by no means a realistic racing game and the laws of phyisics are thrown out the window, so if that's what you are looking for, look elsewhere. What this game is is a ton of fun. It's probably my favorite arcade style racing game I've played. All the tracks are unique, (from a Christmas themed track, to a cold war beach and an airplane graveyard) and the vehicals are just fantastic and all handle differently. My personal favorite is "Kitty With Claws." It may not be the fastest or the biggest, but I think it stears the best.
You have three different weapons at your disposal to create chaos on the track and take out other vehicals. Each weapon is replenished by picking up power ups laying on the track in the form of different color barrels. Each vehicle has their own brand of weapons and are very satisfying to use when executed correctly. The only problem is that there is hardly anyone playing online anymore. But I have had a fantastic time against the AI in all the tracks. Since I have always been terrible at racing games, (realistic or arcade style) I find playing on easy mode gives me a good enough challenge and still maintains its fun factor. Give this game a try if you are into racing games but want something different.

This is a beautiful, yet most infuriating game.
I read reviews where people complained about the controls, but to be honest I had zero troubles with them as they're super simple (basically just one button and one stick for each, and hardly anything else). Both with a keyboard and with a controller I was able to use both brothers without issue (even if the keyboard wasn't particularly comfortable)... that is, until the game bugged out.
This game is beautiful in that it has pretty graphics and (for the first half) a very lovely story. The puzzles are very, very simple, the only time I ever got stuck was because, again, the game bugged out. If you've played Ico (PS2) you might like this one. It reminds you a bit of it, but it's a lot simpler and has a much crappier ending.
Besides the ending not being to my taste, the game is, as I said, filled with bugs that made it impossible for me to play properly. When it wasn't crashing with a "P13" error and needing to be re-verified for the third time in the same day, it was a checkpoint bugging out that not even a chapter restart could solve (just to count a few I had: puzzle not working, character disappearing through ground and falling to death, character disappearing, cutscene not playing and thus having to restart chapter to move on, character not jumping though the keys/buttons were pressed and falling to death, character jumping across gap... and then jumping right back and refusing to move forward except to jump forward and jump back again.... all that in less than 3hrs gameplay.)
What could improve this game: Besides a completely different ending, this game would be highly improved if they fixed the bugs, and would be even more interesting if it had an option to play real co-op with someone else (that is not on the keyboard next to you) if you wanted to. I love controlling both brothers at once, but I think it'd be slightly more challenging if you had to cooperate with another person rather than yourself. :P There's not enough co-op games where you actually have to plan and co-op with someone, which is why this would be nice.
To sum it up: I recommend it for the first part of the story, and because I love these kind of games. I recommend it only if it's on a bundle or super cheap, otherwise don't bother because the bugs are too annoying. And I'd recommend it even more if it weren't because of the bugs (maybe you luck out and have none, or maybe you get the curse I did and have them all.)
If you want a really really nice story tho, go play Ico.

After eighteen hours played total I can finally review this game and it's a beauty. It's totally 'radical' as the kids call it, 'bodacious' or something along those lines.
So, what is WASTED? To put it simply, it's a First Person Shooter with Rogue-like elements in it, it has procedurally generated dungeons and loot, it has permadeath and the like. It's set in the '80's when there was a war between America and Russia in some sort of nuclear war, you know, the Fallout style story. There are these vaults called Coolers (so-called because of the names of said vaults being called Cool Air) that are supposed to be housing the brightest minds of the human generation but something goes awry, everything gets messed up and, well, years later, there's a wasteland of people perpetually stuck in the 80s and you get to play as one of them.
At the start, you get the ability to customize your character, although you're limited in options first off as you can unlock more styles later down the line and, even then, you cannot customize your character outside of the intro without a certain unlock later down the line. And dying as your customized character will generate a randomly generated character that you may or may not like the look of with a name that only a careless drunkard of a parent would give them.
So, either way, you get a small tutorial to ease yourself into the first Cooler and you're sent on your merry way. Pretty cool, huh? Indeed. The game from there is pretty straight forward, move around the floor of the randomly generated Cooler picking up weapons, ammo, armor, and rubber duckys along the way while fending off the inhabitants within. It plays very much like a Fallout game and it shows.
So, why are you raiding a Cooler? Simple. Because of Booze. You drink booze to gain buffs and bonuses (or penalties) based on what you drink as a Hangover, there's also weaker Booze that are called Flasks that'll give you a temporary boost or penalty to any of your stats. The only way to leave a Cooler when you enter is to either die, have a Hangover, or reach the 10th floor of each Cooler and clear out the secret depths within. Did you know that this game actually has more of a story than it first lets on in the intro? It's true, and when you conquer your first cooler, well, there's more where that came from.
So, here's the ups and downs that I've encountered when I've been playing through this game:
+ Unique, lovable characters - There's a guy named, well, the censor won't let me say his name but let's just say there's a guy who has two heads in the main hub that you'll be visiting plenty of throughout the game. There's some dude who lost his wife, there's another dude who makes deliveries for those who are on death's door, and more.
+ Weapon variety - Okay, sure, there's not an awful lot of weapons that are available to you, at first, but if you know Fallout games, you should know that more powerful and more awesome weapons will become available down the line. Not only that but certain weapons do certain things like forcing you to shoot the enemy's groin to deal full damage and more. Also, there's weapon mods that you can rarely find throughout the game to make your favorite weapons just that little bit more special. Also, melee is not totally useless in this game if you build it right, although I just went for the shooty build.
+ Randomly Generated dungeons - It should help stave off the repetition of going through the same cooler over and over and over again as the dungeons are built up of set pieces that you can recognise with enough hours of playing. It can make for some interesting Coolers, let me tell you.
+ Cool music - The music for the game is top-notch and totally tubular dude, especially the ones that play on the radio.
+ Replay Value - There's a lot of replay value tucked away in this tiny game, enough to beat the $1/hour goal at the very least. If you're burnt out from playing the main storyline, there's a tougher mode called Courier runs where you play as a randomly generated character as you delve deep into a seemingly endless Cooler filled with increasingly tougher enemies. The goal? To stash away the most valuable treasure you can find before you die. Oh, and you can do it once per real world day.
+ Difficulty - The difficulty is based in the how stealthy you can be to take out enemies quickly as you make your way through the cooler while also juggling the exploration aspect of the game and taking the time out to find goodies that'll aid you in your quest to get as Wasted as possible. I didn't really find the game to be too difficult but more on that down in the cons section.
+ Permanent buffs and temporary boons (or banes) - The hangovers can give you an advantage (or disadvantage) which can make the game easier (or harder) depending on what you take and they stay with you until you die. On the other hand, there are flasks that can give you a boon or a bane in your current Cooler run, it's a hard gamble and inevitably they start falling off late-game when you've amassed a large amount of good hangovers.
- Random Generation can screw you over - Sometimes, life just hates you and throws you into a room with a Tripping Hazard and five explosive barrels that blows you up. Sometimes, you get a dead end as you're being chased by the game's physical manifestation of a time limit.
- Knockback is a ♥♥♥♥♥ then you die - When you get hit (or an enemy gets hit), knockback happens. When that happens, you're unable to do anything until you land, which can make for some frustrating deaths if you're not careful. On the bright side, you can abuse this mechanic on them, too, but it's still annoying to deal with.
- The time limit can be limiting at times - It sometimes feels like five seconds before the Purifier shows up and sometimes it can take forever. While you are encouraged to go explore, you have to keep the hidden limit in mind. And the purifier can catch you off guard the first time with his minigun that can pin you against the wall if you're not careful. Plus he seems to home in on you no matter if you're stealthed or not, which can be lame if you're trapped in a dead end with no escape. He does get easier to deal with later on in the game, though, so it's about learning when to explore and when to beat it.
- Difficulty - Game can be easy but it can also be quite hard at times with the game throwing several curveballs at you, sometimes ending in your own death. Random generation can end up with multiple people with shotguns for instance or several suicide bombers, that sort of stuff.
- Inventory Management is a pain - Dear god, it's hard to carry all the things and manage ammo and wear armor and keep a hold of healing items at the same time. Happily, the game relieves some of the stress of clicking by snatching things that you already have from the container if they can be stacked but it can be frustrating at times to play about with the small item limit you have at the start. Fanny packs can alleiviate this somewhat but it only delays the inevitable. Lesson learned. Never hoard things.

Here's some extended gameplay if you want a good idea of how WASTED plays:
WASTED is part rogue-lite, part Fallout parody, and part toilet humor.
The gameplay borrows liberally from Fallout 3:  shoot, loot, switch to 3rd person if you want, pick from a list of dialogue options, and do quests. Lock picking has been replaced by prying doors open with can-openers. Vaults have been replaced with Coolers. There are buildings to explore, but the interiors are randomly (semi-randomly?) generated. Each building requires you to go down as many levels as you can before you reach your goal or you find some booze to drink yourself into a coma with. If you do the latter you wake up in your house with all of your loot in-tact. If you die trying to accomplish the task at hand then you'll lose the loot you've been carrying around.
Combat is generic. Shoot with guns, melee with bats/knives/crowbars, and slap people around with your fists if all else fails. It works well enough, but it isn't anything special. Sometimes it’s hard to hit faster moving enemies if they get close to you, as your melee attacks aren’t usually very fast.
Unlike the series it’s parodying, this game isn't quite open world. Instead, you get from place to place via fast-traveling in your car. This isn't a huge deal, as the game can feel kind of repetitive as it is, so cutting out wandering through a desert might have been for the best.
Graphically the game is fine. The art style it uses is kind of cutesy, kind of gross. It serves the tone of the game well. There were few graphical errors to be found.
The music is highly similar to 80s apocalypse movies. If you like that kind of tune then you'll be in luck. Think synth-y. There are radios to be found that play more pop-like music as well. The music also serves a purpose during gameplay. Spending too much time on any floor of a Cooler will eventually lead to you getting hunted by an SOB (Soldier of Buzzkill, or something like that). These enemies have high health, high damage, and their mini-guns knock you back into the wall so hard that there’s essentially no fighting back. When one of these guys starts coming for you the music will change and the HUD will indicate that someone is hunting you. This makes each level tense, as there’s a lot to loot and little time to do it.
The characters are interesting enough, though many of them spout something obnoxious. Sometimes this seems purposeful, but other times you get the feeling that whoever wrote the line you just heard didn't realize how dated it sounds. Some jokes are genuinely funny, others sound like they came from a 2006 meme website. It's a mixed bag. There are a lot of pop culture references, some more obscure than others. I was particularly fond of♥♥♥♥♥♥ who seemed to be based on Richard Nixon. His genitals have mutated into a character in and of itself, who is named KissinJerk. Talking to them is certainly unique.
If you're a huge Fallout fan and you want something that makes fun of it with poop jokes and alcoholism, then this is your game. If you're an Adult Swim fan who likes their other games then this is also probably going to be something you enjoy. It's a game that you can easily lose a few hours to while you try to find your way out of a dungeon, dodging machine gun fire, and drinking liquid bread.
If you don't like Fallout (or if you're a hardcore Fallout purist who would be frustrated by a dumbed-down version of the mechanics) then you might not get as much out of this. It could still be fun for you, but not if you take it too seriously.

Overall this game is unique, fun, and well made. I give this game rating 8/10.

If you're buying this game, you probably already know what you're getting: a bunch of wacky scenarios where you get to play with surgical tools. The main problem is that while the controls can be fun for a little while, the novelty quickly wears off and leaves you mostly with frustration as you try mostly in vain to actually perform surgery. What starts as merely difficult becomes almost impossible if you accidentally jab yourself with a hallucinogen, which adds psychedelic vibes to an already clumsy interface. I get that the point of the game is that you're not supposed to be in much control, but the problem lies in the fact that that also means you can't really play the game well in general. It's more a joke game than anything.
That said, the game does have some nice things. The art direction, sound, and music are all really nice, and the theme tune is really catchy and suits the game well. Too bad these aren't really good enough reasons to buy the game.
If you have the patience to try to overcome the stumbling blocks the game throws at you or you're just really interested in messing with the physics, then you might consider buying this when it's on sale. Everyone else should probably skip it.

Great fun and enjoyable, Train Simulator gives a feel for the real world train driving experience with real world routes and locomotives/rollingstock.
Loads of scenarios to choose from, ranging from yard shunting work to long distance passenger and freight and more.

I'm not going to say much in this review that other reviews have left unsaid, so bear with me. Three main points with this one.
The individual trains themselves for the most part look fantastic. The stations are close to their real life counterparts (at least on the Southern and London Overground networks where I spend 80% of my travelling time IRL) and even the stretches of rail between stations are faithfully recreated. I was very impressed with this.
Apart from that the graphics suck, and I mean SUCK. Trees look like dollops of guacamole, brick walls look like crabsticks and the actual railway looks like it was rendered in 480p. I'm going to make a lot of comparisons to the other great transport simulator I enjoy (ETS2) in this review, but by god there is simply no comparison. Outside the trains, the graphics in this game are just god awful.
This camp's pretty divided. It's either condemnation for ridiculous DLC from most reviewers, or slight praise for having such a variety of choice out there. My two cents is simple: the DLC ARE TOO EXPENSIVE CONSIDERING WHAT THEY ARE. As mentioned above, the graphics are hideous and have not improved in recent years. You will be paying for something that includes at most about eight scenarios you could have made yourself on a stretch of rail which will wear out its novelty factor very fast. This brings me onto -
This was the killer for me. I live two hours' commute away from anywhere in real life, so I spend a HELL of a lot of time on TfL (Transport for London). I've never driven a train before, but I've taken them every day for the past eight years so I expect there to be some level of complexity.
As far as I am aware, this game has three buttons. Two in some cases: a reverser (you'll touch it once at the start and never again) and a throttle, brake or combination of the two.
. Unlike ETS2 where there is an element of constant concentration and relaxation, TS2018 is literally just leaving a button where it is and remembering not to speed. Not just that, but due to the lack of appropriate scaling most if not all of the scenarios in the game take well over half an hour, if not closer to an hour. It's just soul destroying.
If you really like trains, spend a lot of time on them IRL and notice that your local train line is available as a DLC? Get this game, but don't expect to play it for long before you get tired of it.

(PREFACE: I have beaten this game before, but before Steam Achievements were added and GFWL was removed, so I don't have steam achievements for having beaten the game yet. Hopefully I'll finish my playthrough sometime this century)
Regarding Off The Record specifically, it's a slight improvement over Dead Rising 2 all-around. From what I've heard DR2 is slightly more stable (I experienced no real gamebreaking bugs and only FPS drops in the new Uranus Zone but that's just me), and DR2 is certainly of more value if you want to follow Dead Rising's canon story (dunno why you'd want to do that after DR3 started to derail the series slightly and DR4 finished the job, but whatever), but gameplay-wise Off The Record is absolutely the superior version.
The changes are fairly minimal, but it includes, among a few other details, a new zone into the map, new combo weapons, combo weapons from Case West have been imported, and the camera mechanic also returns from Case West. It's pretty much Dead Rising 2.1. (There's also a few psychopaths with a new coat of paint, primarily the final boss)
Another large selling point is the all-new Sandbox Mode, which is an alternate gamemode that does away with both the missions and the timelimit, and just lets you roam around the map killing zombies, psychopaths, and doing fairly enjoyable challenges. If you just want to screw around and kill zombies, this is what you've wanted. It's also a nifty feature for those who don't like replaying Dead Rising games over and over in order to get better at the game and eventually get the best ending, as you can level up to 50, get combo cards and so on without the time pressure getting to you.
Now, a general summary of the game rather than simply what OTR includes. Dead Rising can be difficult to describe, but it's a 3rd person beat-em up (for lack of a term I'm more familiar with) where you plough through hordes of zombies. A large gimmick of the series if your ability to pick up anything that isn't nailed down in order to use it as a weapon (I'm still being surprised by how many random items there are I've never seen before, or seeing new moves I didn't know certain weapons had), and Dead Rising 2 introduced the ability to combine weapons into significantly stronger Combo Weapons.
So, the core gameplay of Dead Rising is effectively buttonmashing into hordes, and finding better stuff with which to buttonmash into hordes. This is where Dead Rising puts twists on the gameplay to make it consistently enjoyable, rather than making it Dead Rising 4.
For one thing, durability is a thing. Weapons in Dead Rising are NOT things you can just keep around. A combo weapon might get you through 60 zombies if it's an especially durable one. Taking out a crowd of zombies will take several weapons' worth of durability. You need to figure out if it's worth burning your combo weapons, or if you can scavenge enough mediocre weapons from your immediate environment to deal with the zombies fine.
Secondly, Psychopaths. Psychopaths require preperation, careful management and skilful gameplay in order to get past them. It's not Dark Souls or anything, but a single Psychopath is far more of a threat than any amount of zombies, and many of them are used in pretty clever ways- For example, during a certain period of time, three snipers set up in the centre of the map. You could invest time in clearing them out, or side-step them on the map, and it's the player's choice to figure out which approach they'd rather take as well as which approach they think will consume the least time.
And speaking of time, yes, Dead Rising's stories have a time limit. This isn't just something the game implemented to be a♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's to add degrees of strategy to... Basically everything. Farming PP (exp, basically) will cost time. Getting money will cost time. The more time you consume, the closer you get to having negative consequences- Sidequests each have individual time limits, critical story missions have time limits and you will fail the main quest if you aren't on time for one, and Frank himself needs to consume Zombrex every 24 hours or he'll succumb to his infection. If you're going for 100% completion, this results in an extremely strategic and really awesome balancing act. I was turned off from the series when I heard about the time limit, but after playing it, the time limit really isn't an issue. Don't let it stress you out and see it as another objective- "Okay, I need to be here within 20 minutes, but that's 20 minutes of time to do whatever I want in the meantime... Hey, who wants to raid a zombie-infested casino?!" (or, if you're being pragmatic, you'd be picking up magazines you want for your build. But nobody plays Dead Rising to be pragmatic)
I can absolutely, highly recommend this game. IMO it's the overall best Dead Rising game. The original still has a lot of value, and if you JUST want to ♥♥♥♥ around and kill zombies without caring about the series' other elements Dead Rising 3 is arguably superior, but DR2 executes a lot well as a sequel, and Off The Record improved its problems.

Yet again we have an example of an indie game that doesn't need any help. With an approval rating of 96% it should be fairly obvious that Brothers is a purchase worth making. If however you aren't entirely certain what makes it good, allow me to elaborate.
Brothers is an esthetically pleasing narrative about two brothers whos' mother is dead and father has fallen ill. It is up to them to travel to a another land and retrieve the only means to cure him. Brothers is a puzzle game that blends its mechanics seamlessly with its story. You control both brothers individually and must coordinate their efforts and make use of their unique advantages in order to solve a variety of puzzles. The game is incredibly straight forward with just you. the brothers, and your wits. The game's story is also told with out dialog but none the less manages to be engrossing from start to finish and the fantasy world the brothers inhabit is breathtaking and mystifying.
Around three hours, the game is actually quite short and can be completed in one sitting. In addition it has very little replayability. These may be a factor on whether you want to wait for a sale but ultimately Brothers will make an excellent addition to your library.

This is what happens if Motorstorm and Twisted Metal have a baby, and that baby has a case of dwarfism.  Gameplay wise, P.A.M. is enjoyable, playing almost like a motorstorm game but with similar weapons and weapon systems to an older twisted metal game. The nine cars (Three in DLC) that the game has are all rather unique and pretty well balanced, and at least one makes homage to, again, Twisted metal by having a weaponized ice cream truck. But then again, you can also play as a school bus with a plow or, better yet, a nuclear-powered smart car. Each one of them has three different weapons, one for the front, one for the back, and one for the sides. They're all absurd and many of them are variants of tossing mines on the field, but they do it in differing way, to the credit of the designers.
When you're actually in a race, it's certainly different than most other racing games. Laps don't matter too much in the grand scheme of things, nor is your placement in the actually racing around. The tracks are so damn big that you usually only get one lap anyhow. But what matters most is your kills. Even if you're in last palce when the timer runs out, but you have the most kills, you win the race. This means you can be a cheeky sonuva♥♥♥♥♥, grab a side weapon, and then slow down and time out the weapon to catch the majority of the opposing racers. Works well, try it.
But my main complaint about this game is content. The cars are decent, sure. The price of the dlc isn't bad either; $2 for three cars. But you only have six tracks and a remodeled version of the first one made for christmas. (Yes, really.) The tracks, though, are amazing- Plenty of alternate routes, tons of insane terrain, and plenty of pillars to run your♥♥♥♥♥into when boosting at full speed. All are enjoyable and very long except for one of them, from what I remember. But that's all this game has. Nine cars, six tracks... and that's it. The only two gameplay modes are arcade and "Apocalyptic Challenge", and all the latter is is just playing all six tracks in a row for a total, final score. It can certainly get boring quick, but it's enjoyable while it lasts.
Oh yes, the achievments in this game or stupidly easy to get at times. I got one for switching off the in-game music... -_-

I'm a fan of the old point and click games, I grew up with Monkey Island and Grim Fandango. I've yet to find something similar that captures the humour, atmosphere and style of those games. Deponia seemed like a good, recent take on the genre so I thought I'd give it a shot. If you're a fan of point and click adventure games, I would recommend it. Otherwise, I'd say try Monkey Island first (particularly the remastered versions if nostalgia alone isn't enough to see past the older graphics.)
Deponia is ok all round, the art style is pretty cool and the environments are well drawn. The dialogue is pretty hit and miss though, and if I'm honest I didn't find it all that funny.
One thing that really stood out to me as quite poor was the sound design. Some of the sound effects get really repetitive, to the point of being annoying in some scenes, and the robotic effect on the Organon voices were far too loud and irritating. The music isn't great, although the mechanical sounding elements lend themself well to the locations and world, they just lacked the charm that I've heard in other point & click adventure classics.
The characters are ok, a little underdeveloped but the storyline is fairly decent. Doc and Bozo deserved more introduction in my opinion.
The puzzles on the most part are logical, with enough hint in the dialogue frome looking at objects to help you along but there are the occasional frustrating puzzles that I admit I couldn't figure out on my own.
Overall, it's worth getting this if you're a fan of the point & click genre, but I'd grab it while it's on sale.

Crafting is also constantly used and gets harder (you need to constantly upgrade yoru workbench/furnace), however its fine to use. but hard to navigate through at first.
Combat is really linear, you attack a monster (you cant move whilst attacking), you wait for its attack animation, you dodge roll and repeat. Some monsters are ranged, some are flying and some run away when at low health.
However the gameplay cycle is really, REALLY, bland. Let me explain it in a nutshell: Explore world -> Kill monsters and gather resources -> Find a dungeon -> Get dungeon loot -> Find Portal -> Go to next World -> Repeat
This is a really nice concept and I enjoy this part of it, IF the world wasn't so damn small. It feels like every world you go to is the same size and there feels pretty much no diffrence between them except for the diffrent monsters/resources you find.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Clear Sky is second installment of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series and is a prequel to the first game Shadow of Chernobyl.
Game is set in Chernobyl zone five years after second Chernobyl disaster. Player is given control of Scar, a mercenary who is employed by Clear Sky faction to go after a group of stalkers trying to breach the center of the zone.
Since Shadow of Chernobyl, this game offers interesting addition of faction wars system. Different factions struggle for territory, either attacking other faction for territory gain or defending one already owned.
Game also include new system of weapon customization with the ability to repair gear and add new modifications to it. New system of anomalies, which are harder to notice and one can obtain artifacts only by using special detector.
NPC's AI also improved since first game, making fight's harder, more dynamic and more interesting.
Although much improvement has been made, this game is not superior to it's predecessor. Throughout the game I have found many bugs which forced me to load previous saves so I could progress in story. But most disappointing thing for me was ending. I'm not going to spill any detail but for me it was like developers wanted to hasten it and it lost part of immersion.
In any case I still recommend this game. I really liked the improvements and various mods that can enhance gaming experience even better.

A rather buggy game that really needed an auto-save when you rescue people. The first few hours are tough until you get a few levels and one speed upgrade. Has an issue with crashing unless you manually save often, has very glitchy textures in cutscenes, loading areas sometimes freezes your controls in one direction until you mash the buttons enough to get him to stop moving. Has AI issues the deeper you get into the game, to where armed humans ignore you if you attack them. The final stretch having (queen immune) mutant zombies endlessly hound you to where you can get stunlocked when you fight humans and the whole time hear an endless cacophony of very loud dinosaur screams while they swarm you in larger numbers. You need to restart a couple times, because you ran out of time doing something or that being low leveled gets you killed in four hits or one second.
If you can get past all that bad stuff, you have a game that gets enjoyable as you mix drinks that makes you ten times stronger, or turns off zombie AI, or shrugs off boss attacks that would otherwise knock chunks of your HP off. Survivors also get buffed from your drinks, so you can have granny NPCs with oversized weapons you gave them, running at 80MPH. There are enough variations with bosses to keep you busy, but a health magazine and painkillers will get you through most of them quickly. Don't expect to save everyone or for them to remain alive to the very end. Survivors exist to level you up very fast.

I rarely fall in love with games that are outside my favorite gaming genre: high fantasy RPGs. Mount & Blade is one such exception. Any time I start a new campaign, I know many an evening will be spent gaming away.
The basic premise of the game is pretty straightforward; real time clashes of troops or self-organized miscreants such as bandits, with elements of town/village management, war campaign management, troop management and faction relationship building and various stand-alone quests given by in-game dignitaries.
I find the combat addictive every time, and also like that the difficulty slider can be either very challenging or quite forgiving based on player preference and skill. The challenge also changes depending on your campaign premise: free-lance, straight playing vassal, or power grabbing for a claimant or yourself.
What is essential in holding my interest is that the game events are randomised: relative strenghts of factions, personalities of gameworld lordlings, war declarations etc. If that's not enough, there is quite the impassioned modding scene for this game.
The appeal that M&B holds for me beats me, frankly. I even normally hate horse-riding in games! Any time a village has unbearable poverty, I just end up doing the hateful cattle quests and cursing the fool I am! I get pangs of guilt in the final battle sequence when my glorious troops may end up slaugtering but three poor souls! I am currently wrenched by my ambition of becoming empress of all lands, but feel immoral in declaring war! And so on and so forth...
To me, this title just has that "je ne sais quoi..."
The one thing I meanwhile wish the developer will one day implement in future title is "Wilhelm Tell" questline, or chance to reject the feodal noble outlook, and form and fight for a republican confederacy, Swiss style of yore.

This game starts out as a funny, slapstick comedy, but soon you realise that it doesn't progress from that point. The developer seems to have assumed that people will enjoy the fact that the control system is unreliable, unfinished, and inconsistent. (The basics of the game were developed in just TWO DAYS as part of a competition, and it shows.) True, it is funny the first one or two times when you accidentally sever the patients' oesophagus instead of removing a rib. (At least I THINK that's his oesophagus, it's hard to tell.) But when you find that the first (and ONLY) operation available to you can't be completed due to this "humour", you quickly stop smiling. The only reason I discovered a second operation to try is because I became so frustrated with the operating theatre that I went back to the reception area and started messing around with the objects there. If you somehow manage to insert the video cassette into the player (how quaint!), you get a bonus operation made available to you. This game is definitely a funny joke, for about five minutes. The question is, who is the joke being played on? The cartoon patient? Or the buyer of the game?
Please DON'T buy this at full price, you'll be regretting it within a few minutes. Buy it (like I did) in a Steam sale, if you like a few minutes of laughter. Personally, I've had the laughs, now I've also experienced the frustration, and I'm probably not going to touch this game again.

A decent, entertaining game, but it constantly slaps you with several dumb bugs. I understand the difficult controls and the difficult way it is to grab things, but clipping in this game is really annoying. There is focus on such a small area that clipping is an utter eye sore. A silly game is not a good excuse to let bugs slide like this. Is clipping fun, interesting, funny, or entertaining? Not really. It looks like lazy development.
And then you have your hand getting stuck on things like coffee mugs, bones, etc. Most stuck related issues can be tied to clipping, in the first place. It's like the engine doesn't know what to do when your finger gets stuck in the side of a coffee mug. The mug vibrates in confusion in your hand as the Unity engine racks its brain trying to figure out how to fix the situation. A good few shakes will get it off, but I'm not really feeling how this helps the atmosphere/humor of the game. Just prevent polygons from going through other polygons.
Besides my complaints, it's a fun game to play. The different enviorments are very challenging and interesting. Graphics are pretty decent, even with their cartoon-like qualities. The main menu is fun and creative. Plus $10 is a fair asking price, however this game goes on sale very often. I got it for around $3. Just add it to your wishlist and wait.
I feel confident enough to say that I can now transplant brains.

I have bought and played every single Tekken game since the very first one many years ago on the PS1. Always have loved the series. I will write this review from an old school perspective. First, the game plays very well on PC. The graphics are very good, and do not require a crazy powerful graphics card to run. I use an RX470 and it runs ultra 1080p at solid 60fps. So yes, it runs great, no crashes or glitches. The story mode is ok, entertaining the first play through. Online works well, for the most part. To me, Arcade mode is a very important mode. I grew up with arcades, so having the ability to recreate that experience at home is important. My largest gripe with Tekken 7 is the fact that the arcade mode is so short, it borders on non existant. A total of 5 battles including the 2 boss battles? Are you kidding me? Also, no character endings at the end to look forward to. Namco, PLEASE create an 'extended arcade mode' where I can actually fight a good 8-10 battles before the boss fights. Also, add in some proper endings. Im sure some of us old school gamers really miss this. The game is good, it plays well, but it is sparse on the ability to just play a good old fashioned arcade style game that isnt over in 5 rounds.
In terms of characters, there are some new, and some old. I miss a few of the mainstays, and certainly do not want to have to buy them via season pass dlc. I hate the whole idea of buying a game, then having to buy 'more' of a game. Usually, Namco shyed away from this practice, but not here, apparently. Ok so is it good and worth buying? Yes, but with the warning that after you complete story mode, the single player / offline modes are lacking, especially arcade mode. Online is great for awhile, but eventually players will be hard to come by. This is why single player content is so essential, in addition to online. Will Namco fix this? I hope so.

This is another one of those games that you can't really rate on gameplay, but rather storyline.  Think of it as an interactive movie.
I must say, it was a unique experience controlling two characters at once.  Combining this with platforming made the puzzles and action sequences challenging and rewarding - but not frustrating.
I loved the setting and I loved the set pieces and I loved the touching character moments.  I loved the mystery and intrigue - what was the giant war all about?  Who was that invisible snow beast? Was he the same creature that froze all those people? How did that spider woman come to be?
That being said - what I felt disappointing was the overall storyline (bland - you are on a fetch quest to get a magic potion to save your sickly father) and the theme.  I didn't understand what I was supposed to take away from the conclusion of the game.  I won't spoil - but let's just say this game isn't all sunshine and roses.  Though it's very simplistic, don't think this is a child's game.  No.  I would not let a child play this.  It has some very dark and very morbid moments - but it has some heart warming, uplifting moments as well.
Overall, I would recommend this game for its powerful story, unique gameplay mechanics, and rewarding yet challenging puzzles and platforming.  If you like to come out of a game feeling happy - don't play this!  This game is a mixed bag in that respect.
Here's hoping for a sequel.

Spelunky HD stays mostly true to the original with only a few new items. I like this part. This review is positive so far, right? But in other ways, Spelunky HD seems like a version of Spelunky designed only to make you angry. It feels like there are problems with controls, for example the Spelunker hangs on ledges too easily, wasting time and causing accidents, particularly with speedy incoming bats. Unfortunately, it's also twice as bad when you have climbing gloves. Then there are things that could cause problems if you're not lucky, for example, in the Ice Caves a spring pad can spawn next to the exit door, and a freezy-goat-thing can spawn above the door, forcing you to try to land directly between them just to get to the door and end the level.
I'm not trying to hate on Spelunky HD just because it's the sequel to a game I loved very much. I just feel like the game was never play-tested quite enough, or any problems found were ignored. It's also not about the game being slightly harder than the original. It's that the problems with the game make it irritating to play.
That said, there is of course much to be said about the amount of effort put into this remake. The graphics, music, and sound effects are shiny and new. I believe it can stand up to the original just because it's still such a familiar game overall, but it could be better, maybe even better than the original, with a few loving fixes.
